cards.title: P versus NC
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NC}\), where NC consists of decision languages recognized by logspace-uniform Boolean circuit families of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have such a circuit family?
cards.definitions: P is deterministic polynomial time on ordinary Turing machines. For \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{NC}\) there must be fixed constants c,k,C and a family \((C_{n})_{n}\ge 0\) such that \(C_{n}\) decides membership in L correctly on every n-bit input, has at most \(C(n+2)^{c}\) gates, and has depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{k}\). Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; fan-out is unrestricted and one output bit is designated. Depth is the longest input-to-output gate path. A deterministic \(O(\log (n+2))\)-space transducer given \(1^{n}\) must output the description of \(C_{n}\); its polynomial output bound is part of the size requirement. Constants and the generator may depend on L but not on n. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered Boolean gate DAG, its input-bit values, and an output-gate index; it asks whether that gate evaluates to 1. Its input length n is the entire binary encoding length, and malformed encodings are rejected. No randomization, advice, oracle, or restriction to monotone gates is permitted. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every language in P has a logspace-uniform family of polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth circuits, or prove that some language in P has no such family. By the stated completeness result, the affirmative answer is equivalent to Circuit Value belonging to NC, and the negative answer to Circuit Value not belonging to NC. Excluding only one fixed depth exponent, nonuniform monotone circuits, or one evaluation procedure does not establish \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NC}\).
cards.why: This asks whether a feasible computation can require intrinsically many sequential stages even when polynomially many processors are available. It is the central unresolved premise behind P-completeness as an explanation for resistance to parallelization, spanning graph algorithms, simulation, optimization, and language processing.

progress.text: Ladner establishes that Circuit Value is logspace complete for P, giving a concrete universal target for efficient parallelization.
Greenlaw, Hoover, and Ruzzo organize the theory of P-completeness and its open P-versus-NC question, including uniform circuit and parallel-machine formulations.
Raz and McKenzie prove monotone \(\mathrm{NC}\ne\)monotone P and a strict monotone NC hierarchy. These results restrict the gates used by the computing circuits.

Cavalar and coauthors prove perfect matching requires monotone circuit size \(2^{n^{\Omega (1)}}\), improving Razborov’s quasipolynomial lower bound. The November 2025 revision appears in STOC 2026; general Boolean circuits are not covered.

context_blocks.text: Circuit evaluation makes the apparent obstacle concrete. A sequential algorithm visits the gates in their supplied topological order and computes every value in polynomial time. The question is whether the Boolean function described by an arbitrary such circuit always has an efficiently constructible, much shallower evaluation circuit. Depth of the supplied circuit and depth of an algorithm that evaluates it are different quantities.

For example, a long chain that successively ANDs input bits can be replaced by a balanced tree of AND gates with logarithmic depth. Thus a long chain in the input is not by itself a lower bound on the time needed to evaluate it. Circuit Value allows arbitrary sharing and combinations of gate types, rather than promising this particular associative form.

Ladner proved Circuit Value complete for P under logarithmic-space reductions. These reductions themselves admit NC computation, and NC is closed under their composition. An NC algorithm for this one problem would therefore parallelize every problem in P. P-completeness supplies this conditional consequence; it does not already prove the absence of a parallel algorithm.

The resource tradeoff is polynomial total circuit size against polylogarithmic dependency depth. The exponent of the polynomial work budget may be large, so a positive answer would not automatically provide nearly linear work or useful speedups on a small machine. Logspace uniformity prevents the circuit descriptions from supplying arbitrary nonuniform information. The union over all fixed depth exponents also makes this broader than asking whether P equals \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\).

Restricted circuit models reveal real obstructions. Raz and McKenzie separate monotone NC from monotone P, and separate consecutive levels of the monotone NC hierarchy. Their lower bounds restrict the computing circuit to AND and OR. A monotone function can still have a substantially more powerful circuit when NOT gates are allowed, so the restriction cannot be removed from the conclusion.

Recent matching lower bounds sharpen this caution. Cavalar and coauthors prove a stretched-exponential monotone circuit-size lower bound for perfect matching, a problem with polynomial-time general algorithms. The separation measures the cost of forbidding negation. It supplies progress in circuit lower bounds while leaving the general uniform parallel-computation question untouched.

cards.title: Perfect matching in NC
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C,a,b>0\) and a logspace-uniform family of Boolean circuits which, on the adjacency matrix of every n-vertex simple undirected graph, output a perfect matching or correctly report that none exists, with at most \(C(n+2)^{a}\) gates and depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{b}\)?
cards.why: I include this because perfect matching is a basic polynomial-time graph problem for which randomization and parallelism interact in a particularly sharp way. The question asks whether randomness is needed to find globally compatible choices quickly, and whether the structural tools for odd cycles can be made as parallel as the algebraic ones.
cards.definitions: The input is the \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix of a graph on \([n]\), with symmetry and zero diagonal promised. A perfect matching is a set of edges with exactly one edge incident to each vertex. Output is a flag and an \(n\times n\) binary incidence matrix for the chosen matching; when the flag reports nonexistence the remaining output bits are ignored. The empty graph has the empty perfect matching. Circuits use fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\), fan-in-one NOT, constants 0,1 and unrestricted fan-out. Depth counts gates on the longest input-output path and size counts gates; the \(n^{2}\) output positions are specified as part of the description. A deterministic Turing transducer on unary input \(1^{n}\) writes the description using \(O(\log _{2}(n+2))\) work bits, with read-only input and write-only output. Constants and generator are fixed across n; every valid input must receive an exact answer. No randomness, oracle, advice, bipartiteness or other structural graph promise is supplied.

progress.text: The randomized parallel approach of Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani uses isolation to single out a matching. Svensson and Tarnawski review this starting point and the need to derandomize it.

Svensson and Tarnawski give a deterministic general-graph algorithm in $O(\log^3 n)$ parallel time with $n^{O(\log^2 n)}$ processors. It achieves quasi-NC, leaving a quasipolynomial-versus-polynomial resource gap.
Chakraborty and coauthors’ revision constructs maximum matchings in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. The restored auxiliary-memory model does not by itself yield ordinary NC.
The bipartite NC preprint reaches revision 2, covering weighted and search versions and extending to linear matroid intersection. General-graph matching is outside the stated theorem.

cards.status_note: The general quasi-NC result, the bipartite preprint’s revision 2 of 15 July 2026, and the catalytic-logspace revision of 1 June 2026 were checked on 11 September 2026. Subsequent-result searches found no deterministic NC search algorithm for arbitrary graphs. The newly cited preprint proofs have not been independently audited.

context_blocks.text: A polynomial-time sequential algorithm is known, so the issue is how many dependent stages remain when the work is spread across many processors. Polynomial total size is essential: evaluating exponentially many candidate matchings in parallel is outside NC. The output requirement is also explicit. The circuit must select a set of edges forming one matching, or certify nonexistence with its output flag.

Choosing matching edges independently can give incompatible decisions. On a four-cycle, deleting any one edge leaves a perfect matching. Deleting all four edges at once leaves none. This small example distinguishes a collection of individually valid existence statements from the coordinated selection required for a search output.

General graphs also need more structure than the bipartite case. Two disjoint triangles have an even total number of vertices and admit a fractional assignment of one half to every edge, giving total incident weight one at each vertex. They have no perfect matching. This example shows why degree constraints alone do not describe the general matching polytope; odd vertex sets impose additional conditions.

The June 2026 bipartite preprint, updated on 15 July, gives NC algorithms for bipartite matching and extends the results to search and weighted variants and to linear matroid intersection. Its scope restriction matters: an arbitrary graph need not be bipartite. The July revision does not state the general-graph theorem asked here.

A separate June 2026 revision places maximum-matching construction in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. Catalytic space means a larger auxiliary memory tape may begin in an arbitrary state and must be restored on termination. This additional resource is different from ordinary logarithmic workspace, and the result does not establish an NC circuit family. It is a nearby complexity improvement whose model must remain attached to its conclusion.

The 2017 quasi-NC result already obtains polylogarithmic parallel time, but permits \(n^{O(\log ^{2} n)}\) processors. Such a quantity eventually exceeds every fixed polynomial. The open gap is therefore the total resource bound for arbitrary graphs, not simply finding any parallel algorithm with a short dependency chain.

cards.title: Distributed Lovász Local Lemma in \(O(\log  \log  n)\) rounds
cards.formal: Does there exist an integer \(c\ge 2\) such that, for every fixed integer \(d\ge 2, a\) uniform randomized LOCAL algorithm \(A_{d}\) and a constant \(K_{d}\) solve every n-event variable Lovász Local Lemma instance of dependency degree at most d and maximum bad-event probability p with \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\), within \(K_{d}(1+\log _{2}\log _{2}(n+2))\) rounds, with probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\) of avoiding all bad events simultaneously?
cards.why: The question asks whether sparse dependencies can always be resolved within a log-logarithmic communication radius under fixed polynomial slack. This would determine the complexity of a widely used distributed primitive and clarify a central scale in the LOCAL complexity hierarchy.
cards.status_note: The original conjecture, primary distributed bounds, the 2025 locality result and the August 2026 resilient-LLL paper were checked on 11 September 2026. No result settling the exact bounded-degree \(O(\log  \log  n)\) worst-case target was found. The fixed factor \(1/2\) and order of slack/degree quantifiers preserve the saved precise interpretation. Node averages and results for stronger communication models are not substituted for this guarantee.

cards.definitions: There are \(n\ge 2\) bad events, each a predicate on a specified finite subset of finitely many mutually independent variables. Each variable has a finite nonempty alphabet and a rational probability distribution; event predicates and distributions are given by finite tables. Variables occurring in no event can be omitted. Two distinct event nodes are adjacent exactly when their variable sets intersect; this graph is the communication network. Its maximum degree is at most d. The number p is the largest probability of an event under the product of the specified distributions. Each node initially knows n,d, its own event table, its variables and their distributions, its neighbours and their identifiers. Node identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\); shared variables have consistent names. LOCAL means synchronous rounds with arbitrarily long finite messages in each direction on each edge, and unrestricted terminating local computation. Nodes have private independent fair random bits. A single finite program is used at all nodes, independently of n and the instance. Each node outputs one value for each of its variables. Success requires agreement on shared variables and falsity of every event. The round bound holds on every random tape; the success probability is over all node coins for each fixed instance and identifier assignment. Constants and the algorithm may depend on d; the slack exponent c is chosen before d. No preprocessing using the full instance is supplied. The factor \(1/2\) removes the low-degree ambiguity recorded in the source conjecture.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed integer \(c\ge 2\) admits, for every fixed \(d\ge 2\), algorithms \(A_{d}\) and constants \(K_{d}\) with the stated round and global-success bounds on all eligible instances. Alternatively, prove that for every candidate c there is a fixed d for which no such algorithm and constant exist. An obstruction at one slack exponent alone does not refute the existential choice of c. Bounds averaged over nodes, expected round bounds, or a higher fixed power of log log n do not meet the stated guarantee.

context_blocks.text: The Lovász Local Lemma concerns many individually unlikely failures that share only limited dependencies. In a variable instance, a bad event is a condition on some independent random variables. The goal is to choose the variables so that none of these conditions holds. The distributed question asks how quickly processors located at the events can agree on such choices when communication follows the dependency graph.

For an illustrative instance, independently color the vertices of a hypergraph red or blue, and let each hyperedge define the bad event that all its vertices receive the same color. A hyperedge containing k vertices is monochromatic with probability \(2^{1- k}\). Events are adjacent when their hyperedges share a vertex. A successful assignment is a two-coloring with no monochromatic hyperedge. This example explains the objects; the card allows arbitrary finite event tables, rather than only coloring events.

Small individual probabilities do not mean that one simultaneous random assignment succeeds with high probability globally. Even n mutually independent events of probability p are all avoided with probability \((1- p)^{n}\), which can be tiny. The LLL guarantees existence in a suitable probability-and-dependency regime. A distributed algorithm must obtain a globally valid assignment with the much stronger success guarantee stated on the card.

The slack condition \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\) is deliberately stronger than the usual existence threshold. One universal constant c must work before the degree bound d is chosen; choosing an exponent that grows with n would answer a different question. Each d is fixed while n grows, so constants in the round bound may depend on d. This bounded-degree convention is essential to interpreting the conjecture.

In LOCAL, messages have no bandwidth limit, but information still crosses only one dependency edge per round. After r rounds a node can depend only on information and random choices within its r-hop neighborhood. Shared variables also require agreement: two neighboring event processors cannot assign different colors to the same underlying variable and count that as a solution.

Fischer and Ghaffari gave a sublogarithmic algorithm under polynomially strengthened criteria. Subsequent derandomization tools and Davies’s algorithm yield bounds of the form \(O(d/\log  d + (\log  \log  n)^{O(1)})\) in the relevant regime. For fixed d this is polynomial in log log n, but it does not give a bound linear in log log n. The conjecture targets that remaining distinction.

The 2025 locality paper gives an \(O(\log  \log _{1/p} n)\) node-averaged guarantee while retaining a larger worst-case round bound. The average measures how long a typical node remains active; it can be small while a few nodes keep working. This card requires every node to finish within the same \(O(\log  \log  n)\) budget. cards.context:
The Lovász Local Lemma concerns many individually unlikely failures that share only limited dependencies. In a variable instance, a bad event is a condition on some independent random variables. The goal is to choose the variables so that none of these conditions holds. The distributed question asks how quickly processors located at the events can agree on such choices when communication follows the dependency graph.

For an illustrative instance, independently color the vertices of a hypergraph red or blue, and let each hyperedge define the bad event that all its vertices receive the same color. A hyperedge containing k vertices is monochromatic with probability \(2^{1- k}\). Events are adjacent when their hyperedges share a vertex. A successful assignment is a two-coloring with no monochromatic hyperedge. This example explains the objects; the card allows arbitrary finite event tables, rather than only coloring events.

Small individual probabilities do not mean that one simultaneous random assignment succeeds with high probability globally. Even n mutually independent events of probability p are all avoided with probability \((1- p)^{n}\), which can be tiny. The LLL guarantees existence in a suitable probability-and-dependency regime. A distributed algorithm must obtain a globally valid assignment with the much stronger success guarantee stated on the card.

The slack condition \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\) is deliberately stronger than the usual existence threshold. One universal constant c must work before the degree bound d is chosen; choosing an exponent that grows with n would answer a different question. Each d is fixed while n grows, so constants in the round bound may depend on d. This bounded-degree convention is essential to interpreting the conjecture.

In LOCAL, messages have no bandwidth limit, but information still crosses only one dependency edge per round. After r rounds a node can depend only on information and random choices within its r-hop neighborhood. Shared variables also require agreement: two neighboring event processors cannot assign different colors to the same underlying variable and count that as a solution.

Fischer and Ghaffari gave a sublogarithmic algorithm under polynomially strengthened criteria. Subsequent derandomization tools and Davies’s algorithm yield bounds of the form \(O(d/\log  d + (\log  \log  n)^{O(1)})\) in the relevant regime. For fixed d this is polynomial in log log n, but it does not give a bound linear in log log n. The conjecture targets that remaining distinction.

The 2025 locality paper gives an \(O(\log  \log _{1/p} n)\) node-averaged guarantee while retaining a larger worst-case round bound. The average measures how long a typical node remains active; it can be small while a few nodes keep working. This card requires every node to finish within the same \(O(\log  \log  n)\) budget. Results for local-computation queries, MPC or the congested clique also have different access and communication rules.

Its broader general-LLL question must not erase the bounded-degree upper bounds already known here. Lower bounds from sinkless orientation explain why log log n is a central scale, with the precise LLL criterion relevant when transferring such a bound.

The question has broad consequences because distributed conflict-resolution tasks can be expressed as avoiding overlapping bad events. cards.title: One-cycle versus two-cycles conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the following conjecture true? For every fixed sublinear local-memory exponent \(0<\delta<1\), every uniform randomized MPC algorithm \(A\) that distinguishes a single cycle of length \(n\) from two disjoint cycles of length \(n/2\), with high probability and linear total memory as specified below, requires \(\Omega(\log n)\) worst-case synchronous rounds. More precisely, for every fixed positive integer confidence parameter \(h\), there must be constants \(c_{A,h}>0\) and \(n_{A,h}\) such that
\[T_A(n,h)\ge c_{A,h}\log_2 n\]
for every even \(n\ge n_{A,h}\). Correctness has probability at least \(1-n^{-h}\) on each promised graph and every admissible initial placement of its edge list.
cards.why: I include this because the input removes most graph-theoretic complications and leaves the cost of assembling global connectivity information. It is a standard conditional-hardness benchmark for massively parallel algorithms, and a resolution would clarify whether limited memory creates an inherent logarithmic coordination cost even on degree-two graphs.
cards.definitions:
The input is an edge list of a simple undirected graph with vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), for even \(n\ge6\). It is promised to consist either of one cycle through all \(n\) vertices or of exactly two disjoint cycles, each through \(n/2\) vertices. Every edge appears once as its pair of endpoints; the orientation of that pair and list order are arbitrary. Both cases have exactly \(n\) edges and degree two at every vertex. The vertex names carry no order around a cycle. Inputs outside the promise impose no correctness requirement.

Here is a fixed finite-word version of linear-total-space MPC. For a fixed \(\delta\), use \(p(n)=\lceil n^{1-\delta}\rceil\) machines, indexed from one to \(p(n)\). For each fixed \(h\), the algorithm may choose constants \(K_h\ge4\) and an integer \(B_h\ge2\), independent of \(n\). A word has \(B_h\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits. Each machine can store at most \(K_h\lceil n^\delta\rceil\) words, including its input, work state and communication buffers. Thus the sum of memory capacities is \(O(n)\) words for fixed \(h,\delta\). Initially each edge record is placed on one machine, and every placement fitting these local capacities is allowed. Other mutable memory is initially blank. Each machine knows \(n,p(n),h\) and its own index; fixed model parameters are part of the program.

Each synchronous round allows arbitrary finite local computation within that memory and communication with arbitrary other machines. Each machine sends at most \(K_h\lceil n^\delta\rceil\) words in total and receives at most that many; words may encode arbitrary information rather than whole graph records. Recipient addresses count as part of the communicated data. The algorithm must respect both send and receive bounds on every promised input and every random tape. Messages arrive before the next round. Local computation must terminate but has no time bound. Machines have private independent fair random bits and may additionally use a common read-only fair random tape; random bits retained for later use occupy memory. There is no further advice or oracle.

All machines execute one finite program with their indices as input. The program is uniform over \(n,h\); it can depend on the fixed exponent. It suffices to quantify over rational \(\delta\in(0,1)\), so all machine counts and capacity bounds are effectively specified: any fixed smaller real exponent is dominated by a rational exponent below one, and a lower bound for every rational exponent covers it. Constants in the resource bounds may depend on the program and fixed confidence parameter, but not on the input or placement.

Machine one must eventually output ONE or TWO. On every promised input and placement, the output must be correct with probability at least \(1-n^{-h}\), jointly over all random bits. No machine may exceed the resource bounds even on a tape leading to an incorrect answer. Let \(T_A(n,h)\) be the supremum of the number of synchronous rounds until this output, over all promised inputs with exactly \(n\) vertices, all initial placements and all random tapes. Eligible algorithms have finite \(T_A(n,h)\) for each \(n,h\). The target is a worst-case round bound, not expected time.

High probability means that every fixed positive integer \(h\) can be requested as an input parameter; integer parameters also imply every fixed real failure exponent. The lower-bound constants may depend on \(h,\delta,A\). No component-stability, comparison-only or indivisible-record restriction is imposed. In particular, graph distance does not bound the distance a message can travel between machines.

cards.title: Explicit superconstant lower bounds in the congested clique
cards.formal: Does there exist a Boolean predicate P of finite simple undirected graphs on \([n]\), decidable from the full adjacency matrix by one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, such that every uniform deterministic unicast congested-clique algorithm computing P has worst-case round complexity \(R_{A}(n)=\omega (1)\)? cards.definitions: For each \(n\ge 2\), the communication network is the complete graph on processors \(1,\ldots ,n\). The input is a separate simple undirected graph G on the same labeled vertex set. Initially processor v knows n, its identifier v and the \(n- 1\) adjacency bits for edges incident to v in G. No other input or certificate is supplied. In a synchronous round every processor performs a finite, otherwise unrestricted amount of local deterministic computation and sends a separate message of at most \(\operatorname{ceil}(\log _{2} n)\) bits to each other processor; all messages arrive before the next round. Local memory is unrestricted. All processors execute one fixed finite algorithm with their identifiers and n as inputs; no nonuniform advice, randomness, oracle or free communication is allowed. The cost counts communication rounds only, not local computation. Node 1 must halt with \(\mathrm{P}(G)\) on every input; requiring all nodes to receive this one bit changes the cost by at most one round. \(R_{A}(n)\) is the maximum number of rounds until node 1 outputs, over all n-vertex input graphs. The statement \(R_{A}(n)=\omega (1)\) means that for every integer \(B\ge 1\) there is N such that \(R_{A}(n)>B\) for every \(n\ge N\); it is stronger than a lower bound at only infinitely many sizes. The chosen predicate may depend on vertex labels, as in Korhonen–Suomela’s graph-language model. “Explicit” is fixed by the source proposal’s centralized polynomial-time condition: one deterministic Turing machine computes P on every adjacency matrix within \(C(n+1)^{k}\) steps for constants C,k independent of n. There is no polynomial bound imposed on processors’ local work. A constant multiple of log n message bits can be simulated by a constant factor more rounds and does not change the \(\omega (1)\) target.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a single graph predicate with a proved centralized polynomial-time decision procedure and proves the displayed \(\omega (1)\) lower bound against every correct uniform deterministic protocol in the specified model. A negative resolution proves the logical negation of that existence statement. A two-round lower bound, a lower bound for broadcast messages or restricted local computation, or a hard predicate without the centralized polynomial-time guarantee does not settle the target.

context_blocks.title: The network and the input graph differ
context_blocks.text: Even if the input graph is a long path, the processors can communicate directly with every other processor. The path’s large diameter therefore does not force a long wait for information to travel from one endpoint to the other. The obstacle, if any, must arise from the amount and arrangement of the information needed for the decision, while each individual communication link carries only logarithmically many bits.

context_blocks.title: One bit can be much easier than collecting the input
context_blocks.text: For example, deciding whether G has an edge takes two rounds: every processor sends node 1 one bit saying whether it has an incident edge, and node 1 can broadcast the answer. Computing the decision at node 1 itself takes just the first round. Although the whole input contains quadratically many potential edge bits, this predicate does not need those bits collected individually. Input size alone is not a lower bound for an arbitrary one-bit output.

context_blocks.title: Why unicast is essential
context_blocks.text: In the unicast model, a processor may send different pieces of information to different recipients in the same round. Broadcast restricts it to one common message. The latter can admit bottleneck arguments that do not remain valid once a sender uses all its links separately. Drucker, Kuhn and Oshman study both versions and explicitly distinguish their lower bounds. A theorem for the broadcast version cannot be silently transferred here.

context_blocks.title: The explicitness requirement
context_blocks.text: Counting arguments show that some Boolean functions require many rounds. Korhonen and Suomela also establish a uniform time hierarchy by selecting hard functions through exhaustive enumeration. Such a selection supplies computability, but not the polynomial-time centralized algorithm demanded by this card. The desired separation concerns a task that is computationally manageable once its entire graph is available, while still resisting distributed communication with unrestricted local computation.

context_blocks.title: Connections and known limitations
context_blocks.text: The 2014 circuit simulations relate distributed lower bounds to difficult circuit lower bounds, with important bandwidth and depth qualifications. In particular, the introduction distinguishes a superconstant bound with one-bit links from an \(\Omega (\log  \log  n)\) bound with logarithmic links. These are not interchangeable claims for the weaker \(\omega (1)\) target here. Robinson’s PODC 2023 result rules out one-round MST computation at logarithmic bandwidth under its edge-output convention. It proves a genuine limitation, but two rounds are still a constant, and outputting a spanning tree differs from computing one decision bit.

cards.title: Work-efficient parallel directed reachability
cards.formal:
Does directed single-source reachability admit nearly linear work and polylogarithmic depth simultaneously in the uniform randomized CREW PRAM model specified below? Precisely, is the following statement true?
\[
\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists A_c,K_c,a_c,b_c,q_c\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall G\ \forall s\in V(G),
\]
\[
\Pr\!\left[\begin{array}{l}
A_c(G,s)\text{ terminates with the exact reachability indicator,}\\
W\le K_c(n+m)L^{a_c}\ \text{and}\ D\le K_cL^{b_c}
\end{array}\right]\ge1-n^{-c},
\]
where \(G\) ranges over every directed graph on the labeled vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(m=|E(G)|\), and \(L=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\)? Here \(K_c\ge1\), \(a_c,b_c\ge0\) and \(q_c\ge3\) are integers independent of \(n,G,s\); \(A_c\) is one finite program independent of input size. The word length is \(q_cL\). The required event jointly bounds total work \(W\), depth \(D\), and correctness of the entire output on each fixed input. The confidence exponent is requested as a fixed constant before choosing the program. The one-vertex case has the prescribed output consisting of a single 1 and is omitted only to avoid a vacuous probability bound.
cards.why: Directed reachability is a basic graph operation with a linear-work sequential solution. The unresolved issue is whether its dependencies can be processed in polylogarithmic parallel time while retaining nearly that work bound on every input. A resolution would determine whether a fundamental sequential graph task admits efficient use of many processors, rather than a speedup purchased with polynomially more computation.
cards.definitions:
Graphs are unweighted and directed. Their edge sets satisfy \(E\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}^{2}\); loops are allowed and repeated copies of an edge are absent. A vertex is reachable from \(s\) when there is a finite directed path from \(s\) to it, including the length-zero path. No assumption of strong connectivity, acyclicity, bounded diameter or a lower bound on \(m\) is imposed.

The input is an outgoing adjacency-array representation in shared read-only word memory. Cells 0, 1 and 2 contain \(n,m,s\). The next \(n+1\) cells contain offsets \(o_0,\ldots,o_n\), with \(0=o_0\le\cdots\le o_n=m\). The next \(m\) cells contain target labels \(t_0,\ldots,t_{m-1}\). The outgoing neighbors of vertex \(v\) are exactly the distinct labels \(t_j\) for \(o_{v-1}\le j<o_v\). Neighbor order is arbitrary. The output occupies the next \(n\) cells, one word for each vertex in label order: its value must be 1 for a reachable vertex and 0 otherwise. Thus the answer is the entire exact set, represented by \(n\) Boolean values, and does not include distances or a transitive closure.

For the chosen program, words are unsigned \(w=q_cL\)-bit integers. Shared cells and processor identifiers are numbered from 0 to \(2^w-1\). Every processor has a fixed finite number of word registers and runs the same finite program, with its identifier available in a designated register. These register counts and the program may depend on \(c\), but not on the graph or its size. Noninput cells and all other registers initially contain zero. There is no advice, oracle, precomputed graph index or uncharged preprocessing. The polynomial address space is the only imposed working-space limit.

Execution is synchronous. One active processor executes one primitive instruction per round. Instructions read or write one shared cell by its word address; copy words; add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\); perform bitwise AND, OR, XOR or complement; shift a word left or logically right by an integer between 0 and \(w-1\); compare unsigned words; branch; or obtain one fresh unbiased random bit. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Instructions use a constant number of registers. Reads observe the memory at the beginning of the round, and writes commit at its end. Several processors may read one cell, but at most one processor may write a given cell in a round, even if competing writes would contain the same value. Input cells cannot be written. Programs must obey these CREW access rules on every execution.

To account explicitly for activation, only processor 0 starts active. A unit-cost fork instruction activates one previously unused processor with a specified identifier, a program entry label and a constant number of copied registers; it starts in the next round. Two simultaneous forks may not name the same processor. Halting a processor costs one instruction; halted or not-yet-activated processors do no work. All input-independent setup, processor activation, data movement, auxiliary graph construction and output writes count toward work. Work is the total number of executed primitive instructions, and depth is the number of synchronous rounds until all activated processors halt. Nontermination gives infinite depth and does not satisfy the success event. The fork convention makes processor initialization explicit and allows ordinary parallel scheduling with polylogarithmic overhead.

All random-bit instructions draw mutually independent fair bits; the probability is over these bits for each fixed input representation. The required probability concerns correct output and both resource bounds together, not three expectations or an average over graphs. On the exceptional event, the program may return an incorrect answer, exceed a resource bound or fail to terminate. The notation \(\widetilde O(n+m)\) and polylogarithmic depth in the motivating question is replaced by the explicit logarithmic powers and constants in the statement.

progress.text: Jambulapati, Liu and Sidford give directed single-source reachability with \(\widetilde O(n+m)\) work and \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) depth with high probability. This entry uses the corrected fourth arXiv version of their FOCS 2019 paper.

Ashvinkumar, Bernstein, Probst Gutenberg and Saranurak give \(\widetilde O(m)\) work and \((n^{\omega+o(1)}/m)^{1/(2\omega-2)}\) span for \(m\ge n\). Here \(\omega\) is the exponent used for parallel matrix multiplication. Their dense-graph bound is \(n^{0.136}\); this is not a polylogarithmic bound on arbitrary inputs.

Kogan and Parter claim polylogarithmic-depth single-source reachability with \(\widetilde O(T^{\omega/2})\) work, where \(T\) is the number of ordered pairs in the reflexive transitive closure. The arXiv record reports FOCS 2026 acceptance. The claim concerns work in terms of \(T\), which need not be nearly linear in \(n+m\).

cards.title: Sublogarithmic distributed MIS
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform classical randomized LOCAL algorithm \(A\), taking a positive integer confidence parameter \(h\), such that for every fixed \(h\ge1\), on every \(n\)-vertex simple undirected graph with \(n\ge2\), its vertex outputs form a maximal independent set with probability at least \(1-n^{-h}\), and its worst-case elapsed round count \(T_A(n,h)\) satisfies
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{T_A(n,h)}{\log_2 n}=0?
\]
The guarantee ranges over all degrees, all valid distinct identifier assignments and all port numberings. Local computation, storage and message lengths are unrestricted; vertices have private random bits and may know \(n\) and the maximum degree.
cards.why: This isolates the communication needed for a basic symmetry-breaking task whose feasibility is easy to check locally. I include it because either outcome would change the benchmark for distributed graph algorithms: a faster algorithm would supply a stronger primitive, while a logarithmic lower bound would expose a substantial limitation of local coordination.
cards.definitions:
The network is the input finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\); disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are included. Vertex \(v\) eventually outputs a bit \(b_v\). Set \(I=\{v:b_v=1\}\). Independence requires that no edge have both endpoints in \(I\), and maximality requires that every vertex outside \(I\) have a neighbor in \(I\). Maximal does not mean maximum cardinality. For the one-vertex graph the algorithm must output its vertex, without an asymptotic restriction beyond finite time.

Vertices have pairwise distinct identifiers in \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\). Each vertex initially knows its own identifier, its degree, the identifiers of its neighbors, the exact \(n\), the exact maximum degree \(\Delta\), and \(h\). An arbitrary port numbering bijectively labels each vertex's incident edges by the integers from one to its degree. The two endpoints need not give an edge the same port number. Knowing neighbors initially instead of after an identifier-exchange round changes the count by at most one round and does not change the little-o target.

The LOCAL model runs in synchronous rounds. Each vertex can send a different finite binary message of arbitrary length along each incident edge, with messages delivered before the next round. There are no other channels, graph preprocessing, advice strings or shared random tape. Each vertex runs the same finite program with its own sequence of independent fair random bits. Local storage and intermediate computation are unbounded but must be finite and terminate on every random tape between rounds. The program is uniform over \(n,\Delta,h\) and vertex identifiers. After a vertex emits its output it may send fixed dummy messages until all vertices have finished.

For fixed \(n,h\), \(T_A(n,h)\) is the supremum of the number of elapsed rounds until all outputs are available, over every graph with exactly \(n\) vertices, identifiers, ports and random tapes. This supremum must be finite. The displayed success probability concerns the entire output labeling simultaneously on each particular input, not each vertex separately. The time guarantee holds even on tapes on which the output is wrong.

The limit means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every fixed integer \(h\ge1\), some \(n_0\) has \(T_A(n,h)\le\varepsilon\log_2n\) for every \(n\ge n_0\). The threshold may depend on \(h,\varepsilon\) and the program, but not on the graph, degrees or identifiers. Positive integer confidence parameters suffice for every requested real constant failure exponent. No common bound uniform in unbounded \(h\) is required. This explicit confidence-input convention realizes the saved high-probability requirement.

A bound on awake rounds, expected rounds, node-average rounds, or graphs avoiding short cycles is not the all-input worst-case elapsed-round bound in the question.

progress.text: The known degree-sensitive approach replaces dependence on \(n\) by \(\log\Delta\) plus a slower-growing residual term. The checked 2025 introduction explains why this leaves polynomial-degree graphs unresolved.
Theorem 1 gives sublogarithmic MIS for graphs without cycles of length at most six, while Open Question 1 and the discussion retain the general-graph target.

The companion primary paper proves a randomized maximal-matching lower bound \(\Omega(\min\{\log\Delta,\sqrt{\log n}\})\), which transfers to MIS on general graphs but not to MIS on trees. It is compatible with the requested little-o-logarithmic upper bound.

cards.title: Logarithmic-round deterministic maximal independent set
cards.formal:
Do there exist one uniform deterministic LOCAL algorithm \(A\) and an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that on every finite nonempty simple undirected graph with \(n\) vertices, and every valid identifier assignment and port numbering, all vertices output the membership bits of a maximal independent set within
\[C\log_2(n+2)\]
synchronous communication rounds? Vertices may know \(n\) and the maximum degree. No random bits are available, and the constant is independent of graph degree.
cards.why: This measures the quantitative cost of removing randomness from a basic distributed task. I include it separately from randomized sublogarithmic MIS because the algorithm must work against every identifier assignment with no failure probability. An \(O(\log  n)\) result would match the familiar randomized worst-case benchmark and propagate through reductions to other symmetry-breaking problems.
cards.definitions:
The network is the input graph \(G=(V,E)\), which can be disconnected and can have isolated vertices. Its maximum degree \(\Delta\) may be any integer from zero to \(n-1\). A set \(I\subseteq V\) is independent if no edge has both endpoints in \(I\). It is maximal if every vertex outside \(I\) has a neighbor in \(I\). This is inclusion maximality, not maximum cardinality. Each vertex outputs exactly one bit indicating its own membership, and the joint labeling must satisfy both conditions on every instance.

Identifiers are arbitrary pairwise distinct integers from \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\). At a vertex of degree \(d\), its incident edges receive distinct local ports \(1,\ldots,d\); port numbers at the two endpoints need not agree. Initially a vertex knows its own identifier, its degree and ports, the identifiers of its neighbors, the exact \(n\) and the exact \(\Delta\). Supplying neighbor identifiers initially saves at most the one round required to exchange them.

In each LOCAL round every vertex may perform an arbitrary finite deterministic local computation and send a separate finite binary message to each neighbor. The message lengths and local working memory are unrestricted. Messages arrive before the next round. Communication is possible only along graph edges; there is no centralized graph preprocessing, shared memory, nonuniform advice or external oracle. Every local computation terminates. All vertices execute one finite program independent of the graph size, with the listed information as input.

A halted vertex has fixed its output and may subsequently send dummy messages. The round count is elapsed synchronous time until all vertices have output, not the sum of their work or a count of active rounds. The displayed bound includes all graphs, identifiers, ports and degrees simultaneously. The use of \(\log_2(n+2)\) handles the one-vertex case; after changing the constant it is equivalent to an eventual \(O(\log n)\) guarantee on \(n\ge2\).

For a correct algorithm \(A\), let \(T_A(n)\) be the largest elapsed round count on the allowed instances of exactly \(n\) vertices. The question is \(\exists A\,\exists C>0\,\forall n\ge1:T_A(n)\le C\log_2(n+2)\). Its negation must exclude every correct uniform deterministic program, not merely algorithms using a particular decomposition or rounding method.

cards.title: Almost-linear-work parallel exact maximum flow
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), do there exist one uniform randomized priority-CRCW PRAM algorithm \(A_a\), constants \(C_a\ge1\) and \(B_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge a+3}\), and a function \(h_a:\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\to[1,\infty)\) with
\[
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\log h_a(N)}{\log N}=0,
\]
such that the following holds? On every explicitly given directed graph with \(n\ge2\) vertices, \(m\) arcs, distinct terminals \(s,t\), and integral capacities \(0\le u_e\le n^a\), the algorithm outputs an exact integral maximum flow with probability at least \(2/3\), and every execution satisfies
\[
 W\le C_a(m+n)h_a(m+n),\qquad
 D\le C_a h_a(m+n).
\]
Here \(W\) is total work and \(D\) is parallel depth in the word model below. In asymptotic notation the requested simultaneous bounds are \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) work and \((m+n)^{o(1)}\) depth.
cards.definitions:
The vertex set is \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Input memory contains \(n,m,s,t\) and an explicit ordered array of arcs \(E\), each with its two endpoint labels and integer capacity. There are no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. The range is \(0\le m\le n(n-1)\), and isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and zero capacities are permitted. No planarity, acyclicity, density or expansion promise is assumed. The fixed integer \(a\) specifies the admitted capacity regime and may be built into the program.

A feasible output is an integer \(f_e\) for every original arc, in input order, such that \(0\le f_e\le u_e\) and
\[
 \sum_{(v,z)\in E}f_{(v,z)}=
 \sum_{(z,v)\in E}f_{(z,v)}
 \quad(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}).
\]
Its value is outgoing flow minus incoming flow at \(s\). It must maximize that value over all feasible flows. Integral capacities admit an integral maximum flow. Any maximizing flow is acceptable, but the entire arc vector must be output explicitly. A maximum-flow value, a cut or an implicit flow alone is not the required output. If no positive flow is possible, the exact optimum is zero.

The computational model is a synchronous parallel random-access machine with shared memory and priority concurrent reads and writes (priority CRCW PRAM). Simultaneous reads of one cell are allowed. If multiple processors try to write one cell in a round, the lowest-index writer succeeds. Each active processor executes at most one word-RAM instruction per round, using its own local registers and the shared memory. Processor identifiers and memory addresses are word values. Processors follow one finite program with their identifiers available; there is no input-length advice or precomputed table. Processor activation and all program-controlled initialization count as work; a hidden computation cannot be assigned to an uncharged processor. Initially only the explicit input and fixed machine constants are present, and unused memory and registers are zero.

Words have length
\[
 w=B_a\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil.
\]
Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, copying, comparisons, branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. A shift by at least \(w\) positions returns zero. Each processor may generate a fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit word in one instruction; all such random words are mutually independent. Operations on longer integers are implemented by multiple charged instructions. There are no unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic operations or real-number oracles. The chosen \(B_a\) must accommodate every processor identifier and address used by the algorithm.

Work \(W\) is the sum of all executed processor instructions, including activation, input access, preprocessing, random generation and output writes. Depth \(D\) is the number of synchronous rounds until the complete output is available. Both resource bounds must hold on every execution, including executions returning an incorrect answer. Correctness means that the whole vector is feasible and exactly optimal, with probability at least \(2/3\) over the machine's coins for each fixed input. The success probability is not averaged over graphs, and resources are not merely bounded in expectation. Deterministic algorithms are allowed as a special case.

The program, word constant, multiplicative constant and overhead function may depend on \(a\), but not on the graph, its input ordering or its capacities. One algorithm for the fixed \(a\) must achieve the asymptotic bounds over all sizes. In particular, for every \(\delta>0\), its work is eventually at most \((m+n)^{1+\delta}\) and its depth at most \((m+n)^\delta\), after increasing a size threshold depending only on \(a,\delta\). Allowing a different algorithm for each \(\delta\) would be a different claim. The overhead function is an analytic bound, not advice supplied to the machine.

Subpolynomial depth is the requested target; polylogarithmic depth would suffice but is not required. The same computation must have almost-linear total work. An algorithm with small depth and polynomially more work, or with almost-linear work and a fixed positive power of \(n\) in its depth, does not meet the simultaneous endpoint. Using \(m+n\) accounts explicitly for the vertex set even when the graph contains few arcs.

context_blocks.text: Sequential almost-linear-time algorithms do not guarantee few dependent computation stages. This question asks whether exact directed flow can retain almost-linear total work while reducing those stages to subpolynomial depth.

The DAG-projection result gives efficient parallel reductions between exact directed flow and suitable approximation tasks on directed acyclic graphs. A reduction transfers a future algorithm; it does not itself supply the missing endpoint.

The August 2026 revision of the dense-instance result gives \(\widetilde O(m+n^{3/2})\) work and \(\widetilde O(\sqrt n)\) depth. Its work is near-linear on sufficiently dense inputs, but its depth is still polynomial in graph size.

The separate strongly polynomial parallel result supports arbitrary real capacities with \(\widetilde O(mn)\) work and \(\widetilde O(m)\) depth. Neither bound supplies the almost-linear-work and subpolynomial-depth combination asked for here.
Approximate flow in undirected graphs is a different regime in the source’s classification. Exactness, direction and the simultaneous resource limits are essential parts of this card.

cards.why: This is a central unresolved parallelization problem for exact network optimization, asking whether near-optimal sequential work can coexist with subpolynomial dependence depth.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence claim or its logical negation.

A positive answer must cover every fixed capacity exponent \(a\), with a uniform algorithm for that exponent, the simultaneous worst-case work and depth bounds, and the per-input probability of an exact explicit integral maximum flow. A result with stronger bounds also qualifies if it supplies this full output and model guarantee.

A negative answer must prove that for at least one fixed \(a\) no admissible algorithm and constants satisfy the target. A conditional obstruction, a lower bound for one algorithmic framework, or a difficulty confined to a more demanding capacity model does not establish the unconditional negation. An approximation algorithm, a restricted graph-family result, or a reduction to another task alone is insufficient unless the remaining task is also solved with the required resources.

cards.title: Deterministic volume gap
cards.formal:
For every fixed locally checkable labeling problem \(\Pi\) on all finite graphs of some fixed maximum degree \(\Delta\), is the following implication true?
\[
\bigl[\exists\text{ correct deterministic VOLUME algorithm }A:\lim_{n\to\infty}V_A(n)/n=0\bigr]
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl[\exists\text{ correct deterministic VOLUME algorithm }B\ \exists C>0\ \forall n\ge1:\ V_B(n)\le C(1+\log^* n)\bigr].
\]
The function \(V_A(n)\) is the largest number of distinct vertices visited to determine one requested output on an allowed input with at most \(n\) vertices. Algorithms know the exact size \(N\) of their input graph, and distinct vertex identifiers lie in \(\{1,\ldots,N^2\}\). The model and input class are defined below.
cards.definitions:
The problem \(\Pi\) fixes an integer degree bound \(\Delta\ge2\), an integer verification radius \(r\ge1\), finite nonempty input and output alphabets, and a finite collection of permitted rooted radius-\(r\) neighborhoods. A neighborhood records the graph, its root, vertex input and output labels, degrees and local port numbers. Vertices within graph distance at most \(r\) are shown, with their induced edges and incident degrees. The rule ignores identifiers and graph size and is unchanged under rooted isomorphism preserving labels and ports. An output labeling is legal exactly when each vertex sees a permitted neighborhood.

Instances include every finite nonempty simple undirected graph of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), with every input labeling and every port numbering, including disconnected graphs. A port numbering assigns, independently at each vertex of degree \(d\), its incident edges bijectively to \(\{1,\ldots,d\}\); port numbers at opposite ends need not agree. There is no global graph-structure promise. A problem with unsatisfiable instances simply has no correct algorithm and cannot witness the premise.

A computation requested at vertex \(v\) starts with that vertex visited and with its identifier, input label, degree and port names, the problem description and exact graph size \(N\). A probe chooses an already visited vertex \(w\) and one of its ports, discovers the neighbor \(u\) reached by that edge, and returns \(u\)'s identifier, input label, degree and local port names. It adds \(u\) to the visited set. Repeated probes are permitted. A program can explore only by following edges from visited vertices: it cannot jump to a vertex merely by guessing its identifier. The returned input does not supply the identities of all unvisited neighbors for free.

Only the number of distinct visited vertices, including the initial vertex, is charged. Intermediate computation and working memory have no time or space bound but must terminate on every input. Each algorithm is one finite deterministic program, uniform over all graph sizes. There is no advice, random tape, preprocessing of the graph, persistent shared state or communication between separately requested output computations. Their answers nevertheless must combine into a valid labeling on every allowed instance and every distinct identifier assignment.

For \(n\ge1\), \(V_A(n)\) maximizes this visit count over all such instances with \(1\le N\le n\), all identifiers and all requested vertices. The exact size known to the algorithm in that maximization is \(N\), not the outer bound \(n\). For a correct terminating algorithm this maximum is finite. The constants and the programs in the implication may depend on the fixed problem \(\Pi\), including its degree bound and verification radius, but not on \(n\).

Define \(\log^*n\) as the number of successive applications of \(\log_2\) needed to reach a value at most one; in particular \(\log^*1=0\). The limit in the premise means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), some integer \(n_0\) has \(V_A(n)\le\varepsilon n\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). The all-\(n\) bound in the conclusion is equivalent to an eventual big-O bound after enlarging its constant to handle finitely many small sizes. The claim concerns deterministic connected exploration, not randomized VOLUME algorithms or local computation algorithms allowed to probe distant vertices.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal implication or a fixed LCL counterexample. A counterexample must include a correct sublinear-volume algorithm and prove that every correct deterministic algorithm \(B\) fails the iterated-logarithmic bound: for every \(C>0\) and \(n_0\), some \(n\ge n_0\) has \(V_B(n)>C(1+\log^*n)\). Randomized intermediate complexities, bounds for one graph promise, or an unproved assertion that an optimal algorithm exists do not suffice.

cards.title: Quantum 3-coloring of cycles in \(o(\log^{*}n)\) rounds
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform quantum-LOCAL protocol \(A\) and a function \(T:\mathbb N_{\ge3}\to\mathbb N\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge3\) and every injective identifier assignment \(\lambda:V(C_n)\to\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\), all nodes of the consistently oriented cycle \(C_n\) finish within \(T(n)\) communication rounds on every possible execution branch, and their classical outputs \(c_v\in\{1,2,3\}\) satisfy
\[
\Pr\bigl[\forall\{u,v\}\in E(C_n),\ c_u\ne c_v\bigr]\ge1-\frac1n,
\qquad
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{T(n)}{1+\log^{*}_2n}=0?
\]
The probability is over the protocol's quantum measurement outcomes. Initially the quantum state is a product of local zero states. Each node knows \(n\), its own identifier and the predecessor/successor ports, and communication in both directions is permitted.
cards.definitions:
For specification only, \(C_n\) has vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_{n-1}\) and edges \(\{v_i,v_{(i+1)\bmod n}\}\). Its consistent orientation tells each node which port leads to its successor and which to its predecessor. The indices \(i\) are not inputs to the protocol. Identifiers are distinct integers in \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\), represented in binary. Nodes receive no distinguished leader, numerical position, neighbor identifiers, list of all identifiers, or other global information beyond \(n\). The identifier assignment is fixed before quantum randomness; the success bound holds for every such assignment.

All nodes execute the same fixed finite classical control program. Its initial classical input consists only of \(n\), the node's identifier and its two port labels. Classical computation manipulates finite binary strings by ordinary Turing-machine operations and may determine which local qubits to use next. There is no bound on local computation time, local storage or message length, but every local phase and every message must be finite on every possible branch. No advice depending on \(n\), the identifiers or the graph is supplied.

Local quantum storage is a finite tensor product of qubits. A node may append a fresh qubit in state \(\lvert0\rangle\), discard a local qubit, apply \(H\) or \(T\) to one local qubit, apply CNOT to an ordered pair of distinct local qubits, or measure a local qubit in the computational basis, with subsequent classical control depending on the outcome. The gates are
\[
H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{\mathrm i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathrm{CNOT}\lvert x,y\rangle=\lvert x,x\mathbin{\oplus}y\rangle
\quad(x,y\in\{0,1\}).
\]
Here \(\mathrm i^2=-1\) and \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. On a global density operator \(\rho\), a local gate acts by unitary conjugation on its chosen registers; discarding a register takes its partial trace. A computational-basis measurement with outcome \(b\in\{0,1\}\) has probability \(\operatorname{tr}(P_b\rho)\) and, when that probability is nonzero, leaves normalized state \(P_b\rho P_b/\operatorname{tr}(P_b\rho)\), where \(P_b\) projects the measured qubit onto \(\lvert b\rangle\). Classical random choices may be obtained by such measurements. There is no postselection that discards unsuccessful outcomes from the success probability.

A communication round consists of finite local processing followed by simultaneous noiseless transmission of finite quantum registers along the cycle edges. Each node may send registers to both neighbors and receives their sent registers before the next local phase. Sending transfers ownership of the qubits; it does not copy unknown states. Classical messages can be encoded as computational-basis registers. A final finite local phase may produce the node's color without another round. There is no communication between nonneighbors, no information conveyed by elapsed local computation time, and no additional inter-node channel. The initial global quantum state is the tensor product of all freshly initialized local \(\lvert0\rangle\) registers; there is no shared randomness or preshared entanglement. Entanglement created by the protocol through counted communication is allowed.

Every node must output one color and halt, including on branches where the resulting coloring is improper. A possible branch is one whose finite measurement outcomes have nonzero Born probability. The round bound holds on every such branch and uniformly over all identifier assignments of the same size, rather than merely in expectation or with high probability. Local operations, message lengths and numbers of qubits are not charged to round complexity. The program has no real-number oracle or arbitrary exact unitary as an extra primitive; the gate set above retains the card's existing concrete uniform interpretation.

For real \(x\ge1\), \(\log^{*}_2x\) is the least nonnegative integer \(r\) for which applying \(\log_2\) repeatedly \(r\) times reaches a value at most \(1\), stopping as soon as that occurs. The displayed limit means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(N\) such that \(T(n)\le\varepsilon(1+\log^{*}_2n)\) for every integer \(n\ge N\). The probability target is global correctness of all edges simultaneously, not separate correctness probabilities for individual nodes.

A conditional lower bound alone does not prove nonexistence. A lower bound limited to anonymous probability-one protocols, to one-way one-round communication, to two-coloring, or to growing-degree trees does not settle the stated protocol class.

cards.title: Optimal exact single-source shortest paths in CONGEST
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(b\ge 1\), do there exist constants \(K,c>0\) and a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm which, on every connected simple undirected graph with \(n\ge 2\) vertices, integer edge weights in \([0,n^{b}]\) and a designated source s, makes every vertex output its exact weighted distance from s in at most \(K(\sqrt{n}+D)(\log _{2}(n+2))^{c}\) rounds on every execution, with simultaneous correctness probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\)? Here D is the diameter of the unweighted graph.
cards.why: This asks whether exact weighted shortest distances can be computed as quickly as the general communication lower bound permits, up to logarithmic factors. It separates the cost of exact optimization from the costs of network diameter and limited link bandwidth.
cards.status_note: Primary exact CONGEST bounds, randomized distance lower bounds, the approximation result and later-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No algorithm or impossibility theorem settling the full stated polylogarithmic-overhead target was found. The inherited 2026 paper is retained as related-work provenance, rather than used alone as evidence of the current best bound.

cards.definitions: A path length is the sum of its edge weights; the distance is the minimum path length, and the source distance is zero. D is the maximum over vertex pairs of the minimum number of edges on a path between them. The graph itself is the network. In each synchronous round, each endpoint of each edge can send at most \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits to the other endpoint, for a constant B depending only on b. Nodes initially know n,b, the source identifier, their own identifiers, and the identifiers and weights of incident neighbours. Identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\). Local computation and memory are unrestricted, but each local computation between rounds terminates. Nodes use independent private fair random bits. One finite program, allowed to depend on b, runs at all nodes; no global graph description, advice, routing tables or preprocessing is supplied. The graph, weights, source and identifiers are fixed before randomness is drawn. Output at v is an ordinary binary integer for \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\), stored locally. The guarantee concerns all vertices together, over all coins. All communication, including finding termination and any preprocessing, counts in the round bound. K,c,B are independent of n,D and the instance; no value of D is initially supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed weight exponent b there is a single uniform algorithm meeting the stated \(O((\sqrt{n}+D)\operatorname{polylog} n)\) round bound on every execution and the simultaneous \(1- n^{- 3}\) correctness probability on every eligible network. Alternatively, prove that this is impossible for at least one fixed b, for every choice of algorithm and fixed constants K,c,B. An approximation guarantee, an \(n^{o(1)}\) overhead not bounded by a fixed power of log n, or a result for only one diameter regime is not the stated affirmative answer.

context_blocks.text: Every vertex must learn its distance from one designated source, measured by the sum of edge weights. The processors sit at the vertices and can communicate only along the graph’s edges. The question is about the number of synchronous communication rounds, rather than the time a single processor would spend on an adjacency-list representation.

There are two different notions of distance. If s is joined directly to v by an edge of weight 10, but a two-edge route has weights 2 and 2, the weighted distance is 4 even though v is one communication hop from s. The parameter D ignores weights and measures the largest hop distance between vertices. A minimum-weight path can contain many more edges than a minimum-hop path.

Each edge transports only \(O(\log  n)\) bits per direction in one round, while different edges can communicate simultaneously. A distance fits in \(O(\log  n)\) bits because weights are polynomially bounded, but many different pieces of information may need the same link. The \(\sqrt{n}\) term in the benchmark reflects a bandwidth obstacle in worst-case networks; the D term reflects how far information has to travel.

The requested output is distributed: vertex v stores \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\). Collecting all distances at s, printing full paths, or making every vertex learn the whole distance table would impose additional communication requirements. Conversely, a local estimate that is merely close to the shortest distance is not the exact output required here.

Chechik and Mukhtar give an exact randomized bound \(\tilde\{O\}(\sqrt{n} D^{1/4}+D)\), where the tilde hides factors polynomial in log n. Their theorem also handles directed weighted graph inputs over an undirected communication network, so it covers the undirected case retained on this card. The extra \(D^{1/4}\) factor is not absorbed by the logarithmic allowance when D grows polynomially with n.

Cao and Fineman’s 2023 theorem supplies another bound, \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{2/5+o(1)}D^{2/5}+\sqrt{n}+D)\), for polynomially bounded weights. This improves the comparison in part of the diameter range. For \(D\approx n^{1/2}\), its displayed terms give \(n^{3/5+o(1)}\), while the target is \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{1/2})\). This comparison of proven bounds displays a remaining gap; it does not prove that any particular graph requires \(n^{3/5}\) rounds.

The notation \(n^{o(1)}\) allows factors larger than every fixed power of log n. Such a factor cannot automatically be treated as the polylogarithmic overhead specified in the statement. Similarly, a theorem for one fixed diameter regime does not supply the single bound required for all connected networks.

Near-optimal algorithms for \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate undirected distances provide an important contrast. For fixed \(\varepsilon\) they may return a nonzero relative error. Since integer distances can be as large as \(n^{b+1}\), forcing exactness by taking \(\varepsilon\) extremely small can increase the algorithm’s complexity through its \(\varepsilon\) dependence. A fixed-accuracy approximation theorem therefore does not imply this exact result.

The inherited 2026 reference studies programmable matter with reconfigurable circuits that transmit signals in a different way. Its related-work section is useful background for CONGEST, but its own polylogarithmic algorithm is not a solution in the present model. The card now cites the original CONGEST results as well, including the 2023 bound missing from that summary.

Resolving the question would determine whether exact numerical optimization has an additional distributed cost beyond the familiar bandwidth-and-diameter benchmark. Shortest distances are also a primitive in other distributed constructions, so a faster exact computation would affect more than routing from one source.

cards.title: Directed reachability with nearly linear memory and polylogarithmic passes
cards.formal: Do there exist constants a,b,C and a uniform randomized streaming algorithm that decides directed s–t reachability on every n-vertex graph using at most \(Cn(\log (n+2))^{a}\) bits of memory and \(C(\log (n+2))^{b}\) passes, with success probability at least \(2/3\) for every adversarially ordered edge stream?
cards.definitions: The input is a finite simple directed graph on the labelled vertex set \([n], n\ge 2\), with distinct designated vertices s,t. The algorithm knows n,s,t before reading the edges. Each directed edge occurs once in an insertion-only stream, in an arbitrary order fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. Each pass scans this same stream in the same forward order. The input is read-only: there are no adjacency queries, random-access reads, sorting operations on external storage, or writable auxiliary streams. All mutable working storage counts toward the bit bound; fresh independent random bits may be read from a one-way random source. The memory and pass bounds hold on every execution. Computation between successive input items is unrestricted but must terminate; no running-time bound beyond termination is imposed. A yes answer means that there is a directed path from s to t in the input graph. The constants and algorithm are independent of n, the graph, and the edge order.

context_blocks.text: Directed reachability asks an elementary question: can one vertex eventually lead to another by following arrows? With the whole graph in memory, a search answers it in linear time. In a graph stream, the difficulty is that the next useful edge may already have gone past before the algorithm learns that its tail is reachable. Repeated scans provide another opportunity to use the edge, but every scan revisits the entire input.

Nearly linear memory means linear in the number of vertices, up to powers of a logarithm. It can store labels, several values per vertex and a sparse auxiliary graph, but a dense input may have quadratically many edges. The card allows every fixed polylogarithmic memory overhead: it does not ask for an especially restrictive exact n-bit implementation. Conversely, allowing storage proportional to all the edges would erase the intended obstacle.

A simple baseline maintains the set of vertices already reached from s. Whenever an edge leaves this set, its head is marked reachable. After at most \(n- 1\) scans every reachable vertex has been found, using a bit per vertex and counters. A path whose edges appear in reverse path order makes this particular algorithm advance slowly. That example is not a lower bound for all algorithms: a path has only linearly many edges and fits entirely in the permitted memory.

The undirected analogue has a much stronger one-pass solution: maintain connected components with union–find. Direction removes the equivalence-relation structure that makes this summary sufficient. Strongly connected components can still be contracted in a digraph, but their directed reachability relation is another graph rather than just a partition. A small summary must somehow preserve the information needed for the specified source and target.

Jambulapati, Liu and Sidford give a randomized parallel reachability algorithm using nearly linear work and \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) depth. Their shortcut construction can also be implemented in the streaming model. Assadi and coauthors explicitly state the resulting \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-pass semi-streaming path-finding algorithm as Proposition 4. This supplies the relevant upper bound through a concrete simulation, rather than through an assumption that every shallow parallel computation automatically yields a streaming algorithm.

A reachability-preserving shortcut is an extra arc \((u,v)\) added only when the original graph already contains a directed path from u to v. Such arcs can reduce the number of edges in a path without changing which vertices are reachable. The cited streaming upper bound constructs and uses a sparse collection within its memory budget; its pass guarantee is part of that implementation, not a consequence of the existence of shortcuts alone.

On the lower-bound side, Guruswami and Onak extend earlier path-output barriers to the decision problem itself. Their multipass space bound implies that semi-streaming reachability requires \(\Omega (\log  n/\log  \log  n)\) passes. The exact theorem includes polynomial factors in the pass count and logarithmic factors in n; these should not be dropped when comparing parameters. The conclusion rules out constant passes but leaves the polylogarithmic target available.

Chen, Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, Song and Yu prove that \(o(\sqrt{\log  n})\) passes require \(n^{2- o(1)}\) space. This is a striking strengthening of how much memory is necessary when the pass budget is very small. It is not a larger asymptotic lower bound on the number of passes with nearly linear memory than the \(\Omega (\log  n/\log  \log  n)\) statement above. The two results describe different parts of the tradeoff.

Azarmehr and coauthors’ September 9, 2026 revision still identifies \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) as the fastest known semi-streaming reachability pass bound. Their Theorem 9 links an improved streaming approximation for distance to monotonicity to an improved reachability algorithm. This is evidence that the question controls progress beyond reachability itself, and gives a recent explicit check of the benchmark used on this card.

A positive answer would show that repeated sequential access with a compact memory can recover global directed information surprisingly quickly. A negative answer would establish a fundamental barrier to that access pattern, even without restricting local computation time. Either result would help explain the difference between graph problems admitting compact summaries and those that require many rounds of discovering dependencies.

cards.title: Depth-first search in NC
cards.formal: Does there exist a logspace-uniform family of deterministic Boolean circuits of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth that, on the adjacency matrix of every finite simple undirected graph, outputs a valid depth-first-search forest? The roots and the order of visiting neighbors may be chosen freely for each input.
cards.why: DFS is a basic graph structure whose standard construction has a long chain of sequential choices. Resolving this question would determine whether randomness can always be removed from its efficient parallel construction while retaining polynomial total resources.

progress.text: Aggarwal and Anderson give a randomized NC algorithm for undirected DFS, as documented in the 2025 paper’s introduction. This permits randomness.
Ghaffari, Grunau and Qu give a randomized algorithm with \(\widetilde{O}\)\((m+n)\) work and \(\widetilde{O}\)\((\sqrt{n})\) depth; this addresses work efficiency with a larger depth bound.

Chauhan, Datta and Praveen prove deterministic parallel bounds for bounded-genus and undirected single-crossing-minor-free graphs, and a logspace bound for bounded treewidth. The general question remains open in their statement.
