cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) the input is the \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal adjacency matrix of a graph G on \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). The output is a parent array \(p\in \{0,\ldots ,n\}^{n}\), with 0 denoting a root. If \(p(v)\ne 0\), require \(\{v,p(v)\}\in E(G)\); repeatedly taking parents must reach 0 from every vertex. These parent edges define a rooted forest, and each connected component of G must be spanned by one of its trees. A vertex u is an ancestor of v if u lies on the tree path from v to its root. The forest is a DFS forest if, for every edge \(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\), one endpoint is an ancestor of the other. For undirected graphs this is exactly the class of forests produced by recursive depth-first search under some choices of roots and neighbor orders. Encode each parent entry in \(\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Each circuit \(C_{n}\) has \(n^{2}\) input bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) output bits, uses AND and OR gates with at most two inputs and NOT gates with one input, and has size at most \(O(n^{c})\) and depth at most \(O((\log _{2}(n+2))^{k})\), for fixed constants c,k independent of n and G. Logspace uniformity means that one deterministic Turing machine, given \(1^{n}\), writes the description of \(C_{n}\) while using \(O(\log (n+2))\) working space, excluding its read-only input and write-only output tapes. Correctness is required on every valid adjacency matrix; behavior on other bit strings is unrestricted. The empty graph has the empty output. No randomness or input-length-specific advice is supplied. NC here refers to computing a valid encoded output, rather than deciding a Boolean language.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct one circuit family satisfying all the stated correctness, uniformity, size and depth requirements, or prove that no such family exists. The output may be any valid DFS forest. A randomized algorithm, a quasipolynomial-size circuit family, an algorithm only for a restricted graph class, or a lower bound for one prescribed traversal order does not settle this question.

context_blocks.text: Depth-first search explores an unvisited neighbor, completes the recursive exploration from that neighbor, and only then tries another neighbor of the current vertex. The resulting parent pointers form a spanning forest. The question asks whether that structure can always be assembled in a small number of parallel stages, even though the familiar sequential procedure follows one exploration at a time.

Being a spanning tree is not enough. In a triangle with vertices 1, 2 and 3, a tree rooted at 1 with children 2 and 3 fails: edge \(\{2,3\}\) joins different branches. The path with parent pointers \(p(1)=0, p(2)=1\) and \(p(3)=2\) is a valid DFS tree. The ancestor condition makes this distinction explicit without prescribing a traversal order.

The height of the output tree is not the running time being bounded. A path graph may require a DFS tree of height \(n- 1\), yet its n parent entries may be computed in parallel. Conversely, a sequential algorithm with linear running time need not have polylogarithmic parallel depth.

The freedom to choose a valid output matters. Reproducing the lexicographically first DFS order under fixed choices is P-complete according to the cited source. That hardness result does not exclude efficient parallel computation of a different valid DFS forest.

The general undirected problem has a randomized NC algorithm, and a deterministic parallel algorithm with quasipolynomially many processors is known. The latter exceeds the polynomial resource bound in this question. Deterministic NC algorithms are also known for several restricted graph families. The 2025 source still leaves general deterministic NC open.

There is a separate goal of keeping total work close to the input size. The 2023 algorithm obtains work \(\widetilde{O}\)\((m+n)\) and depth \(\widetilde{O}\)\((\sqrt{n})\), where m is the number of edges and \(\widetilde{O}\) suppresses factors polynomial in logarithms. Its depth bound is sublinear but does not establish the polylogarithmic depth required here.

Uniformity requires one small-space procedure to describe the circuits for every input length. The circuits cannot be unrelated choices supplied separately for each n. Both this requirement and the polynomial size bound belong to the target; merely showing that suitable circuits exist with larger resources leaves a different question.

sentences: A depth-first-search forest records the parent choices of recursive graph exploration.
For an undirected graph, it is a rooted spanning forest in which every graph edge joins a vertex to one of its ancestors.
The problem asks for a deterministic, uniformly specified parallel computation that constructs any such forest with polynomial resources and polylogarithmic depth.
Randomized NC algorithms and deterministic results for restricted graph classes are known, but those guarantees do not settle the general target.
A solution would show whether this basic search structure can always be built efficiently in parallel without random choices.

cards.title: Two-dimensional sandpile prediction in NC
cards.formal: Is the language \(\mathrm{SP}_2\) defined below in logspace-uniform \(\mathrm{NC}\)? An instance explicitly supplies a finite stable rectangular array of sand grains and cells \(p,q\) inside that rectangle. Extend the array by zero to all of \(\mathbb Z^2\), add one grain at \(p\), and accept exactly when \(q\) eventually topples under the simultaneous four-neighbor rule. The question concerns one uniform circuit family with polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth for all input lengths.
cards.definitions:
Let \(W,H\ge1\), let \(B=\{0,\ldots,W-1\}\times\{0,\ldots,H-1\}\), let \(c:B\to\{0,1,2,3\}\), and let \(p=(p_x,p_y),q=(q_x,q_y)\in B\). Define \(\bar c(v)=c(v)\) on \(B\) and \(\bar c(v)=0\) elsewhere in \(\mathbb Z^2\). Set \(c_0(v)=\bar c(v)+\mathbf1_{\{v=p\}}\). With
\[
E=\{(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)\},
\]
define, for every integer \(t\ge0\) and every \(v\in\mathbb Z^2\),
\[
c_{t+1}(v)=c_t(v)-4\mathbf1_{\{c_t(v)\ge4\}}+
\sum_{e\in E}\mathbf1_{\{c_t(v-e)\ge4\}}.
\]
Here \(\mathbf1_A\) is \(1\) when assertion \(A\) holds and \(0\) otherwise. Every unstable cell topples once per simultaneous round; its threshold and the number of grains sent to each neighbor are fixed. The required output is \(1\) exactly when \(\exists t\ge0:\ c_t(q)\ge4\). All cells outside the supplied rectangle participate in the same dynamics. There is no absorbing boundary, periodic identification, missing neighbor or cell-dependent weight.

For a nonnegative integer \(z\), let \(s(z)\) be its ordinary binary expansion without leading zeros, using \(s(0)=0\), and let \(b(z)=|s(z)|\). Encode \(z\) as \(1^{b(z)}0s(z)\). A valid binary input is the concatenation of these codes for \(W,H,p_x,p_y,q_x,q_y\), followed by exactly \(2WH\) bits encoding the entries of \(c\): list rows in increasing \(y\), and within each row increasing \(x\), using \(00,01,10,11\) for \(0,1,2,3\). Dimensions must be positive and the encoded coordinates must belong to \(B\). Strings not meeting these conditions are rejected. Let \(N\) be the complete binary string length, including all array entries. Extra zero rows or columns are permitted, but their entries still count; this is not a sparse or succinct configuration encoding.

Membership in logspace-uniform \(\mathrm{NC}\) means that there exist fixed integers \(a,k\ge1\), a fixed real \(K\ge1\), and a deterministic finite Turing-machine program generating a Boolean circuit \(C_N\) from the unary input \(1^N\), for every \(N\ge0\). It must halt, use at most \(K\log_2(N+2)\) work-tape cells, and write an explicit gate-and-wire description to a write-only output tape. Its input tape is read-only. The circuit has \(N\) input bits and one output, uses AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates of fan-in one and constants \(0,1\), has at most \(K(N+2)^a\) gates and depth at most \(K(\log_2(N+2))^k\), and decides \(\mathrm{SP}_2\) exactly on all length-\(N\) strings. Gate descriptions use binary indices in topological order and specify the output gate. There is no advice or oracle. The constants, circuit generator and gate basis are independent of the instance. Randomized error is not allowed; no time \(t\) is supplied as part of the instance.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of membership of this language in the specified uniform circuit class, or a complete Lean proof that no such circuit family and generator exist. Polynomial sequential simulation alone is insufficient. A proof of P-completeness under logspace reductions would imply nonmembership only with the additional assumption that P differs from NC; it is not an unconditional negative answer.

cards.title: Lifting CSP sketching resistance to sublinear streaming resistance
cards.formal: For every finite family \(\Pi\) of Boolean predicates of a fixed arity, does the following implication hold? If no \(o(\sqrt n)\)-bit sketching algorithm nontrivially approximates Max-CSP(\(\Pi\)), then no \(o(n)\)-bit single-pass streaming algorithm nontrivially approximates it. Nontrivial approximation, sketching and the polynomial stream-length convention are defined below.
cards.why: A universal implication would upgrade a broad sketching classification to a fundamental limitation on all small-memory streaming algorithms. A counterexample would show that some CSPs admit an informative sequential summary even though every substantially smaller mergeable summary is approximation resistant.
cards.status_note: The 2025 source states this as a conjecture. A substantial April 2026 theorem now gives LP-gap-based linear-space lower bounds, but the checked text does not explicitly establish or refute Conjecture 8 for every sketching-resistant family. Status remains uncertain rather than certifying that the 2025 question survives that theorem. The card’s mathematical statement is complete, and its polynomial-length convention is identified explicitly.

cards.definitions: Fix an integer \(k\geq1\) and a nonempty finite family \(\Pi\subseteq\{\pi:\{0,1\}^k\to\{0,1\}\}\). A constraint on \(n\geq k\) variables consists of a predicate \(\pi\in\Pi\) and an ordered tuple of \(k\) distinct indices in \([n]\). An instance \(\Phi\) is a nonempty list of such constraints; repetitions are allowed and every occurrence has unit weight. For an assignment \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), its value is the fraction of constraint occurrences it satisfies, and \(\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\) is the maximum over assignments. Let \(\rho(\Pi)=\inf_{n\geq k,\Phi}\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\). Padding with unused variables makes this the limiting trivial approximation threshold. A nontrivial approximation has a fixed \(\delta>0\), with \(\rho(\Pi)+\delta\leq1\), and outputs a value \(v\) satisfying \((\rho(\Pi)+\delta)\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\leq v\leq\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every instance and order. The algorithm need not output an assignment. A deterministic streaming algorithm has a finite state represented by \(s\) bits, a fixed initial state, an update map taking the current state and next constraint, and a final output map. It reads the constraint list once in an adversarial order. A randomized algorithm is a distribution over deterministic algorithms, chosen independently of the list. Local computation and the choice of this distribution are unrestricted; this is the nonuniform randomness model used for the source’s lower bounds. A sketching algorithm additionally has a state map \(K\) on lists and a binary combination map \(H\), with \(K(\sigma\tau)=H(K(\sigma),K(\tau))\) for every pair of lists whose concatenation is allowed; its updates append a singleton through this map, and its output depends only on the sketch. Randomized sketches are distributions over such deterministic schemes. Commutativity and linearity of the sketches are not separately required. Editorial length convention: an algorithmic space regime must handle every fixed polynomial length bound. Precisely, to admit nontrivial approximation in \(o(b(n))\) space means that there is one fixed \(\delta>0\) such that, for every fixed integer \(d\geq2\), there is an algorithm family for all lists of length at most \(n^d\), with worst-case state size \(s_d(n)\) satisfying \(s_d(n)/b(n)\to0\). The algorithm may depend on \(\Pi,d,\delta,n\), but not on the input list; the ratio improvement \(\delta\) does not depend on \(n\) or \(d\). The two occurrences of “no” in the conjecture negate this full definition.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the implication for every predicate family in the stated model, or give a fixed family that is resistant to nontrivial o(√n)-space sketching and a nontrivial o(n)-space streaming approximation for that family. Both parts of a counterexample need proofs. A faster approximation for a family already admitting nontrivial small sketches, or a lower bound under an additional condition not proved for all families in the premise, is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: This is Conjecture 8 of Singer’s column. It simultaneously enlarges the algorithm class and the permitted memory, while asking only whether any fixed improvement over the trivial ratio is possible. It does not claim that every approximation threshold of every CSP stays unchanged as space increases.

The sketching dichotomy gives polylogarithmic-space algorithms or square-root-space lower bounds, with a small slack in the approximation thresholds. Its definition of a sketch permits general mergeable summaries; restricting the premise to linear sketches would be a different statement.

Max-DiCut illustrates why the premise matters. Its trivial ratio is one quarter, while small sketches already give a ratio approaching four ninths. Better streaming approximations using more memory therefore do not by themselves refute the resistance implication in this card.

Singer, Tulsiani and Velusamy’s April 2026 manuscript proves linear-space lower bounds from integrality gaps of the basic linear programming relaxation. That relaxation assigns a distribution of local assignments to each constraint and requires consistent one-variable marginals on shared variables. Its ratio is not defined by the sketching premise in this card.

The same manuscript gives a tight classification for bounded-degree instances and explicitly continues to distinguish general sketching lower bounds from streaming lower bounds. Applying its theorem to Conjecture 8 requires a theorem connecting every resistant predicate family to the needed LP gap. This review does not claim that such a connection has been proved or disproved.

cards.title: Optimal measurements and near-linear decoding for universal ℓ₂/ℓ₁ sparse recovery
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants \(C,B>0\), \(a\geq0\), and a deterministic recovery scheme such that, for every \(n\geq1\) and \(1\leq k\leq n\), one fixed matrix \(A_{n,k}\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(m\leq Bk\log_2(en/k)\) permits recovery from \(A_{n,k}x\) in at most \(Bn\log_2^a(n+2)\) operations, with \[\|x-\widehat x\|_2\leq \frac{C}{\sqrt{k}}\min_{z:\,|\operatorname{supp}(z)|\leq k}\|x-z\|_1\] simultaneously for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\)?
cards.why: The target combines information-efficient sensing with fast, uniformly reliable reconstruction for arbitrary signals. Resolving it would show whether the strongest standard universal mixed-norm guarantee can be obtained without sacrificing near-optimal compression or practical asymptotic decoding time.
cards.status_note: The 2009 source poses this universal mixed-norm tradeoff, and the checked later for-all recovery paper still distinguishes it from its ℓ₁/ℓ₁ result. No matching resolution was located in the bounded September 2026 check. The arithmetic/preprocessing convention is explicit; efficient explicit matrix generation is not asserted to be part of the original target.

sentences: A fixed matrix compresses every real signal to a short vector of linear measurements.
The decoder must work for all signals with error controlled by the best k-sparse ℓ₁ tail divided by √k.
The conjecture combines O(k log(en/k)) measurements with near-linear deterministic decoding.

cards.definitions: The support of a vector is the set of its nonzero coordinates; a vector is \(k\)-sparse if its support has size at most \(k\). The norms are \(\|v\|_1=\sum_i|v_i|\) and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The minimum in the statement is the sum of absolute values outside the \(k\) largest-magnitude coordinates of \(x\); ties may be broken arbitrarily. The decoder receives \(n,k\), the exact real measurement vector \(y=A_{n,k}x\), and read-only access to the fixed description of the scheme. It receives neither \(x\) nor its support, and must output all \(n\) coordinates of \(\widehat x\). The output need not itself be sparse. Measurements are linear and selected independently of the unknown signal. We use the real-arithmetic model: real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero number, square root of a nonnegative number, comparison, and access to an addressed stored entry each cost one operation; ordinary integer index operations cost one as well. The decoder is one fixed algorithm, with polynomial-size read-only advice depending only on \(n,k\), including the matrix and any preprocessing data. Reading advice is charged. Advice generation and forming the original measurement vector are outside the requested decoding bound. No polynomial-time explicit matrix construction is required. Once the scheme is fixed its decoder is deterministic and the guarantee holds for all real signals; a matrix chosen by the probabilistic method is admissible only if a single fixed choice works for all signals. Constants, the polynomial advice exponent and the decoding exponent are independent of \(n,k,x\). Measurements are noiseless; no additional post-measurement perturbation is included.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction or existence proof of a scheme meeting both resource bounds and the universal mixed-norm error guarantee in the specified arithmetic model, or prove that no such scheme exists. A guarantee holding with high probability separately for each input, an ℓ₁/ℓ₁ error bound, or optimal row count with slower decoding is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The source’s “deterministic” target is universal recovery from one matrix: the same measurements must work for every signal. Editorial model convention: this card makes the arithmetic-operation and preprocessing conventions explicit, without adding the separate challenge of efficient deterministic matrix generation. It also uses \(\log(en/k)\) and \(k\geq1\) to remove the source formula’s undefined or zero endpoint expressions.

For exactly \(k\)-sparse signals the right-hand side is zero, so the scheme must recover them exactly. For nonsparse signals, recovery quality depends on the entire tail and gains a factor \(1/\sqrt{k}\). Merely outputting a plausible support does not establish this robust guarantee.

The original question emphasizes achieving optimal measurement count and fast reconstruction together. Classical constructions achieve the two features separately for this error criterion, whereas some fast optimal-measurement schemes use a different norm on the reconstruction error.

The later for-all sparse-recovery work of Gilbert, Li, Porat and Strauss improves measurements and decoding for the ℓ₁/ℓ₁ formulation, and explicitly lists mixed-norm recovery as a remaining direction. Its use of a matrix fixed for all signals is compatible with a nonconstructive probabilistic existence proof.

The inequality \(\|v\|_2\leq\|v\|_1\) does not convert an \(\ell_1/\ell_1\) theorem into the requested result: it loses the essential \(1/\sqrt{k}\) factor. Likewise, an input-dependent success probability does not imply that one random seed works simultaneously over the uncountable set of all real inputs.

When \(k\) is comparable to \(n\), storing the full vector is consistent with the measurement bound. The compression challenge lies in the sparse regime. Counting the output cost explains why near-linear decoding remains a meaningful target even when the number of measurements is much smaller than \(n\).

cards.title: Characterizing separable distances approximable in small streaming space
cards.formal: Characterize the functions \(\phi:\mathbb N_0^2\to\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\) in the domain below for which the separable dissimilarities \[d_\phi(f,g)=\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(f_i,g_i)\] admit arbitrarily accurate relative approximation by one-pass algorithms using space polynomial in \(\log(n+M+2)\) and \(1/\varepsilon\), under deletions that preserve nonnegative frequencies. Equivalently, determine the classification function \(\chi(\phi)\in\{0,1\}\), equal to one exactly for functions with such algorithms.
cards.why: A full classification would explain which local comparisons of large frequency vectors retain enough structure for accurate compression under deletions. It would connect individual distance estimators and impossibility results through a general mathematical criterion, including dissimilarities that are not norms or even metrics.
cards.status_note: The source asks for a broad characterization. This card explicitly fixes an effective separable streaming variant rather than attributing every resource convention to the source. The 2016 one-variable result is only a partial classification, and the later metric counterexample concerns another model. No full characterization for the specified domain was located in the bounded September 2026 check.

sentences: A local nonnegative cost φ defines a dissimilarity by summing over corresponding frequency coordinates.
The stream may insert and delete frequencies while keeping both vectors nonnegative.
The selected task classifies exactly which effectively evaluable costs admit polylogarithmic-space relative approximations.
The criterion must cover the entire specified domain and include both algorithms and impossibility proofs.
Known offset obstructions, difference-based aggregate classifications and norm-sketching results cover only parts of this domain.

cards.definitions: The domain consists of all fixed total functions \(\phi\) with \(\phi(t,t)=0\) for every \(t\geq0\), whose rational value on binary integers \(a,b\) can be computed in time polynomial in \(\log(a+b+2)\). Numerators and positive denominators are output in binary; the polynomial may depend on \(\phi\). Symmetry, the triangle inequality, homogeneity and dependence only on \(a-b\) are not assumed. A stream starts with \(f=g=0\) in \(\mathbb N_0^n\). Each item selects one vector, a coordinate \(i\in[n]\), and a change \(+1\) or \(-1\); no intermediate coordinate may become negative. The total number of updates is at most a given bound \(M\geq1\), so all coordinates are at most \(M\). Inputs \(n,M\) and a rational accuracy \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\) are known in advance. The algorithm reads each update once, in an arbitrary order independent of its coins, and at the end outputs a nonnegative rational \(D\). For every valid stream it must satisfy \((1-\varepsilon)d_\phi(f,g)\leq D\leq(1+\varepsilon)d_\phi(f,g)\) with probability at least \(2/3\); zero dissimilarity must therefore produce zero on a successful execution. The algorithm is a uniform randomized Turing machine that may depend on the fixed function \(\phi\). It may read fresh independent random bits, but remembered randomness, counters, work tapes and evaluation of \(\phi\) all count toward its working space. The read-once input and final write-only output are separate tapes and cannot serve as auxiliary storage. No running-time bound is required beyond termination on every run. Define \(\chi(\phi)=1\) if there are such an algorithm and constants \(B,a,b\), depending only on \(\phi\), using at most \(B\varepsilon^{-b}\log^a(n+M+2)\) working bits on every input and every coin outcome; otherwise define \(\chi(\phi)=0\). This definition ranges over all \(n,M,\varepsilon\). It does not require that a single decision program classify arbitrary descriptions of \(\phi\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a noncircular necessary-and-sufficient condition on the numerical function \(\phi\), expressed without quantifying over streaming algorithms or communication protocols, and prove the classification completely in Lean. The positive direction must establish the specified approximation scheme; the negative direction must rule out every space bound of the stated form. As a function-valued benchmark answer, a supplied real-valued classification \(h\) must satisfy \(|h(\phi)-\chi(\phi)|\leq1/100\) throughout the domain. An exact zero-one characterization satisfies this tolerance. Repeating the definition of \(\chi\), covering only a proper subclass, or giving an uncertified list of examples is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The source asks broadly which distances and dissimilarities can be compressed, especially when updates can delete items. Editorial specialization: this card fixes the separable, effectively evaluable rational-valued family, one-pass nonnegative-frequency deletion model and polylogarithmic-space approximation regime. The classification function makes the domain and acceptance precision explicit without requiring an algorithm to decide the classification from source code.

The source gives a linear-space obstruction when the cost of the same coordinate difference varies too much with its offset. This explains why dependence on the vector difference is a natural candidate property, but a necessary obstruction alone does not classify all admissible functions or provide matching algorithms.

The admissible family includes \(\phi(a,b)=|a-b|\), \(\phi(a,b)=(a-b)^2\), and coordinate disagreement \(\phi(a,b)=1\) when \(a\ne b\), zero otherwise. The last is not homogeneous. Thus “must be a norm” cannot be used literally as the characterization of every dissimilarity covered by the question.

Braverman, Chestnut, Woodruff and Yang characterize a large class of sums \(\sum_i h(|f_i-g_i|)\), including nonmonotone functions, with a specific exceptional class. Their work explicitly describes this as a partial answer to the Guha–Indyk question. It does not cover arbitrary two-argument \(\phi\).

The source’s norm-sketching update concerns a geometric characterization for normed spaces and a different constant-size communication formulation. Khot and Naor subsequently show that the corresponding norm characterization fails for general metric spaces. Neither statement is a characterization of the whole streaming class defined here.

An additive error proportional to the total frequency would be much weaker when two large vectors are very close. Relative error and exact treatment of zero are therefore central to the lower bounds and must be retained. Insertion-only algorithms or summaries of normalized probability distributions have different guarantees and input models.

cards.title: Fast merging of summaries for symmetric streaming computations
cards.formal: Does every total, order-invariant Boolean stream function computable deterministically in polylogarithmic space and polylogarithmic time per item also admit a deterministic summary scheme with polylogarithmic message size, working space, and time per merge, correct for every binary merge tree? The uniform families, input lengths and costs in this question are specified below.
cards.why: Fast merging would allow any efficiently maintained order-independent statistic to be computed from independently processed pieces without an expensive reconstruction step. A separation would expose an inherent computational cost of parallel aggregation even when communication and memory are small.
cards.status_note: The cited paper establishes a space-preserving simulation but explicitly identifies its high running time as a limitation. This card selects a precise uniform polylogarithmic-time refinement, with no promise or randomness. No matching general simulation or separation was located in the bounded September 2026 check; the literal malformed source sentence is not treated as evidence.

sentences: The input statistic is a total Boolean function invariant under reordering the stream.
A streaming program computes it using polylogarithmic memory and time per item.
The selected question asks for equally efficient local summaries and merging on every binary aggregation tree.
A known simulation preserves small space but can use superpolynomial merge time.

cards.definitions: For each integer \(N\geq2\), let \(f_N\) map every nonempty sequence over \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\) of length at most \(N\) to one bit. Totality means every such sequence is in its domain. Order invariance means permuting any sequence leaves its value unchanged; it is stronger than merely swapping two players. A streaming algorithm is one fixed deterministic program given \(N\) in binary, which starts with an initialized state, reads one item at a time, and produces \(f_N(x)\) when the stream ends. There must be constants \(B,c\), depending on the family but not \(N\), for which initialization, each update and final output take at most \(B\log^c(N+2)\) steps, and the stored state and temporary workspace use that many bits. A merge scheme consists of three fixed deterministic programs: a map \(\Phi_N\) from one item to a summary, a map \(\mu_N\) from two summaries to a summary, and a decoder \(\eta_N\) from a summary to a bit. Summaries may include their represented length. For every valid sequence and every rooted binary tree whose leaves are its items in any order, apply \(\Phi_N\) at the leaves, \(\mu_N\) at internal nodes and \(\eta_N\) at the root. The resulting bit must equal \(f_N(x)\). Intermediate summaries may depend on the tree; only the decoded answer must be invariant. Each message, workspace and invocation time is bounded by \(B_1\log^{c_1}(N+2)\), for constants depending on the family. Time means steps of a standard deterministic multitape Turing machine on binary representations; input and output tapes have the usual sequential access. The programs receive \(N\) and their local arguments, with no advice or precomputed data depending on \(N\). Both models are exact and deterministic. The conclusion is existence of a merge scheme for each streaming-computable family, not a promised efficient compiler from arbitrary program descriptions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal simulation, including the time, memory and arbitrary-tree guarantees. Alternatively give a total symmetric family with a qualifying streaming algorithm and prove that no qualifying merge scheme exists. A slow merge procedure with short messages, a separation using a promise, or a private-randomness separation does not decide this specified question.

context_blocks.text: The workshop page asks broadly whether good streaming algorithms yield good sketches and compares one-way with simultaneous communication. Editorial specialization: this card selects the deterministic, total-function question with efficient merging. This is the time-sensitive refinement motivated by the paper cited on that page, rather than a claim that the already established space-only simulation remains unknown.

Feldman, Muthukrishnan, Sidiropoulos, Stein and Svitkina show that symmetric deterministic streaming computation can be distributed through a binary aggregation tree with comparable message size and polynomially related space. Their simulation uses reachability search and can take superpolynomial time. The retained target asks whether that time cost can always be avoided.

A sequential chain of merges is itself a streaming computation. The converse must support balanced trees and every other arrangement, even when the stream algorithm’s intermediate states record order-dependent information that disappears from the final answer.

The cited paper also gives failures of analogous comparisons for promises, multiple permissible outputs and private randomness. This card removes those routes to a separation by requiring a total Boolean function and deterministic exact computation. The malformed final sentence on the workshop page is not used as a theorem statement.

Associativity of the summary representation is not required: two different trees can leave different internal summaries provided both decode correctly. Demanding identical summaries would strengthen the problem beyond the aggregation model used here.

Recent turnstile-to-linear-sketch simulations address algebraic update streams and space preservation. Their hypotheses and conclusions do not provide this uniform polylogarithmic-time merging theorem for arbitrary insertion streams and arbitrary total symmetric functions.

cards.title: Wait-free exact FIFO queues in Common\(_{2}\)
cards.formal: For every fixed number \(n\ge 2\) of asynchronous processes, is there a deterministic wait-free linearizable implementation of an initially empty, unbounded FIFO queue using only atomic read/write registers and atomic Test&Set bits? Every process may perform both Enqueue and Dequeue, repeatedly and in any order. The implementation must satisfy exact FIFO semantics in every execution, including executions with arbitrary delays and crashes. This is the source’s Common\(_{2}\) question; “some objects with consensus number two” is not a free choice of base types that could include the desired queue itself.
cards.why: Would determine whether the familiar consensus-number-two primitives suffice for an exact queue with individual progress guarantees, clarifying the limitations of the consensus hierarchy as a guide to object implementation.
cards.status_note: Read the source’s model and Common\(_{2}\) paragraph, the earlier explicit Test&Set formulation, the journal abstract and footnote 7, and the 2026 strong-linearizability theorem statements in arXiv v3. Checked later exact-queue and Common\(_{2}\) searches through 12 September 2026. No general ordinary-linearizable resolution found; searches are not exhaustive.

references.authors: Castañeda, Armando; Rajsbaum, Sergio; Raynal, Michel

cards.definitions: There are n sequential processes with distinct identifiers \(1,\ldots ,n\). Each invokes a new high-level operation only after its previous one returns. The scheduler interleaves atomic shared-memory steps arbitrarily; a process may stop forever at any point. A register stores a finite value and supports atomic Read and Write. A Test&Set object is a bit initially 0 whose atomic operation returns the old bit and sets it to 1; arbitrarily many initially fresh objects and registers are available. Private computation and storage are allowed. No bound on memory growth or on the number of operations in a history is imposed, but every performed step manipulates finitely represented data. No Compare&Swap, stronger atomic multi-object operation, or queue base object is supplied. Sequential queue state is a finite sequence of values from \(\{0,1\}\)*. \(Enqueue(v)\) appends a new occurrence of v and returns an acknowledgement. Dequeue removes and returns the first occurrence if one exists; otherwise it returns a distinguished EMPTY symbol outside the value set and leaves the queue empty. Equal values may be enqueued multiple times, but each enqueue occurrence may be removed only once. Linearizability means that each finite concurrent history can be completed by responses to some pending invocations and deletion of the others, so that its completed operations have a legal sequential FIFO order preserving each process’s order and real-time order: an operation that returns before another is invoked precedes it. Wait-freedom means that any invoked operation whose process continues taking steps returns after finitely many of that process’s own steps, regardless of other processes’ speeds or failures. No promise that another process will take a step is available. The algorithm may depend on the fixed n; the question does not require one implementation for infinitely many simultaneously participating processes. Common\(_{2}\) denotes types implementable for every finite n from registers and two-process-consensus power; the cited model paper states the queue question equivalently using Test&Set. Equal consensus numbers alone do not assert mutual implementability.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct and prove correct such a deterministic implementation for every finite n, or prove impossibility for some finite n in this model. Both exact linearizability and individual wait-free progress are required. A lock-free implementation that permits starvation, a restriction on the number of enqueuers or dequeuers, duplicated removal of an occurrence, weak-empty responses, bounded histories, or a stronger atomic base type does not meet the target. An impossibility result only for strong linearizability does not rule out ordinary linearizability.

context_blocks.title: Progress of the system is weaker than progress of every process
context_blocks.text: The original paper contrasts nonblocking exact queues with wait-free relaxed queues. Nonblocking progress ensures that operations keep completing somewhere in the system; wait-freedom also prevents an individual process that keeps running from being postponed forever.

Naming this basis matters because the queue itself has consensus number two; allowing an arbitrary base type of that number would not state the intended implementation problem.

context_blocks.title: A 2026 impossibility concerns a stronger consistency condition
context_blocks.text: Attiya, Castañeda and Enea rule out strongly linearizable queues from interfering primitives in their model, even with only lock-free progress. Strong linearizability requires a choice of linearizations that remains consistent when executions are extended. Ordinary linearizability in this card makes no such prefix-consistent-choice requirement, so that theorem does not settle Common\(_{2}\) membership.

cards.title: Common2 membership of FIFO queues
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true?
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge3\quad
\exists A_n:\quad A_n\text{ implements a linearizable wait-free FIFO queue for }n\text{ processes}
\]
using only the atomic read/write registers and one-shot test-and-set bits defined below? The queue is initially empty and has no capacity bound. Every process may perform arbitrarily many operations of either kind, with arbitrary finite binary strings as enqueued values. Each \(A_n\) is deterministic and has finite code; it may depend on \(n\). The quantifiers do not additionally require one compiler producing all \(A_n\).
cards.definitions:
Fix \(n\ge3\). There are \(n\) named sequential processes with identifiers \(1,\ldots,n\), each knowing \(n\) and its own identifier. A process has unbounded private storage, initially containing only its identifier, \(n\), and its fixed program data. Its local computation is given by a deterministic finite Turing program on finite strings. Shared communication is confined to two countable arrays with natural-number addresses: registers \(R_0,R_1,\ldots\), initially containing the empty binary string, and bits \(B_0,B_1,\ldots\), initially zero. A register read atomically returns its whole current finite string; a write atomically replaces that string and returns an acknowledgement. The primitive \(\operatorname{TAS}(j)\) atomically returns the old value of \(B_j\) and changes it to one. A bit is never reset, and every later test-and-set on that bit returns one. Any process can access any address; using a previously unused address does not require an allocation oracle. There is no fixed bound on addresses used, register bit lengths, private storage or total operations over a whole execution. A finite execution prefix uses only finite data and finitely many primitive calls.

The scheduler interleaves individual local computation steps and atomic primitive calls. Each scheduled process chooses its next action from its private state, its current invocation and previous primitive responses. Processes receive no randomness, clock, failure detector, schedule information or noncomputable oracle. They can be delayed arbitrarily and can stop forever at any point. No fairness assumption constrains other processes. Local Turing steps, primitive invocations and operation responses count as that process's own steps; no bounded step complexity is demanded.

The sequential queue state is a finite sequence of finite binary strings, initially empty. \(\operatorname{Enqueue}(v)\) appends one occurrence of \(v\) at the end and returns a distinguished acknowledgement. \(\operatorname{Dequeue}()\) removes and returns the first occurrence if the sequence is nonempty; otherwise it returns a distinguished \(\mathsf{Empty}\) value without changing the state. Empty, acknowledgement and string-valued responses have separate tags, so the empty binary string is an ordinary possible item. Repeated equal values represent separate occurrences. Each process can invoke either operation whenever its previous invocation has returned, so it has at most one pending invocation. Clients may choose later invocations from earlier responses; there are no designated enqueuer or dequeuer roles, no bound on the number of calls and no promise that a dequeue finds an item.

Linearizability is required for every finite execution prefix. Take its history of queue invocations and responses. Append responses to any chosen subset of pending invocations and discard the other pending invocations. There must be a total order of the resulting completed operations that preserves each process's order, respects every real-time precedence in the completed history, and gives exactly their responses under the sequential queue specification. Here real-time precedence means that one operation's response occurs before the other's invocation. The choice of this total order may differ between different execution prefixes; it is not required to preserve earlier choices when a history is extended. Infinite executions must satisfy this safety condition at every finite prefix.

Wait-freedom is the following per-process termination property: from any reachable configuration with a pending operation of process \(p\), every continuation in which \(p\) takes infinitely many of its own steps contains a response to that operation after finitely many such steps, regardless of all other processes' delays, crashes or continuing operations. Thus an infinite execution in which one process's pending operation never finishes despite that process continuing to take steps is forbidden, even if other operations keep completing. These definitions specify ordinary linearizability and wait-freedom, with unlimited resource capacity; they impose neither strong linearizability nor a resource bound uniform over all histories.
cards.why: A queue orders work shared by concurrent processes. This question asks whether very weak synchronization suffices to guarantee that each continuing process finishes, even while others stop or interfere. It tests the distinction between consensus power and the ability to implement a reusable data type.

context_blocks.text: The OPODIS 2015 paper, published in 2016, explicitly asks whether an \(n\)-process ordinary linearizable wait-free queue can be built from test-and-set and registers for every \(n\ge3\). This card retains that quantifier order and the unrestricted repeated-operation interface, with finite-string values and explicit deterministic computation conventions.

The consensus number of an object type is the largest number of processes for which copies of that type together with registers can solve wait-free consensus: every continuing process decides one proposed input value and all decisions agree. Test-and-set and queues have consensus number two. That agreement capability by itself does not supply a many-process queue implementation. Common2 is the historical class of types implementable in a wait-free manner from any object type of consensus number two.

Stacks admit Common2 implementations. This result concerns last-in-first-out removal and does not supply the first-in-first-out semantics of the target. The source also studies unbounded numbers of participating processes; the present question allows a separate implementation for each fixed finite process count.

Eisenstat gives a Common2 queue for at most two enqueuing processes and any number of dequeuing processes. The stated restriction on who can enqueue leaves the unrestricted interface in this card unanswered.

The OPODIS 2022 article, published in February 2023, explicitly repeats the open Common2 queue question. Its efficient exact queue uses compare-and-swap, which atomically checks an expected value and conditionally writes a replacement; that primitive is unavailable here. Its separate multiplicity variant relaxes removal semantics.

Strong linearizability requires one choice of linearizations that preserves prefixes across histories. The 2025 paper proves an impossibility for strongly linearizable queues from the relevant weak primitives. Its progress condition is lock-freedom, meaning that infinitely many steps yield infinitely many completed operations somewhere in the system. The stronger correctness requirement prevents this result from being an impossibility for ordinary linearizability.

The PODC 2026 paper extends impossibility results for strongly linearizable queues, including settings with additional primitives and at least four processes. Those results continue to assume strong linearizability. The checked full version therefore does not refute the ordinary wait-free target.

cards.title: One-pass approximation scheme for random-order streaming matching
cards.formal: For each \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\), does there exist a one-pass random-order streaming algorithm returning a matching M with \(|M|\ge(1-\varepsilon)\nu(G)\) with probability at least 2/3, using at most \(C_\varepsilon n\log^c(n+2)\) bits of working space, for an absolute c and finite constants \(C_\varepsilon\)?
cards.definitions:
G is any fixed simple undirected graph on a known labelled vertex set [n]. Its m distinct edges arrive once each in a uniformly random permutation, independently of the algorithm’s coins. The adversary may choose G but not condition the stream order on those coins. The algorithm knows n and rational epsilon, reads edges sequentially without rewinding, and outputs an actual edge set M after the final edge. A matching has no two edges sharing a vertex; nu(G) is the largest matching cardinality.

Space includes stored edge endpoints, counters, retained random bits, and the final output buffer. The output must be a valid matching on every run; the approximation may fail with probability at most 1/3, over both permutation and internal randomness. The same uniform algorithm accepts epsilon as a parameter, and C_epsilon is bounded by some computable function of 1/epsilon. The logarithmic exponent c is independent of epsilon. No polynomial dependence on 1/epsilon is demanded, and no processing-time target beyond termination is imposed. Thus the question is about space at each fixed positive accuracy, not an exact matching algorithm obtained by setting epsilon to 1/n at uniform near-linear cost.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proofs of the one-pass space, validity and approximation guarantees for every fixed accuracy, or prove that no such uniform scheme exists. A hardness result requiring epsilon to shrink with n must account for the permitted dependence of C_epsilon and does not automatically refute this statement.
cards.why: The target asks how much random order can improve a severe streaming-memory constraint.

cards.title: LOCAL coloring below square-root degree dependence
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), one uniform deterministic LOCAL algorithm \(A\), and a constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every supplied integer degree bound \(\Delta\ge2\), and every finite simple undirected \(n\)-vertex graph of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), the algorithm produces a proper vertex coloring with colors in \(\{1,\ldots,\Delta+1\}\) within
\[
C\bigl(\Delta^{1/2-\varepsilon}+\log^*n\bigr)
\]
synchronous communication rounds? The guarantee must hold for every assignment of distinct identifiers from \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\) and every local port numbering. All vertices know \(n\) and \(\Delta\); the same \(\varepsilon,A,C\) must work for all these inputs.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of an algorithm and some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) meeting the stated uniform round bound, or of the logical negation of this existence statement. The improvement may be arbitrarily small but must be one positive constant independent of both \(n\) and \(\Delta\). A negative answer must rule out every positive constant exponent saving in the stated model. Improving a logarithmic factor while retaining degree exponent \(1/2\), or allowing the saving to tend to zero with input size, does not meet the target. There is no prescribed minimum saving and no numerical \(1/100\) answer tolerance for this proposition.
cards.why: I include this because the familiar greedy palette bound hides a distinct distributed coordination problem. A fixed improvement in the degree exponent would reveal new ways to resolve local conflicts, while an impossibility result would explain why the square-root dependence persists across different coloring methods.
cards.definitions:
The network is exactly the input graph. Graphs may be disconnected and may have isolated vertices, but have no loops, parallel edges, weights or additional structural promises. A supplied \(\Delta\) is any upper bound on all degrees, not necessarily the exact maximum. Proper coloring means that every vertex outputs one allowed color and the two endpoints of each edge output different colors. There is no demand that all colors be used.

Each vertex runs the same finite deterministic program, initially knowing its own identifier, its degree, the local names of its incident ports, and \(n,\Delta\). Port names bijectively number the incident edges at each vertex; names at opposite ends need not agree. The identifier range \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\) fixes the polynomial-ID convention explicitly. Identifiers may be assigned adversarially and may be used arithmetically; no order-invariance restriction is imposed. The initial state contains no global graph description, advice or preprocessing result.

In one synchronous LOCAL round, each vertex sends an arbitrary finite binary message along each incident edge, possibly a different message to each neighbor, and then receives all messages sent to it in that round. Local computation and memory are unbounded, but the program must complete its local steps and eventually output at every vertex. There is no bandwidth restriction, randomness, shared random tape or communication along nonedges. Initially exchanging neighbor identifiers, if needed, costs at most one round and is absorbed by the requested bound. Once all vertices have output, the coloring is final. Elapsed rounds to the last output are counted, rather than total messages, local work or average node time.

The function \(\log^*n\) counts successive base-two logarithms until the value is at most one. The fixed constant \(\varepsilon\) is chosen before all graph parameters. It is not an accuracy input; the task does not demand one algorithm for every requested saving. A saving that tends to zero as \(n\) or \(\Delta\) grows is insufficient. Constants hidden in the guarantee cannot depend on graph size, degree bound, port numbering or identifiers.

The target retains only an additive iterated-logarithmic dependence on graph size. A bound polynomial in \(\log n\), even if independent of \(\Delta\), does not establish it in all degree regimes. This is vertex coloring in deterministic LOCAL; results for edge coloring, randomized algorithms, special graph families or massively parallel computation have different guarantees.

cards.title: Randomized parity sketches versus one-way communication for XOR functions
cards.formal: Are there universal constants \(C>0\) and \(a\geq0\) such that, for every \(n\geq1\) and every Boolean function \(f:\mathbb F_2^n\to\{0,1\}\), \[R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\leq C\bigl(1+R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\bigr)\log^a(n+2),\qquad f^+(x,y)=f(x+y)?\] Here the two complexities use worst-input error and shared randomness as defined below. This fixes the polylogarithmic-loss convention in the source’s conjecture.

sentences: The input is an arbitrary Boolean function on a binary vector space.
A parity sketch measures a fixed random collection of linear forms and then decodes their bits.
A one-way protocol may instead send any randomized message about Alice’s vector to Bob.
The conjecture asks whether parity sketches lose only a universal polylogarithmic factor for the associated XOR function.
Known deterministic and uniform-input comparisons do not establish the required worst-input randomized bound.

cards.definitions: The field \(\mathbb F_2\) has elements zero and one, with addition modulo two; vector addition is bitwise XOR. A randomized parity sketch of length \(k\) consists of a jointly sampled matrix \(A\in\mathbb F_2^{k\times n}\) and a decoder \(g\). Their joint distribution is fixed in advance, independently of the input \(z\). The sketch is the \(k\)-bit vector \(Az\); the decoder knows the sampled matrix and all shared coins, and may depend on \(f\) and \(n\). For each fixed \(z\), its probability of outputting \(f(z)\) must be at least \(2/3\). The minimum possible \(k\), including zero, is \(R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\). Each row of \(A\) specifies a subset of input coordinates whose parity is measured. Rows are chosen before seeing any measurement outcome: adaptive parity queries are not allowed. In the communication model Alice knows \(x\in\mathbb F_2^n\), Bob knows \(y\in\mathbb F_2^n\), and both know \(f,n\) and a public random string independent of their inputs. Alice sends one message; Bob must output \(f(x+y)\). For every fixed pair \((x,y)\), success probability is at least \(2/3\). The cost is the largest message length over inputs and coin outcomes; variable-length messages can be padded. Its minimum is \(R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\). Local computation, the description of \(f\), and shared randomness are free in both models. No uniform polynomial-time construction of optimal protocols is required. Logarithms are base two. The constants in the proposed inequality are independent of the truth table of \(f\), the dimension and its communication complexity. The additive one handles zero-cost constant functions without imposing a convention for logarithms of zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed inequality with fixed universal constants, or prove its negation: for every proposed constants there is a dimension and Boolean function violating the bound. A superpolylogarithmic separation family suffices for a negative answer. Equality for deterministic protocols, average error under the uniform input distribution, or a polynomial rather than polylogarithmic loss does not settle this target.

context_blocks.text: The source asks whether randomized linear sketching and randomized one-way communication of the associated XOR function agree up to polylogarithmic factors. The card spells out the usual dimension-based interpretation at error one third; it does not request exact equality of the two integer complexities.

The easy comparison is \(R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\leq R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\): Alice sends \(Ax\), and Bob forms \(Ax+Ay=A(x+y)\) before using the decoder. The question is whether an arbitrary message can always be replaced, with the stated loss, by information of this linear form.

For deterministic exact computation the complexities agree. The randomized case allows a different error set for each choice of coins, so the deterministic statement does not give the desired simulation by simply fixing a seed.

Kannan, Mossel, Sanyal and Yaroslavtsev prove an analogue under uniformly distributed inputs, with an adjustment of the error constant, and analyze several function classes. Worst-input correctness is stronger: a protocol cannot ignore even a very small exceptional set of pairs.

The 2026 turnstile simulation paper concerns streams of integer-coordinate insertions and deletions. Its discussion treats modular and XOR updates as a separate line of work. A simulation for algorithms that already process long streams does not itself convert a single arbitrary Alice-to-Bob message into a parity sketch.

cards.title: Optimal one-pass randomized space for LIS length
cards.formal:
Determine, up to constant factors, the optimal randomized one-pass streaming space in bits for a factor-two estimate of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of a length-\(n\) sequence over \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).

For every fixed input \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{1,\ldots,n\}^n\), let
\[L(x)=\max\{r:\exists\,1\le i_1<\cdots<i_r\le n,\ x_{i_1}<\cdots<x_{i_r}\}.\]
An admissible algorithm reads \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) once in this order and, after the final item, outputs an integer \(\widehat L\) such that
\[\Pr\bigl[L(x)/2\le\widehat L\le L(x)\bigr]\ge2/3.\]
Find an explicit asymptotic function \(f(n)\) admitting a uniform algorithm with \(O(f(n))\) worst-case bit space and a matching \(\Omega(f(n))\) lower bound for every admissible randomized algorithm. Logarithmic factors are part of the requested answer.
cards.why: This problem tests whether randomness can substantially reduce the memory needed to retain ordered structure in a sequence. The large gap between what is known for deterministic algorithms and what is proved necessary for ordinary randomized algorithms makes it a basic unresolved question about one-pass computation.
cards.status_note: Source-open in Sublinear.info Problem 44, Bertinoro 2011, updated 7 March 2013. The selected version uses one pass over length-n sequences from {1,...,n}, a factor-two underestimate and success at least 2/3. On 16 September 2026 the review checked the SODA 2007 upper bound, Chakrabarti’s 2010/2012 communication result and the published ITCS 2026 paper, whose introduction explicitly leaves ordinary randomized LIS approximation open. Its Theorem 1 is a white-box adversarial result for factor 1.1 and alphabet size at least 3n, so it does not resolve the selected model. A bounded later-work search found no verified matching randomized bounds; this does not certify the entire literature or supply a Lean proof.

progress.text: A deterministic one-pass approximation uses \(O(\sqrt n\log(n+2))\) bits for the selected alphabet and fixed accuracy, giving a valid randomized upper bound.

Chakrabarti proves that the communication problems behind earlier deterministic lower bounds have efficient randomized protocols. Those reductions therefore do not yield matching randomized lower bounds.

Gal, Kol, Saxena and Yu prove a square-root white-box lower bound with the additional model and accuracy conditions stated above; they still describe ordinary randomized LIS approximation as a longstanding open problem.

sentences: The problem asks for optimal bit space to estimate the longest strictly increasing subsequence in one streaming pass.
Inputs are arbitrary length-n sequences of numbers from one to n, fixed before the algorithm chooses its random bits.
The final estimate must lie between half the true length and the true length with probability at least two thirds.
Deterministic upper bounds and recent lower bounds against a stronger adaptive adversary leave the ordinary randomized optimum unresolved.
The requested answer must match upper and lower bounds up to constants, including every logarithmic factor.

cards.definitions:
The stream length \(n\ge1\) is known before the stream begins. The input contains exactly \(n\) integers, each in the ordered alphabet \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), represented in binary. Repetitions are allowed: the input is an arbitrary sequence and need not be a permutation. The asymptotic parameter is the number of items \(n\), whereas memory is measured in bits, not in stored items or machine words. An explicit input list occupies \(O(n\log(n+2))\) bits.

An increasing subsequence retains selected positions in their original order; the positions need not be consecutive. Both inequalities in its definition are strict. In particular, repeated equal values cannot both appear in such a subsequence. The strictly decreasing sequence has LIS length one, while \((1,2,\ldots,n)\) has LIS length \(n\). The problem asks only for the length estimate. It does not require the positions or values of a witnessing subsequence.

A single pass gives sequential access to the items from first to last, with no rewind, rereading, permutation of the stream or random-access queries to earlier positions. The algorithm may retain information about previous items only in its working memory. Its output appears after the whole sequence has been processed. It need not approximate the LIS of every prefix or issue intermediate answers.

For each fixed valid sequence, the probability is taken over independent fair random bits used by the algorithm. The entire input is fixed independently of those bits. The guarantee is required separately for every sequence, including sequences with short LIS; there is no promise that the LIS contains a constant fraction of the input. The algorithm may fail on at most one third of its random executions for a particular sequence. No distribution on input sequences is imposed.

The output convention is an underestimate within a factor two, as in the later paper's multiplicative approximation definition. On successful executions it lies in \([L(x)/2,L(x)]\). This is not the wider interval \([L(x)/2,2L(x)]\). The output can be an integer: rounding up a real output in the chosen interval preserves both bounds because \(L(x)\) is an integer. No additive error is allowed.

Use one finite uniform streaming program at all lengths. Its persistent state and temporary working storage are measured in bits; stored input values, counters, indices, retained random choices and output preparation all count. There is no external scratch storage, reusable random tape containing uncharged information, advice string or oracle. The stream itself is read-only sequential input. Fresh random bits may be consumed during computation; information about past bits can be reused only if it was retained within the counted memory.

Space is the maximum number of working bits used at any time, over every valid input of length \(n\) and every random execution, including executions whose final answer is inaccurate. Call this quantity \(s_A(n)\) for algorithm \(A\). It is not expected space. The algorithm must terminate after processing its input, but the target imposes no separate update-time or total-time bound. Unlimited local computation does not permit additional storage or another pass. Knowing \(n\) does not provide the input's LIS length or any statistic of the sequence.

The requested optimum means matching asymptotic upper and lower bounds in this model. There must be one admissible algorithm \(A_*\), a constant \(C>0\) and a threshold \(n_0\) with \(s_{A_*}(n)\le C f(n)\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). For every admissible randomized algorithm \(A\), there must be constants \(c_A>0,n_A\) with \(s_A(n)\ge c_A f(n)\) for all \(n\ge n_A\). The constants are independent of the input and its random bits. The answer must state \(f\) explicitly and establish both directions; merely defining \(f\) to be the unknown optimum is not an answer.

All factors growing with \(n\), including \(\log n\), iterated logarithms or a slowly growing multiplier, must be retained. Determining only an exponent in \(n\), or proving bounds that match only after hiding logarithmic factors, does not meet the selected precision. No numerical additive tolerance applies to an asymptotic space bound.

The white-box adversarial model is different: its input generator may inspect the algorithm's previous random choices and internal memory before selecting the next item. A lower bound against algorithms required to survive that stronger input generator need not hold when the sequence is fixed beforehand. Deterministic algorithms, multiple-pass algorithms, algorithms with reordered access and additive approximations are also separately specified variants. The original source mentions both one and constantly many passes; the user selected exactly one pass and the alphabet \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give an explicit function \(f(n)\) and complete Lean-checked proofs of the matching uniform upper and randomized lower space bounds defined above. The algorithm must meet the factor-two interval and success probability on every fixed input, using one pass and counted worst-case bit space. The lower bound must apply to randomized algorithms in this same fixed-input model and alphabet, not only to deterministic or white-box adversarial algorithms. A single improved bound without a matching other direction, an additive approximation, an algorithm for a larger approximation factor or bounds differing by a logarithmic factor do not complete the selected constant-factor determination.

The user selected one pass, length-n sequences over the alphabet {1,…,n}, success probability at least two thirds and optimal bit space up to constant factors. The strict-increase convention and the multiplicative output interval are stated explicitly.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase; user-approved pass count, alphabet and asymptotic precision

context_blocks.text: The length of the longest increasing subsequence measures how much ordered structure survives inside a sequence. Computing or estimating it differs from sorting: only a number is requested, yet information from distant positions can determine which choices combine into a long subsequence.

Gopalan and coauthors give a deterministic one-pass approximation algorithm using \(O(\sqrt n)\) stored input symbols for fixed relative accuracy. With alphabet \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the corresponding bit bound is \(O(\sqrt n\log(n+2))\). Their discussion explains how to handle strict rather than nondecreasing subsequences. This is an upper bound for randomized algorithms as well, because they may ignore randomness.

Deterministic lower bounds leave open whether randomness saves substantially more memory. Chakrabarti shows that the communication problems used in those lower bounds admit inexpensive randomized protocols. This establishes a limitation of those particular lower-bound arguments; it does not provide a small-space randomized LIS algorithm.

The ITCS 2026 paper proves a square-root space lower bound in the white-box model for a 1.1-approximation with an alphabet of size at least three times the stream length. Its theorem differs from this card in the adversary, accuracy and stated alphabet. Its introduction explicitly retains the ordinary randomized approximation problem as open.

An additive approximation to LIS length can be useful when \(L(x)\) is large. An additive error proportional to \(n\), however, can exceed the entire answer when \(L(x)\ll n\). Likewise, an approximation to the complementary quantity \(n-L(x)\), the number of deletions needed to leave a strictly increasing sequence, need not approximate a small \(L(x)\) multiplicatively.

This is an unusual streaming question in which a sublinear-space deterministic algorithm is known but the benefit of randomness remains poorly understood. Matching randomized bounds would explain whether the memory cost comes from the ordered structure of the input or from limitations of deterministic summaries.

cards.title: Full random walks with near-linear streaming space
cards.formal:
Can a randomized graph-streaming algorithm sample a whole \(L\)-step random walk, for every \(1\le L\le n\), with total-variation error at most \(1/100\), near-linear bit space and polylogarithmically many passes?

More precisely, do there exist one uniform algorithm \(A\), constants \(C_s,C_p>0\) and fixed nonnegative integers \(a,b\) with the following property? For every unweighted directed graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), every start \(s\), every \(1\le L\le n\) and every fixed ordering of its edges, \(A\), knowing \(n,L,s\) before reading the stream, uses at most
\[C_s n\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^a\text{ bits and }\left\lceil C_p\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^b\right\rceil\text{ passes}\]
and outputs a tuple \((Y_0,\ldots,Y_L)\) whose distribution \(\nu_{G,s,L}\) satisfies
\[\|\nu_{G,s,L}-\mu_{G,s,L}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le1/100?\]
Here \(\mu_{G,s,L}\) is the joint distribution of the ordinary directed random walk starting at \(s\), with the absorbing convention at a vertex of out-degree zero defined below.
cards.why: Random-walk sampling is a basic graph primitive, and this question asks whether its full trajectory can be recovered with both modest memory and few sequential scans. It isolates a gap between known constant-pass tradeoffs and the possibility of polylogarithmically many passes.
cards.status_note: Source-open in Sublinear.info Problem 22, Kanpur 2009, with a 23 July 2021 update linking the two-pass result. The user selected a full trajectory for 1 <= L <= n, known start, unweighted directed graph and total-variation error at most 1/100. On 16 September 2026 the review checked the original 2011 reconstruction discussion, the 2021 full-version Theorems 1.1–1.3 and the published ITCS 2026 dense-graph result. Constant-pass lower bounds and the stronger unknown-start preprocessing lower bound do not exclude the selected polylogarithmic-pass algorithm; the dense-graph theorem assumes a minimum out-degree bound. A bounded later-work search found no verified resolution for the selected general-graph model. No new sampler, impossibility proof or Lean formalization is claimed.

progress.text: Das Sarma, Gollapudi and Panigrahy establish the near-linear-space, roughly square-root-in-\(L\) pass baseline and discuss full-walk reconstruction separately.
Chen and coauthors establish a two-pass space tradeoff and lower bounds for every fixed constant number of passes. Their full-trajectory and starting-vertex conventions are explicit.
Efremenko, Kol, Saxena and Zhang obtain one-pass sampling bounds exploiting a lower bound on every vertex out-degree. This advances dense-graph instances without settling arbitrary directed graphs.

sentences: The problem asks for one entire random-walk trajectory in a directed graph presented as an edge stream.
The start is known in advance, and the number of steps is at most the number of vertices.
The output distribution must be within 1/100 in total variation of the true joint distribution of all visits.
Near-linear bit space and a fixed polylogarithmic number of passes must suffice for every graph and edge order.
Known constant-pass tradeoffs and improved dense-graph samplers do not settle this general target.

cards.definitions:
The graph has the known labeled vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge1\), and edge set \(E\subseteq V\times V\). There are no multiple copies of an edge; self-loops are allowed. Both directions between distinct vertices may be present independently. Every edge has unit weight. The stream explicitly lists each directed edge once as a binary pair, in an arbitrary fixed order. Empty streams, isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and graphs with highly unequal degrees are allowed. The number of edges need not be known in advance.

For a vertex \(v\), its out-neighbor set is \(N^+(v)=\{w:(v,w)\in E\}\) and its out-degree is \(d^+(v)=|N^+(v)|\). A true random walk starts with \(X_0=s\). At every step, conditional on the complete history so far, if \(d^+(X_i)>0\), then \(X_{i+1}\) is chosen uniformly from \(N^+(X_i)\). New choices are independent conditional on the successive current vertices. Repeated visits and repeated traversal of an edge are permitted; this is not a simple path.

At a vertex of out-degree zero, define \(X_{i+1}=X_i\). This absorbing convention ensures that a length-\(L\) tuple is defined for every input. It is equivalent to adding a self-loop only at each zero-out-degree vertex. The convention is stated explicitly rather than leaving a uniform choice from an empty set undefined. It does not replace directed transitions elsewhere by undirected ones or add restarts from another vertex.

Equivalently, define the transition probabilities \(K_G(v,w)\) as \(1/d^+(v)\) when \(d^+(v)>0\) and \((v,w)\in E\), as one when \(d^+(v)=0\) and \(w=v\), and as zero otherwise. The desired law on \(V^{L+1}\) is
\[\mu_{G,s,L}(v_0,\ldots,v_L)=\mathbf1_{\{v_0=s\}}\prod_{i=0}^{L-1}K_G(v_i,v_{i+1}).\]
The integer \(L\) counts transitions, so the output lists \(L+1\) vertices including the start. The parameters \(n,L,s\) are explicitly available before the first pass. Only one sampled trajectory is requested.

For distributions \(\mu,\nu\) on this finite tuple space, total variation means
\[\|\nu-\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\frac12\sum_{\omega\in V^{L+1}}|\nu(\omega)-\mu(\omega)|.\]
This compares the complete joint distributions, including dependencies between visits. Correct endpoint probabilities or correct single-time marginals alone do not establish the requirement. The output law averages over all internal random choices. The bound is not a probability that a numerical estimate is accurate, so a separate two-thirds-success convention is not substituted for it. Any probability assigned to an impossible trajectory is part of the total-variation error.

The algorithm returns an explicit tuple in \(V^{L+1}\), with initial vertex \(s\), after processing its passes. It must include every intermediate vertex, not just the endpoint, selected checkpoints, transition counts, a random seed or a program for reconstructing a longer object. The tuple may be assembled in working memory and then written to a final output tape. Its \(O(L\log(n+2))\) bits fit inside the allowed near-linear class because \(L\le n\); all working storage used to assemble it is counted.

A pass reads the full edge sequence from beginning to end. Between passes the algorithm may rewind and keep its working memory, but the sequence and its order remain the same. It cannot change the edge list, jump to an old edge, query an adjacency list or ask for a random neighbor except through computations on information acquired from the stream. There is no uncounted external scratch storage. This is an insertion-only arbitrary-order stream, not a randomly ordered or deletion stream.

Use one finite uniform randomized program for all parameter values. It may draw independent fair random bits. All mutable information counts toward bit space, including edge samples, labels, counters, retained randomness, intermediate structures and the assembled output. Old random choices can be reused only through information retained within that space. Pass and memory bounds hold on all executions. The algorithm must produce its tuple with probability one; no additional bound on local running time is imposed. The input graph and its edge ordering are fixed independently of the random choices.

The constants and logarithmic exponents in the statement do not depend on \(n,L,s,G\), its edge order or the random choices. Since \(L\le n\), a fixed polynomial in \(\log(n+2)\) and \(\log(L+2)\) is bounded by a fixed power of \(\log(n+2)\). Thus the displayed pass bound expresses the source's polylogarithmic target in the selected length range. In background bounds, \(\widetilde O\) and \(\widetilde\Omega\) hide fixed logarithmic factors; the target itself specifies their permitted form.

Knowing the start before reading the graph is important. A preprocessing summary that must later support any as-yet-unknown start has a stronger requirement. A lower bound for that stronger preprocessing task does not automatically apply to the present algorithm. Likewise, a theorem with a fixed constant pass count cannot be evaluated at a growing polylogarithmic pass count unless its uniform dependence on that parameter is proved.

The source asks broadly for faster simulation and separately for endpoint-distribution estimation and the most likely endpoints. With the user's approval, this card selects the full trajectory, fixed total-variation accuracy, unweighted directed input and length range \(1\le L\le n\). It retains the known-start and near-linear-space, polylogarithmic-pass objective.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that an algorithm and fixed constants satisfying every condition above exist, or a complete Lean-checked proof that they do not. A positive answer must bound the total variation of the entire explicit output tuple and account for memory and passes on every graph and edge ordering. A negative answer must rule out all fixed logarithmic exponents \(a,b\) in the selected resource bounds, with the start known before streaming. Constant-pass lower bounds, lower bounds only for unknown-start preprocessing, endpoint-only samplers, results on dense graphs or bounds allowing a polynomial factor in \(L\) do not resolve this target. The tolerance \(1/100\) is the specified statistical distance between distributions, not an additive error on asymptotic resource bounds.

source_formulation.text: Panigrahy asks whether random-walk simulation can use near-linear space and only polylogarithmically many passes in the graph size and walk length. The source also asks separate questions about endpoint distributions. The user selected the entire trajectory of length at most n, a known initial vertex, unweighted directed graphs and total-variation error at most 1/100; the absorbing convention makes zero-out-degree inputs well defined.
