context_blocks.text: Random walks are useful for sampling and exploring large graphs, but a streaming algorithm encounters edges in an order unrelated to the trajectory it will eventually follow. Limited memory prevents retaining all possible future choices, while rereading the graph can be expensive.

A distribution on endpoints discards the route taken to reach them. Two samplers can agree at the endpoint while assigning very different probabilities to intermediate visits. The full-trajectory target therefore explicitly checks the joint law of all visited vertices.

Das Sarma, Gollapudi and Panigrahy obtain a near-linear-space simulation with roughly \(\sqrt L\) passes, up to logarithmic factors. Their basic procedure stores endpoints of walk segments; Remark 3.7 discusses reconstructing internal vertices, and §6 charges additional reconstruction space. The present output convention keeps that distinction visible.

Chen and coauthors give a two-pass sampler using \(\widetilde O(n\sqrt L\log(1/\delta))\) space and total-variation error \(\delta\). Choosing an inverse-polynomial \(\delta\le1/100\) meets the requested accuracy. For polynomially long walks, the extra factor \(\sqrt L\) can exceed every allowed logarithmic memory factor.

The same paper proves \(\widetilde\Omega(nL^{1/p})\) space lower bounds for each fixed pass count \(p\), with \(L=\lceil n^\beta\rceil\) and fixed \(\beta\in(0,1]\). These obstruct constant-pass near-linear-space simulation at such lengths, but do not rule out the growing polylogarithmic number of passes asked here. Its separate unknown-start result has a different quantifier order.

The 2026 dense-graph result gives much smaller one-pass memory when every vertex has sufficiently large out-degree. The minimum degree condition is essential to its guarantee; large average degree alone can leave a difficult region containing the chosen start. The result does not handle all directed graphs in the selected near-linear resource range.

cards.title: Local certificate size versus verification radius
cards.formal: Determine the worst-case certificate-size function \[F(s,d)=\max\{c_d(P):P\text{ is a graph property and }c_1(P)\le s\},\qquad s\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\ d\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1},\] in the anonymous local-verification model defined below. Here \(c_d(P)\) is the minimum number of certificate bits per vertex permitting sound and complete verification of \(P\) at radius \(d\), uniformly over all finite graphs. This asks for the whole numerical tradeoff, with pointwise absolute accuracy \(1/100\), rather than only a yes-or-no answer to the source’s proposed inverse-radius scaling.

source_formulation.text: Is it true that if we allow the verification algorithm to look at distance d, then the optimal size is at most \(\alpha  \cdot  s/d [\ldots ]\)
source_formulation.caption: Truncated source excerpt (at most 25 words); PDF p. 3

cards.why: Local certificates let every vertex check a global claim using a small neighborhood. Understanding their dependence on verification radius would distinguish properties for which additional communication reliably reduces stored proof information from properties that retain an irreducible local memory cost.

Checked later radius-reduction, certification-landscape and local-advice results do not determine it; later checks through 2026-09-16 are bounded.

cards.definitions:
Graphs are finite, nonempty, simple and undirected; they may be disconnected and have arbitrary degree. A graph property \(P\) is a set of these graphs invariant under graph isomorphism. Vertices have no identifiers, port numbers, input labels, advice or knowledge of the graph order. Graph distance is the minimum number of edges in a path; vertices in different components have infinite distance.

Fix integers \(d\ge1\) and \(b\ge0\). A certificate assignment is any function \(z:V(G)\to\{0,1\}^{b}\); for \(b=0\) there is one empty certificate. At a root \(v\), the radius-\(d\) view consists of the root, all vertices at distance at most \(d\), their certificates, and precisely the graph edges with at least one endpoint at distance at most \(d-1\) from \(v\). Edges between two vertices at distance exactly \(d\) are not visible. Neither edges leading beyond the view nor the degrees of its boundary vertices outside the view are additional input.

A verifier is one finite deterministic Turing-machine program accepting or rejecting a view. A view is encoded by its finite adjacency matrix, root index and certificate strings; the decision must be invariant under all renumberings of that encoding. Thus encoding indices convey no persistent identifiers. The program halts on every finite view. Its running time and memory are unrestricted, and it may depend on \(P,d,b\), but it is the same program for every graph order and every vertex. It has no oracle, random bits or additional input.

Such a verifier certifies \(P\) with \(b\) bits when, for every allowed graph \(G\),
\[
G\in P\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z:V(G)\to\{0,1\}^{b}\ \ \forall v\in V(G),\
A(\operatorname{view}_d(G,z,v))=\operatorname{accept}.
\]
The existential certificate assignment is unrestricted and may depend on the entire graph. On a graph outside \(P\), every assignment must cause at least one vertex to reject. There is no error probability. The cost is the common maximum number \(b\) of certificate bits stored at a vertex, not the total number of bits in the graph or view. Using a subset of the \(2^b\) strings is allowed.

Define \(c_d(P)\) as the least such integer \(b\), with value \(+\infty\) if no such verifier exists. The domain of the maximum in \(F(s,d)\) consists only of properties with a certificate bound \(s\) independent of graph order. Different properties and different values of \(d\) may use different verifiers; no algorithm receiving a description of \(P\) is required. The set of possible values is a nonempty subset of \(\{0,\ldots,s\}\): the property containing every graph has cost zero, and a radius-\(d\) verifier can restrict its input to radius one. Hence this maximum is finite and attained as a numerical value. All graphs, graph orders, properties and degrees in its definition are quantified; neither \(s\) nor \(d\) is hidden in an unspecified constant.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a mathematically specified function \(g:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\times\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that \(\lvert g(s,d)-F(s,d)\rvert\le1/100\) for every \(s\ge0,d\ge1\). The approximation need not be integer-valued. An unambiguous expression or certified rule can specify \(g\); merely repeating the defining maximum, giving sampled values, or proving only asymptotic upper or lower bounds does not determine this function to the required precision.

This card explicitly selects the source’s anonymous model and the branch of unlabeled graph properties admitting a constant certificate bound for all graph orders. It broadens the threshold question to the underlying worst-case function \(F(s,d)\), following the authorized quantity/function review. Determining this function is a stronger quantitative target, not an assertion that it is equivalent to every version of the source conjecture. Identifier-dependent models, properties with separate vertex inputs and bounds growing with graph order are outside this selected branch.

The radius view follows Definition 15, including the omission of edges between outer-boundary vertices. A finite terminating verification program fixes computational uniformity, while local running time is unrestricted.

The source proves that anonymous radius-one certification of \(k\)-colorability requires exactly \(\lceil\log_2 k\rceil\) bits. Its larger-radius lower bound and upper bounds for selected properties illustrate the tradeoff, without establishing a universal compression theorem.

The later paper on decreasing verification radius studies how certificate sizes grow when a verifier must see less. Its bounds for that direction do not determine the cost of increasing the radius in the model of this card.

The 2025 complexity-landscape paper studies possible certificate growth rates on paths, cycles and trees, with distinctions involving identifiers and knowledge of graph order. These are different from the full worst-case function for constant certificate bounds on arbitrary graphs.

cards.title: Linear-round weighted APSP in CONGEST
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(b\ge1\), does there exist a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm and a constant \(C_b\) that, on every connected simple undirected \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge weights in \(\{0,\ldots,n^b\}\), outputs all exact weighted distances at their respective vertices within \(C_b n\) communication rounds, with probability at least \(2/3\) that all outputs are correct simultaneously?

The bound must hold on every execution, for all \(n\ge2\). “Linear” means \(O(n)\) with no factor growing with \(n\); a bound \(\widetilde O(n)=O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) does not meet the target.

source_formulation.text: The source asks whether exact weighted all-pairs shortest paths can be computed in linear CONGEST time, after proving a linear lower bound and a limitation of the standard two-party lower-bound framework.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of §5, p.10:12, preserving the literal linear-round question; the explicit probability convention is recorded in the definitions

cards.why: Exact APSP is a central global task in bandwidth-limited networks. Closing the remaining logarithmic gap would identify whether transmitting the necessary information is the only asymptotic obstacle, while respecting the established near-linear breakthrough rather than treating its older polynomial gap as open.
cards.status_note: Source-open for the literal O(n)-round question in the 2017 paper. On 16 September 2026 the source model, Theorems 9–10 and Lemma 11 were checked, together with Bernstein–Nanongkai’s STOC 2019 near-linear algorithm and its explicit polylogarithmic overhead. The April 2025 message-complexity preprint still records that near-linear round result; its own improvement concerns message count. Bounded later-result searches did not locate an O(n) protocol or a superlinear lower bound for the specified randomized model. The newer paper is evidence about the known near-linear bound, not an explicit exhaustive certification that the literal O(n) question remains open.

cards.definitions:
The communication network is the input graph \(G=(V,E,w)\). It has \(n\ge2\) vertices, no loops or parallel edges, is connected, and has nonnegative integer edge weights. For a fixed \(b\), each weight lies between 0 and \(n^b\) inclusive and is represented in binary. A vertex is a processor with a unique identifier in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). It initially knows \(n\), \(b\), its own identifier, the identifiers of its neighbors and the weights of its incident edges, but no other part of the topology or other edge weights. The requirement holds for all labelled graphs and therefore all assignments of these identifiers. The usual polynomial-size identifier range is equivalent for this target because identifiers can be renamed in \(O(n)\) rounds.

Computation is synchronous. In each round each endpoint of each edge can send the other endpoint a message of at most \(B_b\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits, for a fixed constant \(B_b\). Both directions operate independently and different neighbors may receive different messages. All messages sent in a round arrive before the next round. Communication is allowed only along edges of \(G\); there are no additional links between non-neighbors. Edge weights affect shortest-path lengths, not message latency or bandwidth. Local storage and finite local computation are unrestricted and uncharged; only the number of communication rounds is counted. The local rules form one finite, computable program, fixed for all \(n\) and inputs, with no topology-dependent advice or preprocessing.

Randomized processors use independent private fair random bits. For every fixed graph, weights and identifier assignment, probability is over these bits. By the prescribed worst-case round deadline every processor must halt and produce its output; an invalid or incomplete output counts as failure. The success event requires all vertices' entire distance tables to be correct in the same execution, with probability at least \(2/3\). Deterministic algorithms are included as a special case. No average over graphs or identifier assignments is used.

For vertices \(u,v\), define
\[d_G(u,v)=\min_{P:u\leadsto v}\sum_{e\in P}w(e),\qquad d_G(u,u)=0.\]
The minimum may be taken over simple paths, since weights are nonnegative. Each vertex \(v\) must output the labelled table \(\{(u,d_G(u,v)):u\in V\}\). Distances are finite integers of at most \((n-1)n^b\); zero-weight edges and equal-length alternative paths are allowed. The output is the exact distance table, without a requirement to list every path. Output and retained local tables are local memory, not extra communication channels.

The constants, bandwidth bound and program may depend on \(b\), but not on \(n\), graph density, diameter, individual weights or the random choices. At most \(C_b n\) rounds are allowed on every execution. There is no message-count bound beyond the per-edge per-round bandwidth. The source's linear-time question is retained literally. The explicit bounded-error convention uses one fixed constant global success probability; it does not impose an additional failure probability tending to zero with \(n\). The source's nonnegative polynomially bounded integer-weight setting includes the zero-weight edges used in its lower-bound example.

The proposition's negation says that for some fixed \(b\), no such uniform bounded-error algorithm has a linear worst-case round bound on all instances. It does not demand an \(\Omega(n^{1+\delta})\) lower bound for a fixed positive \(\delta\); a rigorously unavoidable unbounded logarithmic or slower factor could already refute linear time. The notation \(\widetilde O(n)\) suppresses polylogarithmic factors and therefore must not be read as \(O(n)\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated linear-round existence proposition. A positive answer must give, for every fixed weight exponent \(b\), a uniform protocol with the stated bandwidth, worst-case \(C_b n\) deadline and simultaneous exact correctness probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. A negative answer must rule out every such protocol for at least one fixed \(b\), preserving the communication and randomness conventions. A near-linear bound with an unbounded factor, approximate distances, a result only for unweighted graphs, a deterministic-only lower bound, or an algorithm with communication links outside the input graph is insufficient. Neither an expected-time bound alone nor a per-vertex success probability alone supplies the stated guarantee. The target is exact asymptotic linearity; numerical error tolerance does not apply.

context_blocks.text: Every node needs an entire row of the distance matrix, yet communication occurs only through the original network. The task therefore combines many shortest-path computations that compete for the same bounded-capacity links.

The 2017 source proves an \(\Omega(n)\) lower bound even on a weighted graph with a constant hop diameter. Its example encodes many edge weights that must pass through one communication link. Thus dependence on the network diameter alone cannot describe the cost of this problem.

The same source shows that its standard two-party reduction with a fixed partition of the vertices cannot yield a superlinear weighted-APSP lower bound. This is a theorem about the scope of that reduction framework, not an \(O(n)\) algorithm or a general impossibility of stronger lower bounds.

Bernstein and Nanongkai subsequently obtain a randomized Las Vegas \(\widetilde O(n)\)-round algorithm for exact weighted APSP, with additional generality including directed inputs. Their analysis retains polylogarithmic overhead, so it resolves the near-linear question without establishing the literal linear bound of this card.

The 2025 message-complexity paper still cites that \(\widetilde O(n)\) randomized round bound. Its own weighted-APSP result uses \(\widetilde O(n^2)\) messages and \(\widetilde O(n^2)\) rounds. Minimizing total messages and eliminating the logarithmic overhead in rounds are different objectives.

A resolution would determine whether the information-transfer lower bound fully captures exact weighted distance computation, or whether coordinating distance information imposes an additional asymptotic cost. The remaining gap concerns factors suppressed by near-linear notation, rather than the large polynomial gap present in 2017.

cards.title: Constant-round MIS in the congested clique
cards.formal: Does randomized maximal independent set admit a constant-round algorithm in the unicast Congested Clique? Precisely, for every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized distributed algorithm \(A_c\) and positive constants \(R_c,B_c\) such that, on every simple undirected graph \(G\) with vertex set \([n]\), \(n\ge2\), the algorithm always terminates within \(R_c\) rounds, uses at most \(B_c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) bits per directed communication link per round, and outputs a maximal independent set with probability at least \(1-n^{-c}\)? Constants and program may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\), the graph or its maximum degree.
cards.why: The question measures how much communication exact distributed symmetry breaking needs when every processor can directly contact every other processor. A constant-round solution would establish a sharp capability of this widely studied model. A general lower bound would expose a bandwidth limitation that survives unrestricted local computation and arbitrary global coordination.
cards.definitions: There is one processor for each vertex \(v\in[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Initially it knows \(n\), its own identifier \(v\), the common identifier set, and exactly the identifiers of its neighbors in the input graph. The physical communication network is complete: in each synchronous round every processor may send a separate message to every other processor, even when the corresponding input edge is absent. Messages sent in a round arrive by its end. Each directed link has the stated bit limit independently; processors may send different messages to different recipients. No extra processors or initially centralized graph description are provided. All processors run the same finite program, with their identifier and local input as parameters. Local computation and local storage have no asymptotic bound, but each local computation terminates and reads only finitely many independent private fair random bits on every execution. All communication, including initialization and distribution of any shared randomness, counts toward the round bound. No graph-dependent or size-dependent advice is supplied. At termination each processor outputs one bit, defining \(S=\{v:\text{processor }v\text{ outputs }1\}\). Correctness means both \(\forall\{u,v\}\in E(G):\{u,v\}\nsubseteq S\) and \(\forall v\notin S:\exists u\in S:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\). Thus maximality means that no additional vertex can be inserted while preserving independence; maximum cardinality is not required. The probability refers to the single global event that all output bits together define a valid set. The round and message bounds hold on every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. Restricting the requested fixed failure exponent to positive integers is equivalent to allowing every fixed positive real exponent.

cards.title: Linear-sketch complexity of the nuclear norm
cards.formal:
Determine the optimal number \(m_\varepsilon(n)\) of exact real linear measurements required to estimate the nuclear norm of an arbitrary real \(n\times n\) matrix with relative error at most \(\varepsilon\) and success probability at least \(2/3\), up to matching constant factors in \(n\), for every fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\).

The sketch is randomized and chosen independently of the input matrix. It must satisfy, for every fixed \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\),
\[\Pr_\omega\!\left[(1-\varepsilon)\|A\|_*\le d_\omega(S_\omega A)\le(1+\varepsilon)\|A\|_*\right]\ge\frac23,\]
where \(S_\omega:\mathbb R^{n\times n}\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear and \(d_\omega\) is a decoder that receives only the sketch and the input-independent random choices. The quantity \(m_\varepsilon(n)\) is the smallest possible dimension \(m\).

Give an explicit asymptotic description \(g(n,\varepsilon)\) and prove that for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) there exist \(0<c_\varepsilon\le C_\varepsilon<\infty\) and \(N_\varepsilon\) such that
\[c_\varepsilon g(n,\varepsilon)\le m_\varepsilon(n)\le C_\varepsilon g(n,\varepsilon)\qquad(n\ge N_\varepsilon).\]
The constants may depend on the fixed accuracy, but not on \(n\). Logarithmic factors in \(n\) must be resolved; determining only a polynomial exponent does not meet this target.
cards.why: Determining this complexity would explain whether summing singular values permits a materially smaller linear summary than storing a general matrix, and exactly how much compression is possible. It would also locate a central matrix norm within the sharply differing sketching behavior of the Schatten family.
cards.status_note: The exact asymptotic order up to constant factors remains source-open in the checked material. The original question is Woodruff’s 2014 survey Open Question 4. The 2019 journal article’s model and linear lower bound were checked. A bounded search on 16 September 2026 found Yang’s arXiv:2608.22247v3, revised 27 August 2026: its stated near-quadratic lower and upper bounds leave logarithmic factors unresolved, as explicitly discussed in §6. This review inspected its model, theorem statement and remaining-gap discussion, not a full independent verification of its 94-page proof; no verified journal acceptance is asserted. The recent bounds are therefore identified as preprint claims, and even as stated they do not complete this card’s matching-constant-factor criterion.

sentences: The nuclear norm of a matrix is the sum of its singular values.
The question asks for the smallest number of randomized exact real linear measurements that suffice to approximate this norm for every fixed input matrix.
The requested answer must give matching upper and lower bounds up to constant factors for each fixed relative accuracy.
Published results separate this matrix problem from ordinary vector norms, bilinear sketches and finite-bit streaming complexity.
An August 2026 preprint claims near-quadratic bounds but leaves logarithmic factors unresolved, and its proof is not independently verified by this review.

cards.definitions:
Let \(n\) be any positive integer. For a real square matrix \(A\), its singular values \(\sigma_1(A),\ldots,\sigma_n(A)\) are the nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues of \(A^{\mathsf T}A\), with multiplicities and zeros included. Its nuclear norm, also called the trace norm or Schatten-1 norm, is
\[\|A\|_*=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_i(A).\]
No symmetry, positive-semidefiniteness, rank, sparsity, integrality or bounded-entry promise is imposed. In particular, this is not the entrywise sum of absolute values. A symmetric positive semidefinite matrix has nonnegative eigenvalues, and for that restricted class the nuclear norm equals the trace; the target covers all real matrices.

An \(m\)-measurement randomized linear sketch for given \(n,\varepsilon\) is specified by an input-independent probability space of random seeds \(\omega\), a real linear map \(S_\omega\), and a decoding function \(d_\omega:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\). Equivalently, each measurement has the form
\[(S_\omega A)_t=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n B_{tij}(\omega)A_{ij},\qquad1\le t\le m,\]
where all coefficients are fixed once the seed is sampled, before inspecting any entry of \(A\). The map may depend on \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(A\). The seed may also specify independent decoder randomness. The coefficient functions and the combined decoding map \((\omega,y)\mapsto d_\omega(y)\) are measurable with respect to their probability space and the usual Borel sigma-algebra on finite-dimensional real spaces, so every displayed success probability is defined.

All randomness is over the seed. The matrix is fixed before that seed is chosen, with the quantifier order \(\exists\text{ sketch distribution}\;\forall A\;\Pr_\omega[\text{success on }A]\ge2/3\). The same seed need not work simultaneously for all matrices. Conversely, a guarantee only for a random input matrix is insufficient. For \(A=0\), success requires the output to be exactly zero. For nonzero inputs the error bound is multiplicative, equivalently \(|d_\omega(S_\omega A)-\|A\|_*|\le\varepsilon\|A\|_*\).

The cost is the fixed number \(m\) of data-dependent real scalars retained. Coefficients, measurements and arithmetic are exact real objects. Their bit lengths, the description of the seed, evaluation time, and the decoder's auxiliary working space are not counted. No finite-precision or efficient-sampling requirement is added. The decoder can be nonlinear and have unbounded computational cost. This is an information measure for general linear sketches, not a claim of a Turing-machine implementation. Separate choices of distribution and decoder for each \(n,\varepsilon\) are allowed; an algorithm constructing them uniformly in polynomial time is not part of the target.

Define
\[m_\varepsilon(n)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\text{ an admissible }m\text{-measurement sketch satisfies the stated guarantee}\}.\]
This minimum is finite and attained as a minimum over integers: retaining all \(n^2\) entries is a linear sketch from which the norm is defined exactly. The target seeks a noncircular asymptotic description of this optimization, with upper bounds witnessed by admissible sketch distributions and lower bounds applying to every such distribution and decoder.

A restricted bilinear sketch retains a matrix \(UAV\) for input-independent matrices \(U\) and \(V\); its scalar entry count is one possible general linear-sketch dimension. General sketches are not restricted to this form. Lower bounds for one selected architecture do not automatically extend to all real linear maps. Likewise, bits of streaming memory and real measurement dimension are different resources. An entry update can be reflected linearly in the sketch, but this does not identify the number of exact counters with their finite binary storage cost.

The source asks for a constant-factor approximation without fixing the constant. This review spells out the family of fixed relative accuracies \(0<\varepsilon<1\), with constant success probability \(2/3\), in the standard model made explicit in the subsequent literature. Each accuracy is held constant while \(n\to\infty\); the answer need not optimize a joint regime where \(\varepsilon\) tends to zero with \(n\). The requested precision for the optimal dimension is equality of asymptotic order up to multiplicative constants, including every unbounded logarithmic factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular asymptotic description of \(m_\varepsilon(n)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of matching upper and lower bounds for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), with the quantifiers and input domain above. An upper bound must give a valid input-independent sketch and decoder with the per-matrix success guarantee. A lower bound must apply to arbitrary measurable decoders and all general randomized real linear maps. Bounds matching only up to polylogarithmic factors, only the exponent in \(n^{\alpha+o(1)}\), a result confined to positive semidefinite matrices, or a finite-bit streaming bound alone do not determine the requested order. The parameter \(\varepsilon\) is the sketch's relative error; the benchmark's default additive numerical tolerance does not replace the required asymptotic precision.

source_formulation.text: Woodruff asks for the optimal dimension of a linear sketch that approximates the Schatten-1, or nuclear, norm within a constant factor. The question contrasts it with the much better understood Frobenius and spectral norms.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Open Question 4, with the general real linear-sketch model and constant-factor precision made explicit below

context_blocks.text: The nuclear norm sums the strengths of all singular directions of a matrix. It is a standard matrix norm with uses in low-rank modeling, and its sketching complexity asks how much linear information must be retained to estimate that total without retaining the full matrix.

The neighboring Schatten norms behave very differently: for fixed approximation accuracy, the Frobenius norm admits a constant-dimensional sketch, whereas spectral-norm approximation requires \(\Theta(n^2)\) dimensions. The nuclear norm has long occupied an unresolved position between these extremes.

For real matrices, changing an entry changes the singular values indirectly. Ordinary vector norm sketches therefore do not automatically estimate a Schatten norm. The 2019 paper makes this distinction and connects nuclear-norm sketching to the possibility of small summaries for matrix nearest-neighbor search.

Theorem 4.1 of the 2019 paper gives an \(\Omega(n)\) general-sketch lower bound for nuclear-norm approximation at a sufficiently small fixed relative error. Its stated error probability can be converted to the convention here by constant repetition. The theorem does not by itself identify the optimum or assert the same threshold for every coarse approximation factor.

The August 2026 preprint claims, for each fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), constants \(A_\varepsilon,C_\varepsilon\) with
\[\frac{n^2}{(\log n)^{A_\varepsilon}}\le m_\varepsilon(n)\le C_\varepsilon\frac{n^2\{\log\log(e^e n)\}^2}{\log(en)}\]
for sufficiently large \(n\). These are the claims of its Theorem 1.1, whose full proof has not been independently verified in this review. The paper explicitly retains a logarithmic gap, so the displayed bounds would still fall short of the card’s constant-factor target.

The short description of a “sketch” can hide several inequivalent costs. This card fixes the number of exact real measurements and a guarantee for each fixed matrix. Finite-bit streaming, input-dependent measurements, and recovery of the matrix itself have different requirements.

cards.context:
The nuclear norm sums the strengths of all singular directions of a matrix. It is a standard matrix norm with uses in low-rank modeling, and its sketching complexity asks how much linear information must be retained to estimate that total without retaining the full matrix.

The neighboring Schatten norms behave very differently: for fixed approximation accuracy, the Frobenius norm admits a constant-dimensional sketch, whereas spectral-norm approximation requires \(\Theta(n^2)\) dimensions. The nuclear norm has long occupied an unresolved position between these extremes.

For real matrices, changing an entry changes the singular values indirectly. Ordinary vector norm sketches therefore do not automatically estimate a Schatten norm. The 2019 paper makes this distinction and connects nuclear-norm sketching to the possibility of small summaries for matrix nearest-neighbor search.

Theorem 4.1 of the 2019 paper gives an \(\Omega(n)\) general-sketch lower bound for nuclear-norm approximation at a sufficiently small fixed relative error. Its stated error probability can be converted to the convention here by constant repetition. The theorem does not by itself identify the optimum or assert the same threshold for every coarse approximation factor.

The August 2026 preprint claims, for each fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), constants \(A_\varepsilon,C_\varepsilon\) with
\[\frac{n^2}{(\log n)^{A_\varepsilon}}\le m_\varepsilon(n)\le C_\varepsilon\frac{n^2\{\log\log(e^e n)\}^2}{\log(en)}\]
for sufficiently large \(n\). These are the claims of its Theorem 1.1, whose full proof has not been independently verified in this review. The paper explicitly retains a logarithmic gap, so the displayed bounds would still fall short of the card’s constant-factor target.

The short description of a “sketch” can hide several inequivalent costs. This card fixes the number of exact real measurements and a guarantee for each fixed matrix. Finite-bit streaming, input-dependent measurements, and recovery of the matrix itself have different requirements.

cards.title: Subquadratic metric TSP cost estimation below factor two
cards.formal:
Do there exist an absolute constant \(\delta\in(0,1)\) and a classical randomized distance-query algorithm that estimates the minimum traveling-salesperson tour cost of every \(n\)-point metric within a factor \(2-\delta\), using \(o(n^2)\) distance queries?

For a metric \(d\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge3\), define
\[\operatorname{TSP}(d)=\min_{\pi\in\mathfrak S_n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}d\bigl(\pi(j),\pi(j+1)\bigr),\qquad \pi(n+1)=\pi(1).\]
The algorithm knows \(n\) and can request \(d(i,j)\) for any chosen pair of labels. Its output \(Z\) must satisfy
\[\Pr\!\left[\operatorname{TSP}(d)\le Z\le(2-\delta)\operatorname{TSP}(d)\right]\ge\frac23\]
for every input metric. Only the number of oracle calls is bounded; the output is a cost estimate and need not describe a tour.
cards.why: This is a central test of how well a global optimization value can be estimated from incomplete metric information. Resolving it would determine whether the factor-two barrier is inherent to sparse distance access or reflects limitations of current estimators, with a sharp separation between learning a value and constructing a tour.

sentences: A metric TSP cost query algorithm asks for distances between selected pairs of labeled points.
The question asks whether some fixed approximation factor below two is achievable with a subquadratic number of queries on every metric.
The algorithm is randomized and only needs to output a cost estimate, with success probability at least two thirds.
Nearly linear MST-weight estimation gives the factor-two baseline, while stronger TSP estimates are known for special metrics or with extra spanning-tree information.
The target separates sparse access to a global optimum value from the information needed to construct an explicit tour.

cards.definitions:
The input consists of a known integer \(n\ge3\), the labels \([n]\), and an oracle for a function \(d:[n]\times[n]\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). It is promised that \(d(i,j)=0\) exactly when \(i=j\), that \(d(i,j)=d(j,i)\), and that
\[d(i,k)\le d(i,j)+d(j,k)\quad\text{for all }i,j,k\in[n].\]
Thus all off-diagonal distances are finite positive real numbers. The triangle inequality and symmetry are input promises, not properties that the algorithm must verify. Metrics are arbitrary: no Euclidean embedding, dimension bound, integer-distance restriction, bounded aspect ratio or distribution on inputs is supplied.

One query consists of specifying labels \(i,j\in[n]\) and receiving the exact real distance \(d(i,j)\). It costs one oracle call. Queries may depend on earlier replies and on the algorithm’s private randomness. Repeated calls are charged again. Diagonal values are known to be zero; allowing a paid diagonal call gives no additional information. The metric remains fixed throughout the execution and is chosen independently of the random bits.

The algorithm is uniform: a single finite program works for every \(n\). To specify computation with exact real oracle replies, use a classical real-register machine with rational program constants, ordinary finite control, integer counters, and exact real arithmetic and comparisons. Allowed real operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by a nonzero value; registers may store queried distances and calculated real values. Randomness consists of independent fair bits, which may be used to select labels. Integer computation, local arithmetic, storage and random-bit generation are not charged to the query budget. They must define an algorithm that halts with probability one on each input. No advice depending on the metric or on \(n\), quantum queries, further metric oracle, precomputed spanning tree or access to unqueried matrix entries is available.

This is a query-complexity question, so there is no polynomial-time or subquadratic-time requirement on the computation between calls. In particular, the original source’s suggestion of subquadratic total time is a stronger aspiration, not an additional condition for answering its primary query question. A positive solution with such a time bound would also solve this card, provided it meets all the stated guarantees.

The output \(Z\) is one real value. On a successful execution it is an upper estimate at most \(2-\delta\) times the optimum. An equivalent lower-estimate convention would require \(\operatorname{TSP}(d)/(2-\delta)\le Z'\le\operatorname{TSP}(d)\); multiplication by the fixed approximation factor converts between the conventions without oracle calls. The algorithm may fail to meet the interval on at most one third of its random executions. Success is required for each metric individually, not merely on average over an input distribution.

The query bound is worst case over inputs and random executions, apart from null-probability exceptional executions. Formally, there must exist \(q:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that every \(n\)-point input uses at most \(q(n)\) oracle calls with probability one, and
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{q(n)}{n^2}=0.\]
The constant \(\delta\), the program and this bound are independent of all distance values. There is no hidden dependence on the ratio of the largest to the smallest positive distance. For finitely many small \(n\), all pair distances may be queried without affecting the limit. The little-o condition is weaker than demanding \(O(n^{2-\gamma})\) for some fixed \(\gamma>0\); both a fixed polynomial saving and a genuine slower asymptotic saving would qualify.

The quantifier order is \(\exists\delta\;\exists A\;\exists q\;\forall n\ge3\;\forall d\), followed by probability over the execution of \(A\). The improvement \(\delta\) must be a positive constant; an approximation factor approaching two from below as \(n\) grows is insufficient. The card asks whether any such constant improvement exists, not for the largest possible improvement or a full approximation-query tradeoff.

A tour is a cyclic ordering of all labels, using each exactly once before returning to the start. The cost includes that closing edge. The oracle describes the complete metric, so each tour edge costs the queried distance itself; no separate underlying graph path needs to be output. \(\mathfrak S_n\) is the set of all permutations of \([n]\). The finite minimum in the definition of \(\operatorname{TSP}(d)\) is attained and is strictly positive.

For background, a spanning tree is a connected acyclic graph on all labels, and \(\operatorname{MST}(d)\) is the minimum sum of its edge distances. The familiar inequalities \(\operatorname{MST}(d)\le\operatorname{TSP}(d)\le2\operatorname{MST}(d)\) explain the factor-two threshold. Estimating the weight of an MST does not give its edges. A graphic metric is the shortest-path distance metric of a connected unweighted undirected graph. A \((1,2)\)-metric has every off-diagonal distance equal to one or two. Both are special classes of the general metric inputs here.

This is not a streaming task: a stream reveals entries in an imposed order, whereas the algorithm here chooses each pair it queries. A result that is given a minimum spanning tree as additional input, or promises a spanning tree of unit-distance edges, concerns additional information or structure absent from the target. Full-input approximation algorithms may also use quadratically many distance entries, regardless of their approximation ratio.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of an absolute \(\delta>0\), a uniform classical randomized algorithm and a worst-case query bound \(q(n)=o(n^2)\) with the stated success probability for every metric. A positive answer must prove the cost guarantee, the uniform little-o bound independent of the metric’s scale and aspect ratio, and almost-sure halting in the specified oracle model. It need not output a tour or run in subquadratic total time. A negative answer must refute this quantified existence statement for randomized adaptive algorithms; a lower bound only for deterministic algorithms, near-exact approximation, or a specific algorithm is insufficient. Positive results restricted to graphic or \((1,2)\)-metrics, or assuming an MST is supplied, do not resolve the arbitrary-metric target. Experimental success rates, conditional computational hardness and an improvement that vanishes with \(n\) do not establish the required result.

source_formulation.text: Sublinear.info Problem 71 asks whether some positive constant improvement below approximation factor two is possible for metric TSP cost with fewer than quadratically many pair-distance queries. It presents a subquadratic total running time as an even stronger goal. This card retains the primary query-complexity question and makes the randomness and cost-estimation convention explicit.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Sublinear.info Problem 71; the primary distance-query target is retained

context_blocks.text: A distance matrix contains quadratically many entries. Estimating a global optimum after reading a vanishing fraction of these entries asks how much information about a metric is needed to recover a useful numerical summary, rather than an explicit combinatorial solution.

Czumaj and Sohler estimate metric MST weight within a factor \(1+\varepsilon\) using nearly linear oracle access for fixed \(\varepsilon\). The resulting TSP estimate approaches factor two. Their arbitrary-metric model does not assume a given geometric embedding or a bounded ratio of distances.

Classical tour algorithms can rely on an actual spanning tree and further global structure. The source emphasizes that obtaining the tree itself can require quadratically many distance queries even though estimating its total weight is much easier. This is an information-access distinction between value estimation and producing a witness.

Chen, Kannan and Khanna obtain below-two estimation for graphic and two-valued metrics. They also prove that sufficiently accurate approximation already requires quadratic query complexity on these special classes. That obstruction near factor one does not rule out every fixed improvement below two.

Chen, Khanna and Tan extend below-two estimation to positive integral metrics that either have a promised unit-edge spanning tree or are supplied with an MST. The query cost is \(\widetilde O(n^{3/2})\). Their paper explicitly leaves the unrestricted general-metric query question open.

The 2023 paper also gives streaming algorithms and lower bounds. Those theorems have different access rules and cannot be substituted for a pair-distance query theorem. In particular, a result with an extra pass over every matrix entry need not inspect only a subquadratic number of distances.

The requested estimate need not correspond to a tour produced by the algorithm. A positive answer would establish that useful information about tour cost is accessible with strictly fewer than all pairwise measurements, even where recovering the usual intermediate structures is expensive.

cards.title: Factor-two graph distances in logarithmically many passes
cards.formal:
Can a randomized streaming algorithm estimate the distance between two specified vertices of an undirected, unweighted graph within a factor of two using \(O(\log n)\) passes and \(O(n\operatorname{polylog}n)\) bits of memory?

More precisely, do there exist one uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), constants \(C_s,C_p>0\) and an integer \(k\ge0\) such that the following holds for every simple graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), every specified pair \(s,t\), and every ordering of its edges? The algorithm knows \(n,s,t\) before the stream begins, uses at most
\[C_s n\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^k\text{ bits and }\left\lceil C_p\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil\text{ passes},\]
and, with probability at least \(2/3\), outputs \(D\) satisfying
\[d_G(s,t)\le D\le2d_G(s,t).\]
For disconnected \(s,t\), success means outputting the symbol \(\infty\). All passes read the same edge order.
cards.why: Shortest-path distance is a basic graph quantity whose global dependencies challenge small-memory sequential access. This question isolates the number of scans needed for a useful constant-factor estimate, between new near-logarithmic lower bounds and the best verified upper bounds.
cards.status_note: Source-open in Sublinear.info Problem 14, Kanpur 2006, updated 25 September 2016. The user selected factor-two single-pair estimation in O(log n) passes and O(n polylog n) bits. The SODA 2026 publication of Assadi–Hoppenworth–Sundaresan and its 21 October 2025 full version were checked on 16 September 2026. Their constant-factor upper bound uses O((log n/log log n)^2) passes; their lower bound is Omega(log n/log log n), including fixed-pair unweighted instances and a same-order simulation. These statements leave the selected target unresolved. A bounded later-work search found no verified closure of this gap. No new algorithm, lower-bound proof or Lean formalization is claimed.

progress.text: Problem 14 explicitly asks for distance approximation in logarithmically many passes and records a then-known distance-threshold lower bound.

Assadi, Hoppenworth and Sundaresan publish upper and lower pass bounds leaving a gap between \(\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)\) and \(O((\log n/\log\log n)^2)\) for constant-factor approximation in semi-streaming space. Neither bound settles the chosen \(O(\log n)\) target.

The source and target are known in advance, and every pass sees the same arbitrary edge order.

cards.definitions:
The input graph is finite, undirected, unweighted and simple: there are no self-loops or parallel edges. Its vertices have distinct binary labels in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge1\). Each edge appears exactly once as an unordered pair of labels. The stream lists these edges explicitly in an arbitrary order, with an end marker; it may be empty. Isolated vertices are included in the known vertex set even though they do not appear in any edge. No planarity, sparsity, degree or diameter restriction is imposed.

The vertices \(s,t\) belong to the known vertex set and are supplied before any edge is read. They may be equal. A path has length equal to its number of edges, and \(d_G(s,t)\) is the minimum length of a path from \(s\) to \(t\). Set \(d_G(s,s)=0\) and \(d_G(s,t)=\infty\) if there is no connecting path. Every finite distance is an integer between zero and \(n-1\).

A pass scans the edge list once from beginning to end. After a pass the algorithm may rewind to the beginning and retain its memory, but it cannot reorder or change the stream. Within a pass it has only sequential access. There is no random access to old edges, adjacency-query oracle, external scratch file or separate stored copy of the graph. All passes encounter the same fixed order. The algorithm may stop after fewer passes than its bound; starting another scan counts as another pass.

The output is one integer \(D\) or the distinguished symbol \(\infty\). The algorithm need not output a path, a spanning tree, distances to other targets or a summary supporting later queries. Integer output loses no generality for this factor guarantee: rounding down a nonnegative real estimate in the permitted interval preserves both inequalities when the true distance is an integer. For a connected pair the successful output lies between \(d_G(s,t)\) and \(2d_G(s,t)\), with no additive error. For a disconnected pair the successful output is \(\infty\); for \(s=t\) it is zero.

For every fixed graph, edge ordering and pair, probability is over the algorithm's independent fair random bits. The input and its order are fixed independently of those bits. The success condition concerns the single requested output. It is not an average over graphs or stream orders, and it does not require one random seed to work for all inputs simultaneously.

Use one finite uniform program for every input size. Its memory consists of all mutable working information, including retained edge data, vertex labels, counters, stored random choices and output preparation. Every bit of that information counts. Fresh random bits may be read as needed, but old random bits cannot be revisited unless their information was retained within the space bound. The graph stream is read-only external input. The supplied parameters take only \(O(\log(n+2))\) bits, so charging their storage does not change the target.

Both resource bounds hold throughout every execution, including unsuccessful random executions. The algorithm must halt and produce an output; no bound on local computation time is imposed beyond this termination requirement. Thus the question isolates memory and passes, as in the streaming source. Computationally expensive processing between edges cannot hide extra memory or reread the input. A polynomial local-time algorithm would suffice, but such a time requirement is not added to the target.

The constants \(C_s,C_p\) and the exponent \(k\) are fixed independently of \(n\), the graph, the stream order, the distance and the random choices. The memory notation \(O(n\operatorname{polylog}n)\) permits any fixed power of the logarithm. The pass bound permits only one power: an arbitrary \(O(\log^c n)\) bound for a fixed \(c>1\) is not the requested \(O(\log n)\) result. Binary logarithms with the harmless \(n+2\) offset avoid small-input exceptions.

The term semi-streaming refers to memory proportional to the number of vertices times a fixed power of the logarithm, even though a dense graph can have quadratically many edges. Papers often count \(O(\log n)\)-bit words rather than bits. This changes the permitted logarithmic power by one and therefore describes the same space class here. When a particular logarithmic space bound is quoted, its unit must still be stated.

The selected model is insertion-only and allows every fixed edge ordering. Edge deletions, random-order streams and a source or target revealed only after streaming are separately quantified variants. Likewise, all-pairs distances and single-source shortest-path trees ask for more output than this card. The original source combines several of these questions. With the user's approval, this card retains just factor-two estimation of one known pair in logarithmically many passes.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the algorithm and constants in the statement, including its success probability for every graph and order and its worst-case bit-space and pass bounds. Alternatively, provide a complete Lean-checked proof that no such uniform randomized algorithm exists. The negative direction must rule out every fixed polylogarithmic space exponent \(k\) together with an \(O(\log n)\) pass bound; a lower bound for one narrower space allowance does not suffice. A lower bound of only \(\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)\), or an upper bound with \(O((\log n/\log\log n)^2)\) passes, leaves the selected target unresolved. Improved constants, a larger approximation factor, an additive error, average-order correctness or correctness only for nearby vertices do not settle this exact resource-and-error question.

source_formulation.text: McGregor asks how well the distance between two specified vertices can be estimated from an edge stream, particularly in O(log n) passes, and separately mentions random-order input. The user selected factor two, undirected unweighted graphs, arbitrary fixed edge order, success probability at least two thirds and semi-streaming bit space. These choices narrow the source to one decision question about algorithm existence.

context_blocks.text: A graph may contain far more edges than a small-memory algorithm can retain. One scan can reveal useful local connections, while a short path between distant vertices can depend on edges encountered in an inconvenient order. The question asks how much repeated access is needed even when only one numerical distance is requested.

The original discussion emphasizes spanners. An \((\alpha,\beta)\)-spanner is a subgraph \(H\) preserving all pairwise distances within \(d_G(u,v)\le d_H(u,v)\le\alpha d_G(u,v)+\beta\). Such a summary supports many pairs, whereas this card supplies its only pair in advance. Results that exploit all-pairs summaries do not by themselves characterize the best method for that smaller output requirement.

Exact distance can be obtained with a number of passes depending on the distance. That dependence can be large on arbitrary graphs. The selected target instead demands a logarithmic worst-case pass bound and permits a controlled multiplicative error.

The SODA 2026 result gives a \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation in \(O(\varepsilon^{-1}(\log n/\log\log n)^2)\) passes using \(O(\varepsilon^{-1}n\log^3 n)\) words. Fixing \(\varepsilon=1/2\) meets the accuracy and bit-space requirements here, but the number of passes is asymptotically larger than \(O(\log n)\).

The same work proves a lower bound of \(\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)\) passes for any constant approximation in semi-streaming space, even for one fixed pair in an unweighted graph. It also explains how its communication simulation accommodates the same order in every pass. This rules out substantially fewer passes while remaining compatible with the requested logarithmic upper bound.

A positive answer would improve the known number of scans for a basic distance query without requiring the whole graph in memory. A negative answer would establish a sharper limitation on what repeated sequential access can recover, even with a constant approximation and only one requested pair.

cards.title: Constant-pass weighted matching with O(n log n) bits
cards.formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and fixed integer \(c\geq1\), is there a randomized insertion-only streaming algorithm that, on every \(n\)-vertex simple undirected graph with integer edge weights in \([1,n^c]\), outputs a matching of weight at least \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(p_{\varepsilon,c}\) passes and \(B_{\varepsilon,c}n\log_2(n+2)\) bits of memory, where \(p_{\varepsilon,c},B_{\varepsilon,c}\) do not depend on \(n\)?
cards.why: The question asks whether near-optimal weighted matchings can be found with memory comparable to the explicit output and a fixed number of scans of a dense graph. It isolates the remaining strict memory requirement from the already established existence of constant-pass algorithms with polylogarithmic overhead.
cards.status_note: The broad historical question is substantially resolved: linear-time RAM approximation and constant-pass near-linear-space streaming algorithms exist. This card explicitly retains the stricter O(n log n)-bit streaming variant with polynomially bounded integer weights. The checked general-graph theorems and 2025 overview do not state that precise memory endpoint; no matching resolution was located in the bounded September 2026 check.

cards.definitions: The vertex set is \([n]\). A matching is a subset of edges with no shared endpoint, its weight is the sum of its edge weights, and \(\operatorname{OPT}\) is the largest such sum over all matchings of the graph. The input is a list of distinct edges, each represented by two binary vertex identifiers and its positive binary integer weight. The algorithm knows \(n,\varepsilon,c\). It reads the list sequentially in an arbitrary order selected independently of its random choices. A pass reads the same complete list in that same order; no deletions, changes of order, random access to earlier items, or requests for selected edges are allowed. The algorithm may stop after any number of passes up to the stated bound. At the end it must output the actual edges of a matching, not merely an estimate of its value. The empty graph has optimum zero and admits the empty output. All stored bits, including edge identifiers, weights, random seeds retained for reuse, counters and temporary working memory, count toward space. A final write-only output tape is permitted, but cannot be used as storage during the passes. The bound is worst case over inputs and random choices; success is required for each input and order. Local computation time is unrestricted, and the finite algorithm may depend on the fixed accuracy and weight exponent. Equivalently the space target is O(n) words of O(log n) bits for each fixed pair of parameters. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) is required for the pass count or space constant.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proof of the approximation, actual matching output, pass and bit-space guarantees for every fixed accuracy and weight exponent. Alternatively prove that this family of guarantees is impossible, for some fixed parameters. A constant-pass algorithm with extra logarithmic factors in bits, an algorithm for bipartite graphs only, or a RAM approximation algorithm does not establish the displayed statement.

context_blocks.text: The 2006 page contains two questions: a constant-pass streaming approximation with O(n log n) space, and a linear-time RAM approximation scheme. This card keeps the streaming question as its single target. Editorial convention: space is measured explicitly in bits and weights have polynomially bounded integer encodings, removing an ambiguity in the historical page.

Duan and Pettie resolved the RAM direction with running time \(O(m\varepsilon^{-1}\log\varepsilon^{-1})\) for maximum-weight matching. That algorithm can access and store the graph in ways unavailable to the streaming model. The old RAM question is therefore recorded as solved context rather than repeated as an open demand.

Gamlath, Kale, Mitrović and Svensson obtained arbitrarily accurate weighted matching in a number of passes depending only on accuracy, using memory linear in n up to polylogarithmic factors. This settles the broader constant-pass semi-streaming objective, but the stated space guarantee alone does not supply the exact bit bound retained here.

Huang and Su improve the number of passes to a polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\). Their Theorem 1.2 states \(O(n\log W\,\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon))\) words, where \(W\) is the weight ratio. Under the present weight encoding this can be \(O_{\varepsilon,c}(n\log^2 n)\) bits. One must account for word size before comparing it with the target.

The 2025 overview distinguishes general weighted graphs from bipartite and unweighted cases and tabulates their different pass-space guarantees. Strong bounds for one of those restrictions cannot be silently substituted for the graph class here.

For weighted matchings, improving the objective can involve both alternating paths and alternating cycles. Retaining enough information to coordinate such improvements while storing only a linear number of words is the specific resource issue in this formulation.

cards.title: Classification of robust chemical computation
cards.why: Chemical implementations often have uncertain reaction speeds. This question isolates what can be computed when every positive choice of fixed kinetic constants must lead to the same answer. A classification would distinguish robust computational content from behavior that depends on carefully selected reaction rates.
cards.status_note: The published DISC 2025 paper proves the sufficient directions and conjectures that they are necessary in §4. No resolution of the joint continuous-model classification was found in the bounded review.

cards.definitions:
A chemical reaction network has a finite species set \(\Lambda\) and finitely many reactions indexed by \(R\). Reaction \(r\) has reactant and product vectors \(a_r,b_r\in\mathbb N^\Lambda\), where \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), with \(a_r\ne b_r\). The vectors give integer stoichiometric multiplicities. Empty reactants or products are allowed; there is no restriction to reactions of a particular order.

Choose distinct input species \(X_1,\ldots,X_k\), with \(\Sigma=\{X_1,\ldots,X_k\}\), and a fixed initial context \(i\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{\Lambda\setminus\Sigma}\). For input \(x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{k}\), the initial concentration is \(c_{X_j}(0)=x_j\) and \(c_S(0)=i_S\) for \(S\notin\Sigma\). The context can contain arbitrary nonnegative real constants. It is fixed as part of the computing network and depends neither on the input nor on the rate constants.

For each assignment \(\kappa\in\mathbb R_{>0}^{R}\), the mass-action trajectory solves
\[
\frac{dc_S}{dt}
=\sum_{r\in R}(b_r(S)-a_r(S))\kappa_r
\prod_{T\in\Lambda}c_T(t)^{a_r(T)}
\qquad(S\in\Lambda).
\]
An exponent-zero factor is one, including at zero concentration. Each \(\kappa_r\) is a finite positive real constant, independent of time, with no common upper or positive lower bound assumed. The polynomial vector field has a unique maximal solution from the initial state. A network used in either robust computation definition must have a nonnegative solution defined for every \(t\ge0\), for every input and every \(\kappa\); finite-time blowup does not qualify. Species other than the output need not converge or remain bounded over infinite time.

For predicate computation choose disjoint voter sets \(\Upsilon_0,\Upsilon_1\subseteq\Lambda\). The network robustly decides \(\varphi\) when, for every \(x\) and \(\kappa\), writing \(b=\varphi(x)\),
\[
\liminf_{t\to\infty}\sum_{S\in\Upsilon_b}c_S(t)>0,
\qquad
\forall S\in\Upsilon_{1-b},\quad\lim_{t\to\infty}c_S(t)=0.
\]
The positive lower limiting value may depend on \(x,\kappa\). It is the total correct-voter concentration that must stay away from zero; individual correct voters need not converge. For numerical computation choose one output species \(Y\in\Lambda\). The network robustly computes \(f\) when, for every \(x,\kappa\),
\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}c_Y(t)=f(x).
\]
Input and output species are not required to be disjoint. A predicate or function is called robustly decidable or computable if some finite network with the appropriate fixed data has this property. No bound on time, species, reactions or convergence rate is imposed. The network may depend on the entire predicate or function, but not on a particular input or rate assignment.

A threshold predicate has the form
\[
\theta(x)=\mathbf1\!\left\{\sum_{j=1}^k q_jx_j>h\right\},
\qquad q_j\in\mathbb Q,\quad h\in\mathbb R,
\]
where \(\mathbf1\) is one when its condition holds and zero otherwise. A multi-threshold predicate is a finite Boolean expression using such tests, constants, AND, OR and NOT. This defines boundary behavior at equality exactly.

A rational floor-affine function is
\[
g(x)=\max\!\left\{0,b+\sum_{j=1}^k q_jx_j\right\},
\qquad q_j\in\mathbb Q,\quad b\in\mathbb R.
\]
Here “floor” means clipping below zero, not rounding to an integer. A function \(f\) is threshold-piecewise rational floor-affine if there exist an integer \(\ell\ge1\), multi-threshold predicates \(\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_\ell\), and functions \(g_1,\ldots,g_\ell\) of the displayed form such that, for every \(x\), exactly one \(\varphi_j(x)\) equals one and \(f(x)=g_j(x)\) for that index. The partition is finite; continuity across its boundaries is not required. Slopes are rational, while thresholds and offsets may be arbitrary real constants.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the joint classification. A positive answer must establish both equivalences for every input dimension, with the exact dynamics and convergence conventions stated here. A negative answer must prove the negation of at least one equivalence, for example by fully verifying a robustly computing network whose predicate or function lies outside the specified class. This is an exact yes/no classification, so the numerical \(1/100\) approximation convention does not replace equality of functions or exact Boolean decisions. A result for a single choice of rate constants, leaderless networks only, discrete molecule counts, or time-varying rate laws does not establish the claimed characterization.

source_formulation.text: The authors conjecture that the classes constructed in their positive results exhaust robust predicate and numerical-function computation. The function class is the one defined in Definition 2.3, despite a shortened name in the conclusion.
source_formulation.caption: Paraphrase of the joint tightness conjecture in §4, with terminology expanded from Definitions 2.1–2.7.

context_blocks.text: The continuous model represents molecular amounts by nonnegative real concentrations. Reactions give a polynomial differential equation. Different positive kinetic constants change trajectories, but robust computation requires their eventual output to agree for every such choice.

Stable chemical computation allows a more powerful adversary controlling reaction progress beyond fixed mass-action laws. The paper shows that stable Boolean decisions can inspect which inputs are zero, but cannot in general distinguish arbitrary positive magnitudes. Fixed-constant mass-action robustness admits more predicates.

Theorem 3.7 constructs robust deciders for every finite Boolean combination of rational-weight threshold tests. Initial context permits real threshold offsets. Exact behavior on the threshold itself is part of the predicate, even though the answer is obtained asymptotically.

Theorem 3.10 constructs robust computers for the finite threshold-defined partitions and rational floor-affine pieces in the question. The resulting functions may be discontinuous. Their values are concentration limits, rather than integer molecule counts.

The conclusion conjectures necessity of both constructed classes. It separately discusses removing initial context and representing signed inputs by differences of concentrations. Those alternatives are outside this card’s selected source conjecture.

The 2026 reverse-robust result allows discrete reactions to run backward until a cutoff and then only forward. Its semilinear classification concerns that different execution model and does not establish the continuous mass-action classification here.

cards.title: Work-efficient parallel approximate flow
cards.formal:
Does at least one of the following two problems admit a uniform randomized parallel algorithm with nearly-linear work and polylogarithmic depth, in the precise regime below?

1. Edge-capacitated budgeted minimum-cost flow: given an undirected graph, terminals \(s,t\), edge capacities and nonnegative edge costs, and a total cost budget \(B\), output a feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow whose value is at least \(\mathrm{OPT}/(1+\varepsilon)\), where \(\mathrm{OPT}\) is the largest flow value within both the capacities and budget.
2. Vertex-capacitated maximum flow: given an undirected graph, terminals \(s,t\), and vertex capacities, output a feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow whose value is at least \(\mathrm{OPT}/(1+\varepsilon)\), where \(\mathrm{OPT}\) is the largest capacity-respecting value.

The assertion is a disjunction over the two entire problem classes. The algorithm may choose one class once and for all; choosing an easier alternative separately for each instance is not the assertion.

cards.definitions:
An input graph \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, simple and undirected, with \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\ge2\), \(m=|E|\), and distinct named terminals \(s,t\). It is supplied by an explicit edge list; disconnected graphs and zero capacities are allowed. For each undirected edge \(\{u,v\}\), a flow has nonnegative values \(f_{uv},f_{vu}\). Put
\[
\mathrm{out}_f(v)=\sum_{w:\{v,w\}\in E}f_{vw},\qquad
\mathrm{in}_f(v)=\sum_{w:\{v,w\}\in E}f_{wv}.
\]
Require \(\mathrm{in}_f(s)=\mathrm{out}_f(t)=0\) and \(\mathrm{in}_f(v)=\mathrm{out}_f(v)\) for \(v\notin\{s,t\}\). The value is \(F=\mathrm{out}_f(s)=\mathrm{in}_f(t)\). Fractional flows are allowed. Internal circulations may occur but consume the same capacities and costs as other flow.

For the edge problem, each edge \(e=\{u,v\}\) has capacity \(u_e\ge0\) and cost \(c_e\ge0\). Feasibility requires
\[
f_{uv}+f_{vu}\le u_e,\qquad
\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}c_{\{u,v\}}(f_{uv}+f_{vu})\le B.
\]
There are no vertex constraints in this alternative. The source calls maximization under this cost budget approximate minimum-cost flow; the card uses that source convention.

For the vertex problem, each \(v\) has capacity \(U_v\ge0\). Its load is \(\mathrm{out}_f(v)\) if \(v\ne t\), and \(\mathrm{in}_f(t)\) if \(v=t\). Require load at most \(U_v\) for every vertex, including both terminals. There are no edge capacities or cost objective in this alternative. Equivalently, in a decomposition into directed simple terminal paths, every unit uses capacity at each vertex on its path, including its endpoints; removable internal circulations do not improve the optimum.

In each alternative \(\mathrm{OPT}\) is the maximum \(F\) over feasible real flows. Zero flow is feasible, and instances with \(\mathrm{OPT}=0\) must also be handled. The output explicitly lists rational values for both orientations of every edge. On a successful run all feasibility inequalities hold exactly and \(F\ge\mathrm{OPT}/(1+\varepsilon)\); no capacity or budget violation is permitted.

Here is an explicit polynomial-data and inverse-polylogarithmic-accuracy convention. For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), allow integral capacities and costs in \([0,n^a]\), and a budget \(B=b/d\) with integers \(0\le b\le n^a\), \(1\le d\le n^a\). Let
\[
L=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil,\qquad
\varepsilon=1/q,\quad q\in\mathbb N,\quad 2\le q\le L^a.
\]
Input numbers, labels and \(q\) are encoded in binary. The same algorithm must cover every fixed \(a\); it receives the numerical instance and \(q\), not advice or a precomputed structure for the graph. Reciprocal-integer accuracies specify the source's inverse-polylogarithmic regime: intermediate accuracies can be met by requesting a smaller reciprocal accuracy. This does not require a fully polynomial bound for arbitrary inverse accuracy outside that regime.

Use a synchronous priority-CRCW word PRAM: processors execute one fixed finite program, have labelled shared-memory words, can read concurrently, and simultaneous writes to one location retain the value of the lowest-numbered writing processor. A step performs word arithmetic, comparison, a Boolean operation, a shift, a shared-memory access, or generation of one independent fair random bit. A word has \(C_a L\) bits for a fixed constant \(C_a\); larger integers and rational numerators or denominators use multiple words and their operations are charged accordingly. There is no exact-real or arbitrary-precision unit-cost primitive. Work counts all processor operations, including input handling and output; depth is the number of synchronous steps. The algorithm must halt within the stated bounds on every random tape and succeed with probability at least \(2/3\) on each valid input.

Nearly-linear work and polylogarithmic depth mean that, for every fixed \(a\), there are constants \(K_a>0\) and \(k_a\in\mathbb N\), independent of the graph, its numerical data and \(q\), such that
\[
\mathrm{work}\le K_a(n+m)L^{k_a},\qquad
\mathrm{depth}\le K_a L^{k_a}.
\]
These are explicit editorial model conventions for the source's parallel resource question. They count the finite precision needed by an actual implementation. Polynomially many processors without the work bound, or a subpolynomial factor that is not bounded by a fixed power of \(L\), is insufficient.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of this disjunctive existence assertion. A positive answer must specify one uniform algorithm for at least one whole alternative and establish its feasibility, approximation, per-instance success probability and simultaneous work/depth bounds for every fixed data-and-accuracy exponent \(a\). A negative answer must rule out the asserted algorithm for both alternatives in the stated model. The question is binary; there is no additional numerical \(1/100\) tolerance. A theorem about the optimum value alone must also supply the required flow output, and a capacity-violating bicriteria result alone does not meet the stated feasibility guarantee.

context_blocks.text: An undirected capacity bounds total flow through a resource; a cost budget bounds the sum of flow times edge cost. Vertex capacities instead constrain all traffic passing through a vertex. These impose different feasible regions even when the graph and terminals agree.

The source studies the more general setting with costs and capacities on both edges and vertices. Its single-commodity theorem achieves almost-linear work and subpolynomial depth for inverse-polylogarithmic accuracy. The open question asks for the sharper polylogarithmic factors, already on either restricted alternative.

The full version also treats concurrent and nonconcurrent multicommodity demands. Open Problem 1 is posed even for a single commodity. The broader multicommodity problem and its dependence on the number of commodities are not added to this target.

SODA 2024 gives an undirected edge-capacitated maximum-flow approximation using work O(m ε^{-3} polylog n) and depth O(ε^{-3} polylog n). That result has neither the cost budget of the first alternative nor the vertex capacities of the second.

The ICALP 2026 result concerns unit capacities and unit lengths on expanders. For conductance φ it gives work near m/(εφ) and depth near 1/(εφ), with approximate congestion and cost while routing prescribed demand exactly. Its restricted graph class and bicriteria guarantee leave the general question here unresolved.

The SPAA 2025 exact-flow algorithm has square-root, rather than polylogarithmic, depth. Its near m+n^{3/2} work is nearly linear on sufficiently dense instances; this does not supply the simultaneous bounds sought for all graphs.

cards.title: One-pass semi-streaming depth-first search
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform randomized one-pass streaming algorithm and fixed constants \(C\ge1\), \(k\ge0\) that, for every connected simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\ge1\) vertices, outputs a depth-first-search spanning tree using at most
\[C n\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^k\]
bits of working memory, with probability at least \(2/3\) for every ordering of its edge stream?

The stream lists each edge once, contains no deletions, and can only be scanned from beginning to end. The algorithm may choose the root and neighbor order of the DFS tree. The question concerns the memory and pass bounds, with no additional polynomial-time requirement.

source_formulation.text: The 2020 paper explicitly asks whether DFS-tree computation needs more than one pass with semi-streaming memory. It treats connected simple undirected graphs and distinguishes insertion-only lower bounds from stronger insertion-deletion upper bounds.

cards.why: DFS is a basic graph decomposition tool whose required ancestor structure is stronger than connectivity or an arbitrary spanning tree. cards.status_note: The exact one-pass question is explicitly open in the checked STACS 2020 source, and the 2024 engineering paper records the existing many-pass bounds rather than a general one-pass algorithm. The 2025 statement is not used as a verified resolution, but the conflict prevents a confident current-open certification. Bounded additional searches located no matching theorem. This is a completed formulation and evidence review with its status limit retained.
