cards.definitions:
The graph has labelled vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), is connected and undirected, and has no self-loops or parallel edges. The algorithm is given \(n\) in advance. Its input stream is an arbitrary permutation of the edges \(\{u,v\}\in E\), represented by the two binary vertex labels, followed by an end marker. No adjacency lists, neighbor-query oracle, random access to the graph or second scan are available. The empty stream for \(n=1\) is valid. The requirement is a promise on these well-formed connected graph streams; recognition of the promise is not an additional task.

A rooted spanning tree \(T\) consists of a root \(r\in V\) and one parent in \(V\) for each other vertex, with every parent edge belonging to \(E\). Following parents must reach \(r\) and visit no cycle. A vertex \(u\) is an ancestor of \(v\) when it lies on the tree path from \(r\) to \(v\). The required DFS condition is
\[\forall\{u,v\}\in E:\quad u\text{ is an ancestor of }v\ \text{or}\ v\text{ is an ancestor of }u.\]
For undirected graphs this characterizes a spanning tree obtainable by depth-first search: start at the root, recursively finish exploring a newly discovered neighbor before exploring another, and retain the edges used for first discovery. The root and each vertex's order of neighbors may be chosen by the algorithm. No prescribed or lexicographic traversal must be reproduced, and the neighbor order need not equal edge-arrival order. An arbitrary spanning tree need not satisfy the ancestor condition.

The output is an explicit root and parent table on all \(n\) labels; for \(n=1\), the sole vertex is the root. It has \(O(n\log(n+2))\) bits. The output may be produced after the stream ends using only retained memory and fresh randomness. A write-only output tape cannot be reread as extra storage. Deferring the output to the end does not change semi-streaming feasibility: an earlier root/parent output of this size could instead be retained within the same asymptotic memory regime.

The algorithm has a single finite description, independent of \(n\) and of the graph. It processes the input in one left-to-right pass and may keep at most \(C n(\log_2(n+2))^k\) bits at any time, including retained edges, summaries, counters, random seeds, temporary computation and postprocessing. The bound is worst case over valid streams and random choices. No advice or external writable storage is allowed. Fresh fair random bits are independent of the graph and edge order; old random bits can be accessed again only if retained within the memory bound. The algorithm must finish processing and produce an output with probability one, but no numerical bound on its processing time is imposed. In particular, the question does not silently add efficient offline computation to the streaming space restriction.

For every fixed \(G\) and every fixed edge permutation chosen before the random bits, the probability that the entire root/parent table is a valid DFS tree must be at least \(2/3\). An invalid tree or failure symbol counts as failure. Deterministic algorithms are allowed as a special case. This is a guarantee on arbitrary graphs and orders, not on random graphs or random-order streams.

Semi-streaming space here means \(O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) bits with one fixed exponent. A word of \(O(\log n)\) bits changes only that exponent, but arbitrary-precision words do not have unit storage cost. The source studies both insertion-only and insertion-deletion streams and states its lower-bound convention for insertion-only streams. This card retains the one-pass question in that basic insertion-only setting. A result only for streams with deletions would not refute it, while an algorithm handling deletions would be a stronger positive result.

A negative answer means that no pair of constants \(C,k\) and no such randomized algorithm works on every promised stream. It need not establish a full quadratic-space lower bound: any lower bound excluding \(n(\log n)^k\) for every fixed \(k\) would suffice. Extra passes, a restriction to sparse graphs with \(O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) edges, or a prescribed traversal order change the problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete proof checked in Lean of the existence proposition or its logical negation in the stated insertion-only streaming model. A positive answer must prove that one algorithm makes one pass, respects its worst-case bit-space bound including postprocessing, terminates with probability one, and outputs some valid DFS tree with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid graph and edge order. A negative answer must exclude all fixed polylogarithmic exponents and all allowed randomized algorithms, without relying on a processing-time limitation absent from the model. A lower bound only for a prescribed traversal, directed graphs, streams with deletions or deterministic algorithms does not suffice. Experiments, random-graph guarantees, and a many-pass algorithm do not settle the target. The output is exact; numerical tolerance does not apply.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary depth-first search takes linear time when the entire graph is available in memory. The challenge here is that edges needed later in the traversal may have already passed by, and the full dense graph cannot be retained.

Finding some spanning tree is possible with near-linear memory in one pass. A DFS tree has the additional global ancestor condition: every edge must connect comparable vertices in the rooted tree. On a triangle, a star rooted at its center is a spanning tree but is not a DFS tree, because the two leaves are adjacent.

The source’s Theorem 4 gives a deterministic insertion-only algorithm with \(p\) passes and \(\widetilde O(n^2/p^2)\) bits, for \(1\le p\le\sqrt n\). At \(p\) of order \(\sqrt n\), this yields semi-streaming space, while at one pass its bound is quadratic. The quoted draft missed this improvement from the very paper containing the question.

For insertion-deletion streams the same theorem gives a randomized \(\widetilde O(n^3/p^4)\)-space tradeoff. That is a different input model. Neither tradeoff establishes a one-pass semi-streaming algorithm or a matching impossibility theorem for the target here.

The 2024 engineering paper evaluates practical versions and heuristics, often observing only one or a few passes, and discusses special random-graph behavior. These observations help explain practical relevance but do not give a one-pass worst-case guarantee on arbitrary edge orders.

Current-status evidence has a specific unresolved conflict: the 2025 long-path paper’s introduction asserts a quadratic-space obstruction for BFS/DFS, while the two papers cited there establish maximal-independent-set lower bounds in the inspected statements. No DFS lower-bound theorem or reduction supporting that assertion was located in those references. The card therefore records uncertainty rather than treating that sentence as a verified resolution.

The source’s Theorem 4 gives a deterministic insertion-only algorithm with \(p\) passes and \(\widetilde O(n^2/p^2)\) bits, for \(1\le p\le\sqrt n\). At \(p\) of order \(\sqrt n\), this yields semi-streaming space, while at one pass its bound is quadratic. The quoted draft missed this improvement from the very paper containing the question.

For insertion-deletion streams the same theorem gives a randomized \(\widetilde O(n^3/p^4)\)-space tradeoff. That is a different input model. Neither tradeoff establishes a one-pass semi-streaming algorithm or a matching impossibility theorem for the target here.

The 2024 engineering paper evaluates practical versions and heuristics, often observing only one or a few passes, and discusses special random-graph behavior. These observations help explain practical relevance but do not give a one-pass worst-case guarantee on arbitrary edge orders.

Current-status evidence has a specific unresolved conflict: the 2025 long-path paper’s introduction asserts a quadratic-space obstruction for BFS/DFS, while the two papers cited there establish maximal-independent-set lower bounds in the inspected statements. No DFS lower-bound theorem or reduction supporting that assertion was located in those references. The card therefore records uncertainty rather than treating that sentence as a verified resolution.

cards.title: Optimal clique-detection rounds in CONGEST
cards.formal:
Determine the optimal randomized round complexity
\[
T_{\mathrm{det}}(n,\ell,b)
\]
of detecting an \(\ell\)-vertex clique in an \(n\)-vertex communication graph, when each directed use of an edge can carry \(b\) bits per round. The parameter domain is
\[
n\ge16,\qquad 4\le\ell\le\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor,\qquad b\ge1,
\]
with all three parameters integers.

The requested answer is an explicit asymptotic expression \(F(n,\ell,b)>0\) and absolute constants \(c,C>0\) such that, throughout this domain,
\[
cF(n,\ell,b)\le T_{\mathrm{det}}(n,\ell,b)
                 \le CF(n,\ell,b).
\]
The constants may not depend on \(n,\ell,b\). Polylogarithmic uncertainty is not sufficient. This full constant-factor target, rather than the historical question of whether a linear number of rounds is necessary, is the explicit user choice.

source_formulation.text: The source leaves a gap between its bandwidth-dependent square-root lower bound for clique detection and the linear-round algorithm then known, and asks how much communication detecting cliques actually requires.

cards.definitions:
The input is any finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(|V|=n\); it need not be connected. A clique of size \(\ell\) is a set of \(\ell\) distinct vertices every two of which are adjacent. The communication links are exactly the edges of \(G\), with communication possible in both directions. Nodes have distinct identifiers in \(\{1,\ldots,n^3\}\), under an arbitrary assignment. Initially a node knows \(n,\ell,b\), its own identifier and the identifiers of all its neighbors, but no other edges. There is no instance-dependent advice or free preprocessing.

In a synchronous round, each node performs arbitrary finite local computation and sends one \(b\)-bit word to each neighbor, possibly a different word on every incident edge. Padding permits shorter content; there is no additional uncharged message channel. All of these words arrive at the end of the round, so a word sent in that round cannot depend on a word received in the same round. Nodes use independent private random bits. Local memory, computation and random-bit generation are uncharged, but each local phase terminates. The algorithm is one finite effective program that operates for every valid \(n,\ell,b\) and every identifier assignment.

At termination each node outputs one bit. On each input, with probability at least \(2/3\), the disjunction of all output bits equals the indicator that \(G\) contains an \(\ell\)-clique. Equivalently, a clique-containing graph must cause at least one node to output one, and a clique-free graph must cause all nodes to output zero, each with the stated joint probability. Either kind of error is allowed outside the successful event. The node outputting one need not belong to a clique or output its vertices. Nodes are not required to enumerate cliques, decide their own membership in a clique, or all learn the answer.

For an admissible algorithm \(A\), let \(r_A(n,\ell,b)\) be the least nonnegative integer bounding its number of rounds on every \(n\)-vertex graph, every identifier assignment and every random execution for those parameters; put \(r_A=\infty\) when no such finite bound exists. Define
\[
T_{\mathrm{det}}(n,\ell,b)=\inf_A r_A(n,\ell,b),
\]
where the infimum ranges over all uniform algorithms satisfying the correctness requirement on the entire parameter domain. Cost is thus worst-case bounded rounds, not expected rounds. The infimum is pointwise in the displayed parameters; admissibility never permits an algorithm that is correct only for a selected graph or parameter tuple.

The bandwidth \(b\) is an explicit positive integer, including values outside the usual \(b=\Theta(\log n)\) specialization. Both directions of an edge have their own \(b\)-bit capacity in each round. This is ordinary CONGEST, with different messages permitted for different neighbors. There are no direct links between nonneighbors. An explicit expression for \(F\) must characterize the dependence on the three integers; merely renaming the optimization defining \(T_{\mathrm{det}}\) is not an answer.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of matching upper and lower bounds within absolute constant factors for the entire specified parameter domain. The upper bound must be realized in the stated detection model, and the lower bound must apply to every admissible randomized algorithm. A bound only for listing all cliques, for broadcast communication, for fixed \(\ell\) with constants depending on \(\ell\), or only at logarithmic bandwidth does not by itself determine the requested function. The selected acceptance tolerance is multiplicative by absolute constants; additive \(1/100\) error is not the criterion for this asymptotic resource function.

context_blocks.text: The conference source proves a lower bound of \(\Omega(\sqrt n/b)\) in the range \(4\le\ell=O(\sqrt n)\), and a corresponding \(n/(\ell b)\) scale for larger cliques. At standard logarithmic bandwidth, it compares this with a linear-round upper bound.

The source also establishes a limitation of its two-party vertex-partition method for obtaining stronger clique lower bounds. That is a statement about the scope of the proof method, not an algorithm attaining the lower bound in a distributed network.

The SODA 2021 result lists all \(\ell\)-cliques in \(\widetilde O(n^{1-2/\ell})\) rounds for each fixed \(\ell\ge4\), at standard logarithmic bandwidth. It therefore also gives sublinear detection for every fixed clique size. The tilde hides polylogarithmic factors.
For \(\ell=4\), that upper bound matches the known detection lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors. This does not establish a constant-factor formula even for this specialization.

For larger cliques, the paper’s matching general lower bound concerns listing, which requires reporting every occurrence. It cannot be transferred to existential detection merely because listing implies detection. Constants or other losses in a fixed-clique-size statement also cannot silently be taken as uniform when clique size grows.

The later journal presentation uses a high-probability detection convention. This card explicitly retains the constant-success convention of the original conference question and treats its full bandwidth dependence as the selected editorial continuation.

cards.title: Fractional-edge-cover load for general-message parallel joins
cards.formal:
For every fixed finite natural-join schema \(Q\), is there a randomized MPC algorithm computing its full join in a constant number of communication rounds with load
\[
\widetilde O_Q\!\left(\frac{m}{p^{1/\rho(Q)}}\right)
\]
on every database instance of total input size \(m\), using \(p\) machines with \(2\le p\) and \(p^3\le m\)?

Precisely, for every \(Q\) and every fixed word-size multiplier \(a\ge1\), must there exist one algorithm \(A_{Q,a}\), constants \(C_{Q,a}>0\), and integers \(R_{Q,a},d_{Q,a}\ge1\), such that it halts within \(R_{Q,a}\) rounds on every execution and, for each valid instance and initial distribution, with probability at least \(1-p^{-2}\) both outputs exactly the join and has load at most
\[
C_{Q,a}\frac{m}{p^{1/\rho(Q)}}
       \bigl(\log_2(m+2)\bigr)^{d_{Q,a}}?
\]
Messages may encode arbitrary information; they are not restricted to complete input tuples. This broader model is the explicit user choice.

source_formulation.text: The source asks whether arbitrary join schemas admit constant-round MPC algorithms matching the fractional-edge-cover load scale, up to the polylogarithmic factors used in its algorithmic bounds. It gives such an algorithm for binary-relation schemas.
source_formulation.caption: Paraphrase of §1.2, p. 25:3, with the model of §1.1. The general-message interpretation was explicitly selected after reviewing the later tuple-based lower bound.

cards.why: Parallel join processing must distribute related information so that machines can produce all compatible output tuples. The fractional edge-cover number captures a fundamental structural feature of the query. Whether it still suffices for communication with unrestricted messages separates a general information limit from limitations of algorithms that move database rows intact.
cards.status_note: The source’s general edge-cover load target remains the selected question in unrestricted-message MPC. The 2024 JACM result refutes its atomic-tuple version, but expressly limits the lower bound to that model. The March 2026 kappa-Join preprint also states its lower-bound conjecture for tuple-based algorithms. No matching result for arbitrary message encodings was found in this bounded review.

cards.definitions:
A schema is a finite nonempty attribute set \(V\) and a finite indexed list of nonempty subsets \(e_1,\ldots,e_r\subseteq V\) with union \(V\). Attribute names, arities, relation names and \(r\) are fixed independently of \(m,p\). Schemas may have repeated subsets. An instance supplies a finite set \(R_i\) of tuples on \(e_i\) for each \(i\). A tuple on \(e_i\) assigns one domain value to each attribute in \(e_i\). Relations have set semantics; duplicate copies within a relation do not contribute multiplicity. The total input size is \(m=\sum_i|R_i|\). The output is the full relation
\[
J_Q(R_1,\ldots,R_r)
=\{t:V\to\mathrm{dom}:\ \forall i,\ t|_{e_i}\in R_i\}.
\]
Every attribute is output; there is no projection, aggregation or bag multiplicity.

The fractional edge-cover number depends only on the schema:
\[
\rho(Q)=\min\left\{\sum_{i=1}^r x_i:
x_i\ge0,\quad
\forall v\in V,\ \sum_{i:v\in e_i}x_i\ge1\right\}.
\]
It is finite and at least one. The variables \(x_i\) are real weights on relation schemas, not data values or relation sizes.

For a precise finite encoding, fix an integer \(a\ge1\) and let a machine word contain \(w=a\lceil\log_2(m+2)\rceil\) bits. Domain values are arbitrary \(w\)-bit strings, with equality of strings deciding attribute matches. A tuple occupies a constant number of words depending only on \(Q\), including its relation tag. Quantification over every fixed \(a\) gives the usual polynomial-size-domain word convention. A message word can contain any \(w\)-bit string computed by its sender; its interpretation is not restricted to a tuple, identifier, count or comparison result.

There are \(p\) machines with distinct indices \(1,\ldots,p\), each able to communicate directly with every other machine. The total input is initially partitioned without replication, with each machine holding at most \(2\lceil m/p\rceil\) tagged tuples. The algorithm must work for every such partition. All machines know \(Q,a,m,p\), the encoding and their own index, but receive no other instance-specific advice, preprocessing or statistics for free.

Each synchronous round consists of arbitrary finite local computation followed by message transmission. All messages in the transmission phase must have been prepared before receiving any message from that phase. A machine may send different messages to different recipients, and later rounds may depend on earlier messages. The load is
\[
\max_{\text{round }j,\ \text{machine }u}
\{\text{number of words received by }u\text{ in round }j\}.
\]
Headers and transmitted metadata count; a word sent to several recipients is received separately by each. Local computation, local storage, outgoing traffic as a separate metric, and local output are uncharged. There is no additional memory cap or running-time requirement, but each local phase must terminate.

Output uses a local emission operation on an explicitly written full tuple. Every output tuple must appear on at least one machine, no non-result tuple may appear on any machine, and repeated emissions of a valid tuple are allowed. A factorized representation, tuple count or emptiness bit is not the required output. A machine may derive and emit a tuple from arbitrary received information; it need not have received all its witness input tuples as intact records.

The algorithm is a single finite effective program for each fixed \(Q,a\), with independent private random bits and no advice depending on \(m,p\) or the data. Its joint correctness/load event has probability at least \(1-p^{-2}\) on every instance. All constants in the displayed bound may depend on \(Q,a\), but not on relation contents, input size, machine count or initial partition. The one-machine case is trivial and does not affect the target. The source's polynomial slack condition \(p^3\le m\) is retained rather than enlarged to all machine counts.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the quantified existence assertion. A positive answer must cover every fixed schema, arbitrary data skew and every valid initial distribution, with the required full output and simultaneous round/load guarantee. A negative answer must show that the target fails for at least one fixed schema in the general-message model. An impossibility restricted to transmitting whole tuples or to a single round is insufficient. This is a binary resource-existence question; no numerical \(1/100\) approximation convention relaxes its bound or exact join output on successful runs.

context_blocks.text: The source focuses on data complexity: a schema is fixed, while its input relations grow. It measures communication received by the busiest machine, and treats local processing and emission of output tuples as free. Its binary-relation result uses three rounds and the edge-cover load scale up to polylogarithmic factors.

The source distinguishes one-round bounds from constant-round algorithms. Its one-round structural parameter can exceed the fractional edge-cover number, so a one-round lower bound does not answer the multiround question.

The later JACM result gives a cyclic boat schema with \(\rho=2\) for which tuple-based algorithms need load \(\Omega(m/p^{1/3})\) in the relevant machine regime. This exceeds the proposed scale \(\widetilde O(m/p^{1/2})\). The restriction to tuple-based algorithms is explicit in both its model and theorem.

In that restricted model, input rows are atoms, and reporting an output tuple requires receiving all of its input witnesses. This card allows arbitrary encodings and inferences instead. Consequently the published restricted lower bound is not presented as a refutation of the selected target.

The same JACM article obtains the edge-cover scale for acyclic joins and distinguishes their behavior from cyclic queries in the tuple-based setting. Thus the failure of the universal tuple-based claim does not negate the established special cases.

The March 2026 κ-Join preprint gives a schema-dependent load bound based on a reduced quasi vertex-cover parameter. It conjectures matching lower bounds for tuple-based algorithms and explicitly says that general tightness remains unresolved. It does not establish the claimed edge-cover bound for arbitrary coded messages.

cards.title: Register space of obstruction-free set agreement
cards.formal: For every integer pair \(n>k\ge1\), determine \(R(n,k)\), the minimum number of shared atomic read/write registers sufficient for deterministic obstruction-free one-shot \(k\)-set agreement among \(n\) named processes with input domain \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), in the model below. Supply a real-valued function approximating \(R\) with pointwise absolute error at most \(1/100\) registers throughout this domain.
cards.definitions:
Fix \(n>k\ge1\). There are \(n\) processes with distinct known identifiers \(1,\ldots,n\); each knows \(n,k\) and initially knows only its own input in \([n]\), not other processes' inputs. A protocol may depend on \(n,k\), and is given by finite deterministic programs with unbounded private storage and no bound on finite local computation. No uniform procedure generating protocols for different \(n,k\) is required. A process may invoke the task at most once; it participates when it invokes, and may decide at most once, after which it stops. Any subset may participate.

The only communication is through a fixed array of \(r\ge0\) shared multiwriter/multireader registers with common names \(1,\ldots,r\). Every process can read and write every register. A register stores a finite binary string of unrestricted length; one atomic read returns its entire current string, and one atomic write replaces that string. Initial shared contents may depend on \(n,k\) and the protocol but are fixed independently of the input assignment and participation. All shared storage is in these counted registers. A scheduled process takes a local computation step, including invocation or decision, or performs one atomic read or write with a finite local update; no stronger shared primitive, random choice, clock, or failure detector is supplied.

An execution is any finite or infinite interleaving of such steps; a process may stop forever at any point, representing a crash, with no fairness or timing assumption. In every finite execution prefix, each decided value must be the input proposed by a process that has already invoked, and at most \(k\) distinct values may have been decided.

Obstruction-freedom requires that, from every reachable configuration, every participating undecided process \(p\) decides after finitely many further own steps if only \(p\) is scheduled thereafter. Other processes may subsequently resume, so safety must also hold under every extension. Register widths, private storage and running time are uncharged.

Define \(R(n,k)\) as the least integer \(r\) for which a protocol satisfies these requirements for every assignment of inputs and every schedule. A finite sufficient \(r\) is known, so this minimum exists.
cards.why: This measures how much shared memory is intrinsically needed for synchronization when processes may disagree on a bounded number of proposed values. Resolving the gap would connect the solvability of agreement tasks to their exact memory requirements, even under the weak guarantee of eventual progress in isolation.

context_blocks.text: The known bounds are \(\lceil n/k\rceil\le R(n,k)\le n-k+1\). The lower bound applies to named processes; the upper bound is achieved even by anonymous processes, so it also applies here. Both ends of the parameter range are determined: \(R(n,1)=n\) and \(R(n,n-1)=2\). In the interior, the general bounds can leave a substantial gap.

The upper-bound algorithm uses exactly \(n-k+1\) physical read/write registers, including the implementation of the snapshots appearing in its presentation. The resource is the number of arbitrarily large registers, not their combined bit capacity. The repeated version, in which processes solve a sequence of agreement instances, already has the exact bound \(n-k+1\); this card concerns one invocation per process.

Ellen, Gelashvili and Zhu conjecture in the preprint that the exact register requirement for \(x\)-obstruction-free \(k\)-set agreement is \(n-k+x\), for \(1\le x\le k<n\). Here \(x\)-obstruction-freedom means that all sufficiently active processes finish whenever at most \(x\) processes continue taking steps. The present question fixes \(x=1\) and asks for the full optimal function, an editorial broadening of the resulting conjecture \(R(n,k)=n-k+1\). It also accepts a determination that refutes that conjecture.

The OPODIS 2025 paper published in January 2026 still lists the same lower and upper bounds for the n-valued problem. Its results about different wait-free tasks do not close this gap. Bounds for swap or other stronger shared objects concern different computational models.

A second paper published in January 2026 continues to state the same register-space bounds while studying limitations of particular classes of impossibility proofs. It does not determine the register-space function.

cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguously specified real-valued function \(g\) on all integer pairs \(n>k\ge1\), and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|g(n,k)-R(n,k)|\le1/100\) throughout the domain, with error measured in registers and \(R\) defined by the stated model. The approximation need not be integer-valued. A certified interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies through its midpoint. Exact determination also qualifies. A finite table, an asymptotic estimate, or unmatched bounds outside this precision do not meet the criterion; merely restating the defining minimization does not specify a determination.

The 1/100 tolerance is the atlas acceptance rule, not a tolerance proposed by these papers.

cards.title: Bipartite maximal matching with polynomial-in-degree volume
cards.formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C>0\), \(k\in\mathbb N\) and one uniform deterministic local-query algorithm which, on every finite simple bipartite graph of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), answers each vertex query after visiting at most \(C(\Delta+1)^k\) distinct vertices, such that all answers together specify one maximal matching? A proper two-coloring of the input graph is supplied. The bound has no dependence on the number \(n\) of graph vertices.
cards.definitions: The input is a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(n=|V|\ge1\), an integer bound \(\Delta\ge1\) with \(\deg(v)\le\Delta\) for all vertices, an injective identifier map \(V\to[n^2]\), and a proper coloring \(\chi:V\to\{0,1\}\) satisfying \(\chi(u)\ne\chi(v)\) on every edge. At each vertex \(v\), the incident edges have an arbitrary fixed bijective port numbering by \(\{1,\ldots,\deg(v)\}\); the two endpoints’ port numbers need not agree. A query rooted at \(v\) initially knows only \(n,\Delta\), the identifier, degree and color of \(v\), and its port index set. Its visited set starts as \(\{v\}\). It can adaptively probe port \(j\) of any visited vertex \(w\), thereby learning the corresponding neighbor \(u\), its identifier, degree, color and the reciprocal port of that edge at \(u\). This adds \(u\) to the visited set. Revisited vertices are recognized by their identifiers and counted only once. A probe does not reveal unvisited vertices behind other ports. The explored vertices form a connected set; direct probes of arbitrary identifiers are forbidden. The volume is the number of distinct visited vertices, including the root, at termination. Temporary memory and local computation are unrestricted but finite. Each rooted query starts afresh, with no preprocessing, shared mutable state or information retained from earlier queries. One finite deterministic program must work for all sizes, degree bounds, graphs, identifier assignments, port orders and supplied proper colorings. It receives no advice or randomness. It outputs either an unmatched symbol \(\bot\) or one local port at its root. For the outputs to describe a matching, whenever \(v\) selects its port leading to \(u\), the separate query at \(u\) must select the reciprocal port leading to \(v\). Let \(M\) be the selected undirected edges. Maximality requires that every edge in \(E\) has an endpoint incident to an edge of \(M\). Equivalently, no further edge can be added to \(M\) while keeping all selected edges vertex-disjoint. Maximum cardinality is not required. The same matching must result for every order of queries, and repeating a query must give the same answer. The constants \(C,k\) are independent of all input parameters, including \(\Delta\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction and correctness/volume proof for the quantified algorithm, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A negative result must rule out every universal polynomial degree bound for every correct uniform deterministic algorithm in this connected, stateless model. An algorithm with a factor depending on \(n\), randomized or expected volume guarantees, an oracle allowing arbitrary jumps, a method requiring preprocessing, or an approximation to maximum matching that need not be maximal does not establish the positive statement. A linear-in-degree lower bound alone does not establish the negative statement.
cards.why: This asks how much graph information is needed to answer a single matching query while remaining consistent with all other answers. A polynomial degree bound would give a deterministic local oracle for a basic graph primitive with cost independent of graph size. A superpolynomial lower bound would separate this information requirement from the known linear dependence on degree in communication rounds.

cards.title: Superlinear local certificates for hereditary graph classes
cards.formal:
Does there exist an isomorphism-invariant hereditary class \(\mathcal C\) of finite simple undirected graphs, with connected members of arbitrarily large order, and a fixed real exponent \(c>1\), such that every correct one-round proof-labeling scheme for membership in \(\mathcal C\) has worst-case certificate size \(\Omega(n^c)\) bits per vertex on connected \(n\)-vertex inputs?

More explicitly, for the optimal accepting-certificate size \(s_A(n)\) of a fixed correct local verifier \(A\), as defined below, require
\[\exists\mathcal C\;\exists c>1\;\forall A\text{ correct for }\mathcal C\;\exists a_A>0\;\exists N_A\;\forall n\ge N_A:\ s_A(n)\ge a_A n^c.\]
The exponent and graph class are common to all verifiers. This asks for a polynomial gap above linear certificate size, not merely for a bound that grows faster than \(n\).
cards.why: The question asks whether vertex-deletion stability imposes a fundamental information limit on distributed proofs. A polynomially superlinear example or a general obstruction would clarify how far local verification of structural graph properties can depart from the linear examples now known.
cards.status_note: Explicitly source-open in MFCS 2024 and still explicitly asked in the full arXiv v5 revision of 24 February 2026. On 16 September 2026 the review checked both versions’ local-verifier definitions, Theorem 3.1 and the exact final superlinear question, with the current arXiv revision history confirmed. Bounded subsequent-result searches found no matching hereditary-class resolution. This is current source evidence through the checked revision, not an exhaustive certification of all later literature.

cards.definitions:
A graph class is a set of finite simple undirected graphs invariant under relabelling of vertices. It is hereditary if \(G\in\mathcal C\) implies \(G[U]\in\mathcal C\) for every subset \(U\subseteq V(G)\), where \(G[U]\) retains exactly the edges of \(G\) with both endpoints in \(U\). The class is fixed independently of input size. Membership is certified only on nonempty connected input graphs, as in the source. Closure under induced subgraphs is a property of the full class, including disconnected graphs; it does not require certifying disconnected networks. Requiring arbitrarily large connected members excludes vacuous lower bounds. Such a hereditary class has connected members of every positive order, by taking connected induced subgraphs of larger connected members.

On an \(n\)-vertex input graph, each vertex has a distinct positive integer identifier from \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\), in binary. These are arbitrary identifiers, not part of the graph property. This fixes the source's polynomial-size identifier convention. Every completeness and soundness condition holds for every permitted identifier assignment. The prover knows the entire labelled graph and assigns a finite binary string \(\sigma(v)\in\{0,1\}^{*}\) to every vertex. Certificates may depend on the graph and its identifiers. Their cost is the maximum length at a vertex, \(\max_v|\sigma(v)|\), not the sum of all certificate lengths.

The same deterministic local verifier \(A\) is used at every vertex, on every input size and every certificate assignment. At a vertex \(v\), it sees its own identifier and certificate, and the identifiers and certificates of its immediate neighbors, with the center distinguished. It has no information about edges among neighbors, about more distant vertices, or about a geometric representation of the graph. It outputs either accept or reject. This is the one-round proof-labeling model: certificates are assigned once and examined locally, without further interaction with the prover. The graph order is not supplied as extra global information. There is no randomization or acceptance error.

As in the source's definition, a verifier and prover are mathematical functions with no computational resource bound. The quantity measures the amount of local information, not the running time of deciding a local predicate; no separate computability or recognition-time requirement is imposed on the graph class or those functions. This convention is what makes the source's universal quadratic upper bound applicable to arbitrary graph classes. A scheme must still satisfy both exact logical requirements:
\[G\in\mathcal C\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists\sigma\;\forall v\in V(G):\ A(v,\sigma)=\mathrm{accept},\]
\[G\notin\mathcal C\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall\sigma\;\exists v\in V(G):\ A(v,\sigma)=\mathrm{reject}.\]
These quantify over every connected input and every valid identifier assignment. In the second condition the adversarial strings may be of any finite length; soundness is not restricted to certificates obeying an advertised short length. The prover is untrusted, and acceptance means that every vertex accepts.

For a fixed correct verifier \(A\) and a connected yes-instance \((G,\mathrm{id})\), let
\[\ell_A(G,\mathrm{id})=\min_{\sigma:\ \forall v\ A(v,\sigma)=\mathrm{accept}}\ \max_{v\in V(G)}|\sigma(v)|.\]
Completeness makes this a finite nonnegative integer. Define
\[s_A(n)=\max_{\substack{|V(G)|=n,\ G\in\mathcal C,\ G\text{ connected}\\ \mathrm{id}:V(G)\hookrightarrow\{1,\ldots,n^2\}}}\ell_A(G,\mathrm{id}).\]
Only finitely many labelled graphs and identifier assignments occur at a fixed \(n\), so the maximum is well-defined; if the set is empty it is defined as zero. The target's \(\Omega(n^c)\) means the displayed eventual bound for every sufficiently large integer \(n\). The verifier is fixed before taking the asymptotic limit; a different verifier for each size is not allowed. Since the prover may choose the shortest accepting certificates, this rules out cheap schemes rather than merely identifying inefficient choices of proof.

The source also asks whether the witnessing class can be monotone, meaning closed under all subgraphs obtained by deleting edges as well as vertices. Monotone classes are hereditary, so such an example would satisfy this card's main target, but edge-deletion closure is not required. The source's hereditary question is the main proposition; its stronger parenthetical variant remains context. The stronger locally-checkable-proof model additionally lets a vertex inspect the entire induced graph on its closed neighborhood. The known lower bounds in the paper hold even in that model, but the target here uses its stated proof-labeling model.

To refute the proposition, one must rule out a common positive polynomial gap for every hereditary class in the stated domain. Formally, for each such \(\mathcal C\) and each \(c>1\), there must be a correct verifier \(A\) for which \(s_A(n)\) is not \(\Omega(n^c)\): for every \(a>0\) and \(N\), some \(n\ge N\) has \(s_A(n)<a n^c\). A universal near-linear upper bound would suffice, but the logical negation does not require that particular stronger result.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the quantified existence statement. A positive answer must specify a hereditary class and one exponent \(c>1\), verify the closure and unbounded connected-member conditions, and prove the per-vertex lower bound against every correct verifier in the stated model, even when the prover chooses its best certificates. A negative answer must prove the logical negation for every admissible hereditary class and exponent. A linear lower bound, a bound such as \(n\log n\), a total-certificate lower bound spread over many vertices, or a lower bound for one selected verifier is insufficient. Computational hardness of centralized recognition alone is not a local certificate-size lower bound in this unrestricted-computation model. The target is an exact asymptotic proposition; numerical tolerance does not apply.

source_formulation.text: After proving the first linear local-certificate lower bounds for nontrivial hereditary and monotone graph classes, the authors ask whether some hereditary class has a lower bound with a fixed exponent strictly greater than one, and ask additionally whether it can be monotone.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the final question in MFCS 2024 §8, retained in the February 2026 full revision; the main hereditary variant is preserved

context_blocks.text: A short global proof can be difficult to verify when its readers only see neighboring pieces. Local certification asks how much evidence must be copied or distributed to individual vertices so that all honest instances are accepted and every false instance is rejected somewhere.

Hereditary properties survive deleting vertices. Many geometric intersection classes have this stability: deleting objects leaves a representation of the induced subgraph. The closure condition distinguishes this question from large lower bounds for properties that depend on a particular global size or symmetry.

The source proves linear lower bounds for several geometric classes, including penny graphs, graphs that are subgraphs of the square grid, and 1-planar graphs. These supply substantial examples at the linear threshold but do not establish a fixed exponent \(c>1\).

Theorem 3.1 bounds the local complexity of a connected graph class by \(\log_2|\mathcal C_n|+O(\log n)\), where \(\mathcal C_n\) is its set of isomorphism types with \(n\) vertices. Thus the number of possible graphs in a class gives a general information bound, and every class has an \(O(n^2)\) upper bound. The question concerns where hereditary classes can lie inside this range.

The known examples illustrate how sensitive local evidence can be to the graph property: planar graphs have logarithmic-size certificates, whereas the source proves a linear bound for 1-planar graphs. A 1-planar graph admits a drawing with at most one crossing on each edge. This comparison concerns certificate size even though local computation is unrestricted.

The full February 2026 revision retains the superlinear question. It also keeps the stronger neighborhood-inspection model separate from ordinary proof labeling. This review fixes the latter and records the stronger known lower-bound scope without changing the target.

cards.title: Parallel sampling of planar perfect matchings
cards.formal:
Do there exist constants \(C,k\ge1\) and a uniform family of randomized Boolean circuits \((A_{n,t})_{n\ge0,t\ge1}\) that, for every simple unweighted planar graph \(G\) on \([n]\) with at least one perfect matching, output a distribution \(\mu_{G,t}\) satisfying
\[
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu_{G,t},U_G)\le2^{-t},
\]
with circuit size at most \(C(n+2^t+2)^k\) and depth at most \(C(\log_2(n+2)+t)^k\)?
Here \(U_G\) is uniform over all perfect matchings of \(G\), and the complete input, output, uniformity and failure conventions are defined below. The same constants and uniform circuit generator must work for every graph and precision. This is the user-selected approximately uniform RNC sampling target.
cards.why: This is a concrete test of whether counting and sampling remain equivalent under strong parallel-time constraints. Planarity makes exact counting tractable, so the remaining issue isolates the cost of coordinating random choices rather than the hardness of evaluating the partition function. A resolution would clarify a central boundary in parallel randomized algorithms.
cards.status_note: Open in the inspected November 2025 autospeculation preprint, which explicitly distinguishes parallel planar matching sampling from already parallelizable counting. The source reports a soft-O(n^(1/4)) expected parallel-time application, still above the polylogarithmic target. The 2024 RNC results for Eulerian tours and asymmetric determinantal processes resolve other parts of the inherited broad direction. A bounded search on 16 September 2026 found no resolution of the selected planar approximate-sampling assertion. The June 2026 weighted counting paper concerns arithmetic operation counts and does not settle this target. This review checked model definitions and result scopes, not all source proofs or a Lean formalization.

cards.definitions:
A graph is finite, undirected, loopless and without parallel edges; its vertices are \([n]\). Planarity means it admits an embedding in the plane with edges meeting only at shared endpoints. The input is the upper-triangular Boolean adjacency matrix in the lexicographic order of unordered vertex pairs. An embedding is not supplied. The promise is that the graph is planar and has at least one perfect matching. Inputs outside this promise still obey the resource bounds, but carry no distributional correctness requirement.

A perfect matching is a set of present edges incident to every vertex exactly once. Write \(\mathcal M(G)\) for this finite nonempty set and \(U_G(M)=1/|\mathcal M(G)|\) for \(M\in\mathcal M(G)\). The empty graph has the single empty perfect matching. Disconnected promised graphs are allowed; no bipartiteness, positive-degree lower bound or edge weights are assumed.

The accuracy parameter is a positive integer \(t\), defining error \(\varepsilon=2^{-t}\). These dyadic errors specify arbitrary requested accuracy up to a factor of two. Each circuit has the adjacency bits as ordinary inputs and independent unbiased random bits as additional inputs. Gates are AND and OR of fan-in two and NOT of fan-in one, together with constants; fan-out is unrestricted. Size counts gates, random inputs and output wires. Depth is the longest gate path and is a worst-case bound, independent of the random bits. The output consists of an edge-incidence vector indexed by all unordered vertex pairs and a failure flag. A nonmatching vector or a raised failure flag is interpreted as the single symbol \(\bot\).

Both output measures live on the finite set \(\mathcal M(G)\cup\{\bot\}\), with \(U_G(\bot)=0\), and
\[
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu,U_G)=\frac12\sum_{z\in\mathcal M(G)\cup\{\bot\}}|\mu(z)-U_G(z)|.
\]
Thus failure probability is charged to the error and the approximation is unconditional; conditioning on success cannot conceal a large failure probability. The graph itself is fixed when taking this distribution.

Uniformity means that one deterministic machine, given unary \(n\) and unary \(2^t\), generates the description of \(A_{n,t}\) using \(O(\log(n+2)+t)\) work space and polynomial time in \(n+2^t\). Padding the inverse-accuracy parameter states precisely the permitted polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\); it does not require a bound polynomial merely in its binary bit length. No graph-dependent advice, counting oracle or exact-real random primitive is free. The circuit must implement all needed computation. Boolean depth and size give a precise standard parallel model corresponding to polynomially many bit processors. For inverse-polynomial error, the displayed bounds are polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth in graph size.

The generator, constants and exponent are chosen before \(n,t,G\). An affirmative answer is one such family. A negative answer is the full negation over all uniform families and fixed constants. Finding one perfect matching or computing their number is not the requested sampling task. The source's broader list of determinant-counted objects has been narrowed to this one user-selected graph distribution.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked construction and proof of the asserted uniform circuit family, including worst-case depth, size, fair-bit implementation and the total-variation bound for every promised graph and every \(t\ge1\); or prove the full negation of that existence assertion. A result only about counting, finding one matching, a restricted graph family, conditional-on-success accuracy or sublinear but non-polylogarithmic depth is insufficient. The explicit sampling error \(2^{-t}\), not the default tolerance for numerical-value answers, governs this proposition. An experimental sampler or citation alone is not a Lean proof.

cards.title: Polynomial-in-optimum graph matching in \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\)
cards.formal:
Do there exist constants \(c,\alpha>0\) and a DLOGTIME-uniform family of deterministic Boolean circuits \((C_n)_{n\ge1}\), of constant depth and polynomial size, such that every finite simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is mapped to a matching \(M(G)\subseteq E(G)\) satisfying
\[
|M(G)|\ \ge\ c\,\nu(G)^\alpha?
\]
Here \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum cardinality of a matching in \(G\). The same constants and circuit family must work for all \(n\) and all graphs. The output must identify the actual chosen edges. The scale \(c\,\nu^\alpha\), and the restriction to graph matching rather than general set packing, were explicitly selected by the user.
cards.why: A matching requires many output decisions to be mutually consistent: selected edges may not share vertices. cards.definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph has no loops or parallel edges. Its input is its \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix \(A\), in row-major order, with \(A_{ii}=0\), \(A_{ij}=A_{ji}\in\{0,1\}\), and \(A_{ij}=1\) exactly when \(\{i,j\}\in E(G)\). Thus \(C_n\) has \(n^2\) input bits. Correctness is required on every valid adjacency matrix; behavior on other bit strings is unrestricted.

The circuit has \(n^2\) output bits, interpreted as a matrix \(B\) in the same order. It must satisfy \(B_{ii}=0\), \(B_{ij}=B_{ji}\le A_{ij}\), and, for every vertex \(i\), at most one \(B_{ij}\) is one. The represented matching is
\[
M(G)=\{\{i,j\}:i<j,\ B_{ij}=1\}.
\]
A matching is any collection of edges with pairwise disjoint endpoint sets, and \(\nu(G)=\max\{|M|:M\text{ is a matching in }G\}\). This counts edges, not covered vertices. For an edgeless graph \(\nu(G)=0\), and the output is the empty matching; use \(0^\alpha=0\).

The permitted internal gates are AND and OR of unbounded fan-in and NOT of fan-in one, together with constant zero and one. Circuits are finite directed acyclic graphs; wires may fan out to many gates. There are fixed integers \(D,k\ge1\) and a constant \(K\ge1\) such that every \(C_n\) has depth at most \(D\) and at most \(K(n+1)^k\) gates and wires. Depth is the maximum number of internal gates on any input-to-output path. The circuits receive no randomness, advice or auxiliary graph information.

DLOGTIME uniformity means that the circuits admit gate addresses of \(O(\log(n+2))\) bits and a single deterministic random-access Turing machine describing their local wiring in \(O(\log(n+2))\) time. Given \(n\) in binary and gate addresses, it decides whether an address is valid, the gate type, and whether a directed wire joins two addressed gates; it also identifies the designated input and output gate for an addressed matrix coordinate. Random access means that the machine can query an input bit using its binary address. The machine and constants are independent of \(n\) and of the input graph. Hardwiring a separate arbitrary circuit description for each \(n\) is not uniformity.

The constants \(c,\alpha\) do not depend on \(n\) or on \(\nu(G)\). One may equivalently require rational \(0<c,\alpha\le1\): decreasing either positive constant preserves the assertion for integer \(\nu(G)\ge1\), and \(|M(G)|\le\nu(G)\) rules out a persistent exponent greater than one on graphs with unbounded optimum. The condition asks for a positive power of the optimum; it is not an assertion of a fixed ratio \(|M(G)|/\nu(G)\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of this exact existence assertion. A positive answer must specify the uniform circuit family and fixed constants and prove circuit size, depth, uniformity, output validity and the cardinality inequality for every graph. A negative answer must refute all choices of positive constants and all allowed circuit families. This binary question has no numerical \(1/100\) tolerance. Producing only an estimate of \(\nu(G)\), proving a limitation of monotone circuits, or handling a restricted input class alone does not meet this target.

cards.title: Deterministic linearizable objects for set agreement
cards.formal: Is it true that, for every pair of integers \(n>k>2\), no deterministic linearizable \((n,k)\)-set agreement object is computationally equivalent to the \((n,k)\)-set agreement task? The quantifier includes every proposal domain I with at least n values and every n-ported object satisfying the definitions below. Equivalence means mutual implementation with atomic read/write registers by deterministic wait-free algorithms. The object may depend on n,k and I, may use the chosen port in determining a response, and may be invoked repeatedly; it is not restricted to one call per port.
cards.why: Tests whether deterministic sequential semantics inevitably add coordination power to reusable set agreement objects, clarifying the relation between one-shot tasks and composable shared-memory abstractions.
cards.status_note: Read the OPODIS definitions and conclusion and the cited DISC 2017 implementation model. Checked the publisher’s 2020 Life beyond set agreement abstract and subsequent-work searches through 12 September 2026. No resolution of the universal \(n>k>2\) statement was located. The later paper was checked at the abstract/model-note level, not by a full proof review; searches are not exhaustive.

references.title: On Deterministic Linearizable Set Agreement Objects

cards.definitions: The system consists of asynchronous processes with distinct identities communicating through shared objects and atomic read/write registers. A process can crash by stopping permanently. Algorithms must be correct for every schedule and every pattern of such crashes. Wait freedom means each operation or task invocation of a process that continues taking steps completes after finitely many of its own steps, regardless of the speeds or failures of other processes; no fixed complexity bound is requested. Reductions are deterministic: randomization is not available. The one-shot task \(T(n,k,I)\) has at most n participating processes, each supplying an input in I and deciding once. Every decision is an input supplied by a participant, at most k distinct values are decided, and every participant that continues taking steps must decide. No sequential ordering constraint is added to these task guarantees. An \((n,k)\)-set agreement object O has ports \(1,\ldots ,n\) and an operation \(ProposeSA(v), v\in I\). Each process chooses a port for each call and waits for its response before making another call. Access is well formed if no two pending calls use the same port. Ports are not permanently assigned to process identities; arbitrarily many processes may use the object over its lifetime, but at most n calls may be pending simultaneously. Only well-formed access is required to be implemented. On every such execution, each response is the current call’s proposal or a proposal of a previously invoked call, and across the entire execution at most k distinct values are returned. This agreement bound does not reset after a round or after all processes become idle. All invocations are supported and are wait-free. A finite sequential history S is a sequence of completed triples (port,proposal,response). Determinism requires that for every allowed S, port p and proposal v there is a unique response extending S by a call at p with v; different histories or ports may give different responses. Linearizability requires every concurrent history to admit an ordering of its operations that obeys this sequential specification and preserves real-time precedence: an operation whose response precedes another’s invocation must come first. Incomplete calls may be discarded or assigned responses before ordering them. To implement an object means to produce only its allowed histories, with the required termination, for all well-formed client executions; reproducing every allowed history is unnecessary. O and T are computationally equivalent when copies of O and registers can solve T, and O can be implemented from registers and instances of any correct solver for T. A task instance has n one-shot participant roles; separate instances have independent state, and the implementation must rely only on the task guarantees, not on additional agreement power a particular solver might possess. This is the source’s equivalence to the black-box set agreement task. Any number of fresh instances and registers is allowed; a completed operation uses finitely many steps. The object’s specified initial state is fixed independently of client inputs. O already solves T by one proposal per participant on distinct ports, so the substantive issue is whether a reduction from the task to O can exist.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that no such object and reverse wait-free implementation exist for every \(n>k>2\), or refute the statement by giving a pair \(n>k>2, a\) proposal domain with at least n values, a deterministic linearizable object and a correct wait-free implementation from the set agreement task and registers. A positive proof need not exhibit a stronger set agreement task: that is an additional conjectured explanation in the source, not a required proof method. Restricting objects to port-independent behavior or proving only some parameter pairs does not establish the universal claim.

cards.title: LOCAL lower bounds for 2-ruling sets
cards.formal:
Is it true that every randomized LOCAL algorithm \(A\) that computes a 2-ruling set on every \(n\)-vertex graph with global success probability at least \(1-1/n\), for all \(n\ge2\), has worst-case round complexity
\[
T_A(n)=\Omega\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log_2 n}{\log_2\log_2 n}}\right)?
\]
Precisely, the proposed assertion is that for every such \(A\) there are constants \(c_A>0\) and \(n_A\ge4\) such that the displayed lower bound with multiplier \(c_A\) holds for every integer \(n\ge n_A\). The maximum ranges over all simple graphs, legal identifier and port assignments, and random outcomes in the model below. No maximum-degree or arboricity restriction is imposed.
cards.why: The question tests how much a minimal relaxation of independence-based domination changes the locality of symmetry breaking. It separates the role of randomness, sparse structure and coverage radius from bandwidth restrictions, and would sharpen a central lower-bound boundary for distributed graph algorithms.
cards.status_note: The original source asks whether MIS lower bounds extend to 2-ruling sets. The user selected the unrestricted-graph randomized n-dependent bound stated here. The inspected 2020 lower-bound paper distinguishes deterministic and randomized guarantees; its deterministic bound is not a proof of this randomized assertion. The 14 September 2026 revision of the low-arboricity paper gives much faster algorithms on sparse graph classes and a separate arboricity-dependent bound, neither of which settles the selected worst case over all graphs. A bounded literature check on 16 September 2026 found no resolution of the precise selected target. Source theorem scopes were checked; full source proofs and a Lean formalization were not verified.

cards.definitions:
The communication network is a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(n=|V|\ge2\), possibly disconnected. Distance is the length of a shortest edge path and is infinite between different components. A 2-ruling set is a subset \(S\subseteq V\) with no edge joining two of its vertices and with every vertex at distance at most two from \(S\). In particular, isolated vertices must lie in \(S\). Maximal independent sets require distance at most one, which is a strictly stronger output condition.

Each vertex hosts a processor. Identifiers are an arbitrary injection \(V\to\{1,\ldots,n^3\}\). Each vertex's incident edges receive distinct local port numbers; the two port numbers on one edge need not agree. Initially a processor knows \(n\), its own identifier, its degree, its port numbers and its neighbors' identifiers, but not the whole graph. This fixes the usual polynomial identifier range and neighbor-knowledge convention. Giving neighbor identifiers initially changes the alternative convention by at most one communication round.

Processors execute the same finite algorithm, with identities and initial data as parameters. Rounds are synchronous: each processor performs finite local computation and sends one finite message of arbitrary length on each incident edge, and messages arrive by the end of the round. Local computation and memory are unrestricted and do not contribute to the round count. There are no additional communication links or free global coordination. Each vertex has its own independent stream of unbiased random bits; no correlated or graph-dependent advice is supplied.

Every processor must halt and irrevocably output a bit, marking membership in \(S\). Only algorithms with a finite deterministic worst-case round bound at each input size are under consideration. This is one global correctness event, not a separate success bound per vertex. The constant \(c_A\) and threshold \(n_A\) in the target may depend on the algorithm, but not on an input graph, identifier assignment or random outcome. Logarithms in the formula have base two and the lower-bound formula is used only for \(n\ge4\).

The source asks broadly about extending MIS lower bounds, including degree-dependent forms. The user explicitly selected only the displayed dependence on \(n\), on general graphs, with the stated high-probability guarantee. cards.title: Linear CONGEST lower bound with logarithmic LOCAL complexity
cards.formal: Do there exist a fixed maximum degree \(\Delta\), a locally checkable labeling problem \(\Pi\) on all connected simple graphs of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), and a deterministic LOCAL algorithm solving \(\Pi\) in \(O(\log N)\) rounds, such that every randomized CONGEST algorithm solving \(\Pi\) with global failure probability at most \(1/N\) requires \(\Omega(N)\) worst-case rounds? The common size parameter \(N\ge2\) is known to every vertex, and each algorithm must meet its guarantee on every input with at most \(N\) vertices. Use the models and quantifiers below; no additional promise on the graph or input labels is allowed.

source_formulation.text: More concretely, it is an open question whether there exists an LCL problem that is solvable in \(O(\log  n)\) rounds in the LOCAL model but […]

cards.why: Local verifiability limits what a problem can demand of a global solution, but it need not make that solution easy to construct with short messages. A logarithmic-versus-linear separation would show that bandwidth can cause a near-global delay even when graph distances and local verification permit a much faster solution. The requirement of one total bounded-degree LCL rules out explanations based on an arbitrary promise or an output whose size grows with the network.

The question asks for one problem that is solvable in logarithmic deterministic LOCAL time but needs linear randomized CONGEST time.
Both models communicate along the same bounded-degree graph, while CONGEST restricts each message to logarithmically many bits.
Such a result would isolate an extreme cost of bandwidth despite local verifiability of solutions.

cards.definitions: An LCL specification consists of an integer \(\Delta\ge1\), a radius \(r\ge1\), finite nonempty input and output alphabets \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{in}},\Sigma_{\mathrm{out}}\), and a finite list \(\mathcal C\) of permitted rooted radius-\(r\) neighborhoods with both input and output labels on every incidence \((v,e)\) where vertex \(v\) is an endpoint of edge \(e\). A radius-\(r\) neighborhood is the subgraph induced by vertices at graph distance at most \(r\) from its root; labels on incidences of its included edges are retained. An output is legal if every such rooted neighborhood is isomorphic to one in \(\mathcal C\), preserving roots and input/output labels. Identifiers, the parameter \(N\), and communication-port numbers are not part of this legality test. The problem must have a legal output for every connected simple graph of degree at most \(\Delta\) with every assignment of input incidence labels. All parts of the specification are fixed independently of the input size. Each vertex is a processor; each incident edge has a distinct local port number in \(\{1,\ldots,\deg(v)\}\), chosen arbitrarily. Initially a vertex knows only \(N\), its degree, its ports and its own incidence input labels, together with its identifier in the deterministic model. Communication uses only graph edges. In one synchronous round each vertex sends a separate message to each neighbor using only its state before the round; messages arrive at its end. LOCAL permits any finite message length. A CONGEST algorithm has a fixed integer bandwidth constant \(\beta\ge1\) and sends one padded string of at most \(\lceil\beta\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) bits per directed edge per round; the bound includes all protocol data. Local computation and memory are uncharged but finite and terminating, and each algorithm has one finite program independent of \(N\). The deterministic LOCAL algorithm must work for every injective assignment of identifiers from \(\{1,\ldots,N^3\}\). The randomized CONGEST algorithm receives no identifiers and uses mutually independent fair private random bits at the vertices, with some finite computable bound \(h_B(N)\) on the number used per vertex. It must finish within a deterministic round bound on every coin sequence, and for each graph, port assignment and input labeling, the probability that all output neighborhoods are legal is at least \(1-1/N\). Outputs are labels on the processor’s own incidences. Let \(t_B(N)\) be the maximum rounds until all vertices output, over all such inputs of size at most \(N\) and all coins. The claimed separation means there is one LOCAL algorithm and constant \(C\) with round bound \(C\log_2(N+2)\) for every \(N\), and, for every correct randomized CONGEST algorithm \(B\) with any fixed \(\beta\), there exist \(c_B>0,N_B\) such that \(t_B(N)\ge c_BN\) for all integers \(N\ge N_B\). The constants in the lower bound may depend on \(B\) and its bandwidth, but \(\Pi,\Delta,r\) and the alphabets are fixed first.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean either establishing this existence statement or proving its negation. An affirmative answer must provide the complete finite LCL specification, prove total solvability, give the deterministic logarithmic-round LOCAL algorithm, and prove the linear worst-case CONGEST lower bound against every randomized algorithm in the stated error and bandwidth model. A lower bound only for deterministic algorithms, a lower bound on a promised subfamily without a total LCL on all bounded-degree inputs, or an \(\Omega(N/\log N)\) bound does not meet the target. A negative answer must exclude every qualifying LCL, not merely the existing construction. No numerical tolerance replaces the required asymptotic bounds.

The authors’ known example has an \(O(\log N)\) deterministic LOCAL algorithm and an \(\Omega(\sqrt N/\log^2 N)\) randomized CONGEST lower bound. It establishes a genuine bandwidth effect but falls short of the linear lower bound requested here.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic-space streaming Euclidean MST estimation
cards.formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized one-pass insertion-only streaming algorithm A and absolute constants \(C\ge1\), \(K\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), \(d\ge1\), \(\Delta\ge2\), and every stream of n distinct points in \(\{0,\ldots,\Delta\}^{d}\), A uses at most
\[K\bigl(d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\lceil\log_2(\Delta+2)\rceil\bigr)^k\]
bits of working memory and returns a rational estimate Z satisfying
\[\Pr[\operatorname{MST}(X)\le Z\le C\operatorname{MST}(X)]\ge 2/3?\]
The stream order is arbitrary and fixed independently of the algorithm’s private random bits. The output estimates total Euclidean MST cost; it need not describe a tree. For polynomially bounded integer coordinates, the required space is \(\mathrm{poly}(d\log n)\), as in the community proposal.
cards.definitions:
The point set X consists of the n distinct inserted vectors. Coordinates are nonnegative integers given in binary, and the parameters n,d and the bound \(\Delta\) are supplied before the stream. The graph is complete on X; an edge between x and y has weight \(\|x-y\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^{d}(x_j-y_j)^2)^{1/2}\). The quantity \(\operatorname{MST}(X)\) is the minimum sum of edge weights over all spanning trees of this graph. It is a real number even though the input coordinates are integers.

The algorithm is one fixed finite probabilistic Turing-machine program with a read-once input stream, private independent fair random bits, working tapes, and an output tape used only for the final rational estimate. An input record may be buffered, with those bits charged to memory. All retained state, counters, random seeds and postprocessing workspace count toward the space bound, on every input and every random tape. Consumed input cannot be revisited, and there are no deletions, extra passes, random-order promise, external storage, nonuniform advice or real-number registers. The machine must halt on every random tape; no separate update-time or total-time bound is imposed. The probability is over its coins for each fixed stream. The constants and exponent do not depend on n,d or the coordinate bound.

Dependence polynomial in the bit length of coordinates makes the finite-input convention explicit. In particular, for each fixed integer b and \(\Delta\le n^b\), the bound has the proposal’s \(\mathrm{poly}(d\log n)\) form. The logarithmic coordinate factor is recorded rather than silently treating arbitrary reals as constant-size words. The target allows d to grow, including \(d=\Theta(\log n)\); a bound exponential in d does not qualify. The approximation constant can be any fixed finite C. Requiring the estimate to lie above the true cost is a normalization: a two-sided constant-factor estimate can be rescaled at the cost of changing C. Neither an explicit tree nor a \(1+\varepsilon\) approximation is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm satisfying the stated memory, pass and probability bounds for some absolute finite approximation constant, or prove the negation for every such algorithm and constants. An \(n^{\varepsilon}\)-space algorithm for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), a factor growing with n, a multiple-pass algorithm, or a lower bound excluding only constants near 1 does not settle this target.
cards.why: An MST measures the cost of connecting an entire geometric data set. A small summary that estimates this global quantity within a constant factor would clarify how much connectivity information survives a single streaming pass as dimension grows.

cards.title: Maximum independent set in the congested clique
cards.formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the minimum worst-case round complexity \(T_{\mathrm{MaxIS}}(n)\) for computing an exact maximum independent set of an arbitrary simple undirected graph on \(n\) labelled vertices in the deterministic unicast congested clique defined below. The output is distributed: each processor outputs the membership bit of its own vertex in one common maximum independent set. Local computation and storage have no resource bound, but each local computation must terminate. Only synchronous communication rounds are charged.
cards.definitions: For every integer \(n\ge2\), the vertices and processors have identifiers \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An input is a simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), represented at processor \(v\) by its \(n\)-bit incident-edge row. Initially each processor knows only this row, its own identifier, \(n\), all identifiers and the common protocol; it has no information about edges not incident to it. The communication network is complete, independently of \(E\). Let \(b(n)=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\). In each round and for each ordered pair of distinct processors, the sender supplies one \(b(n)\)-bit string; shorter payloads must use a fixed padded encoding within that string. Different recipients may receive different strings. All messages for a round depend only on the initial state and messages from earlier rounds, and arrive simultaneously at its end. Local computations are deterministic, with finite descriptions and arbitrary finite local memory; no random coins, advice depending on the input graph, or additional communication channel are available. For fixed \(n\), a protocol may depend on \(n\), but it must work for every labelled graph of that size. All processors must produce their final bits after at most its round bound; their set \(S\) must satisfy both independence, \(\{u,v\}\notin E\) for all distinct \(u,v\in S\), and optimality, \(|S|\ge |I|\) for every independent \(I\subseteq[n]\). Ties between maximum sets are unrestricted, provided the output bits describe one such set. Define \(T_{\mathrm{MaxIS}}(n)\) as the least integer round bound of any such protocol, taking the worst case over all input graphs. There is no promise on density or graph structure. This retains the earlier card’s deterministic, logarithmic-bandwidth specialization of the source’s broader question with bandwidth \(b\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous nonnegative asymptotic function \(f(n)\), a computably specified family of correct deterministic protocols, and a complete Lean-checked proof of constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\ge2\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\), the supplied protocol uses at most \(Cf(n)\) rounds on every input graph, while every correct protocol for that size needs at least \(cf(n)\) rounds on some graph. Thus \(T_{\mathrm{MaxIS}}(n)=\Theta(f(n))\) in precisely the stated model. The upper-bound family must be described by one finite procedure taking \(n\), whose local computation is uncharged. Logarithmically separated bounds, a conditional lower bound alone, approximate solutions, or maximal rather than maximum independent sets are insufficient. This is an asymptotic communication-complexity target; the numerical absolute-error convention does not apply to its big-Theta bounds.
cards.why: Exact independent set separates the cost of learning a global optimum from the cost of computing it once the input is known. cards.title: Streaming space for additive \(L_\infty\) estimation
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the optimal worst-case bit space for a one-pass randomized streaming algorithm that returns only an estimate \(z\) of \(\|f\|_\infty\), with \[\Pr\!\left[|z-\|f\|_\infty|\le\frac{\|f\|_p}{k}\right]\ge\frac23.\] The bound must describe its dependence on domain size \(n\ge2\), update budget \(M\ge2\), accuracy parameter \(k\ge4\), norm flag \(p\in\{1,2\}\), and update mode \(b\in\{\mathrm{insert},\mathrm{difference}\}\), in the model below.
cards.why: Separate the memory needed for one largest-magnitude estimate from the information needed to identify heavy coordinates, while accounting for error scale, domain size and cancellation.
