sentences: The output is a single estimate of the largest absolute coordinate of a streamed frequency vector.
The allowed additive error is one over k times the final L1 or L2 norm.
Insertion-only streams and signed differences of two streams are distinct modes of the same resource question.
The target is a tight bit-space characterization in the domain size, update budget and accuracy.
A 2016 paper reports resolving the insertion-only L1 part, while this review does not certify a complete characterization of all cases.

cards.definitions: Parameters \(n,M,k\) are integers supplied in binary before the stream, together with the two flags. The frequency vector starts at \(f=0\in\mathbb Z^n\). There are at most \(M\) updates \((i,\Delta)\), where \(1\le i\le n\). In insert mode every \(\Delta=1\); in difference mode \(\Delta\in\{-1,1\}\), and update \((i,\Delta)\) replaces \(f_i\) by \(f_i+\Delta\). Negative intermediate and final frequencies are allowed in difference mode. Equivalently, positively and negatively tagged insertions describe the difference of two streams, with their combined length bounded by \(M\). Only this bound, not the actual stream length, is known in advance. Set \(\|f\|_1=\sum_i|f_i|\), \(\|f\|_2=(\sum_i f_i^2)^{1/2}\), and \(\|f\|_\infty=\max_i|f_i|\). The additive tolerance is scaled by the final vector, not by the total number of updates; cancellation therefore matters. At the end, output one rational number \(z\) as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. No coordinate identity or list of heavy items is requested. On \(f=0\), the success event requires exactly \(z=0\). The fixed stream is chosen independently of the algorithm’s private independent fair random bits. There is one terminal query, with success at least \(2/3\) separately on every valid stream; there is no requirement of simultaneous success at all prefixes. Use a uniform randomized multitape streaming machine with one fixed finite program for all parameters, no advice, no public random table and no oracle. The parameter header is read-only. An update is available in a read-only buffer until the machine advances to the next update, after which earlier updates cannot be revisited. Every work-tape bit, stored random bit or seed, counter, index, table and input-dependent retained state counts toward space, including all scratch space used during processing and final decoding. Input and write-only output cells do not count; copies do. Address and head-position information accessible to the algorithm that can carry input-dependent state is charged. The unreadable physical position of the one-way stream is not work memory; the number of updates already consumed is not supplied as a free clock. Random bits cannot be reread unless retained. The machine must halt on every valid finite stream and every random tape; computation time is unrestricted. Space is the maximum number of charged bits over all such streams and random tapes for the given parameters, not its expectation. Bounds may be piecewise over parameter regimes and must use ordinary asymptotic notation with all logarithmic factors exposed. The reciprocal-integer accuracy convention \(\epsilon=1/k\), finite update budget, private randomness and bit accounting make the source’s qualitative space question precise.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a tight asymptotic space characterization across the complete parameter domain and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean. It must include uniform algorithms attaining the stated upper bounds, their terminal-error and worst-case-space guarantees, and matching lower bounds for every algorithm in the same model, up to constants independent of all parameters and flags. A one-sided bound, a bound only for identifying heavy items, a word count hiding bit costs, or a result for only one norm or update mode does not determine the whole characterization. This is an asymptotic resource target: the benchmark does not apply an additive 1/100 tolerance to big-O or big-Theta bounds.

context_blocks.text: The largest absolute frequency is a scalar statistic. Identifying which item attains it can require additional information about a large item domain. The source asks whether that distinction can reduce memory when an additive error measured against the full frequency vector is allowed.

The two norms specify different accuracy requirements. For \(f=(3,-2,0)\), the target value is three, while the error scale is either \(5/k\) or \(\sqrt{13}/k\). For a difference stream, many updates can cancel, so an error proportional to the number of processed updates can be much larger than the permitted error.

This card retains both error scales and both update settings from the source as flags in one space-complexity characterization. It asks for their full dependence on the domain, stream budget and accuracy, rather than for a new yes/no claim that every historical bound remains unimproved. The exact finite-input and randomness conventions are editorial specifications.

Bhattacharyya, Dey and Woodruff explicitly report answering the insertion-only \(L_1\)-error part of the 2006 question. For maximum-frequency estimation they report \(O(\epsilon^{-1}\log\epsilon^{-1}+\log n+\log\log t)\) bits, where \(t\) is the stream length, and describe optimality in their stated regimes. Their result is recorded as existing progress, not as an unsolved insertion-only endpoint.

That result does not by itself supply the \(L_2\)-relative or signed-difference cases. In particular, insertion-only \(\|f\|_1\) equals the number of updates, whereas cancellation destroys that equality in a difference stream. A theorem’s norm, update promise, scalar versus item output, and parameter restrictions must all match before it can be counted toward the full target.

The original page explicitly distinguishes bit space from a count of machine words: random-function descriptions and counters also consume memory. The reviewed card preserves that distinction. The requested comparison is therefore about complete memory usage, not only the number of stored counters.

A full characterization would identify which memory costs arise from maintaining frequency magnitudes and which arise from recovering item names. It would clarify the value of scalar summaries for comparing streams over large domains and the cost of allowing deletions or cancellation.

cards.definitions: The communication network is a finite undirected simple graph \(G=(V,E), |V|=n\ge 2\). Every edge has a supplied direction, known to its endpoints; no acyclicity is promised. A vertex’s outdegree is its number of outgoing edges, and every vertex has outdegree at most the supplied bound \(\beta\). Its indegree and total degree may be arbitrarily large. A proper coloring assigns each vertex a label from one common palette so that endpoints of every edge have different labels, regardless of the edge direction. Vertices execute the same deterministic algorithm in synchronous rounds, have unique identifiers of \(O(\log  n)\) bits, know their incident ports and edge directions, and may know n and \(\beta\). Each round allows a separate message of unbounded size to each neighbor in either direction and unrestricted finite local computation. Cost is worst-case round count over graphs, orientations and identifiers. No precomputed coloring or graph decomposition is supplied. The function f may grow arbitrarily fast with \(\beta\), but cannot depend on n, total degree or the orientation’s path lengths. Both the exponent improvement \(\varepsilon\) and the coefficient of \(\log * n\) must be uniform over \(\beta\) and n. Here \(\log * n\) is the number of repeated base-two logarithms needed to reach a value at most one. Edgeless graphs, including the \(\beta =0\) case, can be assigned one color separately.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of the uniform deterministic algorithm with the stated palette and additive round bound, or establish that no such \(\varepsilon\), constants, computable f and algorithm exist. A palette reduction by only logarithmic factors, a runtime depending on total degree, or a multiplicative log n term does not establish this claim.

cards.title: Polynomial-state protocols for Presburger arithmetic
cards.formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(C,k\) such that every Presburger formula \(\varphi(x_1,\ldots,x_d)\), including arbitrary nested quantifiers, has a leaderless pairwise population protocol \(P_\varphi\) with
\[
|Q_\varphi|\le C(1+|\varphi|)^k
\]
that computes its truth value on every input \(\mathbf a\in\mathbb N^d\) with \(\sum_i a_i\ge2\), reaching permanent unanimous agreement under every fair execution?
The size is that of the original quantified formula, using the syntax and encoding below. The constants are independent of the formula and population size. No running-time bound is required for constructing the protocol or for reaching consensus.
cards.why: The question compares the succinctness of logical descriptions with that of anonymous distributed computation. It asks whether quantifier compression forces an unavoidable increase in the number of local states, even when computation time is unrestricted. This separates representational power from synthesis and stabilization complexity.
cards.status_note: Open in the precise source distinction: STACS 2020 §7 asks for polynomial states in the original possibly quantified formula, while its main theorem covers the quantifier-free representation. The inspected 2024 fast-and-succinct result still measures a quantifier-free formula and does not establish the present bound before quantifier elimination. On 16 September 2026 a bounded later-work check found no resolution; the 2026 ordered-agent paper concerns a different model. This is an existential state-size question, not an efficient synthesis claim: the source separately proves a synthesis-time obstruction. Definitions and theorem scopes were inspected; full source proofs, exhaustive literature coverage and Lean formalization are not claimed.

Fast-and-succinct protocols improve the quantifier-free size/time tradeoff, without establishing a bound before quantifier elimination.
Ordered-agent protocols study additional interaction capabilities and therefore a different computational model.

cards.definitions:
All variables range over \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Formulas are finite syntax trees built from linear comparisons \(\sum_i c_i z_i>b\) and congruences \(\sum_i c_i z_i\equiv b\pmod m\), Boolean connectives \(\neg,\wedge,\vee\), and quantifiers \(\exists z,\forall z\). Coefficients and thresholds are integers, and a congruence modulus is an integer \(m\ge2\). A congruence asserts integer divisibility of the difference by \(m\). Comparisons and sums are evaluated in the integers; quantified values remain nonnegative. Equality and other order relations are expressible using these primitives. Coefficient multiplication is by fixed encoded integers, not multiplication of two variables. Remainder atoms are the standard definitional extension used by the source.

The formula has a declared list of \(d\ge1\) free input variables. A sentence can be treated as independent of one dummy input variable. Encode the original syntax tree explicitly, with operator tags, parentheses or equivalent delimiters, variable binding/index information, and signed binary coefficients, thresholds and moduli. The size \(|\varphi|\) is the total bit length, including the free-variable list. Subexpressions are written at each occurrence; there are no shared circuit nodes, macros hiding large formulas, or uncharged quantifier elimination. Standard explicit encodings of this syntax are polynomially interconvertible, so the existence of some polynomial state bound is independent of their routine delimiter choices.

A leaderless pairwise population protocol consists of a finite state set \(Q\), an input map \(\iota:\{1,\ldots,d\}\to Q\), an output map \(o:Q\to\{0,1\}\), and a finite transition relation \(T\). A transition replaces a multiset of exactly two states by another multiset of exactly two states. Thus a rule may have the form \(\{p,q\}\to\{r,s\}\), allowing equal states; two occurrences of a state require two distinct agents in that state. Include the identity rule for every two-state multiset, so every configuration of at least two agents admits an infinite execution. Multiple rules with the same input multiset are allowed and are resolved by the scheduler. All agents are anonymous; there are no identifiers, order comparisons, extra leaders, initially supplied helper agents, or a known bound on the population.

A configuration is a multiplicity vector \(D:Q\to\mathbb N\). A rule with input multiset \(u\) and output multiset \(v\) is enabled when \(D\ge u\) coordinatewise and then produces \(D-u+v\). The input \(\mathbf a=(a_1,\ldots,a_d)\) gives exactly
\[
D_{\mathbf a}(q)=\sum_{\{i:\iota(i)=q\}}a_i
\]
agents in each state \(q\), with no additive initial population. Total population size is conserved. As in the source, correctness is required for all inputs with at least two agents; the zero-agent and one-agent cases are outside this protocol convention.

Write \(D\to^*E\) for reachability by finitely many legal transitions, including zero transitions. An infinite execution \(D_0,D_1,\ldots\) is globally fair if, for every configuration \(E\), whenever the set \(\{j:D_j\to^*E\}\) is infinite, the set \(\{j:D_j=E\}\) is also infinite. This is the source's configuration-reachability fairness, not merely the requirement that each pair of agent identities meet infinitely often.

The protocol computes \(\varphi\) when, for every allowed input and every fair execution starting at \(D_{\mathbf a}\), there is a finite index \(J\) such that for every \(j\ge J\) and every occupied state \(q\), \(o(q)\) equals the Boolean truth value of \(\varphi(\mathbf a)\). All agents must agree thereafter; they need not detect stabilization or stop interacting. The stabilization index can depend on both input and execution.

The resource being minimized is the number of states available to one agent, \(|Q|\), not its bit logarithm, the number of agents, or the time to consensus. Protocol descriptions depend on \(\varphi\) but not on its input vector. All transition rules are explicit finite rules; pairwise state semantics cannot hide an oracle for the predicate. The same \(C,k\) work for all formulas. The assertion is purely existential and does not add an efficient uniform synthesis procedure.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated uniform polynomial bound. An affirmative proof must establish one pair \(C,k\) and the existence, for every original quantified formula, of a protocol with the required state count, leaderless initialization and correctness on every fair execution for every allowed input. A negative proof must establish the negation of that quantified assertion. A polynomial bound only after quantifier elimination, a protocol using extra leaders, or a lower bound only on construction time does not answer this target. No numerical tolerance changes the proposition, and no Lean proof is supplied merely by specifying a finite transition table.

context_blocks.text: Population protocols distribute computation among anonymous agents with a fixed finite repertoire of states. They determine properties of the initial counts of input types. Presburger arithmetic describes exactly the predicates computable in this model, but that expressiveness theorem does not determine how many states a short logical specification requires.

The 2020 theorem gives polynomially many states for quantifier-free combinations of linear thresholds and congruences. A quantified formula can be much shorter than a formula obtained by eliminating its quantifiers. Consequently, applying the known theorem to an expanded quantifier-free formula does not establish a polynomial bound in the original input size.

The source also distinguishes small protocols from efficiently finding them. The present target asks whether small protocols exist; its affirmative answer would not include a polynomial-time synthesis algorithm or a convergence-time guarantee. Later fast-and-succinct results strengthen the quantifier-free case, and their input-size parameter remains crucial.

Recent protocols over ordered agents allow interactions to inspect extra positional information. That changes the anonymous model specified here and does not provide an answer to this state-complexity question.

cards.title: Subpolynomial detection of two-connected patterns
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed finite simple 2-vertex-connected graph H, with at least three vertices, for which exact H-subgraph detection in the randomized CONGEST model can be solved in \(n^{o(1)}\) rounds on every n-vertex network? The pattern is fixed independently of n. Detection means that, with probability at least \(2/3\), every node outputs NO when the network contains no copy of H, and at least one node outputs YES when it does contain a copy.
cards.why: Asks whether any cyclic pattern can be detected almost as quickly as trees under per-edge communication limits. A resolution would clarify a broad boundary in distributed graph algorithms, and its negative direction includes the difficult triangle-detection barrier.
cards.status_note: Read the original question and surrounding graph-class interpretation; checked the 2025 survey’s standard output convention and the newer triangle lower bound. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no subpolynomial algorithm for an eligible pattern or a resolution excluding all of them. The reported logarithmic triangle bound does not prove polynomial hardness. Proofs were not independently audited.

references.title: Lower Bounds for Subgraph Detection in the CONGEST Model

cards.definitions:
The pattern H is an undirected finite simple graph. It is 2-vertex-connected if it has at least three vertices, is connected and remains connected after deleting any single vertex and its incident edges. This excludes an isolated edge and includes triangles and longer cycles. The network G is an arbitrary finite simple undirected graph on n vertices. A copy of H is an injective map \(\varphi :V(H)\to V(G)\) such that every edge uv of H maps to an edge \(\varphi (u)\varphi (v)\) of G. Extra edges among the images are allowed: the task is not induced-subgraph detection, homomorphism, minor containment or property testing with a distance promise.

There is one processor at each vertex. Each knows n, H, its own distinct identifier and the identifiers of its neighbors; identifiers have \(O(\log (n+2))\) bits, and the guarantee must hold for every valid assignment of identifiers. Local edges have identifiable ports. In each synchronous round a node may send a different message of at most \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits to each neighbor, for a fixed constant B independent of n. Messages are received before the next round, and later messages may depend on everything received so far. No communication is allowed across nonedges. Local computation and memory are unrestricted; only communication rounds are charged. This is ordinary CONGEST, with distinct messages permitted on distinct edges, not broadcast CONGEST or the congested clique.

The algorithm is a uniform distributed procedure fixed with H; it may use independent private random bits at the nodes. Deterministic algorithms are included as a special case. It halts within a worst-case bound \(T_{H}(n)\) on every network, identifier assignment and random tape. The success event concerns the joint vector of all node outputs, with probability over all random bits. In an H-free network all outputs must be NO simultaneously; in a network containing H one YES anywhere suffices. There is no requirement that the detecting node belong to a copy, identify its vertices, list all copies, or notify distant nodes. Disconnected networks are permitted and the same global output convention applies.

The required bound \(n^{o(1)}\) means that one such algorithm exists with \(\log (\max \{2,T_{H}(n)\})/\log  n\to 0\) as \(n\to \infty\). Equivalently, for every fixed \(\delta >0\) its worst-case round bound is at most \(n^{\delta}\) for all sufficiently large n. Constants and the threshold length may depend on H and \(\delta\). A family of different algorithms, one for each \(\delta\), is not silently identified with that single-algorithm claim. A bound \(n^{\alpha _{H}}\) with a fixed positive \(\alpha _{H}\), even a very small one, is not subpolynomial. The size of H is a constant, not another growing complexity parameter.

The source also asks whether every 2-connected pattern instead requires a polynomial number of rounds. A theorem giving each fixed H a lower bound \(\Omega (n^{\delta _{H}})\) for some \(\delta _{H}>0\) would refute the existence question, but this stronger growth dichotomy is not assumed to be its logical negation. A negative answer here only needs to exclude the stated \(n^{o(1)}\) algorithms for every eligible H.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer provides one fixed eligible H and proves a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm with the stated global success probability and \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case rounds. A negative answer rules out such an algorithm for every fixed eligible H. A lower bound for only one pattern, or a fast algorithm for induced copies, promised-far graphs, listing in another model or a pattern that grows with n, does not settle this existence question.

cards.title: Query complexity of the graph degree distribution
cards.formal:
Determine, up to universal constant factors, the function
\[
Q^\star(n,m,h,w)=
\inf_{A\in\mathcal A}\ 
\max_{G\in\mathcal G(n,m,h,w)}
\mathbb E[T_A(G)]
\]
on every feasible tuple defined below. Here \(\mathcal A\) consists of uniform randomized algorithms which receive only \(n\), access the graph through the three specified query types, and correctly estimate its entire complementary cumulative degree histogram with probability at least \(2/3\). The required simultaneous accuracy is
\[
\Pr\!\left[
\forall d\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\},\
\frac9{10}N_G\!\left(\frac{11}{10}d\right)
\le \widehat N(d)\le
\frac{11}{10}N_G\!\left(\frac9{10}d\right)
\right]\ge\frac23.
\]
The parameters \(m,h,w\) describe the graph on which cost is evaluated; their values, estimates and bounds are not supplied to the algorithm.
cards.why: The degree histogram distinguishes common low-degree vertices from rare hubs. Estimating its whole cumulative profile requires guarantees in the tail as well as where most vertices lie. A sharp query bound would identify which structural features permit reliable graph summaries with limited access.
cards.status_note: The 2019 source asks for improved upper and matching lower bounds. Its displayed bicriteria shifts are reversed; this review uses the original 2018 Definition 1.1. The user selected all four performance parameters, fixed ten-percent error and constant-factor precision, then specified on 16 September 2026 that only n is supplied. The 2018 SADDLES theorem requires suitable parameter-dependent sample budgets. The 2025 preprint uses stronger direct random-edge access. Neither source establishes the full constant-factor, four-parameter minimax envelope for the selected information model. No matching resolution was found in the bounded current review.

cards.definitions:
The input graph \(G=([n],E)\), with \(n\ge2\) and \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), is finite, simple and undirected, with no loops or repeated edges. All labels in \([n]\) are valid query arguments; the edge set is hidden. Put
\[
m=|E|,\qquad
N_G(t)=|\{v\in[n]:\deg_G(v)\ge t\}|\quad(t\in\mathbb R).
\]
Thus a noninteger threshold means its ceiling, \(N_G(t)=n\) for \(t\le0\), and \(N_G(t)=0\) for \(t>n-1\). The output is a list of nonnegative rational estimates \(\widehat N(d)\) for integer \(1\le d\le n-1\); the value at zero is known to be \(n\). The event in the question must hold for all output thresholds together.

The h-index and the second tail parameter are
\[
h(G)=\max\bigl(\{0\}\cup\{d\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}:N_G(d)\ge d\}\bigr),
\]
\[
w(G)=
\begin{cases}
\min\{dN_G(d):1\le d\le n-1,\ N_G(d)>0\},&m>0,\\
0,&m=0.
\end{cases}
\]
The \(z\)-index in the 2018 paper satisfies \(z=\sqrt{w}\). These are integer parameters, with the displayed empty-graph convention. A tuple \((n,m,h,w)\) is feasible precisely when some graph on \([n]\) has those values. Let \(\mathcal G(n,m,h,w)\) be the finite nonempty set of all such labeled graphs. The domain includes edgeless graphs.

Each of the following oracle calls costs one query:

- Vertex: return a uniformly random label in \([n]\).
- Degree(\(v\)): return the exact integer \(\deg_G(v)\).
- RandomNeighbor(\(v\)): return a uniformly random neighbor of \(v\), or a distinguished symbol \(\bot\) if its degree is zero.

Random replies are fresh independent samples conditional on the selected query and the fixed graph. An algorithm may adapt its calls and stopping rule to previous replies and its independent fair random bits. There is no indexed-neighbor, edge-existence or direct uniform-edge oracle. The initial input is the binary encoding of \(n\), without advice. Computation, memory, random-bit generation and output length are unrestricted and do not contribute to the query count.

An element of \(\mathcal A\) is one probabilistic Turing machine, uniform over all \(n\ge2\), which halts almost surely with finite expected query count on every input graph and meets the stated success guarantee on every such graph. Let \(T_A(G)\) count all its calls, including those on unsuccessful runs. Expectation includes both its internal randomness and the oracle randomness. The maximum in the question ranges over the exact parameter class, but membership in that class is not an input promise available to \(A\).

The infimum is taken pointwise over this same class \(\mathcal A\). A witness for an upper bound must still be a machine correct on every graph with only \(n\) supplied. The definition does not demand that one machine attain the infimum, or achieve optimal cost simultaneously for every tuple. In particular, a procedure justified only under a promised value of \(m,h,w\) is not automatically an admissible witness. Querying all \(n\) degrees provides an admissible finite baseline.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply an unambiguous, noncircular description of a nonnegative function \(F\) on the feasible tuples and absolute constants \(c,C>0\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof that
\[
cF(n,m,h,w)\le Q^\star(n,m,h,w)\le CF(n,m,h,w)
\]
for every feasible tuple. Upper bounds must use admissible algorithms or an approaching family establishing the infimum bound; lower bounds must apply to all admissible algorithms. Merely repeating the optimization defining \(Q^\star\) is not a determination. Hidden logarithmic factors are not permitted in this constant-factor answer, and no additive \(1/100\) tolerance applies to the asymptotic target. Bounds for average degree alone, only the high-degree tail, a stronger query oracle, or algorithms given the hidden parameters do not settle the requested function.

context_blocks.text: A cumulative degree histogram counts vertices above each degree threshold. Approximating only its normalization in an additive distributional distance can overlook a small but structurally important population of high-degree vertices. The bicriteria requirement controls this tail while allowing a small shift of the threshold.

Uniform vertices and random neighbors have different sampling biases. The model makes these access costs explicit and includes degree queries. The question therefore concerns information available through local graph access, rather than the cost of reading an adjacency matrix.

The 2018 paper introduces the \(z\)-index alongside the usual h-index. In its Standard Model, Theorem 3.1 gives expected cost \(O((n/h+m/w)\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/\delta))\), for positive parameters and sample budgets meeting the theorem’s hypotheses, with simultaneous success probability at least \(1-\delta\). The sample-budget conditions in that theorem depend on graph parameters. Because this card supplies only the vertex count, an upper-bound proof must account for obtaining suitable information or otherwise justify its stopping rule. The source theorem is not silently promoted to an unknown-parameter guarantee.

The 2025 preprint gives nearly matching bounds on an \(m/h\) scale in a stronger query model, using direct random-edge samples. Its general interface also includes indexed neighbors and edge-existence tests. Those guarantees do not determine the cost when an edge sample must be obtained using only the three calls in this card.

The original entry also raises tail-only estimation, testing degree-distribution properties and replacing uniform vertex samples by other access. Those are separate variants. This card retains the full cumulative profile and the original three types of access.

cards.title: Two-stage group testing with arithmetic progressions
cards.formal:
Do there exist absolute constants \(C,D>0\) such that, for every pair of integers \(n\ge2\) and \(1\le k\le n\), an unknown set \(S\subseteq[n]\) with \(|S|\le k\) can be identified exactly by the following deterministic two-stage scheme?

The first stage uses at most \(Ck\log_2 n\) tests. Each test asks whether \(S\) meets a finite arithmetic progression contained in \([n]\), and every first-stage test is fixed before any answers are received. After seeing all first-stage answers, the second stage chooses at most \(Dk\) individual indices and learns their membership in \(S\). All second-stage indices must be chosen before receiving any second-stage answer. The final output must equal \(S\) for every admissible hidden set.

The constants must work simultaneously for all \(n,k,S\). The resource being bounded is the number of tests in each stage; neither constructing the scheme nor decoding the answers is subject to a running-time bound.
cards.why: This question tests how much measurement restrictions can cost in sparse identification even when one follow-up round is available. A resolution would distinguish what arbitrary pooling achieves from what regularly spaced queries can support, a distinction motivated by pattern matching rather than by a new statistical noise model.
cards.status_note: Source-open in the Kanpur 2009 question reproduced as Sublinear.info Problem 33. The active status reflects that dated source and limited search, not a recent author confirmation or exhaustive literature certification.

sentences: A hidden set of at most k positions must be identified by noiseless yes/no tests.
Every first-stage pool must be an arithmetic progression fixed before any answers are seen.
After receiving those answers, the scheme may query only O(k) individual positions in one final stage.
The question asks whether O(k log n) first-stage tests suffice for every hidden set, improving the bound reported in the 2009 source by one logarithmic factor.
The restriction models regularly spaced queries motivated by pattern matching, and unrestricted pooling results do not settle it.

cards.definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input parameters \(n\) and \(k\) are known; only the subset \(S\) is hidden. The promise is an upper bound \(|S|\le k\), not knowledge of its exact size. In particular \(S=\varnothing\) is allowed. The elements have their fixed integer positions, and the arithmetic-progression constraint refers to these positions. There is no ability to permute the hidden input and then declare arbitrary pools to be progressions.

An admissible first-stage pool has the form
\[T=\{a,a+d,\ldots,a+(\ell-1)d\},\qquad a,d,\ell\in\mathbb N_{>0},\quad a+(\ell-1)d\le n.\]
Each pool may have its own start, step and length. Singletons are allowed. There is no wraparound modulo \(n\), no repeated item within a pool, and no requirement that the progression be extended to the ends of \([n]\). The answer is the noiseless bit \(b(T,S)=1\) if \(T\cap S\ne\varnothing\), and zero otherwise. It does not reveal the number or positions of the elements in the intersection.

For given \(n,k\), a scheme consists of a nonnegative integer \(m\), a list of admissible pools \(T_1,\ldots,T_m\), a selection function \(J\), and a final decoding function \(F\). The list depends only on \(n,k\); it is identical for every possible hidden set of the promised size. Write
\[y(S)=(b(T_1,S),\ldots,b(T_m,S))\in\{0,1\}^m.\]
The selection function takes any first-stage answer vector \(y\) to a set \(J(y)\subseteq[n]\) of indices with \(|J(y)|\le Dk\). Every selected index is queried separately, giving the function \(z_S:J(y(S))\to\{0,1\}\) defined by \(z_S(j)=1\) exactly when \(j\in S\). The final decoder knows the parameters, the entire first-stage design, \(y(S)\), the selected indices and their individual answers. Correctness means
\[\forall S\subseteq[n]\text{ with }|S|\le k:\quad F\bigl(y(S),z_S\bigr)=S.\]
The decoder may infer membership of unqueried indices from the complete transcript. It is not required to query every element that it finally reports. Queries in the second stage are individual membership tests only; no additional pooled tests or third stage are allowed. Unrealizable first-stage answer vectors can have arbitrary decoding behavior, subject to the same advertised second-stage query cap.

One test is one oracle answer, independent of the pool's cardinality. First-stage pools may be represented by their integer triples \((a,d,\ell)\), and individual indices and parameters in binary, but description length and computational time are not the costs asked about. No noise, random hidden-set distribution, random design, or probability of error is part of this formulation. This records the source's exact identification problem for an arbitrary set, as opposed to average-case recovery. An existence proof for the finite designs and functions suffices; a polynomial-time construction is not an extra requirement. Since all choices for fixed finite parameters can be enumerated and their correctness checked, this convention does not allow an undecidable query operation.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C,D>0\;\forall n,k\;\exists(T_1,\ldots,T_m,J,F)\;\forall S\), with the stated size restrictions. In particular a separate design tailored to the unknown \(S\) is inadmissible. The upper bound uses \(\log_2 n\), not \(\log_2(n/k)\). The source's \(O(k\log n)\) and \(O(k)\) mean absolute constant factors independent of both parameters. Using \(n\ge2\) avoids the irrelevant zero logarithm at one item.

A negative answer is the logical negation: for every proposed pair of constants \(C,D>0\), there are admissible \(n,k\) for which every scheme satisfying both test caps fails on some hidden set. It need not establish a particular alternative asymptotic lower-bound formula. A lower bound for a single family of progressions, a chosen decoder, or a nonadaptive one-stage scheme would not by itself disprove the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of absolute constants and two-stage schemes with the stated bounds. A positive answer must prove the arithmetic-progression restriction, first-stage independence from answers, the \(O(k)\) cap on individual second-stage queries, and exact recovery for every hidden set of size at most \(k\), uniformly over the full parameter domain. A negative answer must rule out all allowed designs and decoders with every proposed pair of constant factors. Results allowing arbitrary first-stage pools, more rounds, non-individual second-stage tests, or error on some hidden sets do not settle this proposition. This is an asymptotic existence question, so additive numerical tolerance is inapplicable.

source_formulation.text: Porat asks whether two-stage exact group testing can use \(O(k\log n)\) first-stage pools when each pool is an arithmetic progression. Only \(O(k)\) individually chosen membership tests are allowed in the second stage. The listed benchmark for the progression-restricted first stage is \(O(k\log^2 n)\).

context_blocks.text: The hidden set represents a sparse collection of relevant positions. A pooled answer identifies whether an entire regular selection of positions contains any relevant element, so many positions can be checked with one bit of feedback.

The central restriction concerns which collections can be tested together. An arithmetic progression has a fixed spacing, as occurs when inspecting regularly sampled positions in pattern-matching applications. A result for arbitrary subsets does not automatically provide such regularly spaced pools.

The source permits one round of adaptation: pooled answers can determine which individual positions will be checked next. Its question asks whether this limited feedback compensates for the restriction on first-stage pools.

The 2009 question reports \(O(k\log^2 n)\) first-stage tests under the arithmetic-progression restriction and asks to remove one logarithmic factor. This is a dated benchmark reported by the problem proposer, not a newly verified 2026 optimality claim.

The unrestricted two-stage setting has order-optimal test-count results in the cited 2005 paper. Its publisher abstract confirms that the main theorem concerns unrestricted intersection queries, with other variants treated separately. This comparison explains why the geometry of the permitted pools is the substantive issue here.

cards.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) that, on every input encoding a polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_m]\) with \(m\geq1\), halts and outputs YES exactly when \[\exists(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m\quad f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0,\] and outputs NO otherwise? The number of variables, degree and coefficients are unrestricted finite input data, and there is no time or space efficiency requirement.
cards.definitions:
The field \(\mathbb Q\) consists of exact fractions \(a/b\), with \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), identifying fractions of the same value; addition and multiplication are the usual exact field operations. A polynomial input describes \(f=\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_j\prod_{i=1}^{m}X_i^{e_{ji}}\), with \(r\geq0\), \(a_j\in\mathbb Z\) and \(e_{ji}\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Repeated monomials and zero coefficients are allowed. The empty sum is the zero polynomial and \(X_i^0=1\), including when evaluating at zero. Constants are represented with all exponents zero. A rational zero is any tuple in \(\mathbb Q^m\) giving exact value zero; there is no bound on its numerators or denominators and no integrality restriction.

Use the following explicit effective binary encoding. For \(u\geq0\), let \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(b\) bits and no leading zeroes. Encode an integer \(a\) by a sign bit followed by \(\operatorname{code}(|a|)\), with 0 denoting a nonnegative integer and 1 a negative integer; negative zero is invalid. A complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(m)\operatorname{code}(r)\), followed for each \(j=1,\ldots,r\) by the signed code of \(a_j\) and \(\operatorname{code}(e_{j1}),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(e_{jm})\), with no trailing bits. Require \(m\geq1\). The machine halts and outputs NO on every malformed encoding.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program with a finite tape alphabet, ordinary discrete transitions and unbounded work tapes, without advice or an oracle. On every input it must halt after finitely many transitions; its running time need not satisfy a polynomial, elementary or other prescribed bound. Its program is independent of \(m,r\), all degrees and all coefficients. The input supplies only the polynomial, without additional height-comparison predicates or a promise of solvability. The question concerns decision of existence; a YES output need not itself contain a rational tuple.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify one effective algorithm and prove termination and exact correctness on every polynomial in the stated domain, together with rejection of invalid input. A negative answer must prove that no such total correct Turing machine exists. Recognizing only polynomials that have a rational zero, excluding polynomial-time algorithms, or proving undecidability for equations with integer-constrained unknowns or added predicates does not establish the required negation. Any conditional result must be identified as conditional and does not alone settle this unconditional question.
cards.why: This asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver. It connects the computability of arithmetic, logical definability and the existence of rational points on algebraic varieties. The unresolved boundary persists despite undecidability over the integers and decidability of polynomial feasibility over the reals and algebraically closed fields; allowing fractions fundamentally changes the permitted witnesses.

progress.text: The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem settles the integer-solution problem negatively; rational solvability remains a different decision problem.
Koenigsmann’s Annals paper gives a universal definition of \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathbb Q\), implying undecidability of the universal-existential fragment but not the purely existential fragment.
Anscombe and coauthors explicitly record Hilbert’s tenth problem over \(\mathbb Q\) as open and review its relation to existential definability.

The height-comparison undecidability paper appears in Journal of Number Theory after its 2023 preprint. It settles an expansion by height predicates, while retaining the ordinary rational question as open.
The Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman article appears online, proving a negative answer over the ring of integers of every number field; its print issue is March 2026.
Poonen’s account reviews the rings-of-integers breakthrough and gives an alternative proof of the relevant Diophantine-definability implication. Its domain restriction remains essential.

references.locator: Published online 1 December 2025; Inventiones mathematicae 243, 1129–1139 (March 2026). Publisher introduction, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 checked: all rings of integers, not their fraction fields.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open over Q in the cited rational-solvability sources. A bounded primary-source check through 14 September 2026 located no resolution of this exact question. Checked recent results prove undecidability over rings of integers or after adjoining height-comparison predicates; neither settles existence of an unrestricted total rational-solvability decider. This is a formulation and source-scope audit, not an independent verification of every cited proof.

context_blocks.text: Rational tuples can be effectively enumerated and tested by exact substitution, so every YES-instance is eventually recognizable. Such a search does not halt on a NO-instance. The target requires termination in both cases, irrespective of efficiency. A solver for all instances would also allow a rational zero to be found when one exists.

The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem proves that no general algorithm decides integer solvability. It does not automatically decide the rational problem: \(2X-1=0\) has a rational zero but no integer zero. A rational solver cannot simply be applied to the unchanged integer equation.

Allowing rational coefficients gives the same decision problem, because their denominators can be cleared effectively. Finite systems of equations are also equivalent to a single equation: over \(\mathbb Q\), \(f_1=\cdots=f_r=0\) holds exactly when \(\sum_i f_i^2=0\). More generally, disequalities can be encoded using inverse variables and disjunctions using products. These equivalences identify the problem with decidability of the existential first-order theory of \(\mathbb Q\) in the language of rings.

An existential definition of \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathbb Q\) would transfer integer undecidability to this problem. Koenigsmann’s Theorem 1 instead defines \(\mathbb Z\) by a universal formula; its Corollary 3 establishes undecidability for universal-existential sentences. Quantifier alternation is essential to that conclusion: the full first-order theory and the universal-existential fragment are already undecidable, while neither fact settles the purely existential target.

Alpöge, Bhargava, Ho and Shnidman prove undecidability over the ring of integers \(\mathcal O_K\) of every number field \(K\). Here a number field is a finite extension of \(\mathbb Q\), and \(\mathcal O_K\) consists of elements satisfying a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. This restricts the solution domain; in particular \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Z\), whereas the present question permits every rational number.

Poonen’s account dated 3 July 2026 reviews the recent proof of undecidability for these rings and supplies an alternative definability argument from rank stability. Its Theorem 4.2 concerns definitions over rings of integers. This account does not extend the negative answer to the whole field \(\mathbb Q\).

Garcia-Fritz, Pasten and Vidaux prove undecidability when rational equations are supplemented with finitely many height-comparison conditions. For a rational tuple \(q\), their logarithmic height is \(h(q)=\log\max\{d,|dq_1|,\ldots,|dq_m|\}\), where \(d\geq1\) is its least common denominator, and the added predicates compare heights of tuples. These extra constraints are absent from the target. Their ordinary rational-solvability question remains explicitly open.

cards.title: Integer factorization in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,c\ge0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm A such that, for every positive integer N in binary, A outputs the complete prime factorization of N with probability at least \(2/3\), and for every random-bit sequence halts within \(C(n+1)^c\) bit steps, where \(n=\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor+1\)? The same A, C and c must work for all N.
cards.definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two representation of N, with no leading zeroes; its length n counts bits, not the numerical value of N. The one-character string 1 represents N=1. The empty string and all strings beginning with 0 are invalid and must be rejected on every random-bit sequence within the same polynomial bound in their length. For \(N\ge2\), the unique correct factorization is the finite list \((p_1,e_1),\ldots,(p_r,e_r)\), where \(p_1<\cdots<p_r\) are primes, each \(e_i\) is a positive integer, and \(N=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}\). A prime is an integer at least 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. The correct list for N=1 is empty. To fix a binary output format, encode a nonnegative integer a by \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary representation of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). A successful output is 1 followed by code(r) and then code(p_i), code(e_i) for i in increasing order, with no other bits; the single bit 0 is the failure or invalid-input symbol. A is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with one finite program, a fixed finite number of tapes and fixed finite alphabets. It has a read-only input tape and initially blank work and output tapes; a transition accesses only cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. It may request one new independent fair bit at a transition. The probability space is \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) with independent uniform coordinates, and the probability guarantee is separate for every fixed input N. The runtime is the total transition count, including all input access, random-bit requests, arithmetic and output writing. Every random-bit sequence obeys the clock; thus only finitely many random bits affect each run. A malformed factor list, an incorrect list and the failure symbol all count as failure on a positive input. The algorithm receives no promise that N is semiprime or belongs to a particular distribution, no advice or precomputed factors, no order-finding or factoring oracle, and no quantum or unit-cost operations on unbounded integers. The task is full factorization, not merely deciding whether N is prime.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one algorithm and constants satisfy the all-input success guarantee and the all-random-sequences polynomial clock, or prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. A negative proof must exclude arbitrary uniform classical randomized algorithms with arbitrary fixed polynomial exponents; excluding deterministic algorithms alone does not suffice. For the affirmative answer, correctness includes every prime base, multiplicity, ordering and product in the complete output. A heuristic complexity estimate, a guarantee for sampled or restricted inputs, or a quantum algorithm does not meet the stated classical worst-case target.
cards.why: Integer factorization is a basic inverse problem in arithmetic and a central test case for the potential power of quantum computation. Its classical complexity has direct consequences for factoring-based cryptography and for algorithms that currently require access to a factoring subroutine.

progress.text: Shor establishes polynomial-time quantum factorization. The full paper’s January 1996 revision explicitly uses quantum computation, which is outside the classical randomized machine model of this card.
Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena publish deterministic polynomial-time primality testing. This makes prime-factor lists efficiently checkable but does not provide their discovery.

Harvey and Hittmeir prove complete deterministic factorization in \(O(N^{1/5}(\log N)^{16/5}/(\log\log N)^{3/5})\) bit operations as N tends to infinity. The 2022 journal result improves a logarithmic factor while retaining an exponential dependence on binary input length.

Harvey and Hittmeir’s revision removes the previous power-of-N lower restriction on the large-order threshold and slightly improves its runtime factor. Theorem 1.1 may return a large-order element instead of a divisor, and Section 1.1 still explicitly identifies polynomial-time factoring as unknown.

cards.status_note: The undated source survey explicitly asks for randomized polynomial-time factoring, and Harvey–Hittmeir Section 1.1 in the 5 June 2026 revision confirms the absence of a known polynomial-time factoring algorithm even with probabilistic methods. Bounded later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution. The cited heuristic estimate and quantum result are not certified as solutions in this classical model, and new proof claims were not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: Multiplying the prime factors is easy, and the factors themselves fit in a polynomial-size output. Discovering them is the unresolved step. Trial division up to \(\sqrt{N}\) is polynomial in the number’s value but exponential in its binary input length. The distinction between N and log N is essential even when a newer algorithm improves the power of N substantially.

Primality testing and factorization are different tasks. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena algorithm decides in deterministic polynomial time whether a number is prime, without necessarily exhibiting a divisor when the answer is composite. It also makes a proposed full factorization efficiently checkable: verify that every listed base is prime and that the product is N.

Efficient verification makes the two common randomized formulations equivalent in existence: bounded-error polynomial worst-case time, and always-correct polynomial expected time with possible nontermination only on a probability-zero set of random tapes. This equivalence uses an all-input expected bound and fresh independent randomness, and the expected-time formulation alone does not give a worst-case clock on each run. The card chooses the bounded-clock formulation to state the success event without any runtime averaging.

The general number field sieve has the familiar heuristic expected-time estimate \(\exp (((64/9)^{1/3}+o(1))(\ln  N)^{1/3}(\ln  \ln  N)^{2/3})\). This is subexponential but still superpolynomial in the bit length. Rigorous deterministic bounds of \(N^{1/5+o(1)}\) make a different tradeoff and remain exponential in that length. Neither bound is a proof that faster classical factoring is impossible.
Shor’s quantum algorithm factors in polynomial time, using quantum order finding. It provides an upper bound in the quantum model and does not establish a classical lower bound.

The newer deterministic large-order theorem has a different output contract: it may produce a certified high-order group element instead of a divisor. Even when the requested order threshold is small and the subroutine is fast, that output alternative does not amount to a complete factorization. Its usefulness within factoring algorithms must not be mistaken for a solution of the entire factoring problem.

A classical polynomial-time factoring algorithm would undermine the corresponding cryptographic hardness assumptions. Neither the efficiency of multiplication nor a conjectured separation \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) provides a proved classical factoring lower bound. Factoring and inverting RSA are also distinct problems; the historical source explains that the reverse general reduction is unknown.

cards.title: Prime-field discrete logarithms in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\), and integers \(C,c\ge1\), such that \(A\) halts within \(C(L+1)^c\) steps on every binary input of length \(L\) and every sequence of its random bits, and has the following correctness property? For every prime \(p\), every generator \(g\) of the multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), and every \(h\in\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), given the binary encoding of \((p,g,h)\) specified below, it outputs the unique integer \(x\in\{0,\ldots,p-2\}\) satisfying \(g^x\equiv h\pmod p\) with probability at least \(2/3\).
cards.definitions: The field \(\mathbb F_p\) consists of residues \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\) with addition and multiplication modulo the prime \(p\). Its multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\) is \(\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\) with multiplication modulo \(p\). The promise that \(g\) is a generator means that \(g^0,g^1,\ldots,g^{p-2}\), reduced modulo \(p\), list these \(p-1\) residues without repetition; hence the requested exponent exists and is unique. Each input integer is represented by its ordinary base-two expansion \(\operatorname{bin}(a)\), without leading zeros and with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Writing \(\ell(a)=|\operatorname{bin}(a)|\), set \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^{\ell(a)}0\operatorname{bin}(a)\). The complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(p)\operatorname{code}(g)\operatorname{code}(h)\), with \(p\) prime and \(1\le g,h<p\). Its length \(L=2(\ell(p)+\ell(g)+\ell(h))+3\) is \(\Theta(\log_2 p)\) on promised inputs. A successful output is exactly \(\operatorname{bin}(x)\); any different output or a designated failure symbol is unsuccessful. For \(p=2\), the sole promised pair is \(g=h=1\) and the answer is \(x=0\). The machine has a fixed finite program, fixed finite alphabets, a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes and an output tape; each transition costs one step, and any random transition reads one fresh independent fair bit. The time bound includes input processing, bit arithmetic, random-bit generation, output and all preprocessing. The same \(A,C,c\) work for every input, with no advice, oracle, precomputed table or supplied factorization of \(p-1\). Arbitrary classical computations on the concrete binary residues are permitted, not just generic group operations. Malformed encodings may be rejected as failure; on well-formed triples outside the mathematical promise, only the global time bound is required. The success guarantee is separately for each promised triple, over the machine’s coins, not over a distribution of primes or targets. The question concerns the multiplicative group of a prime field; additive groups, extension fields and elliptic-curve groups are different models.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of \(A,C,c\) with both the all-input, all-random-sequence time bound and the per-promised-input success guarantee, or a Lean-checked proof that no such triple exists. Equivalently, a negative answer must prove that every machine obeying some global polynomial clock has a promised input on which its probability of outputting the required exponent is less than \(2/3\). Failure of a particular algorithm, an average-case conjecture for a selected prime distribution, or a lower bound restricted to generic group operations does not establish this negation. A quantum algorithm, success only for selected prime families, or a bound polynomial in \(p\) rather than its bit length does not meet the positive target.
cards.why: Discrete logarithms expose a basic gap between efficient modular exponentiation and our ability to invert it. A uniform classical polynomial-time solver would defeat the corresponding finite-field discrete-logarithm assumptions and solve computational Diffie–Hellman in this setting. An unrestricted impossibility proof would establish a fundamental classical lower bound for a concrete arithmetic problem already solvable in quantum polynomial time.

progress.text: Prime-field NFS methods achieve heuristic subexponential estimates, described precisely in the cited 2008 survey. Those historical estimates are distinct from proven expected-time bounds and from a lower bound against arbitrary algorithms.
Shor supplies a quantum polynomial-time discrete-logarithm algorithm; §6 of the inspected manuscript uses the same prime-field and supplied-generator mathematical problem.
Shoup’s Theorem 1 proves a generic-encoding lower bound parameterized by the largest prime divisor of the group order. It does not apply to unrestricted computation on concrete residues.

Kleinjung and Wesolowski’s fixed-characteristic theorem appears in the inspected 18 November 2019 version and the 2022 JAMS article. The expected-time bound and extension-degree parameter do not give a prime-field polynomial-bit algorithm.

Discrete Logarithm Factory analyzes shared preprocessing for a constant proportion of fields of a given approximate size and degree, with individual-target costs separated. Its publisher abstract and full introduction were checked.

Lido’s Finite Fields and Their Applications article concerns small characteristic. The inspected preprint’s Theorem 1.1 requires \(d>p\), so its quasipolynomial guarantee does not settle the prime-field question.

Wu and coauthors explicitly assume worst-case classical hardness of prime-field DLP in a new quantum-complexity preprint. Version 1 remains the sole version on 14 September; its conditional reduction is not a resolution of the assumption.

cards.status_note: The original number-theory survey leaves the classical prime-field problem open. The same generator-input problem is explicitly assumed classically hard in Wu et al., arXiv:2608.15545v1 of 16 August 2026, still its sole version on 14 September. The reviewed 2026 small-characteristic publication and quantum results do not resolve this target. A bounded later-work search found no matching classical polynomial-time solution or unrestricted impossibility proof; source proofs and new conditional reductions were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: For a supplied \(g\) and exponent \(x\), modular exponentiation takes time polynomial in their bit lengths. Inverting this operation would reveal the shared value \(g^{ab}\) from \(g,g^a,g^b\) in the corresponding Diffie–Hellman setting. This implication does not identify discrete-logarithm hardness with every Diffie–Hellman or encryption-security assumption. The card asks a worst-case algorithmic question; a negative answer alone does not prove average-case hardness for a cryptographic parameter distribution.

Candidate answers are efficiently verifiable by checking \(0\le x\le p-2\) and \(g^x\equiv h\pmod p\). Thus, as an elementary consequence of verification, existence of the stated bounded-error algorithm is equivalent to existence of a Las Vegas solver that is never wrong and has a uniform polynomial expected running-time bound on every promised input. Independent verified repetition has bounded expected cost in one direction; truncation at three times an expected-time bound gives success at least \(2/3\) by Markov’s inequality in the other. This does not require every run of a Las Vegas solver to terminate, only probability-one termination and finite expected cost.

Schirokauer’s survey gives a conjectured expected-time NFS bound of the form \(\exp(O((\ln p)^{1/3}(\ln\ln p)^{2/3}))\) in the prime-field regime. This is a heuristic complexity analysis, not an unconditional polynomial-time theorem or an unrestricted lower bound. The displayed scale grows faster than every fixed power of \(\log p\). The 2024 Discrete Logarithm Factory paper separately studies costs shared across fields and targets; any such preprocessing must still fit this card’s complete single-input budget.

Shoup’s lower bound concerns randomly encoded group elements. If \(q\) is the largest prime divisor of a cyclic group’s order, constant success requires \(\Omega(\sqrt q)\) generic group operations in that model. His parameter \(q\) is not the field characteristic \(p\); for this card the group order is \(p-1\). The theorem averages over the random encoding, exponent and algorithm coins. It does not exclude algorithms that use the actual integer residues and their arithmetic structure.

Kleinjung and Wesolowski’s Theorem 1.1 gives expected time \((p d)^{2\log_2 d+O(1)}\) for the multiplicative group of \(\mathbb F_{p^d}\). For fixed \(p\) and growing extension degree \(d\), this is quasipolynomial in the input size. Substituting \(d=1\) supplies at most a polynomial-in-\(p\) guarantee, not the requested polynomial in \(\log p\). The occurrence of the product \(p d\) in their bound must not be confused with the field order \(p^d\).

Lido’s paper, published in March 2026, also proves a quasipolynomial expected-time theorem in small characteristic. In the inspected version its hypothesis is explicitly \(d>p\) for a field of size \(p^d\), excluding the growing prime-field family with \(d=1\). The source’s field-regime restriction remains part of the theorem even though all these problems share the name discrete logarithm.

Shor’s polynomial-time algorithm uses quantum computation. Wu and coauthors’ August 2026 preprint uses the same prime-field generator-input problem as an explicit classical-hardness assumption for a claim about estimating outputs of adaptive shallow quantum circuits. That assumption is not a proved classical lower bound; the reduction and its quantum resource claims were not independently verified in this review.

This would invert a basic arithmetic operation used in finite-field cryptography and match a known quantum capability.

cards.title: Polynomial-time, polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\), a real constant \(K>0\), an integer \(k\geq1\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) such that for every pair of integers \(d\geq n\geq1\) and every explicitly encoded \(B\in\mathbb Q^{d\times n}\) with linearly independent columns, every run halts in at most \(K(N+1)^k\) bit operations and returns a nonzero \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), with
\[\Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\leq n^C\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\geq\frac23?\]
The input length \(N\) includes all matrix entries. The lattice is \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), and \(\lambda_1\) is its shortest nonzero Euclidean length. Randomness consists of independent fair bits on that fixed input. The program and all constants are chosen once, before any input.
cards.definitions:
The input contains \(d,n\) and all \(dn\) rational entries in row-major order. To fix a binary encoding, let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(t\), using the one-bit string \(0\) for zero, and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Dimensions use \(E(d),E(n)\). A rational number is encoded by a sign bit followed by \(E(|a|)E(q)\), where it equals \(a/q\), \(q>0\), and \(\gcd(|a|,q)=1\); zero has positive sign and denominator one. There are exactly \(dn\) entries and no trailing bits. Valid inputs satisfy \(d\geq n\geq1\) and column independence over \(\mathbb Q\). The total number of encoded bits is \(N\). The polynomial clock applies on every binary input; behavior and output on malformed or dependent-basis inputs are otherwise unrestricted.

The Euclidean norm of \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The lattice consists of all integer combinations of the columns, with its usual embedding in \(\mathbb R^d\). Independence makes \(z\mapsto Bz\) injective and makes \(L(B)\) discrete in its real span. Thus
\[\lambda_1(L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2>0\]
is attained. No uniqueness of the shortest vector up to sign is assumed. The algorithm returns the coefficient vector: its \(n\) signed integer coordinates use a sign bit and \(E\) of the absolute value, with positive sign for zero. It must return a valid nonzero vector on every run on a valid input. An unsuccessful run may exceed the norm bound, but may not output zero, fail to halt or omit the vector. The squared norm can equivalently be used in the displayed guarantee with squared factor \(n^{2C}\).

Use one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a finite description independent of all input parameters. Its tapes have a fixed finite alphabet encoding bits. Each transition can read and write only a fixed number of cells and move each head by at most one cell. An additional instruction obtains one fresh independent fair bit at unit cost. This describes ordinary uniform classical bit computation, with no advice, oracle, quantum operations, uncharged preprocessing or unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers. All reading, writing, arithmetic, memory manipulation and random-bit generation count toward the bound. The output uses the integer encoding specified above, and every bit written is charged.

For a given valid input, randomness is the product measure of independent uniform bits on an infinite random tape; the polynomial clock ensures that only finitely many are read. The success event is the displayed norm inequality, separately for every input. All runs, including those outside that event, must return a valid nonzero integer vector within the same clock. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as the special case that uses no random bits. Expected polynomial time alone is not the stated requirement.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C,K,k,A\;\forall d,n,B\), with both the probability guarantee and the all-run clock imposed after choosing the input. In particular, \(C\) may be large but must be fixed. The factor is \(n^C\), determined by lattice rank; it is not a polynomial in the ambient dimension, the coefficient magnitude or the input bit length. In rank one it is exactly one. There is no input-distribution, shortest-vector uniqueness, ideal-lattice, conditioning, modular or basis-quality promise. The problem concerns arbitrary finite rational bases, including ones with very large coefficients.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of one algorithm and constants meeting every requirement, or of the logical negation of that existence statement. A negative answer must rule out every fixed exponent \(C>0\) and every permitted randomized polynomial-time algorithm, rather than only a deterministic algorithm or a selected small approximation factor. A positive answer must establish the actual nonzero-vector output, success on each basis and all-run bit clock, including coefficient and output lengths. A conditional complexity lower bound gives only a conditional conclusion unless its assumption is proved. A gap-decision certificate, a factor depending without a rank bound on the input basis, a uniqueness-promised result, an oracle-call bound excluding subroutine time, or a quantum algorithm alone does not settle this classical search target. No additional numerical tolerance weakens this exact existence proposition.
cards.why: This asks whether efficient classical computation can find short vectors in every Euclidean lattice with a loss bounded by one fixed power of rank. The gap between known general algorithms and this regime is a basic obstacle in lattice complexity. Resolving it would clarify the relation between lattice geometry, efficient approximation and worst-case hardness assumptions used in cryptography; its consequences for particular schemes still depend on the exact problem and parameters.

progress.text: LLL establishes polynomial-time reduction with an exponential-in-rank short-vector guarantee.
Aharonov–Regev give polynomial certificates on both sides of the specified square-root-rank gap-decision problem.
Haviv–Regev obtain nearly polynomial approximation hardness under explicitly randomized complexity assumptions.
Bennett’s survey separates general polynomial-time approximation, search-to-decision questions and cryptographic parameter regimes.
Shenoy’s article is published with a basis-dependent approximation expression; the checked theorem does not supply a uniform rank-polynomial bound.
The checked Hair–Sahai revision gives deterministic subexponential reductions and a subpolynomial approximation gap under its stated hardness assumption.
Sato–Yasuda publish the PotBKZ termination theorem with enumeration and node costs still separate.
Wan’s major revision replaces a false premise in its first version and retains fixed-factor claims while dropping the earlier dimension-dependent claims.
Hirahara–Ogitsuka’s conditional and parameterized hardness results are published at RANDOM.
The revised generic-metric query lower bound has a different access and metric model.

cards.status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The survey’s unrestricted classical polynomial-factor search gap remains the saved target. The checked Shenoy expression is basis-dependent, PotBKZ counts costly enumeration calls, and the 2026 hardness results concern smaller factors, explicit assumptions or a different oracle model. Wan’s 8 September revision expressly withdraws its first version’s dimension-dependent claims. No full solution of this card was found in bounded later-work checks; cited new proofs and Shenoy’s convergence claim were not independently verified. The disputed quantum DCP claim on TCS-7234 is not a classical algorithm.

context_blocks.text: For integer \(M\geq1\), the basis columns \((M,1)\) and \((M+1,1)\) are both long but their lattice contains \((1,0)\). Thus input column lengths alone do not determine the shortest lattice length. More generally, the same lattice has many bases, and the guarantee must be relative to its intrinsic minimum on every supplied basis.

With its standard parameter, LLL gives a nonzero vector of length at most \(2^{(n-1)/2}\lambda_1\) in polynomial bit time. The original paper separately controls the number of arithmetic operations and the binary lengths of their operands. Its approximation factor is exponential in rank even though the running time is polynomial; a runtime statement alone does not specify the quality of the vector.

Bennett’s 2023 survey summarizes improved general polynomial-time guarantees with factor \(2^{O(n\log\log n/\log n)}\). This established upper guarantee is still much larger than any fixed polynomial in rank. It does not prove that every algorithm must lose that much: whether the guarantee can be improved to some \(n^C\) is the existence question on this card.

Haviv and Regev prove hardness at factors \(2^{(\log n)^{1-\varepsilon}}\), for fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), unless NP has one-sided-error randomized quasipolynomial-time algorithms. Under the stronger randomized subexponential-time assumption they obtain \(n^{c/\log\log n}\) for some fixed \(c>0\). Both factors are subpolynomial: for every fixed \(C>0\), they eventually lie below \(n^C\). Their theorem therefore does not rule out the looser approximation asked for here. The randomness assumptions are part of the result.

For \(\gamma\geq1\), GapSVP asks whether \(\lambda_1\leq r\) or \(\lambda_1>\gamma r\), promised one of those alternatives and given \(r>0\). Aharonov and Regev place this decision problem, for some factor \(\gamma=c\sqrt n\), in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\): each promised answer has a polynomial-length certificate verifiable in polynomial time. This is not a polynomial-time method of finding the requested vector. Their full Corollary 1.2 specifies a constant \(c\); it does not assert the result for every smaller factor hidden in big-O notation.

Bennett’s separate search-to-decision question underscores that approximate search SVP, gap decision, unique-SVP and shortest-independent-vectors problems must be distinguished. Cryptographic worst-case-to-average-case reductions concern specified variants at specified approximation and noise parameters. An algorithm here would change the search-SVP landscape; a security reduction alone does not make every cryptographic problem equivalent to it.

Shenoy’s 2024 article advertises an approximation expressed through \(1/(1-\delta)\). In the checked accepted manuscript, Theorem IV.2 defines \(\delta\) from the actual basis, and Corollary IV.3 retains that dependence in a squared-length bound. Merely knowing \(0\leq\delta<1\) supplies no fixed rank-polynomial upper bound on the factor. The manuscript is not counted as a solution of this card; its general convergence claim was not independently verified.

Sato and Yasuda’s May 2026 theorem bounds the number of calls to PotENUM by a quantity polynomial in rank and input coefficient bit length for a fixed reduction parameter. The full Theorem 2 and Remark 2 separately retain an exponential-in-blocksize enumeration factor and the cost of processing each enumeration node. A polynomial number of calls is therefore not a polynomial total bit-time guarantee with arbitrary blocksize.

Hair and Sahai’s April 2026 revision gives a deterministic subexponential-time reduction from satisfiability to Euclidean GapSVP with a subpolynomial approximation gap. Its deterministic hardness conclusion assumes that NP is not contained in the intersection of deterministic time classes \(\operatorname{DTIME}(\exp(m^\eta))\) over all fixed \(\eta>0\), where \(m\) is the source input length. A deterministic reduction does not remove the stated complexity assumption, nor automatically exclude bounded-error randomized algorithms under that same deterministic assumption.

Hirahara and Ogitsuka’s paper, published at RANDOM on September 9, 2026, obtains deterministic constant-factor Euclidean hardness under an explicit lower-bound assumption against nondeterministic circuits. Its parameterized results use another resource measure. Wan’s September 8 revision separately claims unconditional deterministic reductions for every fixed constant factor, but explicitly removes its first version’s dimension-dependent claims after identifying a false tensor-product premise. Neither statement gives unconditional impossibility for all randomized algorithms and all polynomial factors. The new proofs were not independently verified.

The September Wan revision is the version used here: its Theorem 1.2 concerns fixed constant factors, and its introduction expressly withdraws the earlier dimension-dependent consequences. An older abstract or first-version summary must not be used to restore those withdrawn consequences.

Joglekar, Shinde and Agarkar’s September 9 revision concerns a generic metric supplied through a black-box distance oracle, for small constant approximation factors. Its adversary is permitted to perturb the metric. That is distinct from the explicit rational basis and fixed Euclidean norm on this card, and is not an unconditional lower bound for this target.

A classical algorithm satisfying this card also qualifies for the quantum approximation target TCS-7234. The converse is not automatic. Exact quantum search is separately retained as TCS-7169. The present target permits any fixed approximation exponent, rather than asking to optimize that exponent or requiring exact shortest-vector recovery.
