cards.context:
For integer \(M\geq1\), the basis columns \((M,1)\) and \((M+1,1)\) are both long but their lattice contains \((1,0)\). Thus input column lengths alone do not determine the shortest lattice length. More generally, the same lattice has many bases, and the guarantee must be relative to its intrinsic minimum on every supplied basis.

With its standard parameter, LLL gives a nonzero vector of length at most \(2^{(n-1)/2}\lambda_1\) in polynomial bit time. The original paper separately controls the number of arithmetic operations and the binary lengths of their operands. Its approximation factor is exponential in rank even though the running time is polynomial; a runtime statement alone does not specify the quality of the vector.

Bennett’s 2023 survey summarizes improved general polynomial-time guarantees with factor \(2^{O(n\log\log n/\log n)}\). This established upper guarantee is still much larger than any fixed polynomial in rank. It does not prove that every algorithm must lose that much: whether the guarantee can be improved to some \(n^C\) is the existence question on this card.

Haviv and Regev prove hardness at factors \(2^{(\log n)^{1-\varepsilon}}\), for fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), unless NP has one-sided-error randomized quasipolynomial-time algorithms. Under the stronger randomized subexponential-time assumption they obtain \(n^{c/\log\log n}\) for some fixed \(c>0\). Both factors are subpolynomial: for every fixed \(C>0\), they eventually lie below \(n^C\). Their theorem therefore does not rule out the looser approximation asked for here. The randomness assumptions are part of the result.

For \(\gamma\geq1\), GapSVP asks whether \(\lambda_1\leq r\) or \(\lambda_1>\gamma r\), promised one of those alternatives and given \(r>0\). Aharonov and Regev place this decision problem, for some factor \(\gamma=c\sqrt n\), in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\): each promised answer has a polynomial-length certificate verifiable in polynomial time. This is not a polynomial-time method of finding the requested vector. Their full Corollary 1.2 specifies a constant \(c\); it does not assert the result for every smaller factor hidden in big-O notation.

Bennett’s separate search-to-decision question underscores that approximate search SVP, gap decision, unique-SVP and shortest-independent-vectors problems must be distinguished. Cryptographic worst-case-to-average-case reductions concern specified variants at specified approximation and noise parameters. An algorithm here would change the search-SVP landscape; a security reduction alone does not make every cryptographic problem equivalent to it.

Shenoy’s 2024 article advertises an approximation expressed through \(1/(1-\delta)\). In the checked accepted manuscript, Theorem IV.2 defines \(\delta\) from the actual basis, and Corollary IV.3 retains that dependence in a squared-length bound. Merely knowing \(0\leq\delta<1\) supplies no fixed rank-polynomial upper bound on the factor. The manuscript is not counted as a solution of this card; its general convergence claim was not independently verified.

Sato and Yasuda’s May 2026 theorem bounds the number of calls to PotENUM by a quantity polynomial in rank and input coefficient bit length for a fixed reduction parameter. The full Theorem 2 and Remark 2 separately retain an exponential-in-blocksize enumeration factor and the cost of processing each enumeration node. A polynomial number of calls is therefore not a polynomial total bit-time guarantee with arbitrary blocksize.

Hair and Sahai’s April 2026 revision gives a deterministic subexponential-time reduction from satisfiability to Euclidean GapSVP with a subpolynomial approximation gap. Its deterministic hardness conclusion assumes that NP is not contained in the intersection of deterministic time classes \(\operatorname{DTIME}(\exp(m^\eta))\) over all fixed \(\eta>0\), where \(m\) is the source input length. A deterministic reduction does not remove the stated complexity assumption, nor automatically exclude bounded-error randomized algorithms under that same deterministic assumption.

Hirahara and Ogitsuka’s paper, published at RANDOM on September 9, 2026, obtains deterministic constant-factor Euclidean hardness under an explicit lower-bound assumption against nondeterministic circuits. Its parameterized results use another resource measure. Wan’s September 8 revision separately claims unconditional deterministic reductions for every fixed constant factor, but explicitly removes its first version’s dimension-dependent claims after identifying a false tensor-product premise. Neither statement gives unconditional impossibility for all randomized algorithms and all polynomial factors. The new proofs were not independently verified.

The September Wan revision is the version used here: its Theorem 1.2 concerns fixed constant factors, and its introduction expressly withdraws the earlier dimension-dependent consequences. An older abstract or first-version summary must not be used to restore those withdrawn consequences.

Joglekar, Shinde and Agarkar’s September 9 revision concerns a generic metric supplied through a black-box distance oracle, for small constant approximation factors. Its adversary is permitted to perturb the metric. That is distinct from the explicit rational basis and fixed Euclidean norm on this card, and is not an unconditional lower bound for this target.

A classical algorithm satisfying this card also qualifies for the quantum approximation target TCS-7234. The converse is not automatic. Exact quantum search is separately retained as TCS-7169. The present target permits any fixed approximation exponent, rather than asking to optimize that exponent or requiring exact shortest-vector recovery.

cards.title: Vinogradov’s least quadratic nonresidue conjecture
cards.formal:
For an odd prime \(p\), let \(n(p)\) be the least positive quadratic nonresidue modulo \(p\), defined below. Is it true, unconditionally, that
\[\forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists P_\varepsilon\in\mathbb N\ \forall p\ge P_\varepsilon\text{ odd prime},\qquad n(p)\le p^{\varepsilon}?\]
Equivalently, is \(n(p)=p^{o(1)}\) as \(p\) tends to infinity through the odd primes? The threshold may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on the prime. No unproved analytic hypothesis is assumed.
cards.why: A small quadratic nonresidue is a basic witness used in finite-field arithmetic, and its size measures how long the initial integers can all behave like squares modulo a prime. The conjecture asks for uniform cancellation strong enough to beat every fixed power of the modulus. It would cross a long-standing barrier in character sums and bound the range of deterministic searches for such witnesses; subpolynomial size in the modulus is not the same claim as polynomial size in its bit length.
cards.status_note: Tao’s Conjecture 1.1 and Theorem 1.3 and Quesada-Herrera’s June 2025 slides 14–15 were checked on 2026-09-14. The latter retains the unconditional Burgess bound and explicitly labels its stronger recent bound as conditional on GRH. A bounded search including 2026 work found no matching unconditional all-primes resolution. This is source-open status with those limits.

sentences: A quadratic nonresidue is a nonzero residue that is not a square modulo the prime.
Vinogradov’s conjecture says that the least positive one eventually lies below every fixed positive power of the prime.
The threshold may depend on the exponent, but the bound must cover every sufficiently large odd prime.
Conditional logarithmic-square estimates and almost-all-prime results do not establish this unconditional statement.
A refutation would require one fixed positive exponent and arbitrarily large primes violating its bound.

cards.definitions:
For integers \(a,b\) and a positive integer \(p\), the congruence \(a\equiv b\pmod p\) means that \(p\) divides \(a-b\). An integer \(a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\) if there exists \(x\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\) with \(x^2\equiv a\pmod p\); otherwise it is a quadratic nonresidue. Define
\[n(p)=\min\{a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}:\forall x\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\},\ x^2\not\equiv a\pmod p\}.\]
For an odd prime, exactly half of its nonzero residue classes are squares, so the set is nonempty. Representatives are ordered as ordinary positive integers; this is not the least absolute value among positive and negative representatives. Multiples of \(p\) are not counted as nonresidues.

The domain is all odd primes, not composite moduli, almost all primes, or one prescribed congruence class. The prime \(2\) is omitted because every nonzero residue modulo \(2\) is a square. Real powers have the convention \(p^\varepsilon=\exp(\varepsilon\log p)\), where \(\log\) is the natural logarithm.

The statement can equivalently be expressed using only integer powers:
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists P_k\in\mathbb N\ \forall p\ge P_k\text{ odd prime},\qquad n(p)^k\le p.\]
Likewise, the subpolynomial notation means \(\lim_{p\to\infty,\ p\ \mathrm{prime}}\log n(p)/\log p=0\). The source writes \(n(p)=O_\varepsilon(p^\varepsilon)\); since its claim quantifies over every positive exponent, the implicit constant can be absorbed by using a smaller exponent and increasing the threshold. The unit-leading-constant formulation above is therefore equivalent. The conjecture asks for existence of the thresholds, without an extra requirement to compute them effectively.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal statement, or a Lean-checked refutation. A refutation must establish a fixed \(\varepsilon_0>0\) and arbitrarily large odd primes \(p\) with \(n(p)>p^{\varepsilon_0}\). A finite numerical exception cannot refute an eventual bound. A result for almost all primes, a bound with one fixed positive exponent, or a theorem assuming GRH or Elliott–Halberstam is insufficient without also proving the necessary hypothesis.

context_blocks.text: Tao states the conjecture with a constant depending on the chosen exponent and records the general unconditional Burgess bound \(n(p)=O_\eta(p^{1/(4\sqrt e)+\eta})\) for every \(\eta>0\), where \(e=\exp(1)\). That fixed positive base exponent does not imply the conjecture.

The introduction records Ankeny’s stronger \(O((\log p)^2)\) bound under the generalized Riemann hypothesis. It also notes results for almost all primes. Both are separated from the unconditional all-primes target.

Tao’s Theorem 1.3 proves that the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture on primes in arithmetic progressions implies Vinogradov’s conjecture. This is a conditional implication, not an unconditional resolution.

Quesada-Herrera’s June 2025 slides continue to display the Burgess exponent as the unconditional bound. The following slide discusses a better constant in a logarithmic-square estimate and explicitly assumes GRH. That improvement therefore does not settle the statement here.

cards.title: Exact Euclidean SVP in BQP
cards.formal: Do there exist a uniform quantum algorithm and a polynomial p such that, for every integer matrix \(B\in \mathbb{Z} ^{m\times d}\) with \(m\ge d\ge 1\) and linearly independent columns, the algorithm outputs \(z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{d}\setminus \{0\}\) satisfying ||\(Bz||_{2}=\min _{y\in \mathbb{Z} ^{d}\setminus \{0\}}||\)By||\(_{2}\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(p(\mathrm{L})\) elementary steps on every execution? L is the total binary encoding length of m, d and all entries of B.

cards.definitions: The lattice generated by B is \(\Lambda (B)=\{Bz:z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{d}\}; d\) is its rank and m its ambient dimension. Its first minimum \(\lambda _{1}(\Lambda )\) is the minimum Euclidean length of a nonzero lattice vector. Full column rank makes this minimum positive and attained. The output is the signed binary coefficient vector z, so lattice membership and the corresponding integer vector Bz can be recovered without a real-number encoding. Any shortest vector is acceptable, with no uniqueness promise; the zero vector is excluded. Exactness means squared length equals \(\lambda _{1}^{2}\), rather than being within a multiplicative factor greater than one. Use the standard uniform quantum circuit model: a classical polynomial-time machine generates, from \(1^{\mathrm{L}}, a\) circuit on an L-bit input register, zero-initialized ancillary qubits and output qubits, using the fixed universal gates H, T and CNOT, followed by computational-basis measurement and polynomial-time classical decoding. H is the Hadamard gate, \(T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\), and CNOT maps |\(a,b\rangle\) to |\(a,a\oplus b\rangle\). Circuit size, qubit count, input processing and output writing are polynomial in L. No advice, oracle, pre-supplied quantum state or unit-cost access to an exponentially large memory is provided. Failure is allowed on at most one third of runs for each valid input; it is not an average over randomly chosen lattices. Malformed encodings and rank-deficient matrices can be rejected classically. Integer bases are the imported target; clearing rational denominators preserves shortest vectors up to a common scale and increases encoding length only polynomially.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of the algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial cost and exact-search success on every valid basis, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Classical NP-hardness alone does not establish the negative answer for quantum computation. A polynomial-factor approximation, an algorithm for a promised special family, or an exponential-time speedup does not establish the positive answer.

context_blocks.title: The basis can hide a short vector
context_blocks.text: The vectors \((100,1)\) and \((101,1)\) are both long, but their difference is \((1,0)\). Since every nonzero integer vector has length at least one, this difference is shortest in their lattice. SVP searches all integer combinations of the supplied basis, rather than choosing its shortest column.

context_blocks.title: Exactness is a separate demand from probability
context_blocks.text: A successful run must output a genuinely shortest vector. Bounded error permits some runs to fail; it does not permit every run to return a slightly longer vector. Similarly, a quantum state encoding many candidate vectors is not the requested classical answer until a shortest coefficient vector can be extracted with the required probability.

context_blocks.title: Why classical hardness does not settle the quantum question
context_blocks.text: Micciancio proves randomized NP-hardness even for some constant-factor Euclidean approximations, hence also for exact search. A polynomial-time quantum exact solver would therefore put all NP decision problems in BQP, the class with bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithms. This is a complexity consequence of the reduction, not a proved impossibility: \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}\) is not known to be false.

context_blocks.title: Faster exponential algorithms still leave the target open
context_blocks.text: The 2025 paper gives exact quantum algorithms with exponential dependence on rank and explicitly separates QRAM access. Hhan’s August 2026 preprint states expected classical time about \(2^{0.6039d}\) and quantum time about \(2^{0.5411d}\), up to lower-order exponential and polynomial factors; the quantum bound uses exponentially large QRAM. Kim’s concurrent sampling preprint also gives an exponential exact-SVP consequence. These recent claims were checked for scope, not independently proved. None gives polynomial time in L.

context_blocks.title: The recent coset claim has a different lattice consequence
context_blocks.text: Simon’s August 2026 DCP preprint claims polynomial-factor approximate SVP, which would not provide exact shortest vectors even if the algorithm were correct. Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised on 1 September, claims a direct impossibility result for that proposed algorithm. The claim and response therefore do not supply a resolution of the exact-search problem on this card.

A polynomial-time quantum exact solver would therefore put all NP decision problems in BQP, the class with bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithms. This is a complexity consequence of the reduction, not a proved impossibility: \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}\) is not known to be false.

The 2025 paper gives exact quantum algorithms with exponential dependence on rank and explicitly separates QRAM access. Hhan’s August 2026 preprint states expected classical time about \(2^{0.6039d}\) and quantum time about \(2^{0.5411d}\), up to lower-order exponential and polynomial factors; the quantum bound uses exponentially large QRAM. Kim’s concurrent sampling preprint also gives an exponential exact-SVP consequence. These recent claims were checked for scope, not independently proved. None gives polynomial time in L.

Simon’s August 2026 DCP preprint claims polynomial-factor approximate SVP, which would not provide exact shortest vectors even if the algorithm were correct. Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised on 1 September, claims a direct impossibility result for that proposed algorithm. The claim and response therefore do not supply a resolution of the exact-search problem on this card.

cards.title: Quantum polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\), an integer \(k\geq1\), a real constant \(K>0\), and one uniform quantum algorithm \(A\) with the following property? For every pair of integers \(d\geq n\geq1\) and every explicitly given matrix \(B\in\mathbb Q^{d\times n}\) with linearly independent columns, the algorithm terminates within \(K(N+1)^k\) charged operations on every execution and outputs a nonzero integer vector \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), with
\[\Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\leq n^C\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\geq\frac23.\]
Here \(N\) is the full binary input length, \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), and \(\lambda_1(L(B))\) is the length of its shortest nonzero vector. The probability is over the computation’s measurement outcomes on this fixed classical input. All constants and the program are chosen before the input; the approximation exponent depends on neither rank nor coefficient size.
cards.definitions:
The input contains \(d,n\) and all \(dn\) rational entries in row-major order. To fix a binary encoding, let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(t\), using the one-bit string \(0\) for zero, and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Dimensions use \(E(d),E(n)\). A rational number is encoded by a sign bit followed by \(E(|a|)E(q)\), where it equals \(a/q\), \(q>0\), and \(\gcd(|a|,q)=1\); zero has positive sign and denominator one. There are exactly \(dn\) entries and no trailing bits. Valid inputs satisfy \(d\geq n\geq1\) and column independence over \(\mathbb Q\). The total number of encoded bits is \(N\). The polynomial clock applies on every binary input; behavior and output on malformed or dependent-basis inputs are otherwise unrestricted.

The Euclidean norm of \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The lattice consists of all integer combinations of the columns, with its usual embedding in \(\mathbb R^d\). Independence makes \(z\mapsto Bz\) injective and makes \(L(B)\) discrete in its real span. Thus
\[\lambda_1(L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2>0\]
is attained. No uniqueness of the shortest vector up to sign is assumed. The algorithm returns the coefficient vector: its \(n\) signed integer coordinates use a sign bit and \(E\) of the absolute value, with positive sign for zero. It must return a valid nonzero vector on every execution on a valid input. An unsuccessful execution may exceed the norm bound, but may not output zero, fail to halt or omit the vector. The squared norm can equivalently be used in the displayed guarantee with squared factor \(n^{2C}\).

A uniform quantum algorithm means one finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine controller with classical input, work and output tapes and a collection of initially zero qubits. In addition to ordinary bit-machine steps, it may apply a gate from \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\) to explicitly addressed qubits, or measure an addressed qubit in the computational basis and receive its classical result. Qubit indices are written in binary on control tapes; writing and processing them take ordinary charged steps. Initializing a fresh zero qubit is charged, so the number of qubits is also polynomially bounded. The input is supplied as classical bits, not as a quantum state-preparation oracle. Classical input bits may be transferred to qubits through charged computation.

For computational basis states \(|0\rangle,|1\rangle\), the gates are
\[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4}),\qquad
\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle,\]
where \(a,b\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. A register of \(q\) qubits has state a unit vector in \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes q}\). A gate acts on its addressed factors and as the identity elsewhere. Measurement outcome \(a\) has probability equal to the squared norm of the projection onto the subspace whose measured bit is \(a\), after which the state is that normalized projection. Classical control may depend on all earlier outcomes. Probabilities of complete executions are defined by these conditional Born probabilities. Fair classical random bits can be generated by a Hadamard gate followed by measurement; their cost is included.

Each classical Turing-machine step, gate, initialization, measurement and output-bit write costs one operation; any fixed overlap in bookkeeping changes only the constant \(K\). The stated bound holds on every possible measurement branch, including unsuccessful branches. There is no quantum advice, computational oracle, free input oracle, postselection on rare outcomes or arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic. The program is independent of input length and of the particular basis. All classical control, including input parsing and generation of the quantum operations, contributes to the same bound.

The approximation parameter is the rank \(n\), not the ambient dimension \(d\) or the bit length \(N\). In rank one the factor is exactly one. Coefficients may have arbitrary binary length, subject only to being part of the input. There is no promised gap between successive vector lengths, random input distribution, special ring structure, modular form or bound on the basis conditioning. Success is required separately on every valid basis, not on average over bases.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of one algorithm and fixed constants \(C,K,k\) satisfying the entire statement, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must rule out every constant polynomial approximation factor and every uniform quantum algorithm with any fixed polynomial clock in the full bit length; an impossibility for one exponent, one circuit family, one oracle model or classical algorithms alone is insufficient. A valid positive answer must prove the actual nonzero-vector output and success probability on all valid inputs, with every-execution cost including classical processing. A decision algorithm for a length threshold, an algorithm assuming a unique shortest direction, a conditional cryptanalytic reduction, or a numerical experiment is not by itself an answer. Conditional results establish only their conditional conclusions unless the additional assumptions are proved. This is an exact existence proposition; the benchmark’s numerical tolerance does not weaken its approximation or probability requirements.
cards.why: This isolates whether quantum computation changes the polynomial-time approximation boundary for unrestricted Euclidean lattice search. A positive answer would improve the guarantee from a superpolynomial loss to one fixed power of rank on every lattice. A negative answer would establish an unconditional limitation on general quantum computation, far beyond the failure of any particular quantum lattice algorithm. Its cryptographic implications depend on the exact lattice task and approximation exponent.

context_blocks.text: Long basis vectors need not imply a large lattice minimum. The two columns \((M,1)\) and \((M+1,1)\), with integer \(M\geq1\), generate a lattice containing \((1,0)\), although both input columns are long. The objective concerns all nonzero integer combinations. It differs from finding the shortest input column and from minimizing over real coefficients, where arbitrarily small nonzero combinations exist.

Bennett’s survey defines approximate search SVP by the same multiplicative comparison with \(\lambda_1\). It records the classical polynomial-time LLL guarantee \(2^{O(n)}\). The factor \(n^C\) requested here is a much stronger bound for every fixed \(C\), while allowing any such constant is a substantial relaxation of exact shortest-vector search. Small-dimensional experiments or guarantees for a particular basis family do not cover this quantifier order.

The decision problem \(\gamma\)-GapSVP is given a basis and a threshold \(r>0\), with a promise of either \(\lambda_1\leq r\) or \(\lambda_1>\gamma r\), and asks which case holds. It does not output a vector. Bennett’s §4.2 explicitly records the unresolved general search-to-decision connection with polynomially controlled approximation. This card does not silently identify those two tasks. Likewise, unique-SVP assumes that every vector linearly independent of a shortest vector is longer by a promised factor; unrestricted SVP has no such promise.

Regev’s original worst-case-to-average-case theorem says that an efficient solver for specified Learning With Errors parameters yields quantum algorithms for the stated GapSVP and shortest-independent-vectors tasks. Learning With Errors supplies random linear equations with a controlled noise distribution; it is not the classical arbitrary-basis input specified here. The direction, task and parameter losses of a reduction matter. In particular, this theorem is not an unrestricted equivalence between polynomial-factor search SVP and every LWE family.

The Brakerski–Kirshanova–Stehlé–Wen paper explicitly describes Regev’s dihedral-coset reduction as a reduction for unique-SVP, then establishes an LWE connection with extrapolated dihedral cosets under parameter losses. Such coset problems supply particular quantum samples as input. Their efficient solution is a separate claim whose consequences for an arbitrary classical basis require a proved reduction with the appropriate target.

The April 2024 Chen manuscript initially claimed new polynomial-time quantum lattice and LWE algorithms. Its archive entry includes an explicit April 18 author correction: a bug in Step 9 invalidates the stated polynomial-modulus LWE claim, with no repair then known. The surviving old abstract is therefore not evidence of a verified breakthrough.

Zhang’s May 14, 2026 revision analyzes a conditional replacement for part of that procedure. Its current statement requires additional front-end conditions and access to a run-dependent offset residue; the introduction explicitly says the resulting LWE conclusion is conditional. These assumptions do not form a complete arbitrary-basis algorithm in the model of this card. Earlier stronger-looking descriptions are not substituted for the latest revision.

Simon’s ePrint 2026/1591, first posted August 3 and last revised August 17, explicitly advertises a polynomial-time dihedral-coset algorithm and polynomial-factor SVP consequences. The archive also records a correction to the first draft’s Lemma 3 and the author’s acknowledgment of a subsequent refutation. The available abstract alone does not verify the asserted unrestricted search consequence or its bit-complexity conventions. The claim is recorded as disputed, not as a resolution.

Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised September 1, states that Simon’s August 11 algorithm cannot recover even the secret’s least-significant bit with nonnegligible advantage. They provide accompanying Lean 4 code. The repository describes precise rounding and register conventions, and a theorem about the specified bit-output procedure and controllers of its coarse outcomes; it explicitly distinguishes this from a formalization of the full-secret recursion. This audit read those scope declarations but did not build or independently verify the proofs, and could not retrieve either ePrint PDF. The rebuttal is evidence against that proposed algorithm, not a lower bound against all algorithms on this card.

The accompanying repository explicitly states that its full-secret solver recursion is not formalized and that its controller theorem observes prescribed restart/bit outcomes rather than every internal measurement record. Those declared limits must be retained when describing what has been machine checked by its authors.

A classical solution of TCS-6667 with the matching factor would also solve this quantum existence target, and an exact quantum solution of TCS-7169 would supply the stronger approximation guarantee. Neither implication reverses automatically. An algorithm here would be a major lattice-complexity advance, but declaring a particular cryptosystem broken would require checking its problem variant, parameters and reductions.

cards.title: Deterministic polynomial-time construction of a prime of a given bit length
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that constructs a prime of every requested bit length in polynomial bit time?

The input is the unary string \(1^n\), for any integer \(n\ge2\). The output must be the binary expansion of some prime \(p\) satisfying
\[
2^{n-1}\le p<2^n.
\]
The prime may be any one in this interval; no particular choice, such as the smallest prime, is prescribed.

With the finite machine model and output predicate below, the precise assertion is
\[
\exists A\ \exists C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ 
\forall n\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\quad
\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\ 
\bigl(
\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,1^n,y,Cn^k)
\land \operatorname{PrimeOutput}(n,y)
\bigr).
\]
One fixed deterministic program and one polynomial bound must work for every requested length. This retains the source's unary-input prime-construction question and makes its bit-computation convention explicit.
cards.definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge2\), the unary string \(1^n\) consists of exactly \(n\) consecutive copies of the symbol one. Its length, rather than the binary length of the integer \(n\), is the input size. Valid inputs are precisely these strings; other input strings impose no requirements.

A positive integer \(p\) is prime when \(p\ge2\) and every positive integer dividing \(p\) is either one or \(p\) itself. A binary output string \(y=y_0y_1\cdots y_{n-1}\) of length \(n\), with \(y_0=1\), represents
\[
\operatorname{val}(y)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}y_i2^{n-1-i}.
\]
Here each symbol \(y_i\) is identified with the integer zero or one. The predicate \(\operatorname{PrimeOutput}(n,y)\) means that \(y\) has exactly this length, its first bit is one, and \(\operatorname{val}(y)\) is prime. No leading zeros, additional bits, compressed description or separate certificate form part of the output. This predicate is equivalent to requiring the ordinary binary expansion of a prime in the displayed interval.

An algorithm \(A\) is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with one read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes, and a binary output stream. Its finite control, finite tape alphabets and number of tapes are fixed independently of the input. Tape cells have nonnegative integer addresses. Initially all heads are at cell zero, work tapes are blank, the input tape contains the input followed by blanks, and the output is empty. Each transition reads the symbols under the heads, changes the finite control, writes at most one symbol on each work tape, moves each head left, right or not at all by at most one cell, and appends at most one bit to the output. A move left from cell zero leaves the head there. The transition rule is a finite deterministic table, defined on every nonhalting state and tuple of scanned symbols, and a designated halt state ends the computation.

One transition costs one bit-computation step. All computation, preprocessing, reading and writing count, including production of all \(n\) output bits. There are no random bits, quantum operations, oracle calls, input-dependent advice or unbounded integers with unit-cost operations. The finite program may contain fixed constants, but receives no additional information depending on \(n\).

The predicate \(\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,x,y,T)\) means that the computation on input \(x\) reaches its halt state after at most \(T\) transitions and has produced exactly the finite output string \(y\). Requiring positive integer constants \(C,k\) expresses ordinary polynomial time: increasing them covers any fixed polynomial bound. Both constants and the whole finite program precede the universal quantifier over \(n\). The assertion is unconditional; an unproved hypothesis about primes or computational hardness is not an additional assumption.

context_blocks.text: The MFCS 2018 paper explicitly asks whether a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm can output an n-bit prime from the unary input specifying n. It distinguishes this construction task from deterministic polynomial-time primality testing and from probabilistic prime generation.

The 2022 survey formulates deterministic prime construction for every bit length at least two and explains its relationship with short time-bounded descriptions of primes. This card retains that all-length construction requirement and specifies the complete finite bit model.

The revised Chen–Lu–Oliveira–Ren–Santhanam manuscript proves an unconditional polynomial-time randomized algorithm that outputs a fixed prime with high probability for infinitely many requested bit lengths. Its Corollary 1.2 is a pseudodeterministic result: it permits random choices and does not give the deterministic construction required here.

The same manuscript records an unconditional deterministic upper bound of \(2^{(1/2+o(1))n}\) time, still exponential in the requested bit length. Its discussion of conditional polynomial-time construction uses stronger unproved hypotheses, including Cramér’s prime-gap conjecture; these are not assumptions of this card.

cards.why: Prime generation is a canonical example where recognizing a suitable object is efficiently possible but constructing one deterministically remains unresolved. A positive answer would remove randomness from this basic number-theoretic construction at every bit length. A negative answer would establish an unconditional computational lower bound for a concrete total search problem. The connection with succinct descriptions of primes also makes the question central to research on derandomization and time-bounded information.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence assertion or of its full logical negation.

A positive answer must supply one finite deterministic program \(A\) and positive integers \(C,k\), and prove for every \(n\ge2\) that it halts on \(1^n\) within \(Cn^k\) bit steps and outputs exactly the binary expansion of an \(n\)-bit prime. The output prime need not be the first prime in its interval.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\forall A\ \forall C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\quad
\exists n\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\quad
\neg\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\ 
\bigl(
\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,1^n,y,Cn^k)
\land \operatorname{PrimeOutput}(n,y)
\bigr).
\]
Thus each proposed deterministic program and polynomial bound must fail at some length, which may depend on both. Failure includes running longer than the bound, never halting, or producing an invalid prime output. This does not assert that some bit length contains no prime.

A randomized or pseudodeterministic construction, success only at infinitely many lengths, or a bound that is polynomial in the numerical value of the output instead of its bit length does not establish the positive assertion. A conditional result establishes the target only if its additional hypothesis is also proved. A lower bound for one search procedure does not establish the unrestricted negative assertion. This is an exact algorithm-existence question, so numerical \(1/100\) approximation is not a substitute for the required proof.

cards.title: Polynomial-factor Euclidean SVP hardness assuming NP is not contained in RP
cards.formal:
Is the following implication true?
\[
\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{RP}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q,\ 0<\varepsilon<1/2:
\operatorname{GapSVP}^{(2)}_{n^\varepsilon}\notin\operatorname{PromiseBPP}.
\]
Thus the target is a fixed positive power of the lattice rank in the Euclidean norm, with no classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm under the specified standard assumption. The exponent may be arbitrarily small but must be independent of the input.
cards.why: Constant-factor Euclidean lattice hardness does not explain whether even a small fixed power of the rank remains difficult to approximate. Establishing this from the standard randomized NP-hardness assumption would close a major qualitative gap in the approximation landscape.
cards.status_note: The selected Euclidean implication remains unresolved in the checked primary sources through 17 September 2026. The August 2026 theorem resolves a broader any-norm interpretation for p > 2 but excludes p=2, and Wan’s September revision retains only fixed-factor claims. The norm and hypothesis were explicit announced editorial choices after unanswered optional questions; this card does not claim the entire original any-norm direction remains open. cards.definitions:
An input is an integer matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) of full column rank, with \(m\ge n\ge2\), together with a positive rational \(r\). All dimensions, matrix entries and the numerator and denominator of \(r\) are explicitly given in binary with delimiters. Let \(L\) be the complete encoding length. Define
\[
\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\},\qquad
\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2,
\quad \|v\|_2=\left(\sum_i v_i^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
For a fixed \(\varepsilon\), the yes-instances have \(\lambda_1\le r\), the no-instances have \(\lambda_1>n^\varepsilon r\), and the inputs with \(r<\lambda_1\le n^\varepsilon r\) are outside the promise. The task is to output the correct yes/no bit; it does not ask for a lattice vector. The approximation factor is an exact mathematical threshold and depends on rank, not ambient dimension or coefficient bit length.

Membership in PromiseBPP means that there are one uniform classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\), with independent fair random bits, and constants \(K,a>0\), such that every run on a well-formed input halts within \(K(L+1)^a\) bit operations, every yes-instance is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\), and every no-instance is rejected with probability at least \(2/3\). Behavior inside the approximation gap is unrestricted. There are no quantum operations, advice or additional oracles. The machine and its constants may depend on the fixed \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(B,r\).

The class NP consists of finite-bit decision languages with polynomial-length witnesses checked by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier. The class RP consists of languages with a uniform randomized polynomial-time decision algorithm that never accepts a no-instance and accepts each yes-instance with probability at least \(1/2\). The antecedent says that at least one NP language has no such RP algorithm. This is an ordinary decision-complexity hypothesis, not an assumption that a lattice problem is hard.

The conclusion requires one rational exponent for which no machine with the stated bounded-error guarantee exists. It does not merely rule out deterministic algorithms or one particular family of reduction algorithms. Restricting the existential exponent to rational values below \(1/2\) does not remove a possible positive-power hardness result: a solver for a smaller gap would also solve the promise problem for any larger gap. No common algorithm is required across different exponents if the conclusion fails.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed implication, with an explicit rational exponent or a rigorous existence proof and all claimed algorithmic guarantees, or prove its logical negation. A refutation must establish NP ⊄ RP together with PromiseBPP membership for every rational exponent in (0,1/2). Hardness only in a norm p > 2, only for constant factors or for subpolynomial factors, or only under a stronger subexponential-time hypothesis does not settle this target.

cards.title: Quantum-ETH hardness of cryptographic-factor GapSVP
cards.formal:
Does the quantum Exponential Time Hypothesis defined below imply that, for some fixed integer \(k\ge1\), there is no bounded-error uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithm for Euclidean
\[\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma_k},\qquad \gamma_k(n)=n^{3/2+1/k}?\]
Equivalently, the target is the conditional assertion
\[\mathrm{QETH}\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma_k}\notin\mathrm{PromiseBQP}.\]
The source asks for hardness at \(n^{3/2+\varepsilon}\) for some constant \(\varepsilon>0\) under a standard complexity assumption, without selecting that assumption. This card explicitly selects quantum ETH for classical 3-SAT; it is an editorial variant of that research direction, not a claim that the source stated this particular implication.
cards.why: This question asks whether a familiar quantum satisfiability assumption can support hardness of lattice approximation at a scale relevant to worst-case-to-average-case cryptographic reductions. That scale is much larger than constant-factor approximation, and hardness at a small factor does not automatically persist as the promise gap grows. A proof would connect lattice-based security foundations to a separate complexity assumption while addressing quantum algorithms explicitly.
cards.status_note: Bennett’s January 2023 Definition 1.1, Section 4.1 and Open Problem 4.11, Chia–Chou–Zhang–Zhang’s ECCC revision Definition 4.25, Hecht–Safra’s Theorems 1.1–1.2, and Wan arXiv:2603.27398v3 Theorems 1.3/1.8 and surrounding scope were read on 2026-09-14. The recent results concern other norms or constant factors, and the Euclidean preprint proof was not independently verified. A bounded later-work search found no matching hardness theorem or algorithm for the selected cryptographic-factor implication. Quantum ETH is an explicitly chosen assumption variant of the source’s broader question; current source-open status does not assert that this particular implication was posed verbatim by Bennett.

cards.definitions:
An instance consists of an integer \(n\ge1\), a nonsingular rational matrix \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), and a positive rational threshold \(r\). The columns of \(B\) form a full-rank lattice basis. Its lattice and shortest-vector length are
\[\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\},\qquad \lambda_1(B)=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2,\]
where \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^{1/2}\). The minimum exists and is positive for a nonsingular basis. No ideal-lattice, module-lattice, random-lattice or special-basis promise is imposed.

The promise problem has YES instances with \(\lambda_1(B)\le r\) and NO instances with \(\lambda_1(B)>\gamma_k(n)r\). Either condition is promised. For \(r<\lambda_1(B)\le\gamma_k(n)r\), either answer is allowed. This preserves the source’s strict inequality on the NO side. The task is deciding the promise, not outputting a short vector. The dimension in the approximation factor is \(n\), not the bit length of the matrix entries.

Use a binary encoding of \(n\), the matrix entries and \(r\), each rational represented by its signed reduced numerator and positive denominator, with self-delimiting lengths. Let \(L\) denote the total input bit length. A quantum polynomial-time solver is one finite uniform quantum algorithm, for the fixed chosen \(k\), which uses at most \(C(L+1)^a\) elementary operations for constants \(C,a\) on every branch, and returns the correct promise answer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every YES and every NO instance. It must halt on all inputs within the time bound; malformed encodings, singular matrices and inputs outside the promise require no particular answer. This is the meaning of \(\mathrm{PromiseBQP}\) here. The program and polynomial may depend on \(k\), which is not an instance parameter.

For definiteness, uniform quantum computation uses a classical Turing controller, qubits initially in computational-basis states, gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), and computational-basis measurements with the Born probabilities. On one qubit, \(H|b\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^b|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\) for \(b\in\{0,1\}\), and \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\). The controlled-not gate maps \(|a,b\rangle\) to \(|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Classical tape work, input reading, generation of gate instructions, gate applications and measurements are charged. The algorithm has no advice, external oracle, uncharged quantum state or postselection. Adaptive classical control and classical randomization obtained by measurement are allowed.

Quantum ETH in this card is a statement about classical Boolean satisfiability. A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three signed Boolean variables. It is satisfiable if some assignment makes every clause true. Let \(N\) be its number of variables and \(s\) its binary encoding length. The assumption asserts that there exists \(\delta>0\) for which no uniform quantum algorithm decides satisfiability on every such formula, with error at most \(1/3\), in time \(C2^{\delta N}(s+1)^a\) for any fixed constants \(C,a\). Time is worst-case over inputs and measurement outcomes, in the same uniform quantum model. This uses the positive exponential-rate formulation of Definition 4.25 in the cited quantum complexity paper; it is not a hypothesis about the quantum satisfiability or local-Hamiltonian problem.

The exponent increment is fixed before instances or candidate solvers are considered. Writing it as \(1/k\) loses no existence case from an arbitrary constant \(\varepsilon>0\): choosing \(1/k\le\varepsilon\) only reduces the approximation factor, and a solver for the smaller factor also solves the larger-factor promise. The source’s alternative LWE target is not bundled into this card. No lattice-hardness or cryptographic-security assumption is available in addition to the stated quantum ETH premise.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed conditional assertion with these encodings, norm, approximation factor and uniform quantum model. A positive answer may assume quantum ETH as defined but must establish the claimed exclusion of polynomial-time algorithms, rather than assume hardness of GapSVP or LWE. It must obtain a fixed positive exponent increment and cover all promised rational-basis inputs. A lower bound only for classical algorithms, a constant-factor approximation problem, another norm, or exact SVP alone does not establish this target. Refuting the conditional assertion requires more than showing that one proposed reduction fails; likewise, refuting quantum ETH alone would make the implication vacuously true rather than false.

The cited quantum complexity paper defines a positive-exponential-rate quantum ETH for classical 3-SAT. Its assumption provides the premise used here, rather than an already known reduction to lattice problems.

The source surveys worst-case-to-average-case reductions connecting sufficiently large-factor Euclidean GapSVP hardness to appropriate Learning with Errors parameters. cards.title: Exact Euclidean SVP in single-exponential time and polynomial space
cards.formal:
Do there exist one randomized classical algorithm \(A\) and absolute integers \(C,d\ge1\) such that, for every rational lattice basis \(B\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) with linearly independent columns and total binary encoding length \(L\), the algorithm finds an exact shortest nonzero vector of \(\Lambda(B)\) with probability at least \(2/3\), while using simultaneously at most
\[
2^{Cn}L^d\quad\text{bit operations}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
L^d\quad\text{bits of working space}?
\]
Both bounds must hold on every random tape. The exponent parameter \(n\) is lattice rank, and every \(m\ge n\ge1\) and every valid coefficient encoding are included.
cards.definitions:
The input explicitly gives \(m,n\) and every entry of \(B\), in column or row order fixed by the encoding. A rational entry is a signed binary numerator divided by a positive binary denominator, using canonical integer encodings and unambiguous boundaries. Reduction to lowest terms is not required. The bit length \(L\) includes all entries and dimension data; the input is not a generating circuit or an oracle. Full column rank and \(m\ge n\ge1\) are promises. No behavior on unpromised inputs is required for the target.

The rank-\(n\) lattice is
\[
\Lambda(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^m.
\]
The columns are linearly independent over the rationals, equivalently over the reals, so \(Bz\ne0\) for every nonzero integer coordinate vector \(z\). With the Euclidean norm \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^m v_i^2)^{1/2}\), define
\[
\lambda_1(\Lambda(B))=
\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2.
\]
Full rank makes this a discrete lattice in its linear span, so the positive minimum is attained.

Successful output is a finite binary encoding of a nonzero integer vector \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\) with \(\|Bz\|_2=\lambda_1(\Lambda(B))\). Equivalently, it satisfies the exact rational inequalities
\[
\forall u\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\},\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m(Bz)_i^2\le\sum_{i=1}^m(Bu)_i^2.
\]
Any minimizer is acceptable, including either sign and any of several shortest vectors. The integer coordinates refer to the input basis. An approximate length, a short vector with a factor greater than one, or a real-valued coordinate approximation is not this output. The algorithm may report failure or return a nonoptimal vector on unsuccessful executions; all executions remain subject to both resource bounds.

Use a uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machine with read-only input, write-only output and a one-way stream of independent fair random bits. Working space counts every used work-tape bit, including saved random bits, counters, intermediate vectors, basis transformations and precision data. The random source cannot be revisited as free writable storage. No external writable memory, preprocessing oracle or nonuniform advice is available. Input and final output tapes are not counted as working storage, but every operation reading or writing them counts toward time. All arithmetic is charged in bit operations; arbitrary-precision arithmetic is not a unit-cost instruction.

The success probability is at least \(2/3\) separately for every fixed valid input, over the machine’s internal random bits. The time and space bounds are worst-case over those bits, including unsuccessful executions, and include preprocessing and all precision management. The same constants \(C,d\) apply to all ranks, ambient dimensions and coefficient lengths. Different fixed polynomial exponents for time and space can be absorbed into one \(d\). A deterministic algorithm qualifies as a special case.

No uniqueness, reduced-basis, random-lattice or special-lattice promise is imposed. The desired exponential base is any absolute constant \(2^C\); no particular base such as two is required. The task is an exact search-algorithm existence proposition, not a separate numerical approximation of \(\lambda_1\).
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply an algorithm and complete Lean-checked proofs of both simultaneous resource bounds and its exact success probability on every valid rational basis. Alternatively, supply a complete Lean-checked proof that no algorithm and absolute constants \(C,d\) satisfy the displayed requirements.

A single-exponential algorithm using exponential space, a polynomial-space algorithm with \(2^{\Theta(n\log n)}\) time, a heuristic or average-case guarantee, or an approximation algorithm does not settle the question. A counterexample to one enumeration or sieving procedure does not rule out all algorithms. A lower bound conditional on an unproved lattice-hardness assumption is not an unconditional negative resolution.
cards.why: The problem asks whether exact lattice search can retain a single-exponential time bound while avoiding an exponentially large stored collection. It separates two major resource regimes in lattice algorithms and helps clarify which memory assumptions matter when interpreting lattice-based computational hardness.

cards.title: Polynomial-factor approximation of cyclotomic ideal SVP
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that finds a polynomial-factor approximate shortest nonzero vector in every ideal of every power-of-two cyclotomic ring?

More precisely, do there exist one probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(c,C,d\) such that, for every \(n=2^k\) with integer \(k\ge1\), and every nonsingular matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\) whose column lattice \(I_B=B\mathbb Z^n\) is an ideal of \(R_n=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^n+1)\), the following holds? On the explicit binary input \((n,B)\) of length \(L\), every run of \(A\) halts within \(C(L+1)^d\) bit steps, and
\[\Pr\!\left[A(n,B)\text{ outputs }v\in I_B\setminus\{0\}\text{ with }\|v\|_2\le n^c\lambda_1(I_B)\right]\ge\frac23,\qquad
\lambda_1(I_B)=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2.\]
The constants and program are chosen before the dimension and ideal. The approximation factor depends on dimension, not on coefficient bit lengths. The output must be the full integer coefficient vector \(v\).
cards.why: The central issue is whether the algebraic structure used to make lattice cryptography compact also makes a core worst-case search problem efficiently solvable at polynomial approximation. The selected family is a standard cyclotomic family with growing dimension, not a collection of hand-picked easy ideals. Resolving the question would clarify the computational strength of these structured hardness assumptions. An efficient ideal-SVP algorithm would not, merely by reversing a known security reduction, constitute an attack on every ring-LWE or ring-SIS distribution.
cards.status_note: Reviewed on 16 September 2026. The original 2016 source poses a broad direction; the concrete classical polynomial-time polynomial-factor cyclotomic search target is an explicit editorial specialization. Checked later work gives conditional quantum algorithms at larger approximation factors and algorithms or length results for restricted ideal classes. The September Martin and Wan preprints state hardness in different ring families and/or exact regimes, and their proofs were not independently certified here. No matching resolution of this full selected target was found in the bounded search; source_open records that qualified assessment, not exhaustive certification of openness.

The selected family is a standard cyclotomic family with growing dimension, not a collection of hand-picked easy ideals. Resolving the question would clarify the computational strength of these structured hardness assumptions. An efficient ideal-SVP algorithm would not, merely by reversing a known security reduction, constitute an attack on every ring-LWE or ring-SIS distribution. Editorial placement in this pass: a high-priority broad or central question.

sentences: An ideal in a power-of-two cyclotomic ring is a full integer lattice closed under multiplication by the ring.
The selected question asks for a classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm returning an actual nonzero vector within a fixed polynomial factor of the shortest length.
One program and fixed exponents must work for every dimension and every explicitly supplied ideal basis, with all preprocessing and output charged.
This is an expressly labeled specialization of Peikert’s broad question about algorithmic advantages of ideal-lattice structure.
Conditional quantum algorithms, easy prime-ideal classes and the new exact-hardness claims in other rings do not determine this all-ideals target.

cards.definitions:
Identify \(R_n\) with the integer polynomials of degree less than \(n\), with addition and multiplication reduced modulo \(X^n+1\). Coordinates are ordered as the coefficients of \(1,X,\ldots,X^{n-1}\). The coefficient Euclidean norm is \(\|a\|_2=(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}a_j^2)^{1/2}\). For these dimensions, \(X^n+1\) is the cyclotomic polynomial of conductor \(2n\), so \(R_n\) is the full ring of integers of \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_{2n})\). The dimension varies without an upper bound.

An integral ideal is an additive subgroup closed under multiplication by every ring element. In the supplied coordinates, the input promise is exactly that \(B\) is nonsingular over \(\mathbb Q\) and \(S(B\mathbb Z^n)\subseteq B\mathbb Z^n\), where
\[S(a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1})=(-a_{n-1},a_0,\ldots,a_{n-2}).\]
Closure under \(S\) and under integer linear combinations gives closure under every ring element. Equivalently, all entries of \(B^{-1}SB\) are integers. Every nonzero integral ideal has a full additive basis of this form. The basis need not be reduced, canonical, circulant or generated by one ring element. Arbitrary prime and composite ideals are included, and no factorization, short generator or special distribution of ideals is promised. Nonsingularity makes \(I_B\) a discrete full-rank lattice, so its positive shortest length is attained.

The input is a dense, explicitly written integer matrix. To fix a binary convention, encode a nonnegative integer \(a\) by \(U(a)=1^\ell 0b\), where \(b\) is the usual binary expansion of \(a\), without leading zeros, and \(\ell\) is its length; use \(b=0\) for zero. Encode a signed integer by a sign bit followed by \(U(|a|)\), with sign zero for zero. Write \(U(n)\) followed by the signed entries of \(B\) in row-major order. Their total length is \(L\). No omitted zeros, succinct matrix circuits or unit-cost large integers are available. Valid outputs list the \(n\) signed coordinates in the same integer encoding; writing every output bit is charged.

The machine has a fixed finite program, alphabet and number of tapes. Each transition reads and writes finitely many tape symbols and moves each head by at most one cell; an independent fair random bit can be drawn at a charged transition. Time includes reading, arithmetic, any preparation depending on \(n\), and writing the output. The time bound holds on all input strings of length \(L\) and all coin sequences. Mathematical success is required only on promised inputs. Outside the promise, any output is permitted. On a promised input, a failure marker, malformed vector or vector violating the displayed conditions counts as failure. Success probability is over the independent coins for each fixed input, not over a distribution of bases.

No quantum computation, oracle, nonuniform advice, precomputed table depending on the field, unit-group basis or ideal factorization is supplied for free. Such information may be computed only within the stated classical time bound. Polynomial exponents may be large but must be universal. Allowing a fixed multiplicative constant in the approximation would be equivalent after increasing \(c\), since \(n\ge2\).

The norm is fixed explicitly to avoid an embedding ambiguity. For \(\zeta_{2n}=\exp(\pi i/n)\), the canonical embedding lists the \(n\) values \(a(\zeta_{2n}^{2j+1})\), \(0\le j<n\). Its squared Euclidean norm is \(n\sum_j a_j^2\). Thus, in this selected family, canonical and coefficient norms differ by the common factor \(\sqrt n\), which cancels in the relative approximation guarantee. This statement does not identify the two norms in arbitrary number rings.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed existence statement or its full negation. A positive answer must specify one finite classical program and universal constants, with a proved bound on every execution and at least \(2/3\) success on each promised basis. A negative answer must rule out every program and every choice of polynomial approximation and time bounds in this model. In particular, for each machine with a global polynomial clock and each fixed exponent \(c\), some promised input must have success probability below \(2/3\). A conditional consequence under an unproved complexity assumption is not an unconditional negative answer. Algorithms for selected ideals, quantum algorithms, superpolynomial approximation factors, or uncharged field preprocessing do not establish this target. Producing or estimating only the shortest length does not satisfy the required search output.

source_formulation.text: Peikert's 2016 Question 3 asks broadly whether ideal-lattice algorithms, possibly quantum, can substantially outperform general-lattice algorithms, and whether such advances extend to ring-SIS/LWE. It does not choose a field family, approximation scale or running time. Following the user's instruction to replace broad directions by concrete variants, this card selects the standard search-SVP problem with polynomial approximation and classical randomized polynomial time on power-of-two cyclotomic ideals. This is a documented editorial specialization, not a quotation or equivalent restatement of all of Question 3. It does not ask for a proved separation from every general-lattice algorithm or for a direct cryptographic attack. Existing conditional quantum speedups at larger approximation factors answer other parts of the historical direction without deciding this target.

context_blocks.text: The 2016 survey frames the question as a tradeoff between the efficiency gained from ring structure and possible additional algorithmic weaknesses. Its search problem asks for an actual short vector. This distinction is essential: the same survey explains that certain polynomial-gap decision versions on ideals can be easy even when finding an adequately short vector is not known to be efficient.

Multiplication by \(X\) gives a signed rotation of every coefficient vector in the selected ideal. For example, \(q\mathbb Z^n\) is an allowed ideal with shortest length \(|q|\) for each nonzero integer \(q\). Such easy instances do not determine the worst-case question, which also includes ideals without a short generator supplied in the input. A change of additive basis describes the same ideal; the guarantee must hold for every explicit basis and charges its actual bit length.

General lattice algorithms already give polynomial-time approximations whose factors are much larger than polynomials in dimension. Peikert's §2.2.2 records that historical time–approximation landscape. Restricting to ideal lattices is useful here only if the output quality and full running time meet both polynomial requirements. The earlier broad phrasing “outperform general lattices” is replaced by this testable threshold, without claiming a lower bound for all generic algorithms.

Cramer, Ducas and Wesolowski give a quantum algorithm with approximation factor \(\exp(\widetilde O(\sqrt m))\) for cyclotomic conductor \(m\). Their Theorem 5.1 assumes GRH and a class-group generation hypothesis, and its running time also depends polynomially on the real-subfield class number. Polynomial boundedness of that class number is an additional hypothesis used for the advertised polynomial-time consequence. This important advance has a different computation model and a superpolynomial approximation guarantee.

Pan, Xu, Wadleigh and Cheng prove classical polynomial-time exact SVP for prime ideals above rational primes \(p\equiv3,5\pmod8\) in the power-of-two family, and for a specified class of products of such primes. Their introduction stresses that the proportion of easy instances depends on how ideals are sampled. The result does not cover every ideal, and the paper explicitly distinguishes these algorithms from a break of ring-LWE.

The CRYPTO 2022 work of Boudgoust, Gachon and Pellet-Mary extends the easy-instance analysis using ideals preserved by many field automorphisms. Its cryptographic application concerns particular partial Vandermonde knapsack instances. The publisher/ePrint abstract was checked for this scope; it is not evidence of a general polynomial-time algorithm for every ideal.

Cui, Li and Zhuang's January 2026 revision studies further prime-ideal classes. In particular, its Theorem 2 describes shortest lengths above primes \(p\equiv7,9\pmod{16}\). Its hypotheses still restrict the ideals, and a formula for a shortest length is distinct from the full uniform search guarantee. No claim that this preprint resolves the all-ideals target is made here.

Martin’s September 2026 preprint claims a dimension-preserving reduction from generic lattices to ideals in varying totally real monogenic number rings. Theorem 1.1 does not force a chosen cyclotomic field; the surrounding discussion explicitly preserves the possible advantage of field-specific methods. Its separate full-ring-of-integers extension has additional conjectural qualifications. This new hardness claim is not a hardness theorem for the fixed cyclotomic family selected here.

Wan’s September 2026 preprint claims exact Euclidean SVP hardness for ideals of \(\mathbb Z[X]/(X^N-1)\), with \(N=q-1\) for varying odd primes \(q\). That quotient has a different rational algebra from \(\mathbb Q[X]/(X^n+1)\). The paper explicitly makes neither a fixed-factor approximation claim nor a cryptographic key-distribution claim. Even if its proof is correct, the stated exact cyclic result does not determine this polynomial-factor cyclotomic search question.

A worst-case-to-average-case security reduction has a direction: an algorithm for the average-case cryptographic problem would solve an associated worst-case lattice problem with stated parameters. An algorithm for the worst-case lattice problem does not automatically run that implication backwards. The historical second question about direct ring-SIS/LWE attacks therefore remains separate from this card’s selected algorithmic target.

cards.title: A classical reduction from semiprime factoring to polynomial-gap SVP
cards.formal:
Do there exist an absolute rational constant \(\varepsilon>0\) and one classical randomized polynomial-time oracle algorithm that factors every integer \(N=pq\), where \(p\ne q\) are primes, using an oracle for Euclidean \(\operatorname{GapSVP}_{n^{2+\varepsilon}}\)?

Here \(n\) is the rank of the lattice in each oracle query, and the algorithm must output the two prime factors with probability at least \(2/3\) on every promised input \(N\). The oracle may answer arbitrarily inside its approximation gap.
cards.why: This would connect two major sources of computational hardness: factoring integers and approximating shortest lattice vectors by a large polynomial factor. The selected approximation regime is strong enough to connect onward to classical worst-case-to-average-case reductions used for lattice cryptography.
cards.status_note: Source-open in Bennett’s Open Problem 4.10. The card selects semiprime factoring and the highlighted n^(2+ε) approximation factor, using an announced editorial default after an unanswered optional question. Quantum factoring and heuristic lattice embeddings do not settle the classical oracle reduction. Bounded later-work checks through 17 September 2026 found no verified matching resolution. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Classical randomized reduction of factoring a product of two distinct primes to decision GapSVP at the stated n^(2+epsilon) scale.

sentences: The input is an integer promised to be the product of two distinct primes.
The goal is to recover its factors with a classical randomized algorithm taking polynomial time in the integer’s bit length.
The algorithm may query Euclidean GapSVP at approximation factor n^(2+ε), for some fixed ε > 0 and query rank n.
It must succeed on every promised semiprime regardless of how the oracle answers inside its approximation gap.
This would connect factoring to a lattice regime relevant for classical cryptographic reductions; a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation is required.

cards.definitions:
The factoring input is just the binary representation of an integer \(N\ge6\), promised to be the product of two distinct primes. The factors, their bit lengths and any auxiliary information are not supplied. They need not have equal bit length, and the target is worst-case correctness over all such products, not only randomly sampled or balanced ones. Put \(s=\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\). A valid output is a pair of binary integers \((a,b)\), in either order, with \(1<a,b<N\), \(ab=N\), and both entries prime. Under the promise any nontrivial factor determines the required pair.

A well-formed lattice query is an explicit integer matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), with linearly independent columns and \(m\ge n\ge1\), together with a positive rational \(r\). Matrix entries are signed binary integers; \(r\) is given by a binary numerator and positive binary denominator. The dimensions and all entries are included in a length-delimited encoding. Define
\[
\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\},\qquad
\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2,
\]
where \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\). An admissible \(\operatorname{GapSVP}_{n^{2+\varepsilon}}\) oracle \(O\) is any total Boolean function obeying
\[
O(B,r)=1\quad\text{if }\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))\le r,
\qquad
O(B,r)=0\quad\text{if }\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))>n^{2+\varepsilon}r.
\]
For \(r<\lambda_1\le n^{2+\varepsilon}r\), either answer is permitted. No oracle correctness is required on malformed queries. The real-valued factor in this definition is an exact promise threshold; no numerical approximation oracle is supplied.

The reduction is one uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(R\), with independent fair random bits, and constants \(K,c>0\), such that for every promised \(N\) and every admissible \(O\), every execution of \(R^O(N)\) uses at most \(K(s+1)^c\) bit operations and outputs the prime factors with probability at least \(2/3\). Writing queries, reading their one-bit answers and writing the factors count toward the running time; the oracle's internal computation does not. Adaptive polynomially many queries are allowed. In particular query rank, ambient dimension and full bit length are all polynomially bounded in \(s\). The same fixed \(\varepsilon,K,c,R\) must work for all \(N\) and every completion of the oracle's gap answers. There is no quantum computation, advice, factoring hint or additional oracle.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence of the stated classical randomized reduction, including its query encodings, bit complexity and success guarantee for every promised semiprime and every admissible oracle, or a proof that no such fixed ε and reduction exist. An unproved heuristic lattice embedding, an exponential-time reduction, a reduction to exact SVP only, or a quantum factoring algorithm does not establish this target.

The target is the decision promise problem with a large multiplicative gap. An oracle for exact shortest vectors is substantially stronger and cannot simply be substituted for this oracle.

The source highlights n^(2+ε) because known classical reductions connect this approximation regime to learning with errors. The input parameter in that factor is the queried lattice rank, not the number of bits of the integer being factored.

Quantum reductions would give no comparable evidence: a quantum algorithm can already factor without a lattice oracle. Requiring a classical reduction is therefore essential to the requested connection.

Using lattices as a heuristic component of a factoring algorithm does not by itself prove a worst-case reduction to this approximate decision oracle. Both the embedding guarantee and the polynomial bound must hold for every promised input.

cards.title: A classical same-dimension reduction from SIVP to polynomial-modulus LWE
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge3\), do there exist constants \(C,K,a>0\), an integer \(b\ge0\), and one uniform classical randomized oracle algorithm \(\mathcal R_c\) with the following property?

For all \(n\ge2\), all admissible parameters \(q,\alpha,m,t\) below, every rank-\(n\) integer lattice basis \(B\), and every admissible search-LWE oracle \(A\), the algorithm \(\mathcal R_c^A(B,q,\alpha,m,t)\) outputs \(n\) linearly independent lattice vectors of length at most
\[
\gamma(n,\alpha)\lambda_n(\mathcal L(B)),\qquad
\gamma(n,\alpha)=C\frac n\alpha\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^b,
\]
with probability at least \(2/3\) on each input basis, using at most \(K(L+m+t+1)^a\) bit operations and oracle calls on every run? Every LWE query must have dimension exactly \(n\), modulus exactly \(q\), and exactly \(m\) samples with the noise parameter \(\alpha\) in the oracle guarantee. Here \(L\) is the complete binary input length, and the constants and algorithm may depend on \(c\), not on the instance.
cards.why: LWE is a classical noisy linear problem, yet the strongest known worst-case connection to SIVP uses quantum computation. Matching that connection classically at polynomial modulus and unchanged dimension would clarify which parts of the hardness foundation actually depend on quantum operations.

It was an announced recommended editorial default after no reply to an optional question. The 2013 polynomial-modulus classical result does not preserve both the dimension and SIVP starting problem. The finite oracle interface and prime-modulus parameter range are explicit specifications, not a claim to reproduce every part of the broader original request. cards.definitions:
Let \(B\in\mathbb Z^{h\times n}\) have full column rank, where \(h\ge n\). The lattice is \(\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), endowed with \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\). Its last successive minimum \(\lambda_n\) is the least radius of a closed Euclidean ball about zero containing \(n\) linearly independent lattice vectors. The output is a tuple of nonzero integer coefficient vectors \(z_1,\ldots,z_n\) such that \(Bz_1,\ldots,Bz_n\) are linearly independent over \(\mathbb R\) and each meets the stated length bound. They need not form a basis of the entire lattice. This is the shortest independent vectors problem (SIVP), not a shortest-vector decision problem.

The matrix entries, dimensions and all rational and integer parameters are explicitly encoded in binary with delimiters. Admissible parameters have prime \(q\le(n+2)^c\), integers \(1\le m\le(n+2)^c\) and \(2\le t\le(n+2)^c\), and a positive rational \(\alpha=u/v\le1/2\) in lowest terms with \(u,v\le(n+2)^c\), satisfying \(\alpha q>2\sqrt n\). Thus both the modulus and inverse noise rate are polynomially bounded for fixed \(c\).

Define an integer noise variable by drawing a real random variable \(E\) with density
\[
\frac{1}{\alpha q}\exp\left(-\frac{\pi x^2}{(\alpha q)^2}\right),
\]
rounding it to the nearest integer, and reducing modulo \(q\). Denote its exact distribution on \(\mathbb Z_q\) by \(\chi_{q,\alpha}\). Ties have probability zero. This is the rounded Gaussian convention from the original LWE reduction, not an assertion that rounding gives the exact discrete Gaussian on the integers.

A search-LWE test instance is sampled by first choosing a uniformly random secret \(s\in\mathbb Z_q^n\). Independently choose \(m\) uniform vectors \(a_i\in\mathbb Z_q^n\) and \(m\) errors \(e_i\leftarrow\chi_{q,\alpha}\), and give the ordered list
\[
(a_i,\langle a_i,s\rangle+e_i\bmod q)_{i=1}^m
\]
to the oracle. The oracle is any fixed randomized map from such lists to \(\mathbb Z_q^n\cup\{\bot\}\), using fresh independent randomness on each invocation, which outputs the actual sampled \(s\) with probability at least \(1/t\), averaged over the uniformly random secret, all samples and its randomness. There is no per-list guarantee; on other lists it may behave arbitrarily. The reduction must work for every such map, with no access to the secret or the oracle's internal random bits. It may make arbitrary adaptive list queries; their correctness is controlled only by this distributional guarantee.

The reduction is a classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine using independent fair random bits. Its cost includes preparing and writing every finite query, reading the returned vector, processing its input and producing its output, but excludes computation inside the oracle. The exact Gaussian distribution defines the oracle promise. The reduction must implement any sampling or numerical approximation it needs in finite bit time, with its errors included in the final failure probability; it receives no exact-real or Gaussian-sampling primitive. It has no quantum computation, advice or other oracles. The all-run polynomial bound and per-basis success guarantee hold even when the admissible oracle gives adversarial replies away from its average-case guarantee.

The 2013 classical modulus reduction reaches polynomial-modulus LWE but increases the dimension. cards.title: Classical ideal-SVP hardness of ring-LWE in power-of-two cyclotomic rings
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge3\), do there exist constants \(C,K,a>0\), integers \(b\ge0,n_0\ge2\), and one uniform classical randomized oracle algorithm that, for every power of two \(n\ge n_0\), reduces worst-case ideal-SVP in \(R_n=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^n+1)\) to the same-ring search-LWE problem defined below, with approximation factor
\[
\gamma(n,\alpha)=C\frac{\sqrt n}{\alpha}\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^b?
\]
The reduction must succeed with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input ideal basis, for every admissible oracle, and use at most \(K(L+m+t+1)^a\) classical bit operations and oracle calls on every run. Its queries must retain the degree \(n\), modulus \(q\), noise-family bound \(\alpha\) and sample count \(m\). The constants and algorithm may depend on \(c\), but not on the ideal or the other parameters.
cards.why: Ring structure makes LWE-based constructions more compact, but the useful worst-case ideal-lattice connection uses quantum computation. A classical reduction at comparable approximation and modulus scales would strengthen the theoretical understanding of that connection.

The September variable-field ideal-hardness preprint does not give this fixed-ring classical reduction. sentences: Ring-LWE consists of noisy multiplication samples in a finite polynomial quotient ring.
The card asks for a classical reduction from finding a short vector in every ideal of a power-of-two cyclotomic ring.
The target keeps the degree and polynomial modulus and seeks the known quantum approximation scale Õ(√n/α).
Its oracle must solve the full bounded elliptical error family, with explicit dual-ring scaling and finite coefficient rounding.
