cards.definitions:
Put \(K_n=\mathbb Q[X]/(X^n+1)\). Since \(n\) is a power of two, this is a number field with ring of integers \(R_n\). A nonzero integral ideal \(I\subseteq R_n\) is given by a full-rank integer matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\): its columns are the power-basis coefficient vectors of a \(\mathbb Z\)-basis of \(I\). The input is promised to generate a set closed under multiplication by \(X\), hence by every element of \(R_n\). All entries, dimensions and parameters are encoded explicitly in binary with delimiters; \(L\) is their total length.

Let \(\sigma_j\) be the embeddings sending \(X\) to the roots of \(X^n+1\). Use the canonical Euclidean norm
\[
\|v\|_{\rm can}^2=\sum_{j=1}^n|\sigma_j(v)|^2,
\qquad \lambda_1(I)=\min_{v\in I\setminus\{0\}}\|v\|_{\rm can}.
\]
The required output is a nonzero integer vector \(z\) such that the ideal element with coefficient vector \(Bz\) has norm at most \(\gamma(n,\alpha)\lambda_1(I)\). A short vector must actually be produced; deciding whether one exists is not the task. In this ring the canonical norm is \(\sqrt n\) times the coefficient Euclidean norm. Also, multiplying a shortest nonzero element by \(1,X,\ldots,X^{n-1}\) gives independent vectors of the same length, so the first and last successive minima of an ideal agree.

Admissible parameters have a prime \(q\le(n+2)^c\), integers \(1\le m\le(n+2)^c\), \(2\le t\le(n+2)^c\), and a rational \(\alpha=u/v\in(0,1/2]\), in lowest terms with \(u,v\le(n+2)^c\), satisfying \(\alpha q\ge(\log_2(n+2))^2\). Let \(R_{n,q}=R_n/qR_n\); its elements are encoded by \(n\) coefficients in \(\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\).

Here is the exact finite-output family of error distributions. Extend the power-basis coefficient space to \(K_{n,\mathbb R}=\mathbb R[X]/(X^n+1)\). Choose one embedding from each complex-conjugate pair and define the real isometry
\[
\tau(v)=\bigl(\sqrt2\operatorname{Re}\sigma_j(v),\sqrt2\operatorname{Im}\sigma_j(v)\bigr)_{j=1}^{n/2}\in\mathbb R^n.
\]
For any vector \(\rho=(\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_{n/2})\) with \(0<\rho_j\le\alpha\), sample independently two real Gaussian coordinates for pair \(j\), each of density \(\rho_j^{-1}\exp(-\pi x^2/\rho_j^2)\). Let \(e\in K_{n,\mathbb R}\) be their inverse image under \(\tau\). Expand \(nq e\) in the power basis, round each real coefficient to its nearest integer and reduce modulo \(q\). The resulting element of \(R_{n,q}\) has distribution \(\chi_\rho\). Ties occur with probability zero. The factor \(n\) is intentional: it converts rounding in the dual ring \(R_n^\vee=n^{-1}R_n\) to this ordinary-ring representation.

An admissible oracle \(A\) is a fixed randomized map from ordered lists of \(m\) pairs in \(R_{n,q}^2\) to \(R_{n,q}\cup\{\bot\}\). For every fixed \(\rho\) in the family, choose a uniformly random secret \(s\in R_{n,q}\), independently sample uniform \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in R_{n,q}\) and errors \(\eta_i\leftarrow\chi_\rho\), and form
\[
(a_i,a_i s+\eta_i)_{i=1}^m.
\]
On this input the oracle must output the sampled \(s\) with probability at least \(1/t\), averaged over the secret, samples and oracle randomness. The same oracle must satisfy this for every \(\rho\); neither the secret nor \(\rho\) is given as side information. It has fresh independent randomness on every invocation. Away from these distributional guarantees its answers are arbitrary. The reduction may make adaptive finite-list queries and must work for every such oracle.

Computation uses a classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine with fair independent random bits. Query construction, input reading, oracle-answer reading, all numerical approximations and output writing are charged; only the oracle's internal computation is excluded. Exact real Gaussians define probability distributions, not computational primitives available to the reduction. Its implementation must use finite arithmetic and include sampling errors in its total failure probability. There are no quantum operations, advice or additional oracles. This is a family-of-noises search target, not the stronger fixed spherical-noise or decision target.

source_formulation.text: Question 4 asks for a meaningful classical worst-case hardness reduction for ring-LWE and explains why the ordinary GapSVP starting point is insufficient on ideal lattices. This card selects approximate search-SVP in power-of-two cyclotomic rings and the elliptical error family of the known quantum reduction, with explicit finite rounding. User explicitly confirmed the selected scope on 2026-09-18: Classical reduction for ideal lattices in power-of-two cyclotomic rings in the stated quantum-reduction parameter range.
source_formulation.caption: Peikert, A Decade of Lattice Cryptography, §7.1 Question 4, printed p.75 / PDF p.77.

context_blocks.text: The source calls the classical reduction question meaningful only when its worst-case premise carries useful ideal-lattice hardness. It explicitly notes that the decision GapSVP problem is easy at the relevant polynomial factors.

The quantum theorem first reduces an ideal Gaussian-sampling problem to search ring-LWE for an entire family of elliptical errors. It yields an Õ(√n/α) factor for independent vectors, and hence also short vectors in cyclotomic ideals.

The power-of-two dual ring is exactly n⁻¹R. Scaling its secrets to R and rounding the noise in a dual basis explains the n in this card’s finite sample definition. Treating the ordinary coefficient Gaussian as though it had the same canonical parameter would change the problem.

The known search theorem requires a solver for every bounded elliptical shape. A fixed spherical error distribution is a distinct stronger hardness target; classical search-to-decision conversions do not remove the quantum worst-case step.

The September 2026 generic-to-ideal preprint changes the ambient number field with the input and allows monogenic orders. Its abstract qualifies the full-ring-of-integers extension. It does not establish a classical reduction to ring-LWE in the fixed cyclotomic family used here.

cards.title: Scholz–Brauer conjecture
cards.formal: For every positive integer n, is \(\ell\)\((2^{n}- 1)\le n- 1+\ell (n)\), where \(\ell\)\((m)\) is the minimum length of an addition chain for m?
cards.why: The conjecture predicts a precise relationship between optimal multiplication plans for an exponent and for its associated all-ones binary integer. Its restricted-chain theorem shows that the unresolved issue concerns how the freedom to reuse older values affects the best possible length.

Tall, Theorems 2–4, proves the conjecture for a specified infinite family with seven binary ones and \(\ell\)\((2n)=\ell (n)\), and for its doubles.
Wallner states the unrestricted Scholz–Brauer inequality among open addition-chain problems and distinguishes the star-chain result.
Agama’s preprint claims asymptotic density one and explicitly leaves the uniform all-integers version unanswered; not independently proof-audited.
Agama’s later preprint abstract claims the inequality for integers with an optimal chain in its quasi-closed class; abstract-only review.

cards.definitions: For a positive integer m, an addition chain of length r is a finite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers \(1=a_{0}<a_{1}<\cdots <a_{r}=m\) such that, for each \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,r\}\), there exist \(j,k\in \{0,\ldots ,i- 1\}\) with \(a_{i}=a_{j}+a_{k}\). The indices j and k may coincide, and any previously produced value may be reused any number of times. The length counts the r additions, excluding the initial 1. Define \(\ell\)\((m)\) as the minimum such r; this minimum exists because \(1,2,\ldots ,m\) is an allowed chain, and \(\ell\)\((1)=0\). Only additions of two previously available numbers are allowed: subtraction, division, arbitrary preloaded constants and sums of three or more terms in one step are excluded. All additions have cost one, regardless of operand size; this is an operation-count question, not a bit-running-time bound. A star chain, also called a Brauer chain, additionally requires each step to have a representation \(a_{i}=a_{i- 1}+a_{j}\) with \(j<i\). Write \(\ell\)*\((m)\) for its minimum length. Thus \(\ell\)\((m)\le \ell *(m)\); the conjecture uses the unrestricted \(\ell\) on both sides. The integer \(2^{n}- 1\) has n ones in binary, and the quantifier includes \(n=1\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the inequality for every positive integer n, or give an integer n together with rigorous bounds on the two minimum lengths showing \(\ell\)\((2^{n}- 1)>n- 1+\ell (n)\). A positive proof may establish existence of the required chains without an efficient algorithm for finding a shortest chain. Equality is not required. Restricted-chain results, a finite verification range, and validity for a density-one set of integers are weaker than the universal assertion.

context_blocks.text: An addition chain is a plan for reusing intermediate powers. Once \(x^{a}\) and \(x^{b}\) have been computed, one multiplication produces \(x^{a+b}\). Starting from x, a chain for m therefore specifies a multiplication-only computation of \(x^{m}\) with one multiplication per chain step. This correspondence explains the interest in short chains; it does not include algorithms that use division or other algebraic operations.

For \(n=5\), the chain 1,2,4,5 has length three and is shortest, since two additions can reach at most four. The conjectured upper bound for \(2^{5}- 1=31\) is therefore \(5- 1+3=7\). The chain 1,2,3,6,12,24,30,31 attains that upper bound: its last two additions are \(24+6\) and \(30+1\). Exhibiting it checks this instance without claiming that every n admits an analogous optimal pattern.

The target compares the cost of building an integer n with the cost of building a much larger integer whose binary expansion is entirely ones. Its dominant term is \(n- 1\), with only \(\ell\)\((n)\) further additions allowed. Merely finding a chain of order n steps would leave the exact additive allowance unresolved.

Brauer’s theorem gives \(\ell\)*\((2^{n}- 1)\le n- 1+\ell *(n)\). In a star chain, every step must use the immediately preceding value. This proves the desired inequality whenever n has a shortest unrestricted chain that is also a star chain. In general, replacing \(\ell\)*\((n)\) by the potentially smaller \(\ell\)\((n)\) is precisely the distinction that the restricted result does not settle.

Tall’s 2024 paper proves the conjecture for an explicit infinite family of integers with seven ones in binary and \(\ell\)\((2n)=\ell (n)\), and also for their doubles. An infinite family need not cover all possible exponents; its role here is a proved special case, rather than a resolution of the universal target.

A May 2026 preprint claims that the proportion of \(n\le N\) satisfying the conjecture tends to one as N tends to infinity. Its introduction expressly distinguishes this claim from a proof for all n. Even a valid density-one theorem can leave exceptions, and this preprint’s proof has not been independently verified in this review.

There is no contradiction in a chain for \(2^{n}- 1\) being shorter than the displayed bound: the conjecture is an upper bound. Nor must a positive solution provide a fast procedure for computing \(\ell\)\((n)\). These distinctions keep an existence inequality separate from exact-length formulas and shortest-chain optimization.

sentences: An addition chain starts at one and builds its target by repeatedly adding two already available values.
Its length counts additions and corresponds to the number of multiplications in the associated repeated-power computation.
The conjecture asks whether the minimum length for \(2^{n}- 1\) is always at most \(n- 1\) plus the minimum length for n.
The analogous theorem for star chains and known infinite families leave the unrestricted universal inequality open in the checked sources.
Resolving it would explain how efficiently optimal exponentiation plans can control the cost of all-ones binary exponents.

cards.title: Baillie–PSW pseudoprimes
cards.formal: Does there exist a composite integer n that passes the strong base-2 probable-prime test and the strong Lucas probable-prime test with Selfridge’s Method A, including the parameter-search rejection rule specified below?
cards.why: Tests the mathematical reliability of a widely used primality-testing combination.

cards.definitions: A composite integer is an integer \(n>1\) with a divisor strictly between 1 and n. Even integers greater than 2 and perfect squares are rejected; thus a candidate here is odd and nonsquare. Write \(n- 1=2^{s} d\) with d odd. The strong base-2 test accepts if \(2^{d}\equiv 1\) (mod n), or \(2^{2^{r} d}\equiv - 1\) (mod n) for some integer \(0\le r<s\). For the Lucas test, examine \(D=5,- 7,9,- 11,13,- 15,\ldots\) in that order, namely \(D_{k}=(- 1)^{k}(2k+5)\) for \(k\ge 0\). At each step reject if \(1<\gcd (|D|,n)<n\); otherwise stop at the first D with Jacobi symbol \((D/n)=- 1\). For odd \(n=\prod p_{j}^{e_{j}}\), the Jacobi symbol \((a/n)\) is \(\prod (a/p_{j})^{e}_{j}\), where \((a/p)\) is 0 if p divides a, +1 if a is a nonzero square modulo p, and −1 otherwise. This defines the symbol without requiring factorization as an implementation. Squares were excluded because their Jacobi symbols cannot be −1; for odd nonsquares the search terminates. Set \(\mathrm{P}=1\) and \(Q=(1- D)/4\). Define integer sequences \(U_{0}=0, U_{1}=1, V_{0}=2, V_{1}=\mathrm{P}\) and, for \(j\ge 0, U_{j+2}=\mathrm{P} U_{j+1}- Q U_{j}\) and \(V_{j+2}=\mathrm{P} V_{j+1}- Q V_{j}\). Write \(n+1=2^{t} u\) with u odd. The strong Lucas test accepts if \(U_{u}\equiv 0\) (mod n), or \(V_{2^{r} u}\equiv 0\) (mod n) for some integer \(0\le r<t\). Passing means surviving the parameter search and satisfying both strong tests, with exact integer congruences. The number 2 is accepted separately but cannot answer this composite-existence question. No extra trial-division cutoff, random bases or additional congruence checks are part of the specified variant.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a composite n together with a proof of compositeness and exact verification of the parameter search and both acceptance conditions, or prove that no composite integer passes this specified variant. A finite search bound, a heuristic count of expected counterexamples or a counterexample to only one component does not settle the question.

context_blocks.title: Why combine two tests
context_blocks.text: A composite can imitate some arithmetic properties of primes. For example, \(2047=23\cdot 89\) passes the strong base-2 test because \(2^{1023}\equiv 1\) modulo 2047. It fails the strong Lucas test with \(D=5\). The question is whether a composite can evade both parts together, however large it is.

context_blocks.title: The exact variant matters
context_blocks.text: Selfridge’s Method A fixes \(\mathrm{P}=1\) and \(Q=(1- D)/4\). The main source also describes Method A*, which changes P and Q to 5 when \(D=5\), and proves equivalence of the strong Lucas outcomes for integers coprime to 10. Its proposed strengthened test adds further congruences. This card keeps the imported strong base-2 plus strong Lucas target and spells out Method A.

context_blocks.title: What exhaustive computation establishes
context_blocks.text: The 2021 paper reports that no base-2 Fermat pseudoprime below \(2^{64}\) also passes its Lucas test, giving correctness through that finite range and hence ruling out smaller counterexamples to the strong combination. It reports no known larger counterexample. Such a bound leaves the existence question over all integers unanswered.

context_blocks.title: Recent evidence has finite scope
context_blocks.text: A January 2026 preprint reports that all 200 selected composites in its experiment fail the strong Lucas test despite passing several Miller–Rabin bases. This does not establish correctness for arbitrary integers or a rigorous independence theorem for the two tests. With the specified parameters, the test’s outcome on a fixed n is deterministic; “probable prime” describes the strength of the conclusion, not random choices made here.

cards.title: NP-hardness of Euclidean unique SVP with a fixed gap greater than one
cards.formal:
Is there an absolute rational constant \(\gamma>1\) such that the search problem \(\gamma\text{-uSVP}_2\) is NP-hard under classical randomized polynomial-time oracle reductions?

The input is an explicitly encoded integer lattice basis \(B\), promised to satisfy
\[
\lambda_2(\mathcal L(B))>\gamma\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B)).
\]
The required answer is an exact shortest nonzero lattice vector. The uniqueness gap \(\gamma-1\) must be a positive constant independent of the input dimension and bit length.
cards.why: A constant separation between the shortest lattice direction and every independent competitor is a strong geometric promise. Proving NP-hardness despite that promise would show that isolating a shortest vector does not remove the worst-case difficulty of Euclidean lattice search.
cards.status_note: Source-open in Bennett’s 2023 Open Problem 4.6. The checked 2025 work excludes the Euclidean norm and uses stronger running-time assumptions. Known inverse-polynomial uniqueness gaps, rotation-lattice assumptions and fine-grained reductions do not supply this fixed-gap polynomial-time oracle NP-hardness statement. Bounded checks through 17 September 2026 found no matching resolution.

progress.text: Randomized NP-hardness is established for a gap greater than one by an inverse polynomial, rather than by a fixed constant.
The source explicitly retains the constant-gap Euclidean NP-hardness question; the rotation-lattice result supplies a different conditional hardness statement.
Deterministic unique-SVP hardness is strengthened in norms p>2 under stronger running-time assumptions; this leaves the selected Euclidean NP-hardness target untouched.

sentences: The input is an explicit integer lattice basis in Euclidean space.
It promises that every independent direction is longer than a shortest vector by one fixed factor greater than one.
The task is to recover an exact shortest vector, with either sign allowed.
The question asks whether this promise search problem is NP-hard under classical randomized polynomial-time oracle reductions.
Shrinking uniqueness gaps and hardness in other norms do not establish this target, whose full proof or refutation must be Lean-checked.

cards.definitions:
A lattice basis is a matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) with \(m\ge n\ge2\) and linearly independent columns. Dimensions and all entries are explicitly encoded in binary with delimiters; let \(L\) be the total input length. Its lattice is
\[
\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^m.
\]
All lengths use the Euclidean norm \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The first successive minimum \(\lambda_1\) is the minimum length of a nonzero lattice vector. The second successive minimum \(\lambda_2\) is the smallest radius of a closed ball centered at zero containing two linearly independent lattice vectors. Independence is over \(\mathbb R\). Rank \(n\), ambient dimension \(m\), and coefficient bit length can all grow with the input.

Under the strict gap promise there are exactly two shortest vectors, differing by sign. A valid answer is a binary integer coefficient vector \(z\ne0\) such that \(\|Bz\|_2=\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))\). Either sign is allowed. The gap concerns independent directions, not merely the second distinct vector, which would always include the negative of a shortest vector. The output target is exact recovery, not an approximation of the shortest length.

Use the following randomized Cook-reduction meaning of NP-hardness for this promise search problem. An admissible oracle is any total function which, on a basis satisfying the promise, returns a valid shortest-vector coefficient vector and, on any other query, can return an arbitrary string or a distinguished failure symbol. Bound every response to a query of length \(L\) by \(4(L+1)^3\) bits. This is only an encoding convention: shortest-vector coefficients for an explicit integer basis have a polynomial bit bound of this size, by bounding an invertible minor and using a basis column as an upper bound on shortest length. The oracle need not be computable or choose the same sign on different bases.

NP-hardness here means that there exist one classical probabilistic multitape oracle Turing machine \(R\) and constants \(K,a>0\) such that for every Boolean 3-CNF formula \(F\) of encoded length \(s\), and for every admissible oracle \(O\), every execution of \(R^O(F)\) uses at most \(K(s+1)^a\) bit operations and
\[
\Pr[R^O(F)=1]\ge2/3\quad\text{if }F\text{ is satisfiable},\qquad
\Pr[R^O(F)=0]\ge2/3\quad\text{otherwise}.
\]
The probability is over independent fair random bits of \(R\). A 3-CNF is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three Boolean variables or their negations. The reduction may make adaptive queries; writing them and reading oracle responses are charged, while the oracle's internal computation is not. On well-formed lattice queries outside the gap promise no correctness is presumed of the oracle, and the reduction must tolerate every permitted response. The constants and \(\gamma\) are fixed before any formula is received. Thus a polynomial-time solver for the promise problem would yield a bounded-error polynomial-time algorithm for every NP language.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of such randomized oracle NP-hardness for some fixed γ > 1, including the reduction, its bit complexity and its guarantee for every admissible oracle, or a proof of the negation of this existence claim. Hardness only for a dimension-dependent gap tending to one, a non-Euclidean norm, a superpolynomial-time reduction or a separate nonstandard lattice-hardness hypothesis does not establish the target. Failure of one proposed reduction does not refute it.

source_formulation.text: Open Problem 4.6 asks for randomized NP-hardness of Euclidean unique SVP for some constant uniqueness factor greater than one. The card spells out a bounded-error polynomial-time oracle reduction for the search formulation.
source_formulation.caption: The Complexity of the Shortest Vector Problem, §4.2, Open Problem 4.6, printed p.15 / PDF p.17.

context_blocks.text: The 2023 source distinguishes ordinary approximate shortest-vector hardness from unique shortest-vector hardness. Its explicitly open target is a fixed Euclidean uniqueness factor greater than one.
Aggarwal and Dubey obtain randomized hardness with a uniqueness gap of 1+1/poly(n). Such a gap tends to one and therefore does not supply the fixed positive separation in this card.

The rotation-lattice reduction proves hardness for constant uniqueness factors if finding shortest vectors in rotations of the integer lattice is hard. Its authors explicitly label that source assumption nonstandard; it is not a reduction establishing NP-hardness.

The October 2025 paper gives new unique-SVP hardness for norms with p>2 under hypotheses on subexponential or quasipolynomial algorithms. Its theorems do not cover p=2. Its related-work discussion also distinguishes fine-grained constant-gap results from polynomial-time NP-hardness.

The two signs of a shortest vector cannot be separated by a uniqueness promise. The promise instead compares the first two successive minima, and the oracle convention retains arbitrary behavior whenever that promise fails.

cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time oracle reduction that, using only \(\gamma\)-GapSVP queries on lattices of the same dimension \(n\), solves SVP with approximation factor polynomial in \(n\) and \(\gamma\)? Concretely, do there exist absolute positive integers \(C,a,b\) and one randomized oracle machine \(R\) such that for every \(n\ge1\), every nonsingular \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), every rational \(\gamma\ge1\), and every admissible oracle \(O_\gamma\) below, \(R^{O_\gamma}(B,\gamma)\) runs in at most \(C(N+2)^b\) steps and outputs \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\) with \[ \Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\le C(n\gamma)^a\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\ge2/3? \] Here \(N\) is the bit length of the encoded input, and the probability is over the reduction’s random bits.
cards.why: Search returns a short lattice vector, whereas a decision oracle only certifies which side of a length gap the lattice lies on. Bridging these versions with polynomial approximation loss and no dimension increase would sharpen a basic computational relationship at the center of lattice algorithms and worst-case hardness assumptions in cryptography.

The available oracle only distinguishes short-vector lengths across a multiplicative gap.
The question asks for a classical polynomial-time reduction that keeps every query in the original dimension and loses only a polynomial in dimension and approximation factor.

cards.definitions:
The input lattice is \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), with a rational full-rank square basis whose columns generate it. The Euclidean norm is \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2}\), and \(\lambda_1(L)=\min\{\|v\|_2:v\in L,\ v\ne0\}\). The output is an exact integer coefficient vector \(z\), so its nonzero lattice vector is unambiguously represented even when coordinates are rational. There is no norm other than \(\ell_2\), target point, uniqueness promise, preprocessing of a fixed lattice, or ideal-lattice restriction.

An oracle query is \((\widetilde B,r)\), where \(\widetilde B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular and \(r\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\). An admissible \(O_\gamma\) is any total Boolean function on these valid queries satisfying \[ \lambda_1(L(\widetilde B))\le r\implies O_\gamma(\widetilde B,r)=1,\qquad \lambda_1(L(\widetilde B))>\gamma r\implies O_\gamma(\widetilde B,r)=0.\] When \(r<\lambda_1(L(\widetilde B))\le\gamma r\), its answer can be either bit. The reduction must succeed for every such total completion of the promise problem, including completions with no computability assumption. Repeated identical queries have the same answer because the oracle is a function. The same input value \(\gamma\) applies to every query. At \(\gamma=1\) there is no gap.

Dimension preservation means every oracle lattice has exactly the original dimension \(n\), including its ambient dimension and rank. Queries may use different bases and thresholds, but cannot increase dimension even by an additive constant. This follows the explicit same-\(n\) statement of Open Problem 4.5. Adaptively chosen queries are allowed; this is a Cook (oracle Turing) reduction, not a requirement of one nonadaptive query.

Integers, rational numerators and positive denominators are encoded in binary with signs and delimiters; \(N\) includes the entire basis and \(\gamma\). Use a probabilistic multitape oracle Turing machine with independent unbiased coin flips, a read-only input tape, work tapes and a query tape. Writing a query and reading its one-bit answer are charged; the oracle itself returns that bit in one oracle step. All arithmetic is implemented on binary tapes and pays its full bit cost. The displayed polynomial bounds total time on every random tape and every admissible oracle, and therefore bounds the number and bit lengths of queries and output. Only valid full-rank rational queries are allowed. There is no additional oracle, advice, quantum computation, or free real arithmetic.

The constants and the finite program are fixed before \(n,B,\gamma\) and the oracle are chosen. A bound \(C(n\gamma)^a\) expresses an unspecified polynomial loss uniformly over the domain \(n,\gamma\ge1\); replacing it by any fixed polynomial in these two parameters gives the same polynomial-loss existence target after increasing \(C,a\). The chosen reduction is allowed bounded-error randomness. This makes explicit the classical randomized reduction convention used by the cited near-exact results, rather than adding a deterministic-only requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a reduction and uniform polynomial bounds exist, with correctness against every admissible completion of the promise oracle, or prove their nonexistence. A positive result must bound the output norm, bit complexity, and dimension of every query. Preserving dimension only up to an unbounded factor, obtaining an approximation loss exponential in \(n\), assuming special lattices, or giving only a quantum reduction does not meet the target. The known exact case or approximation factors approaching one alone do not establish the quantified statement.

context_blocks.text: The source asks for polynomial loss in the approximation factor, not exact preservation of that factor. It also explicitly retains dimension. This matters for lattice algorithms whose costs depend exponentially on dimension, and for distinguishing an algorithm that recognizes short vectors from one that actually finds them.

The search and decision versions are known to be equivalent under dimension-preserving reductions in the exact case \(\gamma=1\). The 2016 randomized reduction has search loss \(\gamma^{n/s}\) and running time \(2^{O(s)}\gamma^{O(n)}\), for \(s\ge\log(n+1)\), with input-bit polynomial factors suppressed in that summary. Choosing \(s\) logarithmic gives an efficient useful guarantee when \(\gamma\) is very close to one; it does not give a polynomial-loss polynomial-time reduction for all approximation factors.

Bennett’s 2023 problem is phrased using rational square bases and Euclidean length. The older reduction map uses a relaxed convention that permits an additive constant in dimension, while the card follows the later explicit same-dimension wording. The distinction is recorded so that a looser reduction is not silently counted as satisfying the target.

The source relates a solution at polynomial approximation factors to worst-case search-SVP foundations for lattice cryptography. The Simons list also discusses search-to-decision questions for closest vectors and independent short vectors, including quantum variants. Those questions have different outputs, oracles or computational models and do not settle the reduction here.

cards.title: A classical SIS reduction from sublinear-factor GapSVP
cards.formal:
Do there exist absolute constants \(0<\varepsilon<1\) and \(C\ge1\), polynomially bounded computable modulus parameters as defined below, and a classical randomized polynomial-time worst-case-to-average-case reduction
\[
\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma(n)}\ \longrightarrow\
\operatorname{SIS}_{n,m(n),q(n),\sqrt{m(n)}},
\qquad \gamma(n)=\max\{1,Cn^{1-\varepsilon}\},
\]
in the Euclidean norm? The reduction must solve every promised rank-\(n\) GapSVP instance from a SIS oracle that succeeds on only an inverse-polynomial fraction of uniformly random matrices. It must have polynomial overhead in the inverse of that success probability.
cards.why: Current worst-case guarantees for SIS rely on roughly linear approximation factors when parameters support nontrivial compression. A fixed exponent improvement would base average-case short-integer-solution hardness on a weaker worst-case lattice assumption.

sentences: A random SIS instance is a matrix modulo a polynomial-size integer, and the goal is a short nonzero integer vector in its modular kernel.
The question asks for a classical reduction from every Euclidean GapSVP instance with approximation factor O(n^(1−ε)) for some fixed ε > 0.
The chosen matrix dimensions ensure that a solution exists while excluding the trivial modulus-sized vector.
The reduction must work even when its SIS oracle succeeds only on an inverse-polynomial fraction of uniformly random matrices.

cards.definitions:
The modulus is one integer-valued function \(q(n)\), for \(n\ge2\), computed from \(1^n\) by one deterministic algorithm in time polynomial in \(n\). For some fixed integer \(d\ge3\), require
\[
n^3\le q(n)\le(n+1)^d,\qquad
m(n)=2n\lceil\log_2 q(n)\rceil+1.
\]
The function, its algorithm, and \(d\) are existentially chosen once. Primality is not required. These conventions select a polynomial-modulus, compressing SIS family, without fixing one numerical modulus schedule.

An SIS instance is a matrix \(A\in(\mathbb Z/q(n)\mathbb Z)^{n\times m(n)}\), with entries sampled independently and uniformly from the residues \(0,\ldots,q(n)-1\). A valid solution is a nonzero vector \(z\in\mathbb Z^{m(n)}\) satisfying
\[
Az=0\pmod{q(n)},\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{m(n)}z_i^2\le m(n).
\]
This is an exact Euclidean norm bound, not an infinity-norm bound or a restriction to binary solutions. Encode each coordinate with a sign bit and \(\lceil\log_2(m(n)+1)\rceil\) magnitude bits, allowing unused encodings to be rejected. The trivial vector with a coordinate equal to \(q(n)\) is too long. Every matrix has a valid solution: since \(2^{m(n)}>q(n)^n\), two distinct binary vectors have the same image under \(A\), and their difference meets the displayed bound.

A worst-case input is an explicit full-column-rank integer matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{h\times n}\), with \(h\ge n\ge2\), and a positive rational radius \(r\). Entries, dimensions, and the numerator and denominator of \(r\) are given in binary; their complete length is \(L\). Write
\[
\mathcal L(B)=\{Bv:v\in\mathbb Z^n\},\qquad
\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))=\min_{v\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bv\|_2.
\]
The promise is either \(\lambda_1\le r\), a yes-instance, or \(\lambda_1>\gamma(n)r\), a no-instance. The algorithm need not decide inputs between these thresholds.

The oracle formulation makes the average-case guarantee precise. For any integer \(t\ge1\), a permitted SIS oracle at parameter \(n\) is a fixed, possibly randomized map from matrices to either a valid solution in the stated encoding or a failure symbol \(\bot\), with
\[
\Pr_{A,\,O}[O(A)\ne\bot]\ge1/t
\]
when \(A\) is uniform. Calls use fresh independent oracle coins; the oracle has no mutable state between calls. It may fail on any selected set of inputs consistent with this average guarantee. No distributional assumption is made about its valid solutions, and the oracle need not be efficiently computable.

The desired reduction is one uniform classical probabilistic multitape oracle Turing machine \(R\) and constants \(K,a>0\). On input \((B,r,1^t)\), it may make adaptive queries to this rank-\(n\) SIS oracle, all with the parameters above. For every \(n,t\), every promised \((B,r)\), and every permitted oracle, it must output the correct yes/no answer with probability at least \(2/3\), over its own independent fair coins and the oracle coins. Every execution takes at most \(K(L+t+1)^a\) bit operations, including parameter computation, queries and responses; only the oracle's internal computation is free. For \(t\) polynomial in \(n\), this is the usual polynomial overhead for a non-negligible average success probability. There is no advice, quantum computation, auxiliary short-vector hint or other oracle.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of a reduction with some fixed ε > 0 and the stated SIS parameters, overhead and universal oracle guarantee, or a proof that no such choice exists. Improving only the modulus, assuming a solver correct on every SIS matrix, supplying hints with the matrices, or allowing superpolynomial reduction time does not establish this target. The two LWE alternatives in the source are not substitutes for the selected SIS branch.

cards.title: NP-hardness of Euclidean covering radius
cards.formal: Is exact Euclidean lattice covering radius NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic polynomial-time map sending each Boolean 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\) to a rational full-column-rank matrix \(B\) and a positive rational threshold \(r\), such that \[\varphi\text{ is satisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mu_2(L(B))\le r?\] Unsatisfiable formulas must map to instances with \(\mu_2(L(B))>r\). This is the exact decision problem, with approximation factor one and no promised gap between the two cases.

source_formulation.text: In particular, we reiterate that the problem of showing NP-hardness of exact GapCRP in the l2 norm (the most important special case) remains open.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 7

cards.why: The covering radius measures how far a point can be from its nearest lattice point. It is a central lattice invariant with connections to integer programming and to worst-case lattice problems used in cryptography. Establishing even exact Euclidean NP-hardness would close a basic gap in the complexity classification of lattice problems, without requiring the stronger approximation-hardness results known in other norms.

cards.definitions: The input basis is a matrix \(B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), where \(m\ge n\ge1\) and the \(n\) columns are linearly independent over \(\mathbb R\). Its lattice is \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\). For \(v\in\mathbb R^m\), the Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^m v_j^2)^{1/2}\). Define \[\mu_2(L(B))=\sup_{t\in\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(B)}\inf_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\|t-Bz\|_2=\max_{w\in[0,1]^n}\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\|B(w-z)\|_2.\] The points \(t\) range over the real linear span of the lattice, not the whole ambient space when \(n<m\). The compact fundamental parallelepiped \(B[0,1]^n\) gives the equivalent finite-radius maximum. The minimum ranges over all integer combinations, including coefficients outside \(\{0,1\}\). The exact decision language contains precisely valid pairs \((B,r)\) with \(r\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\) and \(\mu_2(L(B))\le r\); equality is a YES instance and any strict excess is a NO instance. Encode dimensions and signed rational numerators and positive denominators in binary, with explicit delimiters and all matrix entries listed. Complexity is measured in total encoding length, including entry precision and the threshold, not just dimension. A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three Boolean variables or their negations, with variable indices encoded in binary; it is satisfiable when some Boolean assignment makes every clause true. The requested reduction is one finite deterministic Turing-machine program with a fixed polynomial bit-time bound. It must output a valid instance on every valid formula, and the equivalence must hold for all formulas. All output bits and exact rational arithmetic costs count. No oracle, advice, randomness, real-number oracle or unbounded-precision unit-cost arithmetic is available. NP-hardness here is deterministic many-one hardness for every language with a polynomial-time verifier and polynomial-length witnesses, equivalently hardness for the specified 3-SAT language.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a reduction exists, including polynomial bit complexity, valid output bases and both directions of the satisfiability equivalence, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation. A proof of a polynomial-time algorithm would refute NP-hardness only with an appropriate complexity separation; it is not by itself a negative answer. Hardness in another norm, hardness of linear discrepancy or of coding-theoretic covering radius, randomized reductions alone, and a reduction that reverses YES and NO do not establish this target. The task does not require NP membership or a quantitative approximation gap.

context_blocks.text: Bennett and Ly explicitly single out NP-hardness of exact \(\ell_2\) covering radius in Section 1.4 of their September 2026 proceedings paper. Definition 4 specifies the decision orientation: small covering radius is YES, while radius strictly above the threshold is NO.

cards.definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two expansion of N without leading zeroes, and \(n=\lfloor \log _{2}N\rfloor +1\). The output is the list of distinct increasing primes \(q_{1}<\cdots <q_{r}\) and positive integer exponents \(e_{i}\), all in binary, with \(N=\prod _{i} q_{i}^{e_{i}}\). A prime input has the single pair \((N,1)\). The oracle returns the same unique prime-factorization representation on M. Queries may be adaptive but must all satisfy \(\lfloor \log _{2}M\rfloor +1<n\) relative to the original input length. Merely requiring \(M<N\) would be weaker and is not the target. The ordinary Turing-machine cost includes writing queries, reading answers and writing the output; supplying a correct oracle answer is the sole oracle operation. The output length of prime factorization is polynomial in n. There is no randomness, advice or nonuniform family of reducers. The reduction must work for every input, with one polynomial bound independent of its factorization.

cards.title: coNP certificates for GapSVP at the square-root n/log n scale
cards.formal:
Is there an absolute constant \(C\ge2\) such that Euclidean \(\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma_C(n)}\) belongs to coNP, where
\[
\gamma_C(n)=C\sqrt{\frac{n}{\log_2(n+2)}}\ ?
\]
Concretely, must every input lattice whose shortest nonzero vector has length greater than \(\gamma_C(n)r\) admit a polynomial-length, deterministically polynomial-time verifiable certificate, with no accepted certificate when the lattice has a nonzero vector of length at most \(r\)?
cards.why: A short certificate that no sufficiently short lattice vector exists would strengthen the known upper bounds on lattice complexity. Matching the better approximation scale of interactive proofs with a single classical certificate would clarify the role of interaction in certifying lattice distance.

cards.definitions:
The input consists of an integer matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), with \(m\ge n\ge1\) and linearly independent columns, and a positive rational radius \(r\). Dimensions, signed matrix entries and the numerator and positive denominator of \(r\) are written in binary using an explicit length-delimited encoding. Let \(L\) be its full bit length. The rank \(n\), ambient dimension \(m\), and all coefficient lengths are part of the input.

Define
\[
\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\},\qquad
\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2,
\quad \|v\|_2=\left(\sum_i v_i^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
The GapSVP promise distinguishes yes-instances with \(\lambda_1\le r\) from no-instances with \(\lambda_1>\gamma_C(n)r\). Inputs between those thresholds are outside the promise. The constant restriction \(C\ge2\) ensures \(\gamma_C(n)\ge1\) at every positive rank; changing finitely many small ranks does not affect the intended asymptotic scale. The logarithm is to base two, and the approximation factor depends on lattice rank, not total bit length.

Membership in coNP for this promise problem means that there are one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(V\), constants \(K>0\) and integers \(a,b\ge1\), with the following properties on every well-formed input. A certificate is a finite binary string \(w\) with \(|w|\le K(L+1)^a\), and verification takes at most \(K(L+1)^b\) bit operations for each such certificate. The same verifier and constants must satisfy
\[
\lambda_1>\gamma_C(n)r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists w:\ |w|\le K(L+1)^a\ \land\ V(B,r,w)=1,
\]
\[
\lambda_1\le r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\forall w:\ |w|\le K(L+1)^a\ \Longrightarrow\ V(B,r,w)=0.
\]
Longer strings can be rejected. Verification behavior is unconstrained inside the gap. There is no required efficient algorithm for finding certificates, but verification is uniform, classical and deterministic. Certificates contain only finitely many bits; exact real numbers, randomness, quantum states, interaction with a prover and auxiliary oracles are not supplied. Both the choice of \(C\) and all resource bounds are fixed independently of each input.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a constant and verifier exist, including certificate length, deterministic bit complexity, completeness and soundness on the promise, or a proof of the negation of this existence claim. A randomized interactive coAM protocol, a polynomial-time verifier only at factor C√n, or a smaller-factor protocol with superpolynomial running time does not establish this target.

cards.title: SVP hardness for fixed-rank cyclotomic modules
cards.formal:
Does exact Euclidean shortest-vector decision remain NP-hard on cyclotomic module lattices when the module rank is an absolute constant?

For each fixed integer \(r\ge1\), let \(\mathcal D_r\) be the decision problem defined below. A valid instance consists of a conductor \(m\ge3\), finitely many generators \(y_1,\ldots,y_s\in R_m^r\) spanning \(K_m^r\) over \(K_m\), and an integer squared threshold \(S\ge0\), where
\[K_m=\mathbb Q(\zeta_m),\quad R_m=\mathbb Z[\zeta_m],\quad M=\sum_{j=1}^s R_m y_j.\]
It is a YES instance exactly when \(\lambda_1(M)^2\le S\), using the canonical product norm below.

The target is the existence of a fixed \(r\), a deterministic multitape Turing machine \(F\), and positive integer constants \(C,d\) such that \(F\) runs in at most \(C(N+1)^d\) bit steps on every input string of length \(N\), and for every well-formed 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\), it outputs a valid instance of \(\mathcal D_r\) satisfying
\[\varphi\text{ is satisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda_1(M_{F(\varphi)})^2\le S_{F(\varphi)}.\]
Thus one rank and one uniform polynomial-time many-one reduction must work for all formulas; the conductor, generators and threshold may depend on the formula.
cards.why: Module lattices retain algebraic structure while permitting much larger families than single ideals. Establishing hardness with a fixed number of module coordinates would show that this compact structure can support a fundamental worst-case geometric obstruction as the field degree grows. The problem tests the boundary between algebraic organization and computational difficulty; exact worst-case hardness alone does not establish the security of cryptographic parameter distributions.
cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. Bennett’s 2023 source poses the constant-rank hardness question. Liu–Feng–Pan arXiv:2609.01469v1, submitted 1 September 2026, now claims a matching positive answer for a prime-conductor cyclotomic rank-two subfamily under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The theorem’s norm, rank, representation and exact decision threshold were checked against this explicit variant. Its full proof was not independently certified, so the card remains uncertain rather than being archived as a verified resolution. The result does not assert the separate power-of-two, rank-one or average-case cryptographic statements.

The fixed-rank SIVP work gives a conditional worst-case-to-average-case self-reduction, as distinct from an NP-hardness reduction for exact SVP.

cards.definitions:
For an integer \(m\ge3\), let \(\zeta_m=\exp(2\pi i/m)\). The degree \(n=\phi(m)\) is the number of integers \(a\) with \(1\le a\le m\) and \(\gcd(a,m)=1\). Define the monic cyclotomic polynomial
\[\Phi_m(X)=\prod_{\substack{1\le a\le m\\\gcd(a,m)=1}}(X-\zeta_m^a)\in\mathbb Z[X].\]
The ring \(R_m\) is identified with \(\mathbb Z[X]/(\Phi_m(X))\); it is the full ring of integers in \(K_m\). Every ring element is written uniquely by its \(n\) integer coefficients in the basis \(1,\zeta_m,\ldots,\zeta_m^{n-1}\).

A module generated by \(y_1,\ldots,y_s\) is the set of all sums \(\sum_j a_jy_j\) with \(a_j\in R_m\). Here \(s\ge r\) is finite and may vary. The input promise is that the columns have rank \(r\) over the field \(K_m\). Hence the generated additive group has integer rank \(rn\) and is a full lattice in the real span of its canonical embedding. The ring rank \(r\) stays fixed, while the integer dimension \(rn\) can grow. Generators may be redundant; the module is not promised free over \(R_m\) or principal in rank one. Integral coordinates are required, with no supplied factorization or pseudo-basis oracle.

For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_r)\in K_m^r\), the canonical product norm is
\[\|x\|_{\mathrm{can}}^2=\sum_{i=1}^r\sum_{\substack{1\le a\le m\\\gcd(a,m)=1}}|\sigma_a(x_i)|^2,\qquad\sigma_a(\zeta_m)=\zeta_m^a.\]
Equivalently it is \(\sum_i\operatorname{Tr}_{K_m/\mathbb Q}(x_i\overline{x_i})\), where conjugation sends \(\zeta_m\) to \(\zeta_m^{-1}\). All embeddings, including both members of each conjugate pair, are included. The real lattice dimension is \(rn\), despite representing it with complex coordinates. Set \(\lambda_1(M)=\min\{\|x\|_{\mathrm{can}}:x\in M\setminus\{0\}\}\). Discreteness and full rank make this a positive attained minimum. Squared norms of integral module vectors are integers. The comparison includes equality at the threshold and requires no approximation or gap promise. A threshold of zero gives a valid NO instance.

To specify the bit model, encode each nonnegative integer \(a\) as \(U(a)=1^\ell0b\), where \(b\) is its binary expansion without leading zeros and \(\ell=|b|\); zero uses \(b=0\). Encode signed integers by one sign bit and \(U\) of the absolute value, using the positive sign for zero. A module input writes \(U(m),U(s),U(S)\), then all \(rsn\) signed coefficients, ordered by generator, module coordinate and power-basis coefficient. All coefficients, including zeros, are explicitly present. The fixed \(r\) is a parameter of the language, not part of the input. Invalid encodings, conductors less than three and rank-deficient lists are rejected in \(\mathcal D_r\). The reduction must produce valid inputs on both satisfiable and unsatisfiable well-formed formulas.

A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses with exactly three signed variable occurrences each; repetitions are allowed. Use an encoding consisting of a unary number of declared variables, a binary length-delimited clause count, and three sign/index pairs for each clause, with every index in the declared variable range. The empty conjunction is satisfiable. All clauses and occurrences are written explicitly. Malformed formula strings need not have a correctness guarantee for \(F\), but the global polynomial clock still applies.

The reduction uses one finite classical program and a fixed finite number of tapes. Each step has the usual bounded-symbol read/write and one-cell head movement cost. Arithmetic, construction of the conductor and ring data, and every written output bit are charged. No randomness, quantum computation, advice, hard-instance table depending on input length or uncharged oracle is allowed. The output length is bounded by the same polynomial clock. The chosen rank and constants are independent of formula size. The statement asks for hardness at at least one fixed rank over the specified family, not at every rank or at a fixed conductor. This exact decision language is a yes/no target; it is not a request to estimate a shortest length numerically.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence or its full negation. A positive answer must supply a fixed rank, a uniform deterministic reduction and universal polynomial clock, and prove validity and the YES–NO equivalence for every well-formed formula. A negative answer must rule out such a reduction for every fixed rank, rather than refute a proposed construction or fail to establish hardness at one rank. A randomized reduction, a Turing reduction making several oracle queries, growing module rank, hardness for a non-Euclidean norm, or a security assumption about random keys does not establish this specified claim. It is not necessary to prove \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) in order to prove a reduction.

source_formulation.text: Bennett’s Open Problem 4.9 asks for NP-hardness at some constant module rank over some family of base rings, with power-of-two cyclotomics given as an example. The example is not a mandatory restriction. This card makes the cyclotomic-family variant precise by allowing all conductors, choosing the canonical Euclidean product embedding, integral finite generator lists, exact squared thresholds and deterministic many-one reductions. It retains the existential fixed-rank quantifier, rather than requiring rank two, rank one or hardness for every fixed rank. The family/embedding choice is an explicit editorial specification of the source’s choices. Hardness on the prime-conductor rank-two subfamily would answer this variant affirmatively; it would not establish the separate power-of-two or rank-one questions.

context_blocks.text: A fixed module rank is compatible with an unbounded geometric dimension: rank \(r\) over a degree-\(n\) number field gives integer dimension \(rn\). The hard-instance family must therefore vary the underlying field as inputs grow. Treating “rank two” as a two-dimensional integer lattice would erase the central distinction in the question.

Rank-one modules include ideals, whereas higher rank permits interactions between several ring coordinates. Bennett presents the fixed-rank module question after the ideal-lattice hardness question as a broader target. The distinction between module rank and the number of listed generators also matters: redundant generators do not increase the rank over the field.

The original survey distinguishes exact decision SVP from approximate decision and search variants. Its use of GapSVP does not itself require an approximation gap: factor one is the exact threshold decision problem. The card therefore uses an exact squared threshold and asks for a deterministic reduction, with the norm and representation fixed explicitly.

Felderhoff, Pellet-Mary and Stehlé relate a promised module unique-SVP problem to NTRU and give a random self-reduction with an ideal-SVP oracle qualification. Those are reductions between structured lattice problems with an exceptional-short-vector promise. The checked abstract does not claim a deterministic reduction from an NP-complete problem to the exact decision language in this card.

De Boer, Page, Toma and Wesolowski’s 2025 preprint, presented at STOC 2026, gives a worst-case-to-average-case self-reduction for approximate SIVP at fixed module rank. Its abstract specifies the Extended Riemann Hypothesis, a discretized invariant distribution, and a polynomial loss in approximation. SIVP seeks independent short vectors; a self-reduction of that task does not establish NP-hardness of exact SVP.

Liu, Feng and Pan’s 1 September 2026 preprint claims NP-completeness of exact decision SVP for full-rank free modules of rank two over \(\mathbb Z[\zeta_q]\), where the conductor \(q\) ranges over primes congruent to three modulo four. Theorem 1.1 specifies deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, integral generators, a nonzero determinant and an integer squared threshold under the canonical product norm. These instances belong to the card’s family with \(r=2\).

If that claim is correct, it answers the selected existential-rank question affirmatively even with two generators. Its Corollary 1.2 separately states search hardness under Turing reductions. The paper explicitly excludes conclusions about a fixed cyclotomic ring, the power-of-two family, average-case hardness or a cryptographic security reduction. The theorem and model were matched here, but the complete new proof was not independently certified; the card is therefore uncertain.

The earlier ideal-SVP algorithmic advances give an additional reason to distinguish rank one from rank two. Cramer, Ducas and Wesolowski’s cyclotomic ideal result is quantum, has a \(\exp(\widetilde O(\sqrt m))\) approximation scale, and has stated number-theoretic hypotheses for its polynomial-time consequence. It is neither an exact decision algorithm for all fixed-rank modules nor a contradiction to an exact hardness claim.

cards.title: ETH hardness of constant-factor shortest-vector approximation for \(1\le p\le 2\)
cards.formal: Does deterministic ETH imply that for every fixed real \(p\in [1,2]\) there is a constant \(\gamma >1\) for which the gap shortest-vector problem \(SVP_{p,\gamma}\) has no deterministic algorithm running in time \(2^{o}(d)N^{O}(1)\), where d is the ambient lattice dimension and N is the explicit input bit length?
cards.why: Would strengthen the fine-grained hardness basis for constant-factor lattice approximation in the most familiar norm range, using an ordinary satisfiability assumption. It separates a genuine exponential obstruction from lower bounds relying on a stronger gap or randomized premise.
cards.status_note: Published source and definitions checked through 11 September 2026. Hair–Sahai’s 2026 deterministic hardness result was also checked: its subexponential reduction does not supply the displayed \(2^{o}(d)\) lower bound in output lattice dimension. No matching resolution of the ordinary-ETH target for \(1\le p\le 2\) was located.

progress.text: The paper establishes ordinary-ETH constant-gap CVP hardness and randomized-ETH SVP hardness for \(p>2\), while explicitly leaving \(p\in [1,2]\) open.

Hair and Sahai’s revised preprint gives deterministic hardness for all finite norms; its reduction-size regime is different from the dimension-linear fine-grained requirement here. The work is accepted at FOCS 2026.

cards.definitions: An input consists of integers \(d\ge r\ge 1, a\) rational \(d\times r\) matrix B with linearly independent columns, and a positive rational threshold R. All rationals are given by signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators with delimiters; N is the total bit length. The lattice is \(\mathrm{L}(B)=\{Bz:z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{r}\}\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^{d}\). For fixed \(p\in [1,2]\), the norm is \(\Vert x\Vert _{p}=(\sum _{i=1}^{d}|x_{i}|^{p})^{1/p}\), and \(\lambda _{1}^{p}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{\Vert v\Vert _{p}:v\in \mathrm{L}, v\ne 0\}\). \(SVP_{p,\gamma}\) accepts if \(\lambda _{1}^{p}(\mathrm{L})\le R\) and rejects if \(\lambda _{1}^{p}(\mathrm{L})>\gamma R\). Inputs between these thresholds are outside the promise; either answer is permitted there. The requested task is gap decision, not output of a lattice vector. The norm parameter and gap are fixed mathematical constants, not part of the input, and one finite deterministic Turing-machine program must solve all promised inputs for them. A subexponential bound means time at most \(2^{h(d)}N^{c}\) for some fixed c and nonnegative h with \(h(d)/d\to 0\). Bounds and programs may depend on p and \(\gamma\). The dimension convention follows the source’s lower-bound statements for lattices in \(\mathbb{R} ^{d}\); rank \(r\le d\) is displayed separately. ETH here asserts that for some \(\delta >0\) there is no deterministic algorithm deciding 3-CNF satisfiability on v variables in \(O(2^{\delta v}M^{c})\) time for any fixed c, where M is the formula’s bit length. It is the ordinary satisfiability assumption, not a promise that unsatisfiable instances have a constant fraction of violated clauses. Randomized ETH instead excludes bounded-error randomized algorithms and is a different premise. The card follows the literal deterministic-ETH version of Open Problem 1.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute the implication from ordinary deterministic ETH to the stated constant-gap subexponential lower bound for every fixed \(p\in [1,2]\). The constant \(\gamma\) may depend on p but must be strictly greater than one and independent of dimension. A result using GapETH, or only randomized ETH, does not by itself prove this precise implication.

context_blocks.title: The gap concerns the shortest nonzero vector
context_blocks.text: The zero vector belongs to every lattice and is excluded from the minimum. In \(\mathbb{Z} ^{2}\) the shortest nonzero vector has norm one for every p in this range. A YES instance has such a vector within radius R; a NO instance has none within the larger radius \(\gamma R\).

context_blocks.title: A constant approximation gap must survive dimension growth
context_blocks.text: The desired factor \(\gamma\) is fixed once the norm is chosen. A hardness result whose factor approaches one as dimension grows would not meet the question. Conversely, the target does not require hardness for every constant factor, only for some factor greater than one at each p.

context_blocks.title: The source distinguishes its assumptions
context_blocks.text: The paper proves ordinary-ETH hardness for constant-gap closest vector in all finite \(\ell p\) norms. Its shortest-vector result for \(p>2\) uses randomized ETH. Closest vector has a specified target point, while shortest vector looks for a short nonzero vector around the origin; the two tasks and the two ETH variants are kept separate.

context_blocks.title: The missing norm range includes Euclidean geometry
context_blocks.text: At \(p=1\) the norm sums absolute coordinates, while at \(p=2\) it is Euclidean length. The source leaves this whole interval as an open shortest-vector hardness target. Its result outside the interval therefore does not establish the displayed claim.

context_blocks.title: A later deterministic breakthrough has different size guarantees
context_blocks.text: Hair and Sahai give deterministic hardness of approximation in every finite \(\ell p\) norm, including \(p=2\), in a work accepted at FOCS 2026. Their reduction uses a subexponential-size/time regime relative to the SAT instance. This is substantial progress on removing randomization, but its stated hardness does not exclude every \(2^{o}(d)\)-time algorithm in the output lattice dimension, as this card requests.

cards.title: A quantum 2^(0.2075n) lower bound for exact Euclidean SVP from QSETH
cards.formal:
Does the Quantum Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis defined below imply that there are no constants \(K,a>0\) and no uniform bounded-error quantum algorithm which, for every explicitly given integer lattice basis of rank \(n\) and total binary input length \(L\), outputs an exact shortest nonzero vector using at most
\[
K\,2^{83n/400}(L+1)^a
\]
elementary operations on every execution? The exponent is the exact rational number \(83/400=0.2075\), and the norm is Euclidean.
cards.why: Quantum attacks on lattice problems are often estimated from particular sieving algorithms. A rank-sensitive exponential lower bound under an independent SAT hypothesis would provide a much firmer basis for those estimates and would have to overcome substantial limitations of current reductions.

The choice of QSETH was an announced editorial default after no reply to an optional question. The precise gate model and polynomial input-length factor are editorial specifications. cards.definitions:
An instance is a full-column-rank integer matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), with \(m\ge n\ge1\). The dimensions and all signed entries are explicitly encoded in binary with delimiters; \(L\) is the complete encoding length. The lattice is
\[
\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\},\qquad
\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2,
\quad \|v\|_2=\left(\sum_i v_i^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
An acceptable classical output is a binary integer coefficient vector \(z\ne0\) with \(\|Bz\|_2=\lambda_1(\mathcal L(B))\). Either sign and any shortest vector are acceptable. The success probability must be at least \(2/3\) on each individual basis, over all internal measurements and randomness. No average-case or unique-shortest-vector promise is imposed. Reading the input and writing the output count toward the running time. The exponential parameter is the rank \(n\), not the ambient dimension \(m\) or the bit length \(L\).

Use the following uniform finite-gate quantum model for both the lattice problem and the hypothesis. A fixed classical multitape Turing machine controls qubits initialized to \(|0\rangle\), applies gates from \(\{H,T,T^{-1},\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), prepares fresh zero qubits, measures in the computational basis and finally writes a classical answer. Here \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and CNOT maps \(|u,v\rangle\) to \(|u,u\mathbin\oplus v\rangle\). The controller has the explicit classical input and may adapt to measurement outcomes. Each classical bit step, gate, preparation and measurement costs one operation. Gates may act on arbitrary finitely indexed qubits, but computing and writing their binary indices costs classical bit steps. There is no advice, postselection, external oracle or unit-cost coherent memory-lookup operation; any such lookup used by an algorithm must be implemented with counted gates. All classical control time is counted, and time is bounded on every measurement branch.

For an integer \(k\ge3\), a \(k\)-CNF formula is an explicitly listed conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most \(k\) literals on \(N\) named Boolean variables. A literal is a variable or its negation. Let \(M\) be the complete binary encoding length. The Quantum Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (QSETH) here is:
\[
\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\ \exists k\ge3:
\text{there is no uniform quantum algorithm deciding }k\text{-SAT}
\text{ in time }O\!\left(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)N}(M+1)^b\right)
\]
for any constant \(b\), with error at most \(1/3\) on every formula. The algorithm and polynomial exponent may depend on \(k,\varepsilon\). The cost model is exactly the one above. Thus the reference exponent is \(1/2\), reflecting quantum search, rather than the classical exponent 1.

The card asks for the full logical implication from this specific hypothesis. It does not restrict a proof to many-one, nonadaptive or black-box reductions. Its conclusion excludes the displayed running time itself; it is not merely a statement that all still smaller exponents are impossible. The polynomial factor permits arbitrary explicit coefficient lengths.

cards.title: Unconditional exponential hardness of \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\)-GapSVP

cards.definitions: An instance is an invertible rational matrix \(B\in \mathbb{Q} ^{n\times n}\) and a positive rational threshold r, all represented explicitly in binary with numerator, denominator, sign and delimiters included in N. The lattice is \(\mathrm{L}(B)=\{Bz:z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{n}\}\). Its shortest nonzero Euclidean length is \(\lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{(\sum i v_{i}^{2})^{1/2}:v\in \mathrm{L}, v\ne 0\}\); the minimum exists because B is invertible and the lattice is discrete. The promise problem \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\)-GapSVP asks for YES when \(\lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L})\le r\) and NO when \(\lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L})>n^{1+\varepsilon}r\), promised that one holds. There is no correctness requirement in the gap between those cases. The same \(\varepsilon\) is used at every dimension. A bounded-error algorithm must give the correct answer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every promised instance. Use a uniform quantum computation with a fixed finite universal gate set, such as Hadamard, T and controlled-NOT, computational-basis measurements and classical control; qubits begin in the input state and zero auxiliary states, without advice, oracles or special quantum input access. Gate operations, classical control and input handling all count toward total worst-case running time, with the bound applying to every measurement branch. A single machine must work for all dimensions and bit lengths. The factor \(N^{k}\) explicitly accounts for the ordinary polynomial input-processing overhead suppressed in the source’s dimension-based exponential notation. Constants \(c,\varepsilon\) are chosen before the algorithm and may be specified as positive rational numbers, with their values part of a positive resolution; k and the hidden running-time constant may depend on the algorithm. The task is worst-case promise decision, not a claim about a supplied random distribution of bases.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify positive constants \(c,\varepsilon\) and prove, without a complexity-theoretic or cryptographic hardness assumption, that no correct bounded-error quantum algorithm has running time \(O(2^{cn} N^{k})\) for any fixed k. Alternatively, refute the proposition by proving that for every \(c,\varepsilon >0\) there is an algorithm with such a running-time bound for some fixed k. Conditional hardness, exact-SVP hardness with approximation factor 1, and hardness in a different norm do not settle the stated target.

cards.title: Sunflower conjecture
cards.formal:
For every integer \(r\ge3\), does there exist a real constant \(C_r\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(k\ge1\), every finite set \(X\), and every family \(\mathcal F\subseteq\{S\subseteq X:|S|=k\}\),
\[
|\mathcal F|>C_r^k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists\text{ distinct }S_1,\ldots,S_r\in\mathcal F\ \exists K\subseteq X\ \forall i\ne j:\ S_i\cap S_j=K?
\]
The constant may depend on \(r\) but not on the set size \(k\), the ground set or the family. The conclusion is the existence of an ordinary \(r\)-sunflower.
cards.definitions:
A family here is a finite set of subsets, so identical members are not repeated. It is \(k\)-uniform when every member has exactly \(k\) elements. There is no bound on the finite ground-set size \(|X|\). An \(r\)-sunflower consists of \(r\) pairwise distinct members whose pairwise intersections are all the same set \(K\), called the core. For \(r\ge3\), this core also equals the intersection of all selected members. Removing \(K\) leaves pairwise disjoint petals. The core may be empty, in which case the selected sets are pairwise disjoint. For distinct equal-sized members their petals are nonempty.

The quantifier order is \(\forall r\,\exists C_r\,\forall k,X,\mathcal F\). No single base independent of \(r\) is requested. One may equivalently require an integer \(C_r\ge2\), since a larger integer base preserves the upper bound. An eventual bound for all sufficiently large \(k\), with the threshold depending on \(r\), also yields the displayed all-\(k\) formulation by enlarging \(C_r\) to cover finitely many small sizes.

The classical sunflower lemma bounds the size of any sunflower-free \(k\)-uniform family by \(k!(r-1)^k\), independently of its ground set. Consequently the largest such size \(S_r(k)\) exists as a finite integer, even though the ground set is unrestricted. The conjecture is equivalently \(S_r(k)\le C_r^k\) for all \(k\). It does not ask for the exact value, a numerical estimate or constant-factor asymptotics of \(S_r(k)\).

The source also states the conjecture for sets of size at most \(k\). Padding every smaller set to size \(k\) with fresh elements unique to that member preserves pairwise intersections and reduces that variant to the displayed one. This observation is not a claim about robust sunflowers: their probabilistic coverage requirement is stronger, and lower bounds for that stronger structure do not refute the ordinary conjecture.

There is no computational requirement on finding the sunflower or computing the constants. This is a quantified extremal-combinatorial proposition, so the numerical absolute-error convention does not replace it.

context_blocks.text: The classical lemma forces a sunflower only after a factorial-sized threshold. The conjecture would replace this by an exponential whose base is independent of the set size.

Modern bounds remove most of the classical growth but still have a base growing logarithmically with the set size. The robust sunflower method has its own obstruction at that scale, which does not settle ordinary sunflowers.
Sunflower structure supports computational lower bounds and other combinatorial reductions. A uniform exponential threshold would strengthen the general principle used in such applications.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed conjecture or its negation. An affirmative proof must establish a finite base for every fixed \(r\ge3\). A negative proof must supply one fixed \(r\ge3\) for which every candidate base \(C\ge1\) admits a \(k\)-uniform family of more than \(C^k\) members with no \(r\)-sunflower. Improving known superconstant bases, proving only the case of one petal count, or disproving a robust-sunflower variant does not decide the full statement.

cards.definitions: For an integer \(n\ge2\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A partial order \(\le_P\) is a reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive binary relation on \([n]\). Distinct elements \(x,y\) are incomparable if neither \(x\le_P y\) nor \(y\le_P x\); a total order has no incomparable pair. A linear extension is a bijection \(L:[n]\to[n]\) such that \(L(a)<L(b)\) whenever \(a\le_P b\) and \(a\ne b\). Let \(E(P)\) be the finite nonempty set of all linear extensions, \(e(P)=|E(P)|\), and \(e_P(x,y)=|\{L\in E(P):L(x)<L(y)\}|\). Probabilities use the uniform distribution on the entire set \(E(P)\), so \(\Pr[L(x)<L(y)]=e_P(x,y)/e(P)\). The endpoints \(1/3\) and \(2/3\) are included. The pair may depend on the full finite order; there is no algorithmic or representation restriction. In the context, width is the largest size of a set of pairwise incomparable elements, height the largest size of a totally ordered subset, and the cover graph joins \(x,y\) if one is strictly below the other with no element strictly between them. The balance constant is \(\beta(P)=\max_{x\ne y}\min\{e_P(x,y),e_P(y,x)\}/e(P)\).

context_blocks.text: A partial order records comparisons already known, and its linear extensions are all complete rankings still compatible with that information. The conjecture says that unless only one ranking remains, some unresolved comparison splits these possible rankings into two substantial groups. Neither outcome may leave more than two thirds of them. The distribution is uniform over whole rankings, not over the currently available choices in a stepwise topological sort.

Take three elements with \(a<b\) and c unrelated to both. The three linear extensions are abc, acb and cab. The probability that a precedes c is \(2/3\), while the probability that b precedes c is \(1/3\). No incomparable pair is closer to a half. This small example shows that the universal interval cannot be narrowed to \([1/3+\eta ,2/3- \eta ]\) for any \(\eta >0\). In a total order every pair instead has probability zero or one, which explains the excluded case.

Uniform local choices need not produce uniform extensions. In the same example, choosing randomly between the two initially minimal elements a and c gives cab probability \(1/2\), and gives abc and acb probability \(1/4\) each. Those are different from the required probabilities \(1/3\) each. Fixing the probability space prevents a superficially similar random-ordering question from replacing the conjecture.

Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter prove the weaker universal bound \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\ge (5- \sqrt{5})/10\approx 0.2764\). It already guarantees an informative comparison and improves the earlier \(3/11\) bound of Kahn and Saks. The requested value \(1/3\) is a sharper extremal constant, rather than the first guarantee of any fixed positive balance.

The conjecture is known for substantial classes, including width-two and height-two orders, and orders whose cover graph is a forest. Width limits how many elements can be mutually incomparable; height limits the length of a chain. These are distinct restrictions, and neither covers arbitrary finite orders. The Chan–Pak survey states the general question separately from this collection of positive cases.

Aires and Kahn obtain stronger asymptotic balance under size hypotheses: for example \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\) tends to \(1/2\) when width is at least a fixed positive fraction of the number of elements. Their 2025 paper still states the unrestricted \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) bound as a conjecture. A result for a sequence of sufficiently wide orders leaves narrower and exceptional finite orders uncovered.

Gupta’s July 2026 revision reports an exhaustive verification of the stronger Gold Partition property through fourteen elements, implying the balance conjecture for those sizes. Its arithmetic and archived artifacts are described in the paper; this review did not rerun the census. A verified finite range, however large its enumeration, does not establish the universal statement.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every finite non-total partial order has an incomparable pair with \(e(P)/3\le e_P(x,y)\le2e(P)/3\), or a complete Lean-checked refutation: a finite non-total order for which every incomparable pair violates that closed interval. All extension counts and probabilities must use the full set of linear extensions defined here.

sentences: A partial order records known comparisons, and its linear extensions are all compatible complete rankings.
The conjecture asks whether every finite non-total order has an incomparable pair that appears in either relative order in at least one third of all extensions.
The extensions are weighted uniformly, and both endpoints of the interval are allowed.
A three-element order with only one comparison shows that the constant one third cannot be improved universally.
A resolution would identify the sharp balance guarantee for a comparison in sorting with partial information.
